In an uncontrolled paired study of 96 symptomatic C/C-13910 malabsorbers, enzyme given one hour before a 25-g aqueous challenge made 21 breath tests negative, reduced 17 and left 58 similar; this is not a placebo-controlled efficacy estimate or a universal failure rate.

evidence.snippet: Lactase enzyme supplements extracted from yeasts and molds are available as tablets or drops.
evidence.explanation: The chapter describes exogenous digestive enzyme preparations.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Supplies luminal hydrolytic activity to compensate for low endogenous enzyme.

evidence.snippet: Dietitians play a central role in formulating personalized, well-balanced low-lactose or lactose-free diets while ensuring adequate intake of calcium, vitamin D, and other key nutrients.
evidence.explanation: The chapter recommends dietetic support to prevent nutritional consequences of restriction.

treatments/2.description: Provide individualized dietary counseling and maintain adequate calcium, vitamin D, protein and energy intake when dairy is reduced. Assess nutritional adequacy and supplement where appropriate. Restriction-related deficiency is a care concern, not an inevitable intrinsic phenotype of lactase non-persistence.

evidence.snippet: In Booster Alpha, there were no significant differences in any GI symptom between Bi-07 and placebo.
evidence.explanation: A reduction in the primary gas outcome did not establish symptom benefit in the milk trial.

evidence.snippet: In Booster Omega, except for symptoms of nausea, there were no differences between the 3 treatments.
evidence.explanation: The aqueous-lactose trial showed no broad symptom advantage and more nausea with Bi-07.

treatments/3.description: Bi-07 was tested as a high-dose, acute co-ingested preparation in two small randomized crossover trials. Breath-hydrogen exposure decreased relative to placebo, but a consistent symptom benefit was not demonstrated; nausea increased in the aqueous-lactose trial. These findings do not establish routine probiotic therapy, long-term benefit, a class effect or equivalence to lactase across food matrices.

evidence.snippet: Bi-07 effected a decrease in the amount of lactose comparable with those of the commercial lactase and laboratory-grade β-galactosidase
evidence.explanation: Direct in-vitro milk measurements support lactose hydrolysis by this specific preparation.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: The preparation hydrolyzes lactose in milk in vitro; the clinical breath-gas outcome is consistent with improved digestion but does not directly measure the anatomical site of hydrolysis.

evidence.snippet: only a proportion of carbohydrate malabsorbers develop symptoms
evidence.explanation: The guideline distinguishes malabsorption from symptoms.

evidence.snippet: When the periods were compared, there were no statistically significant differences in the severity of these four gastrointestinal symptoms.
evidence.explanation: The crossover trial supports discordance between self-report and symptoms at a modest milk dose, within its small selected cohort.

open_questions/0.rationale: Malabsorption and symptoms are not equivalent. Selected trials and guidelines show dose, meal context, visceral sensitivity and expectation effects. A single small milk trial cannot define a universal tolerated dose; absence of significant severity differences also does not erase its observed excess flatus count. No current source establishes one microbial mechanism for every symptomatic person.

evidence.snippet: Future studies examining chromatin configuration35 at the LCT–MCM6 locus in aging individuals and targeted epigenetic editing with the CRISPR-Cas9 system41 will be necessary to fully understand genetic-epigenetic contributions to lactase persistence and non-persistence.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly identify epigenetic editing as future work.

open_questions/1.rationale: Adult and pediatric intestinal associations support a regulatory epigenetic model, but adult age trends are cross-sectional and pediatric enzyme-defined groups are not symptom cohorts. Deletion and RNAi experiments perturb DNA or RNA rather than methylation. Targeted epigenetic editing and appropriately sampled longitudinal studies are needed to resolve mediation.

evidence.snippet: different groups have demonstrated genetic predisposition to atypical HUS (aHUS) involving five genes encoding for complement components which play a role in the activation or control of the alternative pathway
evidence.explanation: States that the aHUS genes act in the activation or control of the alternative pathway, which is the claim this node makes for the regulator half of that set.

evidence.snippet: Factor H (FH) is an abundant serum glycoprotein that regulates the alternative pathway of complement-preventing uncontrolled plasma C3 activation and nonspecific damage to host tissues.
evidence.explanation: States factor H's identity as an alternative-pathway regulator, which is what the GO negative-regulation binding on this node asserts is lost.

evidence.snippet: We found that patients with aHUS are enriched for ultrarare coding variants in the CFH, C3, CD46, CFI, DGKE, and VTN genes.
evidence.explanation: A variant-burden analysis of 400 patients against 600 Iowa controls and 63,345 non-Finnish European gnomAD individuals independently establishes CFH, CD46 and CFI - the regulators wired to this node - as enriched in aHUS.

evidence.snippet: No homozygous deletions of the CFHR1 and CFHR3 genes, which are frequently associated with the anti-FH Ab in aHUS patients, were found in the GP patients.
evidence.explanation: Sources the CFHR1/CFHR3 route to this node: the homozygous deletion is frequently associated with anti-factor H antibodies in aHUS, which neutralise the same regulator the inherited CFH variants disable.

steps/7.description: Factor H, factor I and membrane cofactor protein together restrain the alternative pathway on host cell surfaces, and loss-of-function variants in any of them remove that restraint. In the CFH case the disease-associated variants cluster in the C-terminal surface-recognition domains, so plasma C3 regulation is preserved while regulation on renal endothelium fails. Homozygous deletion of CFHR1 and CFHR3 reaches the same endpoint acquired rather than inherited, by predisposing to anti-factor H autoantibodies that neutralise the regulator.

evidence.snippet: F286L and K323E aHUS-associated BF mutations are gain-of-function mutations that result in enhanced formation of the C3bBb convertase or increased resistance to inactivation by complement regulators.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gain-of-function convertase mechanism this node represents for the factor B half of the gene pair.

evidence.snippet: The mechanism of pathogenicity is reported to be gain of function.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's definitive C3-aHUS curation records gain of function as the mechanism, placing C3 on the effector side of this node alongside CFB.

evidence.snippet: Only pathogenic variants due to missense changes in CFB with functional data supporting a gain of function effect are scored here.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen scored only gain-of-function missense variants for CFB-aHUS, which is the restriction this node's mechanism claim rests on.

steps/8.description: The effector arm of aHUS genetics. Gain-of-function missense variants in factor B and in C3 act on the C3 convertase itself rather than on its regulators: the C3bBb complex either forms more readily or becomes more resistant to inactivation by complement regulators, so amplification is driven from the enzyme side.

evidence.snippet: DGKE phosphorylates and inactivates arachidonic acid-containing diacylglycerol (AA-DAG) to the corresponding phosphatidic acid.
evidence.explanation: States the phosphorylation reaction that is the diacylglycerol kinase activity bound on this node, and whose loss the node asserts.

evidence.snippet: Atypical HUS (aHUS) can result from genetic or autoimmune factors that lead to pathologic complement cascade activation. Using exome sequencing, we identified recessive mutations in DGKE (encoding diacylglycerol kinase ɛ) that co-segregated with aHUS in nine unrelated kindreds, defining a distinctive Mendelian disease.
evidence.explanation: The paper sets DGKE-aHUS apart from the complement-mediated forms it describes in the preceding sentence, which is why this node sits parallel to the complement arm rather than upstream of it.

evidence.snippet: We found that patients with aHUS are enriched for ultrarare coding variants in the CFH, C3, CD46, CFI, DGKE, and VTN genes.
evidence.explanation: DGKE is enriched in the same 400-patient burden analysis as the complement regulators, establishing it as a genuine aHUS gene despite acting outside the complement cascade.

steps/9.description: The one aHUS mechanism in this entry that is not complement-mediated. Diacylglycerol kinase epsilon phosphorylates arachidonic acid-containing diacylglycerol to phosphatidic acid, terminating a diacylglycerol signal that activates protein kinase C. Biallelic loss of DGKE therefore leaves that signal running in endothelium, platelets and podocytes, producing a prothrombotic state directly rather than through the alternative pathway.

evidence.snippet: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare cause of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) caused by the dysregulation of the alternative complement pathway.
evidence.explanation: This 2025 consensus statement confirms that aHUS is fundamentally caused by alternative complement pathway dysregulation.

evidence.snippet: Tremendous advances in our understanding of the thrombotic microangiopathies (TMAs) have revealed distinct disease mechanisms within this heterogeneous group of diseases.
evidence.explanation: This authoritative review by leading aHUS researchers documents the complement-mediated disease mechanisms underlying aHUS.

steps/10.description: The central mechanism of aHUS is loss of regulation of the alternative complement pathway on endothelial cell surfaces. Normally, complement factor H (CFH), membrane cofactor protein (MCP/CD46), and factor I (CFI) cooperate to inactivate C3b deposited on host cell surfaces. In aHUS, genetic mutations in these regulators or gain-of-function mutations in complement effectors (CFB, C3) lead to unchecked C3 convertase (C3bBb) activity and amplification loop activation on endothelial surfaces.

evidence.snippet: The understanding of the role of the membrane attack complex in some TMAs has led to the introduction of pharmacologic inhibition of complement C5, which greatly improved prognosis.
evidence.explanation: Walsh & Kavanagh 2025 review confirms the central role of MAC in endothelial injury in aHUS and related TMAs.

evidence.snippet: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) is a rare, complex, multisystem disease of dysregulated complement activity, characterized by progressive thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), acute kidney injury, and multiorgan dysfunction
evidence.explanation: This clinical trial confirms aHUS is characterized by complement-driven progressive TMA with multiorgan dysfunction.

steps/11.description: Uncontrolled complement activation generates membrane attack complex (MAC/C5b-9) on endothelial cells, causing direct cell injury. Sublytic MAC deposition induces endothelial activation with upregulation of adhesion molecules, tissue factor expression, and loss of thrombomodulin. Injured endothelium releases von Willebrand factor (vWF) multimers and exposes subendothelial collagen.

evidence.snippet: These all result in pathologic features of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), which cause endothelial damage and organ injury.
evidence.explanation: Confirms TMA pathology involves microthrombus formation causing endothelial damage and downstream organ injury.

steps/12.description: VWF multimers released from activated endothelium and exposed subendothelial collagen promote platelet adhesion and aggregation. Tissue factor expression on activated endothelium triggers the coagulation cascade, generating fibrin-platelet microthrombi in arterioles and capillaries, particularly in the glomerular microvasculature.

evidence.snippet: These all result in pathologic features of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), which cause endothelial damage and organ injury. TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that TMA pathology causes the clinical triad of MAHA, thrombocytopenia, and AKI through endothelial damage.

steps/13.description: Fibrin-platelet thrombi occlude glomerular capillaries and arterioles, causing mechanical shearing of red blood cells (schistocyte formation), consumptive thrombocytopenia, and ischemic injury to renal parenchyma. Progressive thrombotic microangiopathy leads to acute kidney injury and, if untreated, irreversible renal damage with cortical necrosis and progression to end-stage renal disease.

evidence.snippet: extrarenal organ manifestations occur in 19%-38% of patients within six months of initial disease presentation (dependent on organ)
evidence.explanation: Global aHUS Registry evidence supports extrarenal involvement as a recurrent manifestation of complement-mediated TMA.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal involvement was the most common extra-renal manifestation, presenting in 22.2% of patients.
evidence.explanation: In the UK Global aHUS Registry cohort, gastrointestinal involvement was the most common extra-renal manifestation (22.2%), confirming that systemic TMA extends beyond the kidney.

steps/14.description: Although kidney involvement dominates aHUS, thrombotic microangiopathy can affect extrarenal organ systems. Gastrointestinal and neurologic involvement can manifest as diarrhea, seizures, encephalopathy, or stroke.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of TMA is made clinically by the triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and organ damage (mainly acute kidney injury).
evidence.explanation: Brazilian consensus confirms MAHA as part of the defining diagnostic triad.

steps/15.description: Mechanical destruction of red blood cells passing through damaged and thrombosed microvasculature, evidenced by schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, elevated LDH, and reduced haptoglobin.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of TMA is made clinically by the triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and organ damage (mainly acute kidney injury).
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia is part of the defining diagnostic triad.

evidence.snippet: Eculizumab resulted in increases in the platelet count; in trial 1, the mean increase in the count from baseline to week 26 was 73×10(9) per liter (P<0.001).
evidence.explanation: The Legendre NEJM 2013 eculizumab trial documents thrombocytopenia at baseline that improved with complement inhibition.

steps/16.description: Consumptive thrombocytopenia due to platelet consumption in microvascular thrombi. Platelet counts typically 20,000-150,000/uL.

evidence.snippet: progression to ESRD after the first aHUS episode was more frequent in adults (46% versus 16%; P<0.001)
evidence.explanation: The French nationwide series documents that AKI progressing to ESRD occurs in 46% of adults and 16% of children after first episode.

evidence.snippet: 60% of genetic aHUS progresses to end-stage renal disease (ESRD).
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews clinical-characteristics summary puts the eventual renal outcome of genetic aHUS at 60% progressing to end-stage renal disease. This is a different denominator from the French series above, which reports progression after the first episode stratified by age rather than over the whole course, so the two figures are complementary rather than in conflict.

steps/17.description: The kidney is the primary target organ in aHUS. Acute kidney injury results from thrombotic microangiopathy in glomerular capillaries and arterioles, with rapid rise in serum creatinine and oliguria.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals present with aHUS before age 1 year, have persistent hypertension, hematuria and proteinuria
evidence.explanation: Lemaire et al. document persistent hypertension as a clinical feature in DGKE-aHUS, and hypertension is common across all aHUS subtypes.

steps/18.description: Often severe and can be malignant, resulting from renal ischemia and activation of the renin-angiotensin system.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals present with aHUS before age 1 year, have persistent hypertension, hematuria and proteinuria (sometimes in the nephrotic range)
evidence.explanation: Proteinuria is documented as a persistent feature of aHUS.

steps/19.description: Glomerular injury from TMA leads to proteinuria of variable degree.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals present with aHUS before age 1 year, have persistent hypertension, hematuria and proteinuria
evidence.explanation: Hematuria is documented as a persistent feature of aHUS.

steps/20.description: Microscopic or gross hematuria from glomerular endothelial damage.

evidence.snippet: TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury.
evidence.explanation: MAHA inherently involves reduced haptoglobin as a laboratory marker of intravascular hemolysis.

steps/21.description: Serum haptoglobin is reduced or undetectable as a marker of intravascular hemolysis in the setting of MAHA.

evidence.snippet: TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury.
evidence.explanation: Schistocytosis is the defining morphologic finding of MAHA in TMA.

steps/22.description: Fragmented red blood cells (schistocytes) on peripheral blood smear are a hallmark finding of thrombotic microangiopathy, resulting from mechanical shearing of erythrocytes through damaged microvasculature.

evidence.snippet: extrarenal organ manifestations occur in 19%-38% of patients within six months of initial disease presentation (dependent on organ)
evidence.explanation: GI manifestations including diarrhea are among the extrarenal organ involvement documented in the Global aHUS Registry.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal involvement was the most common extra-renal manifestation, presenting in 22.2% of patients.
evidence.explanation: The UK Global aHUS Registry cohort (n=172) identifies gastrointestinal involvement (which includes diarrhea) as the most common extra-renal manifestation, present in 22.2% of patients.

steps/23.description: Gastrointestinal involvement is common in aHUS, with diarrhea being among the most frequent extrarenal manifestations.

evidence.snippet: extrarenal organ manifestations occur in 19%-38% of patients within six months of initial disease presentation (dependent on organ)
evidence.explanation: The Global aHUS Registry documents that 19-38% of patients develop extrarenal organ involvement within 6 months, including neurological.

steps/24.description: Neurological involvement can occur from cerebral TMA, manifesting as seizures, confusion, or encephalopathy. Extrarenal organ manifestations occur in 19-38% of patients.

evidence.snippet: extrarenal organ manifestations occur in 19%-38% of patients within six months of initial disease presentation (dependent on organ)
evidence.explanation: Stroke is among the extrarenal TMA manifestations documented in the Global aHUS Registry.

steps/25.description: Ischemic stroke from cerebral microvascular thrombosis, occurring in a subset of patients with extrarenal TMA manifestations.

evidence.snippet: These animals represent the first model of aHUS and provide in vivo evidence that effective plasma C3 regulation and the defective control of complement activation on renal endothelium are the critical events in the molecular pathogenesis of FH-associated aHUS.
evidence.explanation: A transgenic mouse expressing a factor H protein equivalent to the human aHUS mutants shows that defective control of complement activation on renal endothelium - with plasma regulation intact - is what converts loss of surface regulation into aHUS.

edges/7.description: With surface regulation lost, C3b deposited on endothelium is no longer inactivated and the alternative-pathway amplification loop runs unchecked.

evidence.snippet: F286L and K323E aHUS-associated BF mutations are gain-of-function mutations that result in enhanced formation of the C3bBb convertase or increased resistance to inactivation by complement regulators.
evidence.explanation: Convertase assays show the two mechanisms by which a factor B gain-of-function variant raises alternative-pathway activity.

edges/8.description: A convertase that forms more readily or resists inactivation produces the same unchecked amplification on endothelial surfaces as loss of regulation, reached from the opposite direction.

evidence.snippet: DGKE is found in endothelium, platelets and podocytes. Arachidonic acid-containing diacylglycerols (DAG) activate protein kinase C (PKC), which promotes thrombosis, and DGKE normally inactivates DAG signaling.
evidence.explanation: Names the cells DGKE acts in and the prothrombotic signal its loss fails to terminate, which is the edge from this node to microthrombus formation.

edges/9.description: Sustained diacylglycerol/protein kinase C signalling in endothelium and platelets drives the same microvascular thrombosis that complement-driven endothelial injury produces, which is why the two genetic routes converge on one clinical syndrome.

evidence.snippet: The understanding of the role of the membrane attack complex in some TMAs has led to the introduction of pharmacologic inhibition of complement C5, which greatly improved prognosis.
evidence.explanation: That inhibiting complement C5 - and hence membrane attack complex formation - improves outcome establishes uncontrolled complement activation as the upstream cause of the MAC-mediated endothelial lesion.

edges/10.description: Unchecked complement activation generates C5a and membrane attack complex on endothelial cells.

evidence.snippet: These all result in pathologic features of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), which cause endothelial damage and organ injury.
evidence.explanation: The review places endothelial damage upstream of the thrombotic microangiopathic lesion. PARTIAL because the abstract does not separately describe the VWF/collagen-mediated platelet recruitment step.

edges/11.description: VWF multimer release and subendothelial collagen exposure recruit and activate platelets on the damaged endothelial surface.

edges/12.description: Fibrin-platelet thrombi occlude glomerular capillaries and arterioles.

edges/13.description: Complement-driven microthrombi can also affect extrarenal vascular beds.

evidence.snippet: TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia is named as a defining manifestation of the thrombotic microangiopathic process, i.e. downstream of microthrombus formation.

edges/14.description: Platelet consumption in microthrombi produces thrombocytopenia.

edges/15.description: Gastrointestinal TMA involvement can manifest with diarrhea.

edges/16.description: Cerebral TMA can produce seizures as a neurologic extrarenal manifestation.

edges/17.description: Cerebral vascular thrombosis can cause ischemic stroke.

evidence.snippet: TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury
evidence.explanation: Acute kidney injury is named as a manifestation of the thrombotic microangiopathic lesion, placing it downstream of renal microvascular thrombosis.

edges/18.description: Glomerular and arteriolar microthrombi cause acute renal ischemic injury.

edges/19.description: Glomerular endothelial injury and capillary thrombosis disrupt filtration barrier function.

edges/20.description: Glomerular endothelial damage produces hematuria.

edges/21.description: Renal microvascular ischemia contributes to severe hypertension.

evidence.snippet: TMAs manifest with a microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and commonly acute kidney injury
evidence.explanation: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia is named as a defining manifestation of the thrombotic microangiopathic lesion in the renal microvasculature.

edges/22.description: Erythrocyte shearing through thrombosed microvasculature produces MAHA.

edges/23.description: Mechanical shearing through microthrombi produces schistocytes.

evidence.snippet: Sixty-one percent of patients had mutations in their complement genes.
evidence.explanation: The French nationwide series confirms high frequency of complement gene mutations in aHUS, with CFH being the most common.

evidence.snippet: Patients with a Complement Factor H mutation had reduced ESRD-free survival, whereas Membrane Cofactor Protein mutation was associated with longer ESRD-free survival.
evidence.explanation: Global aHUS Registry data confirm that CFH mutations carry the worst renal prognosis among complement gene mutations.

evidence.snippet: ESKD-free survival was negatively influenced by CFH, C3, or CFI variants.
evidence.explanation: The UK Global aHUS Registry cohort independently confirms that CFH (with C3 and CFI) variants adversely affect ESKD-free survival, corroborating the poor renal prognosis of CFH-associated aHUS.

evidence.snippet: CFH | HGNC:4883 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome | MONDO:0016244 | SD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the CFH-atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome gene-disease relationship as definitive with semidominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: We report a patient with a novel heterozygous complement factor H (CFH) variant, p.Glu1198Asp (c.3594A>T), who received ravulizumab three months after disease onset. Ravulizumab was administered for relapse prevention in the chronic phase, and no recurrence of thrombotic microangiopathy was observed during the follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Case report documents a novel heterozygous CFH variant (p.Glu1198Asp) associated with aHUS, confirming that distinct CFH variants can drive disease pathogenesis and respond to C5 inhibitor therapy.

evidence.snippet: Membrane Cofactor Protein mutation was associated with longer ESRD-free survival.
evidence.explanation: MCP mutations are confirmed to have better renal prognosis than CFH mutations.

evidence.snippet: The frequency of relapse after 1 year was 92% in children with MCP-associated HUS and approximately 30% in all other subgroups.
evidence.explanation: MCP-aHUS is notable for high relapse rate (92%) in children but better overall renal outcome compared to CFH mutations.

evidence.snippet: CD46 | HGNC:6953 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome | MONDO:0016244 | SD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the CD46-atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome gene-disease relationship as definitive with semidominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Complement Factor I and Membrane Cofactor Protein mutations were more common in patients with initial presentation as adults and children, respectively.
evidence.explanation: CFI mutations are documented to be more common in adult-onset aHUS.

evidence.snippet: CFI | HGNC:5394 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome | MONDO:0016244 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the CFI-atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome gene-disease relationship as definitive with autosomal dominant inheritance.

evidence.snippet: Sixty-one percent of patients had mutations in their complement genes.
evidence.explanation: CFB is among the complement genes with identified mutations in this nationwide series.

evidence.snippet: CFB | HGNC:1037 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome with B factor anomaly | MONDO:0013042 | AD | Moderate | SOP9
evidence.explanation: ClinGen grades CFB-aHUS Moderate rather than Definitive - the weakest grade among this entry's causative complement genes - while recording that no contradictory evidence has emerged.

evidence.snippet: Sixty-one percent of patients had mutations in their complement genes.
evidence.explanation: C3 is among the complement genes with identified mutations.

evidence.snippet: C3 | HGNC:1318 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome with C3 anomaly | MONDO:0013043 | AD | Definitive | SOP9
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's Complement-Mediated Kidney Diseases expert panel classifies the C3-aHUS relationship as definitive, curated against the C3-anomaly subtype term separately from C3 glomerulopathy.

evidence.snippet: No homozygous deletions of the CFHR1 and CFHR3 genes, which are frequently associated with the anti-FH Ab in aHUS patients, were found in the GP patients.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that CFHR1/CFHR3 homozygous deletions are frequently associated with anti-factor H antibodies specifically in aHUS.

evidence.snippet: 214 patients with aHUS were enrolled between 2000 and 2008 and screened for mutations in the six susceptibility factors for aHUS and for anti-factor H antibodies.
evidence.explanation: Anti-factor H antibodies are recognized as a key susceptibility factor in the French national aHUS registry.

genes/5.notes: Typed RISK_FACTOR rather than CAUSATIVE because the deletion is neither necessary nor sufficient: it is a common polymorphism, most carriers never develop anti-factor H autoantibodies or aHUS, and this record's own features describe it as predisposing to autoantibody development rather than causing disease. The GeneReviews chapter frames it the same way, warning that predictive testing on a predisposing factor is problematic because it is only one of several risk factors required for aHUS. SUSCEPTIBILITY would also fit; RISK_FACTOR is used because the claim here is about an inherited structural variant raising risk, with the antibody as the proximate lesion, rather than about a susceptibility locus mapped by association. The autosomal recessive inheritance is retained: it describes transmission of the deletion itself, which is biallelic, not the penetrance of aHUS.

evidence.snippet: we identified recessive mutations in DGKE (encoding diacylglycerol kinase ɛ) that co-segregated with aHUS in nine unrelated kindreds, defining a distinctive Mendelian disease.
evidence.explanation: Landmark paper identifying DGKE as a cause of aHUS through a non-complement mechanism involving prothrombotic DAG signaling.

evidence.snippet: DGKE is found in endothelium, platelets and podocytes. Arachidonic acid-containing diacylglycerols (DAG) activate protein kinase C (PKC), which promotes thrombosis, and DGKE normally inactivates DAG signaling.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the prothrombotic mechanism whereby loss of DGKE leads to sustained DAG/PKC signaling in endothelial cells and platelets.

evidence.snippet: In summary, there is definitive evidence supporting the relationship between DGKE and autosomal recessive atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's Complement-Mediated Kidney Diseases expert panel classifies DGKE-aHUS as definitive with autosomal recessive inheritance.

evidence.snippet: We found that patients with aHUS are enriched for ultrarare coding variants in the CFH, C3, CD46, CFI, DGKE, and VTN genes.
evidence.explanation: A variant-burden analysis of 400 patients places DGKE among the genes enriched in aHUS, independent of the original kindred-based report.

evidence.snippet: Eculizumab therapy may not be beneficial to those with aHUS caused by pathogenic variants in DGKE.
evidence.explanation: The therapeutic corollary of the non-complement mechanism: C5 blockade, which is first-line for the complement-mediated subtypes, may not help in DGKE-associated disease. This is the clinical reason DGKE-aHUS is curated as its own subtype rather than folded into the complement forms.

evidence.snippet: Genetic variants in THBD, which encodes thrombomodulin, have been reported to cause aHUS (PMID: 19625716) however, analysis of large aHUS cohorts (PMIDs: 23307876, 37369098, 37567446) and enrichment analysis (PMIDs: 29500241, 30377230) have failed to reproduce these findings.
evidence.explanation: ClinGen's expert-panel review states that large cohorts and enrichment analyses failed to reproduce the reported THBD-aHUS association, which is the basis for grading this relationship DISPUTED.

evidence.snippet: THBD | HGNC:11784 | atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome | MONDO:0016244 | AD | Disputed | SOP10
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease validity row records the Disputed classification itself, with the mode of inheritance under which it was evaluated.

evidence.snippet: We found that patients with aHUS are enriched for ultrarare coding variants in the CFH, C3, CD46, CFI, DGKE, and VTN genes.
evidence.explanation: One of the two enrichment analyses ClinGen cites against THBD. Its enriched-gene list, derived from 400 patients against 600 Iowa controls and 63,345 non-Finnish European gnomAD individuals, does not include THBD.

evidence.snippet: The genes associated with genetic aHUS include C3, CD46 (MCP), CFB, CFH, CFHR1, CFHR3, CFHR4, CFHR5, CFI, DGKE, THBD, and VTN.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews chapter continues to list THBD among the genes associated with genetic aHUS. Recorded here as the source this entry is departing from, which is why the relationship is retained as DISPUTED rather than removed.

genes/7.notes: Retained as a DISPUTED relationship rather than deleted, because the disputing panel's own summary says more evidence is needed either to support or to refute THBD's role rather than that the gene is excluded. Consistent with this, the 400-patient variant-burden analysis in PMID:30377230 reports enrichment for CFH, C3, CD46, CFI, DGKE and VTN and does not list THBD. Not given a has_subtypes row: MONDO:0013044 (atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome with thrombomodulin anomaly) would assert a gene-defined subtype on a relationship ClinGen currently disputes. The two sources do disagree: the GeneReviews chapter cited below still lists THBD among the genes associated with genetic aHUS, and this entry follows ClinGen's later expert-panel reassessment on the strength of the cohort and enrichment data it cites.

evidence.snippet: Eculizumab inhibited complement-mediated thrombotic microangiopathy and was associated with significant time-dependent improvement in renal function in patients with atypical hemolytic-uremic syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Landmark NEJM 2013 trial demonstrating eculizumab efficacy in aHUS with improvement in both hematologic parameters and renal function.

evidence.snippet: In trial 1, dialysis was discontinued in 4 of 5 patients. Earlier intervention with eculizumab was associated with significantly greater improvement in the estimated GFR.
evidence.explanation: Eculizumab enabled discontinuation of dialysis and earlier intervention was associated with better renal outcomes.

evidence.snippet: This advance facilitated the development of novel, rational treatment options targeting terminal complement activation, e.g., using an anti-C5 antibody (eculizumab).
evidence.explanation: International consensus confirms eculizumab as the rational treatment targeting the underlying complement pathophysiology.

evidence.snippet: Eculizumab was used in 82.5% of cases. The median time from diagnosis to treatment initiation was 3 days (IQR 1–5).
evidence.explanation: Real-world corroboration of the trial evidence above: in the Spanish MATUCIP registry (20 pediatric intensive care units, 40 children treated with a complement inhibitor for thrombotic microangiopathy), eculizumab was the agent used in the large majority of cases, initiated a median of 3 days after diagnosis. Non-peer-reviewed preprint — supporting evidence only, not the sole support for eculizumab as an aHUS treatment.

treatments/0.description: Humanized monoclonal antibody that binds complement component C5, preventing cleavage to C5a and C5b and blocking MAC formation. First-line treatment for aHUS that has transformed outcomes, with rapid hematologic response and renal function improvement.

evidence.snippet: This analysis reveals that ravulizumab administered every 8 weeks is efficacious with an acceptable safety profile for the long-term treatment of adults with aHUS and provides additional clinical benefit beyond 6 months of treatment.
evidence.explanation: Phase 3 trial demonstrates long-term efficacy and safety of ravulizumab with every-8-week dosing in adults with aHUS.

evidence.snippet: Ravulizumab was administered for relapse prevention in the chronic phase, and no recurrence of thrombotic microangiopathy was observed during the follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Case report demonstrates sustained remission with no TMA recurrence in a CFH-aHUS patient treated with ravulizumab for relapse prevention in the chronic disease phase.

treatments/1.description: Long-acting C5 inhibitor engineered from eculizumab with extended dosing interval (every 8 weeks vs every 2 weeks). Non-inferior efficacy with improved convenience.

evidence.snippet: Iptacopan/LNP023, a novel, orally administered C3 convertase inhibitor that has shown efficacy in C3 glomerulopathy and paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria, is going to be tested in patients with atypical haemolytic syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Case report documents iptacopan mechanism and its emerging role in complement-mediated TMA including aHUS refractory to anti-C5 therapy.

evidence.snippet: Trials on novel complement inhibitors, regenerative medicine, targeted therapy, and stem cell therapy may also improve future treatment options.
evidence.explanation: 2026 review confirms that trials on novel complement inhibitors beyond eculizumab represent an emerging therapeutic frontier in aHUS management.

treatments/2.description: Novel oral small-molecule inhibitor of complement factor B, targeting the alternative complement pathway at the level of C3 convertase (C3bBb), upstream of the C5 inhibition site targeted by eculizumab and ravulizumab. Under clinical investigation for aHUS following demonstrated efficacy in C3 glomerulopathy and paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Case reports document rescue use in complement-mediated TMA refractory to anti-C5 agents.

evidence.snippet: Plasma exchange or infusion may transiently maintain normal levels of hematologic measures but does not treat the underlying systemic disease.
evidence.explanation: The NEJM trial background confirms plasma exchange as prior standard of care that provided only transient hematologic improvement.

evidence.snippet: patients were submitted to plasma therapy (plasma exchange and/or plasma infusion) and/or liver transplantation, procedures that are not free of serious complications and that do not address the underlying pathophysiology of the disease.
evidence.explanation: Confirms plasma therapy was used historically but has limitations as it does not address the underlying complement dysregulation.

evidence.snippet: A multidisciplinary approach, including therapeutic plasma exchange (TPE), was employed, resulting in gradual clinical improvement, although the patient remained dialysis-dependent at discharge.
evidence.explanation: Case report of secondary aHUS triggered by severe leptospirosis demonstrates therapeutic benefit of plasma exchange as rescue intervention for complement-mediated complications in systemic infection.

treatments/3.description: Historical first-line therapy before eculizumab. Plasma exchange removes mutant complement factors and autoantibodies while replacing functional complement regulators. Still used as bridging therapy and for anti-factor H antibody-mediated aHUS.

evidence.snippet: patients were submitted to plasma therapy (plasma exchange and/or plasma infusion) and/or liver transplantation, procedures that are not free of serious complications
evidence.explanation: Brazilian consensus documents that liver transplantation (combined with kidney transplantation for CFH mutations) was used historically and remains a consideration for refractory cases.

evidence.snippet: associated with a high rate of recurrence in kidney transplants causing a post-transplant thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA). Prophylactic eculizumab can prevent disease recurrence in select patients.
evidence.explanation: Newcastle National Renal Complement Therapeutics Centre case series documents the high rate of aHUS recurrence in kidney transplants and that prophylactic eculizumab can prevent recurrence in selected patients, supporting genotype-informed transplant management.

evidence.snippet: 34.6% of recipients had an identified complement pathway defect. Median time to presentation with post-transplant TMA was 8.4 months.
evidence.explanation: In 26 patients treated with eculizumab for post-transplant TMA, only a third had an identified complement defect and outcomes were poor for late (>12 months) presentations, indicating eculizumab is not uniformly protective once transplant TMA is established.

treatments/4.description: For patients who progress to ESRD. Risk of disease recurrence in the transplanted kidney varies by genotype (high for CFH mutations, low for MCP mutations). Combined liver-kidney transplantation has been performed for CFH mutations to correct the source of mutant protein.

evidence.snippet: Autoantibodies targeting factor H (FH), which is a main alternative complement pathway regulatory protein, have been well characterized in atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS)
evidence.explanation: Confirms anti-FH autoantibodies as a well-characterized pathogenic mechanism in aHUS, providing the rationale for immunosuppressive treatment to reduce antibody production.

treatments/5.description: For autoimmune aHUS with anti-factor H antibodies, combination of plasma exchange with immunosuppressive therapy (mycophenolate mofetil, rituximab, or cyclophosphamide) to reduce antibody production.

evidence.snippet: half had suspected CM-HUS, while the remaining half received off-label therapy. Patients with suspected CM-HUS initiated treatment significantly earlier than patients with other TMA subtypes.
evidence.explanation: Documents that in real-world pediatric critical care half of complement inhibitor use for TMA is off-label because the complement-mediated mechanism cannot be confirmed at the time of the treatment decision, and that diagnostic uncertainty tracks with later initiation. Non-peer-reviewed preprint.

evidence.snippet: In trial 1, dialysis was discontinued in 4 of 5 patients. Earlier intervention with eculizumab was associated with significantly greater improvement in the estimated GFR.
evidence.explanation: Establishes why the diagnostic delay matters mechanistically rather than only administratively: the timing of complement blockade is associated with the degree of renal recovery.

open_questions/0.rationale: Genetic and functional confirmation of a complement lesion takes far longer than the therapeutic window, and a negative result cannot exclude the mechanism because no complement variant is identified in a substantial minority of clinically definite aHUS. The consequence is visible in real-world practice: in the Spanish MATUCIP pediatric intensive care registry only half of the children who received a complement inhibitor for TMA had suspected CM-HUS, the other half being treated off-label, and those non-CM-HUS patients started therapy roughly 2.5 days later than the suspected-CM-HUS group. The landmark eculizumab trial separately reported that earlier intervention was associated with significantly greater eGFR improvement, so diagnostic delay is plausibly on the causal path to the renal outcome rather than merely a documentation artefact. This is a genuine gap in the mechanism model as curated: the entry asserts that complement dysregulation drives renal microvascular thrombosis, but supplies no measurable, time-resolved readout of that dysregulation usable prospectively at presentation.

evidence.snippet: A homozygous premature stop codon in exon 6 of PIK3R1 was identified in a young woman with colitis and absent B cells.

evidence.snippet: E555K in the transfected cells localized normally to the nucleus and resulted in a dominant negative effect when bound to DNA as a homodimer with wild-type E47.

evidence.snippet: Complete AR TCF3 deficiency is associated with reduced B cells, hypogammaglobulinemia, dysmorphic phenotypes, and B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL)

evidence.snippet: The immunodeficiency results from hypomorphic mutations of SLC39A7, which encodes the endoplasmic reticulum-to-cytoplasm zinc transporter ZIP7.

evidence.snippet: We studied six unrelated agammaglobulinemic patients, each harboring a heterozygous mutation (four de novo, two unphased) of SPI1, the gene encoding PU.1.

evidence.snippet: Patient SPI1 mutations encoded destabilized PU.1 proteins unable to nuclear localize or bind target DNA.

evidence.snippet: 6 were clinically well with laboratory evaluations documenting serum antibody and circulating B-cell concentrations within age- adjusted normal ranges.
evidence.explanation: Six variant-carrying relatives had normal clinical and laboratory assessments at the study time; ascertainment and possible later onset limit penetrance estimates.

evidence.snippet: FNIP1 deficiency is a novel inborn error of immunity characterized by early and severe B-cell development defect, agammaglobulinemia, variable neutropenia, and HCM.

genes/10.notes: Biallelic FNIP1 deficiency is a syndromic B-cell immunodeficiency with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and variable neutropenia. evidence.snippet: In three families with Hoffman syndrome 9,10, we identi ﬁed three heterozygous mutations affecting the TOPRIM, or DNA gating, domain of the type II topoisomerase TOP2B.
evidence.explanation: Three families establish the reported human syndrome; mechanistic assays use separate yeast and mouse systems.

evidence.snippet: There are an additional 6 cases of homozygous PIK3CD gene mutation resulting in LOF of PIK3 delta enzyme complex. These patients also displayed hypogammaglobulinemia or agammaglobulinemia as well as decreased B cells [34].

genes/12.notes: Biallelic loss of the p110-delta catalytic subunit can cause severe antibody deficiency with reduced B cells. This is distinct from dominant activating PIK3CD variants causing activated PI3K-delta syndrome. The historical numbered AGM series does not exhaust the modern disease spectrum.

evidence.snippet: One (D.II.1) of 5 patients receiving live-attenuated oral polio vaccine developed iatrogenic paralytic poliomyelitis.
evidence.explanation: Direct SPI1 cohort evidence of a live oral polio vaccine complication; the small exposed denominator is not a general vaccine-risk estimate.

treatments/2.description: Avoid live viral vaccines, especially oral polio vaccine, in severe antibody deficiency under immunology guidance. Inactivated polio vaccine is used for affected people and family contacts. The SPI1 cohort directly documents vaccine-associated paralytic poliomyelitis; this does not quantify all vaccines or all genotypes.

evidence.snippet: Complete blood count with differential and quantitative serum immunoglobulins at least annually; chest and sinus imaging as needed to assess for chronic lung and/or sinus disease.
evidence.explanation: XLA surveillance schedule provides a clinical framework, adapted for genotype, age, complications and treatment.

treatments/3.description: Monitor infections, blood counts and immunoglobulins; assess chronic lung or sinus disease when clinically indicated. Follow genotype-specific skin, cardiac, gastrointestinal and inflammatory complications. Surveillance detects complications; it does not itself inhibit the molecular defect.

evidence.snippet: (P1 and P2, family 1) additionally showed severe blistering dermatosis (Fig. 1b), failure to thrive and thrombocytopenia, prompting hematopoietic stem cell transplantation; this resulted in cure of immunologic abnormalities and amelioration of skin disease.
evidence.explanation: Two siblings among six ZIP7-deficient patients had severe skin disease, poor growth and thrombocytopenia; transplantation outcomes are specific to them.

evidence.snippet: Five years after transplantation, he remains IRT dependent because of undetectable serum immunoglobulin (IgA) and IgM despite naïve B-cell reconstitution and >99% donor peripheral blood engraftment in B-cell, T-cell, and myeloid cell compart- ments.

Two severely affected ZIP7 siblings had correction of immunologic abnormalities and improvement of skin disease. In SPI1 disease, one recipient remained replacement-dependent five years after full trilineage donor engraftment; another failed engraftment after receiving cells from an unknowingly variant-carrying sister. These contrasting small series do not establish a uniform curative strategy.

treatments/5.description: Explain gene- and allele-specific inheritance, test at-risk relatives after a molecular diagnosis, and reassess initially mild SPI1 carriers over time. A clinically healthy related donor can carry the familial variant; donor assessment should include this possibility.

evidence.snippet: Immune modulating treatments successfully used for inﬂammatory bowel disorder included mesalamine, mycophenolate, and tumor necrosis factor inhibition (adalimumab). treatments/6.description: Treat inflammatory complications according to the affected organ and infection risk. In the SPI1 cohort, mesalamine, mycophenolate and adalimumab were reported for bowel inflammation, whereas multiple agents had limited success in one refractory arthritis case. These are uncontrolled treatment experiences, not comparative efficacy evidence or a disease-wide regimen.

Forced mutant expression and global null mouse studies use different allele mechanisms; preserved null-mouse antibody function cannot establish or refute a dominant human effect. open_questions/1.rationale: The 2025 cohort has22 agammaglobulinemic patients,5 relatives with milder antibody abnormalities and6 apparently unaffected relatives. Its81.8% estimate concerns any antibody phenotype and is affected by familial ascertainment and possible later onset. No hematologic malignancy was observed over514 patient-years, but the small cohort cannot establish zero risk. The L180F family has marked within-family variation; a simple PU.1 abundance-to-severity relationship is not established.

evidence.snippet: Specifically, p4EBP1 and pAkt473 were significantly activated ( 12.46±1.86 vs 4.00±0.53, p = 0.00 02; 3.82±1.78 vs 0.97±0. 09, p = 0.029). As opposite, no difference could be found in S6 phosphorylation (1.46±0.14 vs 2.70±0.51, p = 0.14).

evidence.snippet: B -cell precursors did not show evidence of a maturation block, unlike classical agammaglobulinemia14, although a relative increase of earlier maturation stages (pro-B and pre-B1) and a significant reduction of immature B-cells was observed (Figure 1E and supplemental Figure 8).
evidence.explanation: One patient had altered precursor proportions without a discrete maturation block, limiting a universal pro-B arrest model.

evidence.snippet: Indeed, circulating P1 B-cells exhibited increased numbers of mitochondria and mitochondrial activity relative to healthy control (HC) B-cells (Figure 1F and supplemental Figure 9 ).
evidence.explanation: Mitochondrial dye readouts were measured in rare circulating B cells from one patient compared with a healthy control; they do not establish a general ATP-production flux.

The original marrow observation lacks a discrete block, and later cases differ in neutrophil number and stimulus-dependent function.

steps/1.description: The BRAF V600E mutation causes constitutive activation of the RAF kinase by mimicking the phosphorylated active state. This results in ligand-independent activation of the MAPK pathway driving thyroid follicular cell proliferation and dedifferentiation.

steps/2.description: Mutant BRAF constitutively phosphorylates and activates MEK1/2, leading to sustained ERK1/2 activation. This drives uncontrolled proliferation and is the rationale for combined BRAF/MEK inhibition therapy.

steps/3.description: BRAF V600E-driven MAPK activation suppresses expression of thyroid differentiation genes including NIS (sodium-iodide symporter), leading to radioiodine refractoriness. This loss of differentiation is associated with more aggressive disease behavior.

evidence.snippet: Significant correlations were found between expression of BRAF V600E and that of PD-L1 and PD-1.
evidence.explanation: Supports adding a PD-L1/PD-1 immune-evasion mechanism linked to BRAF V600E-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma.

steps/4.description: BRAF V600E-positive papillary thyroid carcinoma is associated with increased PD-L1 and PD-1 expression in the tumor microenvironment. This checkpoint pattern provides a mechanistic immune-evasion axis relevant to refractory BRAF-mutant thyroid cancer.

edges/1.description: Constitutive BRAF activation drives downstream MEK-ERK signaling

edges/2.description: MAPK activation suppresses thyroid differentiation gene expression

edges/3.description: BRAF V600E-positive tumors show correlated PD-L1 and PD-1 expression.

evidence.snippet: The common gene mutations in PTC include BRAF V600E,RET/PTC rearrangement,and RAS mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports BRAF V600E as a common mutation in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

genes/0.notes: BRAF V600E is the most common mutation in papillary thyroid cancer, occurring in 40-60% of cases. Associated with extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastasis, and radioiodine refractoriness. Targetable with BRAF/MEK inhibitors.

evidence.snippet: Coexisting BRAF V600E and TERT mutations independently elevated the risk of loss of radioiodine avidity (OR = 4.8, P = .009).
evidence.explanation: Supports TERT promoter mutation as a prognostic modifier in BRAF V600E differentiated thyroid cancer.

genes/1.notes: TERT promoter mutations co-occur with BRAF V600E in a clinically important subset of differentiated thyroid cancers and increase risk of radioiodine avidity loss, recurrence, and poor prognosis.

treatments/0.description: Total thyroidectomy with or without lymph node dissection is the primary treatment for papillary thyroid cancer regardless of BRAF status. Extent of surgery guided by tumor size and nodal involvement.

treatments/1.description: Adjuvant radioactive iodine (I-131) therapy is used for intermediate and high-risk disease. BRAF-mutant tumors may have reduced radioiodine avidity due to dedifferentiation and NIS suppression.

treatments/2.description: Combined BRAF inhibitor (dabrafenib) and MEK inhibitor (trametinib) is approved for BRAF V600E-mutant anaplastic thyroid cancer and shows activity in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer.

treatments/3.description: Multi-kinase inhibitors approved for radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer regardless of BRAF status. May be used when BRAF-targeted therapy is not available or has failed.

evidence.explanation: Supports radiation exposure as the leading established environmental risk factor for papillary thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: The common gene mutations in PTC include BRAF V600E,RET/PTC rearrangement,and RAS mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports the major early driver classes emphasized in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

evidence.snippet: In most tumors of follicular cell origin, the primary molecular events are RAS or RAS-like (follicular-patterned tumors) and BRAF p.V600E or BRAF V600E-like (conventional papillary carcinomas) alterations.
evidence.explanation: Anchors the characterization of these driver events as the primary (early) molecular alterations in follicular-cell-derived thyroid tumors.

steps/1.description: Early oncogenic alterations in papillary thyroid carcinoma commonly include BRAF V600E, RET/PTC rearrangements, and RAS-family mutations. These driver events arise in thyroid follicular cells and establish the genotype-phenotype patterns that distinguish conventional papillary tumors from more follicular-patterned neoplasms.

evidence.snippet: In most tumors of follicular cell origin, the primary molecular events are RAS or RAS-like (follicular-patterned tumors) and BRAF p.V600E or BRAF V600E-like (conventional papillary carcinomas) alterations.
evidence.explanation: Supports the dominant BRAF-like and RAS-like molecular programs that organize papillary thyroid carcinoma biology.

evidence.snippet: BRAF V600E, the most common oncogenic driver in papillary thyroid carcinoma, activates the MAPK pathway and suppresses genes involved in iodine metabolism and differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the role of BRAF-driven MAPK activation and reduced differentiation in a major papillary thyroid carcinoma subset.

steps/2.description: Driver alterations converge on chronic MAPK signaling, which promotes thyroid follicular cell proliferation and malignant transformation. BRAF-like tumors especially depend on this pathway and often show loss of thyroid differentiation programs relevant to iodine handling.

evidence.snippet: Progression of thyroid tumors to advanced and less-differentiated carcinomas requires additional oncogenic alterations, including TP53 and TERT promoter mutation, and aberrant PI3K-PTEN-AKT signaling.
evidence.explanation: Supports the progression model linking additional alterations to aggressive and less-differentiated thyroid carcinoma states.

steps/3.description: A subset of papillary thyroid carcinomas acquires additional alterations such as TERT promoter mutation, TP53 disruption, and aberrant PI3K-PTEN-AKT signaling. These changes are associated with progression toward more aggressive, less-differentiated, and radioiodine-refractory disease.

edges/0.description: Driver mutations and fusions converge on persistent mitogenic signaling

edges/1.description: Additional oncogenic hits superimposed on driver signaling promote dedifferentiation and treatment resistance

evidence.snippet: The most common etiologic factor is radiation
evidence.explanation: Identifies radiation as the most common etiologic factor for this cancer, the exposure that generates its driver alterations.

edges/2.description: Radiation reaching the thyroid causes double-strand breaks whose mis-joining produces the rearrangement-type drivers characteristic of radiation-associated disease, so the exposure reaches this node through a known repair-error step.

evidence.snippet: BRAF V600E, the most common oncogenic driver in papillary thyroid carcinoma, activates the MAPK pathway and suppresses genes involved in iodine metabolism and differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Supports BRAF V600E as the dominant papillary thyroid carcinoma driver and a mechanism for MAPK activation.

evidence.snippet: Overall, these findings confirm that BRAF V600E mutation is associated with an increased risk of nodal metastasis and recurrence in papillary thyroid carcinoma.
evidence.explanation: Supports the clinical association between BRAF V600E and adverse recurrence-related features.

evidence.snippet: However, its lack of impact on distant metastases and disease-specific mortality limits its role as an independent prognostic marker in clinical decision-making.
evidence.explanation: The same meta-analysis found no significant association with distant metastases or disease-specific mortality, qualifying BRAF V600E as an incomplete independent prognostic marker.

genes/0.notes: BRAF V600E is the most common single driver alteration in conventional papillary thyroid carcinoma. It activates MAPK signaling and is associated with higher risk of nodal metastasis and recurrence in aggregate analyses. However, a large meta-analysis of 20,570 patients found no significant association with distant metastases (OR=0.75) or disease-specific mortality (OR=0.97), limiting its role as an independent prognostic marker for survival.

evidence.snippet: The common gene mutations in PTC include BRAF V600E,RET/PTC rearrangement,and RAS mutations.

genes/1.notes: RET/PTC rearrangements define an important papillary thyroid carcinoma subset, especially in radiation-associated disease, and converge on the same mitogenic pathways as other canonical drivers.

evidence.snippet: The common gene mutations in PTC include BRAF V600E,RET/PTC rearrangement,and RAS mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports RAS-family alterations as recurrent papillary thyroid carcinoma drivers.

evidence.snippet: In most tumors of follicular cell origin, the primary molecular events are RAS or RAS-like (follicular-patterned tumors) and BRAF p.V600E or BRAF V600E-like (conventional papillary carcinomas) alterations.
evidence.explanation: Supports the distinction between RAS-like follicular-patterned tumors and BRAF-like conventional papillary carcinomas.

evidence.snippet: Progression of thyroid tumors to advanced and less-differentiated carcinomas requires additional oncogenic alterations, including TP53 and TERT promoter mutation, and aberrant PI3K-PTEN-AKT signaling.
evidence.explanation: Supports TERT promoter mutation as a late progression event in aggressive thyroid carcinoma biology.

genes/3.notes: TERT promoter mutations are progression-associated events linked to aggressive, less-differentiated, and radioiodine-refractory thyroid carcinoma states.

treatments/0.description: Surgical resection is the mainstay of treatment for localized papillary thyroid carcinoma.

treatments/1.description: Radioactive iodine is used selectively after surgery for intermediate-risk, high-risk, or metastatic differentiated thyroid cancer.

treatments/2.description: Advanced papillary thyroid carcinoma with actionable driver alterations may be treated with genotype-matched targeted therapy, including RET inhibitors for RET fusion-positive disease and BRAF-directed regimens in BRAF V600E-driven refractory tumors.

treatments/3.description: Multi-kinase inhibitors are standard systemic options for progressive radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer when surgery and radioiodine are no longer sufficient.

evidence.snippet: Patients must have received previous lenvatinib or sorafenib and progressed during or after treatment with up to two VEGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors.
evidence.explanation: Defines the second-line, VEGFR-TKI-refractory population in which cabozantinib was evaluated, downstream of the lenvatinib/sorafenib option already curated here.

evidence.snippet: cabozantinib showed significant improvement in progression-free survival over placebo: median not reached ... versus 1·9 months (1·8-3·6); hazard ratio 0·22 (96% CI 0·13-0·36; p<0·0001)
evidence.explanation: Reports the randomised progression-free survival benefit that supports cabozantinib as an active option after VEGFR-TKI failure.

evidence.snippet: Grade 3 or 4 adverse events occurred in 71 (57%) of 125 patients receiving cabozantinib and 16 (26%) of 62 receiving placebo
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the grade 3-4 toxicity burden stated in the description, so the efficacy claim is not curated without its safety cost.

evidence.snippet: Cabozantinib contributed high-certainty evidence for progression-free survival in radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer after previous VEGFR-targeted therapy
evidence.explanation: GRADE certainty rating from a 2026 systematic review of treatment-resistant malignancies, corroborating (not solely supporting) the COSMIC-311 result above. Non-peer-reviewed preprint; cited only alongside the peer-reviewed trial report.

treatments/4.description: Cabozantinib is a multi-kinase inhibitor (VEGFR2, MET, AXL, RET) used in the second-line setting for radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer that has progressed during or after lenvatinib or sorafenib. This VEGFR-TKI-refractory population previously had no standard of care; the randomised placebo-controlled COSMIC-311 trial met its progression-free survival endpoint at interim analysis, at the cost of substantially more grade 3-4 toxicity (palmar-plantar erythrodysaesthesia, hypertension, fatigue).

steps/1.description: Chromosomal rearrangements fuse the RET tyrosine kinase domain with upstream partners that provide dimerization domains. This creates constitutively active chimeric proteins that signal independently of RET ligands (GDNF family members).

steps/2.description: Constitutive RET kinase activation drives the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade, promoting uncontrolled thyroid follicular cell proliferation. This is a major effector of RET-mediated thyroid tumorigenesis.

steps/3.description: RET activation recruits PI3K and stimulates AKT-mTOR signaling, promoting cell survival and resistance to apoptosis. Combined with MAPK activation, this drives thyroid cancer progression.

edges/1.description: RET fusion activates RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK signaling cascade

edges/2.description: RET fusion stimulates PI3K-AKT survival signaling

evidence.snippet: The common gene mutations in PTC include BRAF V600E,RET/PTC rearrangement,and RAS mutations.
evidence.explanation: Supports RET/PTC rearrangements as common mutations in papillary thyroid carcinoma.

treatments/0.description: Total thyroidectomy with lymph node dissection is the primary treatment. Most RET fusion-positive PTCs have excellent outcomes with surgery alone.

treatments/1.description: Adjuvant radioactive iodine therapy is used for intermediate and high-risk disease. RET fusion-positive tumors generally maintain radioiodine avidity better than BRAF-mutant tumors.

treatments/2.description: Highly selective RET inhibitor approved for RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer that is radioiodine-refractory. Demonstrates high response rates with durable disease control.

treatments/3.description: Another selective RET inhibitor with activity in RET fusion-positive thyroid cancer. Similar efficacy profile to selpercatinib.

treatments/4.description: Multi-kinase inhibitors approved for radioiodine-refractory differentiated thyroid cancer. May be used but selective RET inhibitors are preferred for RET fusion-positive tumors.
