evidence.explanation: Membrane redistribution, not a general increase in GLUT1 abundance.

evidence.snippet: BAY876 and SL327 treatments did not significantly alter GLUT1 trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence.explanation: Primary human brain endothelial-cell transfection experiment; trafficking persists with MEK inhibition.

steps/5.description: KRAS G12V increases GLUT1 localization at the plasma membrane in immortalized HUVECs and primary human brain microvascular endothelial cells, without increasing total GLUT1 expression. SL327 does not reverse trafficking, distinguishing it from MEK-dependent HK2 induction.

evidence.snippet: Quantification of the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) showed that KRASG12V ECs featured a notable elevation of glycolysis in comparison with KRASWT ECs, without changes in mitochondrial respiration as measured by the oxygen consumption rate (OCR)
evidence.explanation: Direct functional metabolic measurements in engineered endothelial cells substantiate the flux claim.

evidence.snippet: siRNA knockdown of HK2 resulted in a dose-dependent reduction of both average sprout length and number per EC spheroid
evidence.explanation: Perturbation of HK2 supports a contribution of glycolysis to the cultured-cell sprouting phenotype.

steps/6.description: Mutant endothelial cells show increased glucose uptake, extracellular acidification and lactate secretion. HK2 knockdown and glycolytic inhibitors suppress selected angiogenic behaviors. Most mechanistic experiments used immortalized HUVECs; primary brain cells and human lesion-derived cultures provide additional validation.

evidence.snippet: expression of mutant KRAS (KRASG12V) in endothelial cells in vitro induced increased ERK (extracellular signal-regulated kinase) activity, increased expression of genes related to angiogenesis and Notch signaling, and enhanced migratory behavior.
evidence.explanation: Engineered endothelial-cell experiments establish several cellular responses; they do not by themselves establish a human identity-switch mechanism.

evidence.snippet: endothelial subsets were enriched for arterial and venous, but not venular or capillary transcriptional identity scores in AVMs
evidence.explanation: Human single-cell comparison identifies the specific zonation disturbance.

steps/7.description: Mutant KRAS promotes angiogenic gene expression, migration and sprouting in endothelial assays. Notch-associated transcripts increase in the 2018 HUVEC experiments, but arterial and venous identity markers did not change there. Human AVM single-cell data instead show loss of capillary and venular signatures in nidus endothelial populations. These are distinct observations rather than proof that Notch activation abolishes all arterial–venous identity. Increased proliferation is model-dependent.

evidence.snippet: N-Cad, Slug, and CD44 were significantly increased, but VE-Cad was decreased, in ECG12V compared to control
evidence.explanation: Cultured mouse brain endothelial cells expressing KRAS G12V.

steps/8.description: KRAS G12V induces mesenchymal markers in cultured mouse brain endothelial cells and engineered mouse AVMs. Trametinib reduces these changes alongside improved barrier measurements. EndMT as the mediator of hemorrhage reduction remains a hypothesis because the treatment affects multiple processes.

evidence.snippet: KRASG12V increased the mRNA expression of the pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1β and IL-6), as well as monocyte chemoattractant protein-1 (MCP-1)
evidence.explanation: Cultured mutant mouse endothelial cells.

steps/9.description: Cultured KRAS G12V mouse endothelial cells increase IL1B, IL6 and CCL2/MCP1 expression and release inflammatory mediators. Mouse AVM tissue also shows endothelial and myeloid cytokine expression. The specific mediators necessary for each downstream effect have not all been isolated experimentally.

evidence.snippet: GPNMB+ Mo3 monocytes, was over-represented in ruptured AVMs
evidence.explanation: Human bulk-RNA deconvolution supported by cellular assays; association with rupture does not establish temporal direction.

evidence.snippet: Normal ECs treated with BV2-MG-CM had decreased mRNA expression of cell adhesion molecules (CDH5 and TJP1) after 48 h of incubation
evidence.explanation: Conditioned medium from primed BV2 cells affected wild-type mouse endothelial cells.

steps/10.description: Human AVMs contain activated and infiltrating myeloid populations. In murine co-cultures, mutant endothelial conditioned medium activates BV2 microglia, and macrophages amplify endothelial barrier dysfunction. BV2 is an immortalized mouse line and does not capture all primary microglial states. GPNMB-positive monocytes are enriched in ruptured human lesions, but cross-sectional enrichment does not establish whether recruitment preceded rupture.

evidence.snippet: VE-cadherin expression was weak and diffuse in bAVM tissue compared to temporal lobe tissue
evidence.explanation: Human lesion tissue staining, with preserved CD31 and ZO-1 staining in the same comparison.

evidence.snippet: normal ECs treated with KRAS-G12V-EC-CM had no changes in the mRNA expression of cell junction molecules
evidence.explanation: Direct mutant endothelial conditioned medium did not reproduce the effect of primed microglial conditioned medium.

steps/11.description: VE-cadherin organization is disrupted in engineered KRAS-mutant endothelial cells and examined human AVM tissue. Murine endothelial and microglial experiments show context-dependent changes in CDH5, TJP1, OCLN and CLDN5; conditioned-medium effects should not be described as degradation of every junction protein.

evidence.snippet: Co-culture of isolated GPNMB+ monocytes from ruptured AVM patients with primary brain vascular smooth muscle cells (VSMCs) increased apoptotic cleaved caspase-3+ VSMCs
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived monocytes with primary vascular smooth muscle cells; an in-vitro functional result.

steps/12.description: GPNMB-positive monocytes isolated from patients with ruptured AVMs increase apoptosis of primary brain vascular smooth muscle cells in co-culture. Soluble osteopontin also increases apoptosis, attenuated by CD44 or integrin blockade. These assays support a possible inflammatory route to mural-cell loss without proving that it initiated rupture in the donor lesions.

evidence.snippet: Brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs) are high-flow vascular lesions characterized by direct arteriovenous shunting without an intervening capillary bed.
evidence.explanation: Defines the nidus lesion in exactly the terms of this node - high flow, direct shunting, absent capillary bed. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

steps/13.description: The nidus contains tortuous vessels connecting feeding arteries to draining veins without a normal intervening capillary network. The resulting low-resistance shunt alters local flow and venous loading. Vessel architecture and drainage differ between lesions.

evidence.snippet: Female sex (1.49, 95% CI 0.96-2.30) and exclusively deep venous drainage (1.60, 0.95-2.68, p = 0.02 in imputed dataset) may be additional predictors.
evidence.explanation: The complete-case estimate for exclusively deep drainage is imprecise and crosses 1; the imputed analysis reaches significance. Neither directly measures venous pressure or proves outflow obstruction.

steps/14.description: High-flow shunting changes venous pressure and mechanical loading, while the degree of venous hypertension depends on drainage anatomy and outflow resistance. Deep venous drainage is an epidemiological risk marker and is not synonymous with venous stenosis or a direct measurement of outflow pressure. Hemodynamic and structural mechanisms may interact in rupture.

evidence.snippet: the presence of Mφ significantly enhanced FITC-dextran permeability in a 3D BBB coculture system
evidence.explanation: Functional permeability assay separates macrophage-dependent dextran leakage from the earlier fall in electrical resistance.

steps/15.description: Barrier dysfunction is demonstrated by reduced electrical resistance in murine endothelial–astrocyte cultures. At the tested early time point, KRAS-mutant endothelium alone did not increase dextran passage; added macrophages did. Mouse tracer leakage is reduced by minocycline. Permeability measurements and microscopic leakage do not by themselves establish prevention or causation of clinical hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: The vessel walls in bAVMs have structural defects, which impair vascular integrity. Mural cells are essential structural and functional components of blood vessels and play a critical role in maintaining vascular integrity. Changes in mural cell number and coverage have been implicated in bAVMs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes deficient mural cell coverage as a structural defect of bAVM vessels impairing vascular integrity. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

evidence.snippet: we found 498 genes downregulated including genes implicated in extracellular matrix composition, the binary angiopoietin-TIE system, and TGF (transforming growth factor)-beta signaling
evidence.explanation: Human bAVM tissue RNA-seq showing downregulation of extracellular-matrix and angiopoietin-TIE programmes, the signalling system that governs mural cell recruitment.

steps/16.description: Altered mural-cell number or coverage can weaken vascular support. Human bulk transcriptomics show reduced extracellular-matrix and angiopoietin–TIE gene programs, but do not directly establish a specific recruitment defect. Patient-derived monocyte co-culture supplies a separate functional mechanism for smooth-muscle apoptosis. Pericyte depletion findings from hereditary AVM models require caution when applied to sporadic KRAS-associated disease.

evidence.snippet: Seizures are a common clinical manifestation in patients with brain AVMs, ranking as the second most frequent presentation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes seizure as the second commonest presentation of brain AVM, the clinical content of this node.

steps/17.description: Perinidal cortical dysfunction can produce seizures. Proposed contributors include altered perfusion, venous congestion, gliosis and iron deposition after bleeding; their relative contributions vary and are not measured directly by surgical outcome cohorts.

evidence.snippet: A total of 141 hemorrhage events occurred during 6,074 patient-years of follow-up (annual rate of 2.3%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.0%-2.7%), higher for ruptured (4.8%, 3.9%-5.9%) than unruptured (1.3%, 1.0%-1.7%) AVMs at presentation.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the natural-history haemorrhage rate and the ruptured-versus-unruptured split that governs management decisions.

evidence.snippet: This large, individual patient data meta-analysis identified hemorrhagic presentation and increasing age as independent predictors of hemorrhage during follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the independent predictors of subsequent haemorrhage in untreated disease.

evidence.snippet: these hemorrhage risk estimates cannot be extrapolated to the entire lifetime of a patient.
evidence.explanation: Full text of PMID:25015366: natural-history follow-up is limited by censoring at intervention and selection; annual estimates are not lifetime constants.

steps/18.description: Rupture of malformed nidus or draining vessels produces intracerebral, intraventricular or subarachnoid haemorrhage - the presentation that makes brain AVM a leading cause of haemorrhagic stroke in the young. In an individual-patient meta-analysis of four untreated cohorts spanning 6,074 patient-years, the annual haemorrhage rate was 2.3% overall, and this figure is strongly conditioned on presentation: 4.8% per year in lesions that had already ruptured versus 1.3% per year in those that had not. Prior haemorrhage and increasing age were the independent predictors.

evidence.snippet: Brain arteriovenous malformations (bAVMs) are high-flow vascular lesions characterized by direct arteriovenous shunting without an intervening capillary bed.
evidence.explanation: Defines the structural lesion. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

steps/19.description: The defining structural lesion: a nidus of dilated vessels shunting arterial blood directly into veins without an intervening capillary bed, demonstrated on catheter angiography, CT angiography or MR angiography.

evidence.snippet: are a leading cause of hemorrhagic stroke in young adults and children
evidence.explanation: Establishes haemorrhagic stroke as the defining clinical danger of brain AVM.

evidence.snippet: A total of 141 hemorrhage events occurred during 6,074 patient-years of follow-up (annual rate of 2.3%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 2.0%-2.7%), higher for ruptured (4.8%, 3.9%-5.9%) than unruptured (1.3%, 1.0%-1.7%) AVMs at presentation.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the annual haemorrhage rate in untreated disease, stratified by whether the lesion had previously ruptured.

steps/20.description: Rupture can cause intracerebral, intraventricular or subarachnoid hemorrhage. Untreated hemorrhage rates depend strongly on prior rupture; the four-cohort meta-analysis estimated 1.3% annually after an unruptured presentation and 4.8% after a ruptured presentation.

evidence.snippet: Seizures are a common clinical manifestation in patients with brain AVMs, ranking as the second most frequent presentation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes seizure as the second commonest presentation of brain AVM.

evidence.snippet: Epileptic seizure was the most common presenting symptom (80.4%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies seizure as the dominant presentation in a surgical series of unruptured lesions. Not mapped to a frequency band because the cohort is restricted to unruptured, surgically treated AVMs.

steps/21.description: Seizures are a common presentation. A retrospective surgical series restricted to 52 unruptured lesions reported epilepsy at presentation in 80.4%; this selected proportion is not a disease-wide frequency.

evidence.explanation: ARUBA Table 2: first hemorrhagic strokes in the randomized intervention and medical-management groups, respectively. These are observed events rather than only an endpoint definition.

steps/22.description: Hemorrhagic stroke is a major clinical consequence. Ischemic stroke also occurred in ARUBA, especially in the intervention arm; treatment-associated events should not be treated as the natural-history frequency of ischemia.

evidence.snippet: In our cohort, epileptic seizures were the most frequent initial clinical manifestation, whereas headaches and focal neurological deficits were less commonly observed.
evidence.explanation: Names focal neurological deficits as a presenting manifestation and places their frequency below seizure in an unruptured surgical cohort. No frequency band is asserted because the source gives an ordering, not a proportion, and the cohort is surgically selected.

steps/23.description: Some clinical series report focal neurological deficits without specifying the affected functions. More specific motor and sensory findings are represented separately where primary patient descriptions permit.

evidence.snippet: whereas headaches and focal neurological deficits were less commonly observed.
evidence.explanation: Primary clinical series of unruptured lesions.

steps/24.description: Headache, including migraine-like presentations, occurs in patients with brain AVM. The observational cohorts do not establish that every headache is caused by the lesion.

edges/2.description: Activating RAS/RAF variants increase downstream ERK activity.

edges/3.description: KRAS G12V changes GLUT1 trafficking in cultured endothelial cells; this response is not reversed by MEK inhibition.

edges/4.description: KRAS-mutant endothelial cells develop an inflammatory secretory phenotype.

edges/5.description: MEK inhibition lowers HK2 in mutant endothelial cells, although ERK stimulation alone is insufficient to induce HK2.

edges/6.description: MAPK-dependent angiogenic transcription and migration promote abnormal sprouting.

edges/7.description: KRAS-dependent mesenchymal-marker changes are reduced by trametinib in mouse and cultured-cell models.

edges/8.description: MEK inhibition restores VE-cadherin organization in engineered endothelial cells.

edges/9.description: Increased surface glucose transport supports greater glucose uptake.

edges/10.description: Increased hexokinase activity supports glucose phosphorylation and glycolytic flux.

edges/11.description: HK2 knockdown reduces excessive sprouting and migration in mutant-cell assays.

edges/12.description: Dysregulated endothelial remodeling contributes to abnormal arteriovenous architecture; endothelial KRAS/BRAF animal models support sufficiency at the pathway level.

edges/13.description: A shift toward mesenchymal characteristics accompanies reduced endothelial junction organization; independent mediation has not been established.

edges/14.description: Direct arteriovenous connections alter flow and expose venous structures to abnormal hemodynamic loading.

edges/15.description: The nidus and direct shunt define the structural phenotype.

edges/16.description: Abnormal loading may contribute to failure of vulnerable vascular walls.

edges/17.description: Altered perinidal perfusion and venous congestion may contribute to cortical dysfunction.

edges/18.description: Mutant endothelial conditioned medium activates BV2 microglia and promotes migration in vitro.

edges/19.description: Primed microglial conditioned medium reduces selected endothelial junction transcripts.

edges/20.description: Patient-derived GPNMB-positive monocytes increase smooth-muscle-cell apoptosis in co-culture.

edges/21.description: Disrupted endothelial junctions reduce barrier resistance and can permit leakage.

edges/22.description: Loss of endothelial barrier integrity may contribute to vessel vulnerability, together with wall support and hemodynamic stress.

edges/23.description: Apoptosis can reduce smooth-muscle support; the degree of in-vivo contribution is unresolved.

edges/24.description: Deficient vascular support may contribute to wall instability; individual human rupture events are multifactorial.

edges/25.description: Epileptogenic cortical activity produces clinical seizures.

edges/26.description: Rupture releases blood into intracranial compartments.

edges/27.description: Clinically symptomatic hemorrhage can produce hemorrhagic stroke.

evidence.snippet: When ruptured, intracranial AVMs usually present with focal neurological deficits, seizures, and sequelae of increased intracranial pressure.
evidence.explanation: Clinical synthesis supports focal neurological deficits following rupture; it does not establish a mechanism for every unruptured presentation.

edges/28.description: Intracranial bleeding can injure or compress neural tissue and produce a focal deficit.

evidence.snippet: If the hemorrhage is large enough to cause a significant increase in intracranial pressure, patients will often present with headache, nausea and vomiting, and a decreased level of consciousness.
evidence.explanation: The chapter links headache to pressure elevation after a sufficiently large hemorrhage; this does not explain all headaches in AVM.

edges/29.description: A sufficiently large hemorrhage can increase intracranial pressure and cause headache.

evidence.snippet: We detected somatic activating KRAS mutations in tissue samples from 45 of the 72 patients and in none of the 21 paired blood samples.
evidence.explanation: Somatic variants were detected in a subset of resected lesions and not in the 21 paired blood samples assayed; this is not a universal statement about all blood-based methods.

evidence.snippet: We identified activating KRAS mutations in the majority of tissue samples of arteriovenous malformations of the brain that we analyzed.
evidence.explanation: Activating KRAS variants occurred in a majority of the sampled lesions; animal and cellular perturbations provide additional causal evidence.

genes/0.notes: Somatic activating KRAS variants are recurrent drivers in lesional endothelium. The founding study detected variants in 45/72 resected lesions and none of 21 paired blood samples. Endothelial enrichment increases detection, while assay sensitivity, tissue composition and low variant allele fractions affect yield. These findings support mosaicism but do not establish the developmental timing or a sharply bounded clone in every patient, or imply that all sporadic lesions are genetically explained.

evidence.snippet: Eight specimens contained KRAS mutations, which included p.G12D (n = 5) and p.G12V (n = 3). Two specimens contained BRAF mutations: p.V600E and p.Q636X.
evidence.explanation: Primary surgical cohort; includes one V600E and one functionally unresolved Q636X BRAF variant.

evidence.snippet: Mice with BrafV600E mutations in brain ECs developed BAVM closely resembled that of human lesions.
evidence.explanation: Engineered activating BRAF model supports causal potential of this allele; does not validate every detected BRAF variant.

genes/1.notes: Activating BRAF variants are less common than KRAS variants. A 2019 surgical series found KRAS variants in 8/16 and BRAF variants in 2/16 lesions. Its BRAF V600E variant is an established activating allele, whereas the functional consequence of Q636X was not resolved. Detection of a BRAF sequence variant alone does not establish gain of function.

evidence.snippet: In the low-risk group, there were no deaths, and poor outcomes were rare (6.8% at discharge; 2.3% at 9 months). Conversely, the high-risk group demonstrated significantly worse outcomes (62.5% poor outcome at discharge, 28.6% at 9 months).
evidence.explanation: Selected surgical cohort shows an association between anatomical grade and outcome; it is not a randomized comparison against observation.

evidence.snippet: Only microsurgical resection was consistently associated with reduced hemorrhage risk in sensitivity analyses.
evidence.explanation: Observational MATCH analysis of AVM hemorrhage or death; it does not directly compare the all-stroke endpoint of ARUBA or establish randomized modality superiority.

treatments/0.description: Microsurgery aims at complete nidus removal and can provide immediate obliteration, with outcome dependent on lesion anatomy and surgical risk. A selected 52-patient retrospective series found better outcomes for supplementary Spetzler-Martin scores ≤6. MATCH sensitivity analyses favored microsurgery for AVM hemorrhage or death, but this observational result does not establish superiority for all patients or all neurological outcomes.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Resection physically removes the shunting nidus, eliminating both the haemodynamic and the inflammatory arms of the lesion at once.

evidence.snippet: Estimated probabilities of AVM obliteration at 5 and 10 yr were 64% and 82%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Estimated obliteration rises over time but remains incomplete in this selected pediatric cohort.

evidence.snippet: The primary endpoint occurred in 14%, comprising hemorrhagic stroke, death, and permanent radiation-induced changes in 6%, 3%, and 8%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the harm profile, including radiation-induced change, that has to be set against the obliteration benefit.

evidence.snippet: Three-year imaging follow-up, available in 79/94 (84%) confirmed AVM occlusion in 51/79 (65%
evidence.explanation: TOBAS prospective SRS registry, predominantly ruptured small lesions; 54% when all enrolled analyzed patients are the denominator.

treatments/1.description: Focused radiation produces progressive vascular injury and eventual nidus obliteration over a latency period. Hemorrhage remains possible before obliteration, and radiation-related injury is an additional risk. A 101-patient retrospective pediatric cohort reported 64% estimated obliteration at five years and 82% at ten years, with permanent symptomatic radiation changes in 8%. A separate prospective TOBAS SRS registry reported three-year occlusion in 51/79 patients with imaging, or 54% of all 94 analyzed patients.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Radiation-induced obliteration progressively closes nidus vessels, abolishing the shunt over a period of years rather than immediately.

evidence.snippet: The ARUBA trial showed that medical management alone is superior to medical management with interventional therapy for the prevention of death or stroke in patients with unruptured brain arteriovenous malformations followed up for 33 months.
evidence.explanation: The randomised trial's conclusion supporting conservative management for unruptured lesions, with its follow-up duration stated.

evidence.snippet: The primary endpoint had been reached by 11 (10.1%) patients in the medical management group compared with 35 (30.7%) in the interventional therapy group.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the difference in death or symptomatic stroke that led the data and safety monitoring board to halt randomisation.

evidence.snippet: After extended follow-up, ARUBA showed that medical management alone remained superior to interventional therapy for the prevention of death or symptomatic stroke in patients with an unruptured brain arteriovenous malformation.
evidence.explanation: The final follow-up analysis, which supersedes the 2014 interim horizon and shows the effect did not decay with longer observation.

treatments/2.description: Observation with treatment of symptoms and coexisting vascular risk factors is an option for selected unruptured AVMs. In the ARUBA randomized trial, medical management reduced death or any symptomatic stroke compared with the pooled intervention strategy over a mean 50.4 months in the final analysis. This is not a comparison of each procedure individually or evidence about ruptured lesions, and longer-term net benefit remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: medical management with interventional therapy (ie, neurosurgery, embolisation, or stereotactic radiotherapy, alone or in combination)
evidence.explanation: Establishes embolization as one of the three standard interventional modalities, as randomised in ARUBA.

evidence.snippet: Only microsurgical resection was consistently associated with reduced hemorrhage risk in sensitivity analyses.
evidence.explanation: The observational sensitivity finding concerns microsurgical resection and does not establish a hemorrhage-prevention benefit for embolization.

treatments/3.description: Catheter-delivered embolic material can occlude components of the shunt. Embolization may be used before resection or radiosurgery, or with curative intent in selected anatomy. Obliteration and procedural risk require individual assessment; partial angiographic occlusion is not equivalent to demonstrated long-term prevention of hemorrhage.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Embolic occlusion of nidus compartments and feeding arteries removes shunting channels, either as definitive treatment or to reduce flow before resection or radiosurgery.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were controlled with phenytoin extended-release 400 mg daily and phenobarbitol 100 mg daily.
evidence.explanation: Patient 1 baseline care; the source misspells phenobarbital.

evidence.snippet: Seizures reported to occur one to two times per month, refractory to levetiracetam 500 mg two times per day.
evidence.explanation: Persistent seizures despite levetiracetam in one patient; this does not establish comparative efficacy among antiseizure drugs.

treatments/4.description: Treat established seizures according to seizure type, response and tolerability. In the bevacizumab pilot, one participant had controlled seizures with phenytoin plus phenobarbital, while another remained symptomatic on levetiracetam. These observations do not rank the drugs or support universal prophylaxis.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Antiseizure drugs suppress seizures generated by perinidal cortex without treating the arteriovenous shunt.

evidence.snippet: have shown stable disease with little to no progression since beginning treatment, although this follow-up timeframe is truncated and further follow-up is needed.
evidence.explanation: Preprint, three uncontrolled cases; imaging stability cannot establish efficacy or prevention of hemorrhage.

evidence.snippet: Patient 3 had a hemorrhagic stroke, but was still deemed ineligible for surgical or endovascular intervention
evidence.explanation: Hemorrhage during an uncontrolled course is a safety/outcome observation, not evidence of efficacy or proof of drug causation.

evidence.snippet: the size and number of bAVMs were not noticeably changed in trametinib-treated mice based on our MRA imaging
evidence.explanation: Counterevidence to anatomical lesion regression in this mouse experiment; it does not negate the separate hemorrhage-volume benefit.

evidence.snippet: at 8 weeks of treatment, the mice treated with 1 mg/kg of trametinib demonstrated significantly lower hemorrhagic volumes than the vehicle treated mice
evidence.explanation: The positive hemorrhage endpoint is distinct from unchanged lesion size/number; this preclinical benefit does not establish clinical efficacy.

treatments/5.description: Trametinib is being explored for brain AVM but clinical efficacy is unestablished. A 2024 preprint describes three uncontrolled compassionate-use cases with relative imaging stability; one patient had a hemorrhagic stroke during treatment, and lesion genotypes were unknown. A separate male-mouse study found prolonged survival and reduced hemorrhagic burden without significant MRA lesion-number reduction. The planned presurgical trial NCT06098872 was withdrawn with zero enrollment.

treatments/5/targets/0.description: MEK inhibition suppresses downstream ERK activation; clinical benefit for brain AVM remains unestablished.

evidence.snippet: No change in bAVM volume was observed 26 or 52 weeks after bevacizumab treatment.
evidence.explanation: Two-patient pilot did not demonstrate radiographic volume reduction; the null finding is limited by sample size.

evidence.snippet: our study is underpowered to detect the hypothesised change in bAVM volume.
evidence.explanation: Explicit limitation of the clinical pilot.

treatments/6.description: A completed single-arm pilot treated two adults with large unresectable unruptured AVMs. Neither had a measurable reduction in nidus volume at 26 or 52 weeks. No clinically important adverse events were identified in this small sample, which is insufficient to establish safety or hemorrhage prevention. NCT06264531 is evaluating symptomatic benefit. Improvement of post-radiosurgery edema in separate reports must not be equated with efficacy against the untreated nidus.

evidence.snippet: coagulopathies should be reversed, and patients should be treated for fever, hyperglycemia, and intracranial hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Current 2026 StatPearls clinical-management chapter; acute supportive care, not trial evidence for elective AVM intervention.

evidence.snippet: External ventricular drainage may be indicated if there is intraventricular hemorrhage extension and hydrocephalus is present.
evidence.explanation: Specific acute neurosurgical indication, conditional on hemorrhage anatomy.

treatments/7.description: Acute hemorrhage requires cardiorespiratory stabilization, management of intracranial pressure and reversal of coagulopathy when present. Ventricular drainage may be required for intraventricular blood with hydrocephalus; a large hematoma with mass effect may require emergency decompression. Stabilization and hematoma management are distinct from the timing and method of definitive nidus treatment.

evidence.snippet: The incidence of death or symptomatic stroke was lower with medical management alone
evidence.explanation: Final ARUBA randomized comparison at mean 50.4 months.

evidence.snippet: the estimated 5-year hemorrhage-free survival was 96.23% (95% CI, 93.95%-97.65%) for the interventional treatment group and 89.00% (95% CI, 86.37%-91.24%) for the conservative management group
evidence.explanation: Different population, endpoint and nonrandomized design; not a direct refutation of the ARUBA all-stroke result.

open_questions/0.rationale: ARUBA randomized adults and measured death or any symptomatic stroke, including ischemic stroke. MATCH emulated a target trial in an observational registry that included younger patients and measured AVM-related hemorrhage or death; its primary outcome excluded ischemic stroke, radiation injury, seizures and cognitive effects. Longer follow-up alone cannot explain the different estimates, and weighting cannot eliminate unmeasured confounding. MATCH high-grade subgroup estimates were imprecise. Diffuse lesions showed benefit at five years but no significant advantage at ten years, rather than uniform absence of benefit.

evidence.snippet: the size and number of bAVMs were not noticeably changed in trametinib-treated mice based on our MRA imaging
evidence.explanation: Distinguishes bleeding reduction from anatomical regression.

evidence.snippet: Patient 3 had a hemorrhagic stroke, but was still deemed ineligible for surgical or endovascular intervention
evidence.explanation: Preprint uncontrolled human observation; no demonstrated hemorrhage prevention.

evidence.snippet: No change in bAVM volume was observed 26 or 52 weeks after bevacizumab treatment.
evidence.explanation: Small clinical pilot limits a broad assumption that pathway inhibition shrinks established lesions.

open_questions/1.rationale: The evidence is no longer exclusively preventive: established-lesion mouse experiments report reduced bleeding and longer survival without clear loss of the nidus, and a preprint describes three uncontrolled human trametinib cases. One of those patients hemorrhaged during treatment. Conversely, a two-patient bevacizumab trial showed no volume reduction. Genotype, mature vascular architecture, dose, treatment duration, rebound after withdrawal and systemic toxicity remain unresolved. NCT06098872 was withdrawn without enrollment; active studies should not be counted as positive efficacy results.

evidence.snippet: the majority of these genetic association results await replication in independent AVM cohorts.
evidence.explanation: Limitation stated by the 2014 review; candidate associations are not treated as validated clinical predictors.

evidence.snippet: PTPN13 was identified as a possible causative gene for non-syndromic inherited bAVM.
evidence.explanation: Candidate proposed from two related affected individuals; not an established sporadic AVM driver.

open_questions/2.rationale: A natural-history review describes candidate IL6, TNF and APOE associations and notes that most awaited independent replication. These associations concern hemorrhage susceptibility, not proven initiating mutations or clinically validated tests. A small familial report proposing PTPN13 also does not establish an alternative cause for unselected sporadic lesions.

evidence.snippet: Here, we present a BOFS patient carrying a heterozygous inversion with one breakpoint located within a topologically associating domain (TAD) containing enhancers essential for TFAP2A expression in human neural crest cells (hNCCs).
evidence.explanation: Identifies the clinical inversion and the affected TFAP2A regulatory domain. The reported hg19 breakpoints also identify patient Nr1 in POSTRE's Table1_LongRange_SVs.tsv.

steps/1.description: A BOFS-associated heterozygous inversion separates an intact TFAP2A allele from neural crest enhancers within its original topologically associating domain. The experimentally studied allele is POSTRE Table 1 patient Nr1. Its physical alteration is distinct from the resulting loss of enhancer contact and reduced expression.

evidence.snippet: the inversion disconnects one TFAP2A allele from its cognate enhancers
evidence.explanation: Patient-derived neural crest cell experiments establish enhancer disconnection.

evidence.snippet: although the inversion shuffles the TFAP2A hNCC enhancers with novel genes within the same TAD, this does not result in enhancer adoption.
evidence.explanation: Limits the mechanism to enhancer disconnection rather than asserting enhancer adoption by neighboring genes.

steps/2.description: Patient-specific hiPSC-derived human neural crest cells demonstrate disconnection of the rearranged TFAP2A allele from its cognate enhancers. Although the displaced enhancers become colocated with other genes in a rearranged domain, enhancer adoption was not observed in this experimental system.

evidence.snippet: leading to monoallelic and haploinsufficient TFAP2A expression in patient hNCCs.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the allele-specific expression consequence in patient-derived human neural crest cells.

steps/3.description: TFAP2A expression is monoallelic and haploinsufficient in neural crest cells differentiated from the inversion carrier's hiPSCs. This measured decrease concerns gene expression, while the encoded protein sequence remains intact. The demonstrated neural crest effect does not establish whether expression is preserved in every other TFAP2A-expressing lineage; LOE versus mLOE is therefore left unclassified.

evidence.snippet: We show that although individual mutations have different effects on DNA binding, they all demonstrate significantly reduced transcriptional activities.
evidence.explanation: In vitro functional assays show BOFS DNA-binding-domain mutations reduce AP-2 alpha transcriptional activity.

evidence.snippet: all mutant derivatives have an altered nuclear:cytoplasmic distribution compared with the predominantly nuclear localization of wild-type AP-2α and several can exert a dominant-negative activity on the wild-type AP-2α protein
evidence.explanation: Mutant AP-2 alpha mislocalizes and several variants act dominant-negatively, supporting an antimorphic mechanism.

evidence.snippet: the individual TFAP2A BOFS mutations can generate null, hypomorphic or antimorphic alleles
evidence.explanation: BOFS variants span a functional spectrum, helping explain variable expressivity.

steps/4.description: Individual TFAP2A BOFS mutations within the DNA-binding region have different effects on DNA binding but all significantly reduce transcriptional activity. Mutant AP-2 alpha proteins show altered nuclear:cytoplasmic distribution compared with the predominantly nuclear wild-type protein, and several can exert dominant-negative activity on wild-type AP-2 alpha. These differences mean individual variants can generate null, hypomorphic, or antimorphic alleles, contributing to the marked phenotypic variability of BOFS.

evidence.snippet: Four additional BOFS patients were found to have de novo missense mutations in the highly conserved exons 4 and 5 (basic region of the DNA binding domain) of the TFAP2A gene in the candidate deleted region. We conclude BOFS is caused by mutations involving TFAP2A.
evidence.explanation: Original identification of TFAP2A coding mutations and a deletion as the cause of BOFS.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a hotspot region in the highly conserved exons 4 and 5 of TFAP2A that harbors missense mutations in 27/30 (90%) families.
evidence.explanation: Missense variants cluster in the conserved DNA-binding domain in the large majority of BOFS families.

evidence.snippet: The occurrence of CL/P, premature graying, coloboma, heterochromia irides, and ectopic thymus, are evidence for BOFS as a neurocristopathy.
evidence.explanation: The constellation of features supports a neural crest origin (neurocristopathy) for BOFS.

steps/5.description: BOFS is caused by heterozygous pathogenic variants affecting TFAP2A, encoding the transcription factor AP-2 alpha. TFAP2A is expressed in premigratory and migratory neural crest cells and regulates gene expression during embryogenesis of the eye, ear, face, and related structures. Most BOFS families carry missense variants clustered in the highly conserved exons 4 and 5 (basic DNA-binding domain); deletions, nonsense, splice-altering, and regulatory (enhancer-disconnecting) variants also cause BOFS. Functional studies show these mutations reduce transcriptional activity, alter nuclear localization of AP-2 alpha, and can act as null, hypomorphic, or dominant-negative (antimorphic) alleles. The combination of cleft lip/palate, premature graying, coloboma, heterochromia irides, and ectopic thymus is cited as evidence that BOFS is a neurocristopathy.

evidence.snippet: concerted inactivation of Tfap2a and Tfap2b in the murine neural crest, even during the late migratory phase, results in a midfacial cleft and skeletal abnormalities
evidence.explanation: Mouse neural-crest TFAP2 loss recapitulates midfacial clefting, modeling a core BOFS feature.

evidence.snippet: Alx1, Alx3 and Alx4 (ALX) transcript levels are reduced, whereas ChIP-seq analyses suggest TFAP2 family members directly and positively regulate ALX gene expression.
evidence.explanation: Identifies a direct TFAP2 to ALX regulatory axis downstream of TFAP2A in midface development.

steps/6.description: In mouse and zebrafish models, TFAP2 paralogs (Tfap2a and Tfap2b) regulate midfacial development of the cranial neural crest. Concerted inactivation in the neural crest produces a midfacial cleft and skeletal abnormalities, with dysregulation of midface gene regulatory network components. TFAP2 factors directly and positively regulate the ALX transcription factor genes (Alx1, Alx3, Alx4); loss of TFAP2 reduces ALX transcript levels. This provides a developmental mechanism linking TFAP2A dysfunction to the midfacial clefting characteristic of BOFS.

evidence.snippet: Branchiooculofacial syndrome (BOFS) is characterized by branchial (cervical or infra- or supra-auricular) skin defects that range from barely perceptible thin skin or hair patch to erythematous "hemangiomatous" lesions to large weeping erosions
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists branchial skin defects as a defining feature of BOFS.

steps/7.description: Bilateral branchial (cervical or infra-/supra-auricular) skin defects, ranging from thin skin or a hair patch to erythematous "hemangiomatous" lesions or large weeping erosions. A cardinal feature of BOFS.

evidence.snippet: ocular anomalies that can include microphthalmia, anophthalmia, coloboma, cataract, and nasolacrimal duct stenosis/atresia

steps/8.description: Small eye(s), part of the spectrum of ocular anomalies in BOFS that also includes anophthalmia.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists nasolacrimal duct stenosis/atresia among the ocular anomalies of BOFS.

evidence.snippet: Branchio-oculo-facial syndrome (BOFS) is an autosomal-dominant condition characterized by three main features, respectively: branchial defects, ocular anomalies, and craniofacial defects including cleft lip and/or palate (CL/P).
evidence.explanation: Cleft lip and/or palate is a defining craniofacial feature of BOFS.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists hypertelorism/telecanthus among BOFS facial anomalies.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists broad nasal tip among BOFS facial anomalies.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists dolichocephaly among BOFS facial anomalies.

steps/18.description: A long, narrow head shape is part of the characteristic BOFS facial appearance.

steps/19.description: Upper lip pits are among the characteristic facial anomalies of BOFS.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes lower facial weakness/asymmetric crying face in BOFS.

steps/20.description: Lower facial weakness (asymmetric crying face or partial weakness of cranial nerve VII) is described in BOFS.

steps/21.description: Malformed and prominent pinnae are common in BOFS.

evidence.snippet: we present CT scan temporal bone anomalies in the familial cases, related to branchial arch defects, highlighting the importance of radiological investigations for differential diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Documents temporal bone anomalies related to branchial arch defects in TFAP2A-confirmed BOFS.

steps/23.description: CT temporal bone anomalies related to branchial arch defects are reported in BOFS and aid differential diagnosis.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommends monitoring for vesicoureteral reflux, a renal-tract anomaly in BOFS.

steps/24.description: Renal structural anomalies (e.g., agenesis, dysplasia, vesicoureteral reflux) occur in a subset (~35%) of individuals with BOFS.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommends assessing teeth for size, number, and malocclusion in BOFS.

steps/26.description: Dental manifestations (abnormal tooth size, number, and malocclusion) occur in BOFS and are monitored during surveillance.

evidence.snippet: we documented TFAP2A mutations in three (10%) probands in our series without a classic cervical cutaneous defect or ectopic thymus
evidence.explanation: Ectopic thymus is one of the cardinal BOFS features in the diagnostic criteria.

steps/27.description: Ectopic (dermal/cervical) thymic tissue is a characteristic finding in BOFS and is one of the cardinal diagnostic criteria, consistent with a neural crest / pharyngeal arch developmental defect.

evidence.snippet: The occurrence of CL/P, premature graying, coloboma, heterochromia irides, and ectopic thymus, are evidence for BOFS as a neurocristopathy.
evidence.explanation: Premature graying is documented as a recurrent BOFS feature supporting neural crest involvement.

steps/28.description: Premature graying of hair is an ectodermal feature of BOFS, occurring in roughly a third of patients, and contributes to the neurocristopathy classification.

edges/3.description: The inversion physically separates the intact gene from its cognate enhancers.

edges/4.description: Loss of cognate enhancer contact prevents normal expression of the rearranged allele in the assayed neural crest cells.

edges/5.description: Reduced availability of functional AP-2 alpha perturbs the neural crest developmental transcriptional program.

edges/6.description: Disrupted neural crest development is mediated in part by dysregulation of the TFAP2-controlled ALX midface gene regulatory network.

edges/22.description: Reduced and dominant-negative AP-2 alpha transcriptional activity is the molecular basis for impaired cranial neural crest development in BOFS.

evidence.snippet: We detected a 3.2 Mb deletion by 500K SNP microarray in an affected mother and son with BOFS at chromosome 6p24.3.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the TFAP2A locus (6p24.3) and a causative deletion in BOFS.

evidence.snippet: Several of these mutations are recurrent. Mosaicism was detected in one family. To date, genetic heterogeneity has not been observed.
evidence.explanation: Documents recurrent variants, mosaicism, and absence of locus heterogeneity in BOFS.

evidence.snippet: BOFS is caused by mutation of the transcription factor AP2-alpha gene (TFAP2A).
evidence.explanation: Confirms TFAP2A as the causative gene; identifies a novel missense variant in the conserved DNA-binding domain.

evidence.snippet: a novel nonsense mutation c.912C>A, p.(Cys304*) (NM_001042425.2) which in exon 6 of the conserved helix-span-helix domain in TFAP2A results in a premature termination codon. It may trigger nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD).
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates a nonsense/loss-of-function TFAP2A mechanism (NMD) causing BOFS.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in TFAP2A (encoding transcription factor AP-2 alpha; gene OMIM 107580, locus 6p24.3) cause autosomal dominant BOFS. The mutational spectrum includes recurrent missense variants in the conserved DNA-binding domain (exons 4-5), nonsense and splice variants, small indels/frameshifts, whole- or multi-exon deletions (including a 3.2 Mb deletion in the original family), and mosaicism. A de novo inversion can also leave TFAP2A coding sequence intact while disconnecting neural crest enhancers and reducing TFAP2A expression. No genetic heterogeneity has been established.

evidence.snippet: In general, children with BOFS should be managed by a multispecialty team including craniofacial specialists, plastic surgeons, otolaryngologists, and speech-language therapists.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends multidisciplinary craniofacial management for BOFS.

treatments/0.description: Children with BOFS are best managed by a multispecialty team including craniofacial specialists, plastic surgeons, otolaryngologists, and speech-language therapists.

evidence.snippet: It is recommended that cleft lip be repaired by an experienced pediatric plastic surgeon.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommends surgical cleft lip repair in BOFS.

treatments/1.description: Surgical repair of cleft lip by an experienced pediatric plastic surgeon.

evidence.snippet: Nasolacrimal duct stenosis or atresia often requires surgery.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews indicates surgical management of nasolacrimal duct obstruction in BOFS.

treatments/2.description: Nasolacrimal duct stenosis or atresia often requires surgical correction.

evidence.snippet: Congenital conductive hearing impairments are described, including hearing rehabilitation and the results of ear surgery.
evidence.explanation: Documents hearing rehabilitation and ear surgery in TFAP2A-confirmed BOFS patients.

treatments/3.description: Standard treatments for hearing loss, including hearing rehabilitation and ear surgery; bone-anchored hearing aids have been used for conductive loss.

evidence.snippet: Once the TFAP2A pathogenic variant has been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes reproductive genetic counseling options for BOFS families.

treatments/4.description: BOFS is autosomal dominant with a 50% recurrence risk to offspring; de novo variants occur in 50%-60%. Once the familial TFAP2A variant is identified, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing are possible.

evidence.snippet: We used non-parametric linkage analysis and genome sequencing to identify a biallelic intronic AAGGG repeat expansion in the replication factor C subunit 1 (RFC1) gene as the cause of familial CANVAS and a frequent cause of late-onset ataxia, particularly if sensory neuronopathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia coexist.
evidence.explanation: Identifies biallelic intronic RFC1 AAGGG expansion as the cause of CANVAS.

evidence.snippet: a recessively inherited, ancient RE located in intron 2 of RFC1 is the predominant cause of CANVAS
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the intron 2 repeat expansion is the predominant cause.

steps/1.description: The usual genotype contains two expanded nonreference pentanucleotide tracts within RFC1 intron 2, overlapping the poly(A) tail of AluSx3. AAGGG is written on the opposite strand to the RFC1 transcript (CCCTT). Motif, interruptions and length affect interpretation; neither intronic location nor repeat size alone proves regulatory loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Together, the findings suggest that the transcript containing truncating variants in RFC1 undergo nonsense-mediated decay leading to RNA degradation.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblast studies characterize the truncating allele in the compound genotype.

steps/2.description: Rare patients carry a coding nonsense allele in trans with an expanded RFC1 repeat. Two siblings with c.1267C>T (p.Arg423Ter) showed mutant-transcript depletion and reduced full-length protein in fibroblasts. The coding single-nucleotide change and its measured consequences are distinct from the intronic repeat alteration.

evidence.snippet: Together, the findings suggest that the transcript containing truncating variants in RFC1 undergo nonsense-mediated decay leading to RNA degradation.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblast studies characterize the truncating allele in the compound genotype.

steps/3.description: Rare patients carry a coding frameshift deletion in trans with an expanded RFC1 repeat. For c.2876del (p.Pro959GlnfsTer24), cDNA sequencing showed depletion of the deletion-bearing transcript and supported the trans configuration. Other reported deletions include c.1739_1740del and c.2191del; the RNA findings should not be assumed measured for every allele.

evidence.snippet: Together, the findings suggest that the transcript containing truncating variants in RFC1 undergo nonsense-mediated decay leading to RNA degradation.
evidence.explanation: Patient fibroblast studies characterize the truncating allele in the compound genotype.

steps/4.description: Allele-specific RNA sequencing and cDNA analysis showed preferential depletion of transcripts carrying p.Arg423Ter or p.Pro959GlnfsTer24, supporting nonsense-mediated decay. This result applies to the coding truncating allele, not directly to the expanded-repeat allele.

evidence.snippet: immunoblotting showed a concordant reduction of the 140 KD full-length RFC1 protein in fibroblasts from affected individuals
evidence.explanation: Protein reduction accompanies allele-specific RNA decay.

evidence.snippet: parents of the affected patients in this study, carrying a truncating variant in RFC1 but no AAGGG expansion on the second allele, did not show a phenotype despite their old age
evidence.explanation: Limits a simple dominant haploinsufficiency interpretation.

steps/5.description: Fibroblasts from two related expansion/p.Arg423Ter patients had approximately 50% lower full-length RFC1 protein. Truncated isoforms were not detected. Repeat-only fibroblasts did not show the same reduction. Unaffected relatives with a single truncating allele indicate that isolated haploinsufficiency is insufficient to explain CANVAS.

evidence.snippet: expression could only be detected when comparing CANVAS lines with their isogenic corrected counterpart, but not when comparing CANVAS lines with non-isogenic controls
evidence.explanation: Unreviewed November 2025 preprint (Currò et al.; DOI:10.1101/2025.11.18.688292). Motor-neuron qPCR showed about 23% lower expression versus isogenic controls; sensory-neuron reduction was about 15%.

evidence.snippet: we were unable to demonstrate a significant effect of the repeat expansion on RFC1 protein.
evidence.explanation: Unreviewed November 2025 preprint (Currò et al.; DOI:10.1101/2025.11.18.688292). The preprint does not establish reduced protein abundance.

evidence.snippet: does not affect RFC1 expression in patient peripheral and brain tissue, suggesting no overt loss of function
evidence.explanation: Original bulk-tissue results argue against a universal expression-loss model.

evidence.snippet: we observed no changes in RFC1 mRNA or RFC1 protein levels between 6-week-old control (n = 3) and CANVAS (n = 3) patient iPSC–derived neurons
evidence.explanation: Published patient-cell observations differ from the later preprint.

steps/6.description: An unreviewed November 2025 preprint reported modest RFC1 mRNA reduction in patient-derived sensory and motor neurons versus isogenic biallelic Alu-repeat deletions, and in targeted analysis of postmortem cerebellum. Protein reduction was not demonstrated. Earlier studies found preserved expression in peripheral cells, limited brain samples and mainly cortical-like neurons. Cell identity, genetic background, RNA quality and assay context may explain discrepancies. Repeat deletion removes more than an expression defect and does not identify the mediator of rescue.

evidence.snippet: we report that the pathogenic RFC1 AAGGG repeats form DNA and RNA parallel G-quadruplex (G4) structures that play a role in impairing biological processes
evidence.explanation: Biophysical assays establish folding capacity of short repeats.

evidence.snippet: The observed DNA polymerase stalling at the center of the (A2G3)10 strand strongly implicates H-r DNA triplex formation
evidence.explanation: A competing structural explanation is supported under other assay conditions.

steps/7.description: Short synthetic AAGGG DNA repeats adopt G-quadruplex or H-r triplex structures under different ionic and temperature conditions. Triplex-sensitive probing and cellular replication assays argue against assigning all stalling to G-quadruplexes. These structures have not been shown to mediate degeneration at the endogenous expanded locus in vulnerable human neurons.

evidence.snippet: Finally, the pathogenic, but not the nonpathogenic, repeat stalls replication fork progression in yeast and human cells.
evidence.explanation: Measures replication impediments in model systems.

steps/8.description: Pathogenic-repeat templates inhibit polymerase progression in vitro. AAGGG tracts also stall replication in yeast plasmids and SV40-origin episomes in human cells, with orientation dependence. Lack of enhancement after PIF1 deletion favors a triplex contribution in yeast. These assays use short repeats or non-native replication systems; they do not establish replication-fork injury in postmitotic CANVAS neurons.

evidence.snippet: we report that the pathogenic RFC1 AAGGG repeats form DNA and RNA parallel G-quadruplex (G4) structures that play a role in impairing biological processes
evidence.explanation: Biophysical assays establish folding capacity of short repeats.

steps/9.description: Synthetic AAGGG RNA forms parallel G-quadruplexes. The RFC1 sense transcript carries the complementary CCCTT sequence; strand and transcript context must be specified before extrapolating AAGGG reporter results to endogenous RFC1 RNA.

evidence.snippet: reduce gene expression via impairing the translation process in a repeat-length-dependent manner
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays support a translation effect in their specific construct context.

steps/10.description: HEK293T reporters containing short upstream AAGGG repeats showed reduced EGFP protein with unchanged reporter mRNA. Stabilizing G-quadruplexes worsened this reporter effect. This measures translation of a construct, not reduced transcription of endogenous RFC1, and is not evidence for a therapeutic effect of G-quadruplex stabilizers.

evidence.snippet: we detected a consistent increase across different tissues of the retention of intron 2 in RFC1 pre-mRNA
evidence.explanation: Original observation in limited tissue samples.

evidence.snippet: no back-spliced reads were identified to map to RFC1 intron 2 or across the RFC1 transcript
evidence.explanation: No detectable circular intronic RNA was found in this study.

evidence.snippet: There were no differences between cases and controls in terms of intron retention or aberrant intron 2 splicing of RFC1 in patient fibroblasts, iPSC-derived neurons, or cortical and cerebellar regions of postmortem brain
evidence.explanation: Direct negative RNA-processing result.

steps/11.description: The 2019 study found increased intron 2 retention in pre-mRNA in small lymphoblast, muscle and brain samples, without aberrantly spliced mature transcripts. The 2024 patient-cell study did not reproduce increased retention or circular RFC1 RNA; the 2025 preprint also found similar transcript processing. A uniform intron-retention mechanism is therefore unproven.

evidence.snippet: RNA fluorescence in situ hybridization of the 2 patients revealed CCTGT- and CCCTT-containing RNA foci, respectively, in neuronal nuclei of tissues with neuronal loss.
evidence.explanation: Autopsy findings support foci formation in two cases; toxicity remains unproven.

evidence.snippet: We did not observe in patient brains the presence of RNA foci of either the sense or antisense repeated unit.
evidence.explanation: Preserves the earlier negative finding.

evidence.snippet: the overall abundance of foci was low, and the specificity was imperfect, with 8.94% of control neurons and 11.3% of CANVAS neurons showing antisense CCCTT RNA foci
evidence.explanation: Patient-neuron signal was small and incompletely specific.

steps/12.description: Repeat RNA foci were reported in two 2024 autopsies with ACAGG or AAGGG configurations. Earlier brain analysis was negative. Reporter foci are readily generated, but 2024 patient neurons showed only a small antisense signal difference with imperfect specificity (11.3% versus 8.94%) and no sense-repeat enrichment. Foci presence does not establish RNA-mediated toxicity.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest that pentapeptide KGREG repeat proteins may be produced from AAGGG repeats in patients with CANVAS in a cell type–specific manner.
evidence.explanation: Postmortem immunoreactivity is suggestive but not perfectly genotype-specific.

evidence.snippet: AAGGG repeats are translated into pentapeptide repeat proteins
evidence.explanation: Reporter assays demonstrate translation.

steps/13.description: AAGGG reporter constructs produce poly-KGREG in HEK cells. Cerebellar granule-layer immunostaining was strong in three of four CANVAS brains, weak in one, and also present in one nonexpanded control; remaining Purkinje neurons lacked staining. Peptide production was not detected in eight-week patient neurons. Short-repeat expression did not reduce rat cortical-neuron survival over ten days, leaving length-, cell- and context-specific toxicity unresolved.

evidence.snippet: repair in CANVAS LCLs was significantly slower, reaching levels comparable to control cells only after 72 h
evidence.explanation: Unreviewed November 2025 preprint (Currò et al.; DOI:10.1101/2025.11.18.688292). Measures delayed repair after a cisplatin pulse.

evidence.snippet: First-derivative analysis of normalized γ-H2AX indicated no differences in the rate of γ-H2AX recovery after UV induction between CANVAS and control neurons
evidence.explanation: The published UV assay limits generalization across forms of DNA damage.

steps/14.description: The unreviewed 2025 preprint found slower removal of platinum-DNA adducts in patient lymphoblastoid cells and greater cisplatin-induced apoptosis in sensory and motor neurons, improved by isogenic repeat-region deletion. Earlier cortical-like neurons had normal UV-induced DNA-damage recovery. The studies test different insults and cell types; neither universal repair failure nor RFC1 mRNA reduction as the causal mediator is established.

evidence.snippet: Gene Ontology (GO) analysis indicated a significant overrepresentation of neuronal signaling processes including synaptic signaling and processes that regulate synaptic signaling
evidence.explanation: Transcriptomic changes converge on neuronal signaling.

evidence.snippet: CANVAS patient iPSC–derived neurons remained devoid of detectable synchronous firing even between 7 and 11 weeks after differentiation
evidence.explanation: Patient neurons had impaired network synchrony.

steps/15.description: Patient-derived predominantly glutamatergic forebrain neurons showed reduced synaptic transcripts and proteins and poorly synchronized network firing. Monoallelic deletion of the Alu-repeat region partially restored these readouts. RFC1 knockdown did not reproduce most abnormalities, and re-expression did not broadly rescue them, although some firing measures changed. These immature cortical-like cultures do not reproduce the selectively vulnerable sensory ganglion and Purkinje populations.

evidence.snippet: Spinal cord pathology demonstrated a marked dorsal root ganglionopathy with secondary tract degeneration.
evidence.explanation: Direct neuropathology in clinically defined CANVAS predating molecular diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: Altered sensation in all limbs in either a length-dependent (distal extremities worse) or non-length-dependent pattern.
evidence.explanation: Clinical distribution does not by itself determine the site of the primary lesion.

steps/16.description: Loss of dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons produces peripheral sensory deafferentation and secondary posterior-column degeneration. Historical autopsies predated RFC1 genotyping, while later genetically confirmed cases show concordant sensory and posterior-column pathology. The primary ganglion lesion does not require a uniformly non-length-dependent clinical distribution.

evidence.snippet: In CANVAS there is a severe cranial sensory ganglionopathy neuronopathy (ganglionopathy) involving the vestibular, facial, and trigeminal ganglia but sparing the auditory ganglia.
evidence.explanation: Historical pathology localizes vestibular failure primarily to ganglion neurons; these donors were not RFC1-genotyped.

steps/17.description: Five temporal bones from four clinically defined, ungenotyped CANVAS patients showed severe vestibular ganglion neuronal loss, with relative preservation of spiral ganglia, sensory hair cells and vestibular nuclei. Trigeminal and geniculate ganglia were also affected. Ganglionic Nageotte nodules reflect glial replacement of lost neurons; they are not psammoma bodies. Relative auditory sparing does not exclude coincident presbycusis or another cause of hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Cerebellar pathology showed loss of Purkinje cells, predominantly in the vermis.
evidence.explanation: Documents selective cerebellar pathology in historical clinical CANVAS.

evidence.snippet: The patient with CANVAS showed severe, widespread depletion of Purkinje cells with associated prominent Bergmann gliosis, while cell density in the granule cell layer was well preserved.
evidence.explanation: The 2019 study documents this pathology in a genetically confirmed CANVAS case.

steps/18.description: Purkinje-cell depletion, often greatest in the vermis, and Bergmann gliosis are documented in clinical CANVAS autopsies and a genetically confirmed 2019 case. This lesion contributes to cerebellar gait, limb, speech and oculomotor dysfunction. Molecular intermediates connecting the repeat genotype to selective adult Purkinje degeneration remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: We observed marked astrocytic gliosis and axonal swelling of the synapse between first and second motor neurons in the anterior horn at the lumbar level.
evidence.explanation: The pathology supports circuit-level abnormality in one patient.

evidence.snippet: Although the second motor neurons in the anterior and lateral horns were preserved
evidence.explanation: Preserved neuronal somata are part of the reported histological finding, not evidence against the described axonal and glial changes.

evidence.snippet: Brisk reflexes, particularly in the upper limbs and at the knees, are commonly observed. Other signs of upper and lower motor neuron involvement, including spasticity and/or Babinski sign, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and weakness, are uncommon.
evidence.explanation: Current synthesis explicitly includes these features.

steps/19.description: Upper and lower motor signs suggest dysfunction of descending motor control and motor-unit circuits in a subset of RFC1 cases. Their lesion-level basis remains uncertain. One genetically confirmed autopsy showed anterior-horn astrocytic gliosis and axonal swelling around motor-neuron somata, with preserved anterior-horn neurons and corticospinal tracts. This supports a possible synaptic component but does not establish generalized motor-neuron death or identify the lesion responsible for upper motor signs.

evidence.snippet: Autonomic testing confirms the presence of a sympathetic and/or parasympathetic dysfunction in half of individuals undergoing specific investigations.
evidence.explanation: Physiological dysfunction is established without assigning a specific ganglionic lesion.

steps/20.description: Sympathetic and parasympathetic dysfunction can affect blood pressure, bowel, bladder, sexual function and sweating. Severity is usually mild but can be substantial. A primary autonomic ganglion lesion has not been established across RFC1 disease; central and peripheral contributions remain possible.

evidence.snippet: cough reflex sensitivity was heightened compared to historical healthy controls
evidence.explanation: Four biallelic participants underwent cough-reflex testing; this is not a contemporaneous controlled comparison.

steps/21.description: Biallelic RFC1 carriers with refractory cough show heightened capsaicin sensitivity relative to historical healthy controls, broadly comparable to other refractory-cough cohorts. edges/3.description: The AAGGG sequence forms noncanonical DNA structures in short-repeat biophysical assays; structure at the endogenous expanded locus has not been demonstrated.

edges/4.description: AAGGG RNA forms G-quadruplexes in defined short-repeat assays; their formation in vulnerable patient neurons is unresolved.

edges/5.description: The founding study detected increased intronic RNA, but later cell assays did not consistently reproduce retention.

edges/6.description: In the unreviewed 2025 preprint, isogenic deletion of the repeat-containing region increased transcript abundance in sensory and motor neurons; preserved-expression studies limit generalization.

edges/7.description: Two genetically confirmed autopsies contained repeat RNA foci, whereas earlier patient brains and later cell assays were negative.

edges/8.description: Short-repeat reporter constructs can produce poly-KGREG; this does not establish toxic peptide accumulation from the endogenous expanded alleles.

edges/9.description: Monoallelic deletion of the Alu-repeat region partially rescued synaptic readouts in one patient-derived neuronal line; the intervening molecular mechanism remains unresolved.

edges/10.description: Sensory neuronopathy is a defining manifestation of genetically confirmed RFC1 disease; the repeat-dependent route to ganglion injury remains unknown.

edges/11.description: Vestibular failure in genetically confirmed disease is consistent with cranial ganglion pathology in historical clinical CANVAS, although those temporal-bone cases were not genotyped.

edges/12.description: A genetically confirmed CANVAS autopsy showed Purkinje depletion and Bergmann gliosis; the repeat-to-cell-death intermediates remain unresolved.

edges/13.description: Autonomic testing documents sympathetic and parasympathetic dysfunction in RFC1 disease; the route from the repeat genotype to autonomic injury and its anatomical site remain unresolved.

edges/14.description: Heightened capsaicin sensitivity is documented in a small group of biallelic carriers with refractory cough; the repeat-dependent process causing reflex sensitization has not been demonstrated.

edges/15.description: Upper and lower motor signs in genetically confirmed cases suggest additional motor-circuit involvement, with axonal and glial abnormalities documented in one autopsy; the repeat-dependent mechanism remains unknown.

edges/16.description: Genetically confirmed CANVAS cohorts show cognitive deficits; the route from the repeat genotype to cerebellar or extra-cerebellar cognitive-network dysfunction remains unresolved.

edges/17.description: Tested premature-termination alleles show preferential mutant-transcript depletion.

edges/18.description: Tested premature-termination alleles show preferential mutant-transcript depletion.

edges/20.description: Reduced expression and altered platinum response co-occur in the preprint, but expression-specific rescue was not performed.

edges/22.description: Repeat folding is implicated in the reporter translation phenotype; relevance to endogenous RFC1 requires testing.

edges/41.description: Cerebellar dysfunction impairs smooth tracking and increases corrective saccades.

edges/44.description: Impaired autonomic cardiovascular control can reduce the blood-pressure response to standing.

edges/54.description: Motor-unit dysfunction can produce fasciculations; the limited pathology permits a synaptic or axonal mechanism without requiring loss of motor-neuron somata.

edges/55.description: Impaired motor-unit innervation can contribute to muscle wasting; this is a provisional explanation rather than evidence of generalized motor-neuron degeneration.

edges/56.description: Motor-circuit or motor-unit dysfunction can reduce force generation; sensory impairment and disuse may also contribute in individual patients.

edges/57.description: The observed impairment of attention, working memory and executive performance is the clinical expression of the proposed cognitive-network dysfunction.

edges/58.description: Executive deficits are a specifically measured component of the cognitive phenotype; their cerebellar and extra-cerebellar substrates remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: We used non-parametric linkage analysis and genome sequencing to identify a biallelic intronic AAGGG repeat expansion in the replication factor C subunit 1 (RFC1) gene as the cause of familial CANVAS and a frequent cause of late-onset ataxia, particularly if sensory neuronopathy and bilateral vestibular areflexia coexist.
evidence.explanation: Identifies biallelic intronic RFC1 AAGGG expansion as the cause of CANVAS.

evidence.snippet: a recessively inherited, ancient RE located in intron 2 of RFC1 is the predominant cause of CANVAS
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the intron 2 repeat expansion is the predominant cause.

evidence.snippet: We show a novel, possibly population-specific CANVAS configuration (AAAGG)10-25(AAGGG)exp, which was the cause of CANVAS in all patients.
evidence.explanation: Documents a population-specific founder repeat configuration.

evidence.snippet: We screened an Asian-Pacific cohort for CANVAS and identified a novel RFC1 repeat expansion motif, (ACAGG)exp, in three affected individuals.
evidence.explanation: Documents the ACAGG pathogenic motif in Asia-Pacific families.

evidence.snippet: the finding of truncating variants associated with CANVAS indicate that full RFC1 sequencing is recommended in cases affected by typical CANVAS and carrying monoallelic (AAGGG)n expansions.
evidence.explanation: Defines the rare second-allele diagnostic route.

evidence.snippet: We identified three novel repeat motifs, AGGGC (n = 6 from five families), AAGGC (n = 2 from one family) and AGAGG (n = 1), associated with CANVAS in the homozygous or compound heterozygous state with the common pathogenic AAGGG expansion.
evidence.explanation: Reports alternative motifs; association in a few families does not settle pathogenicity for every configuration.

evidence.snippet: Unknown significance, reported as part of complex repeats
evidence.explanation: The September 2026 GeneReviews variant table classifies AAGGC as uncertain; its adjacent AGAGG row is also of unknown significance. These interpretations qualify the small 2023 association series.

evidence.snippet: after controlling for potentially confounding covariates such as diabetes and B12 deficiency, this difference no longer reached statistical significance.

genes/0.notes: RFC1 encodes the large subunit of the canonical replication factor C complex that loads PCNA during DNA replication and repair. The usual disease allele is a nonreference intronic short tandem repeat expansion overlapping the AluSx3 poly(A) tail. AAGGG predominates; ACAGG, AGGGC and the Māori AAAGG-flanked AAGGG configuration also occur. Very large AAAGG alleles can be pathogenic, with uncertain penetrance; motif and size must be interpreted together. The September 2026 GeneReviews update still classifies AAGGC and AGAGG configurations as uncertain, despite the pathogenic interpretation proposed in a 2023 series. Rare expansion/truncating, splice or deletion genotypes broaden the allelic spectrum. Reduced expression is directly established for tested truncating alleles; the functional consequence of repeat-only genotypes is context-dependent and unresolved. Monoallelic enrichment in the 2026 neuropathy cohort was nonsignificant after adjustment; that study does not establish dominant RFC1 neuropathy.

evidence.snippet: The goals of treatment are to maximize function and reduce complications.
evidence.explanation: Expert management synthesis; not a CANVAS-specific treatment trial.

treatments/0.description: Coordinate neurology, rehabilitation, ENT, respiratory, speech and swallowing care, with annual neurological and mobility review and more frequent assessment when symptoms change. Current care maximizes function and manages complications; no disease-modifying benefit has been established.

treatments/1.description: Individualized balance, gait and strengthening work, occupational therapy, home adaptations and mobility aids address falls and daily function. Consider vestibular rehabilitation; these recommendations are largely extrapolated from rehabilitation practice.

treatments/2.description: Use speech-language therapy and communication aids as needed. Assess aspiration and nutrition; adjust food consistency for dysphagia based on swallowing assessment.
