evidence.snippet: some hereditary forms of prion disease cannot be rationalized using the concept of mutation-induced thermodynamic destabilization of the cellular prion protein
evidence.explanation: The paper set out to test this exact hypothesis for the FFI (M129/D178N), GSS (P102L) and familial CJD (E200K) variants and concluded against it. D178N could not even be assayed because it aggregated; P102L was indistinguishable from wild-type and E200K only very slightly destabilized.

evidence.snippet: These data suggest that destabilization of PrPC is neither a general mechanism underlying the formation of PrPSc nor the basis of disease phenotypes in inherited human TSEs.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication across all eight disease-associated substitutions in the structured C-terminal domain: five destabilize it and three do not, and the stabilities do not track disease phenotype.

evidence.snippet: propagation of the abnormal, oligomeric prion protein PrP(Sc), which is supposed to be the causative agent of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies, is unlikely to follow a mechanism where kinetic folding intermediates of PrP(C) are a source of PrP(Sc) subunits
evidence.explanation: Refutes the kinetic half of the hypothesis specifically. Stopped-flow folding of the structured domain has a half-life of about 170 microseconds with no detectable intermediates, so a populated folding intermediate is not available as the PrP-Sc precursor. Species/construct caveat: measured on murine mPrP(121-231) carrying an engineered F175W fluorescence reporter - not human PrP and not the D178N-129M haplotype - so the argument is a cross-species extrapolation resting on the conservation of the C-terminal globular fold between mouse and human PrP. The authors show the reporter variant has "the same overall structure and stability as wild-type mPrP(121-231)", which addresses the construct but not the species step.

hypotheses/0.description: The historical model that familial PRNP substitutions cause disease by lowering the thermodynamic (and kinetic) stability of the folded C-terminal domain of PrP-C, so that the native alpha-helical fold more readily slips into a beta-sheet-rich, conversion-competent conformer. It is intuitive and still widely repeated, but it was tested directly and does not hold: measured stabilities of the familial-mutant proteins do not correlate with disease phenotype, and PrP-C folding is too fast and too cooperative to expose a folding-intermediate route to PrP-Sc. Recorded here as a DEPRECATED hypothesis rather than silently deleted, because an earlier revision of this entry asserted it as the mechanism of the "Acquisition of a Conversion-Prone PrP-C State" node, and the intuition is likely to be reintroduced by a future curator unless the refuting evidence stays attached to the claim it refutes.

open_questions/0.rationale: Regional PrPres quantification shows accumulation is broader than the lesions, and that the mediodorsal nucleus is damaged at PrPres levels that leave other regions intact. Neither the 19 kDa strain conformation nor codon-129 phase explains why this particular nucleus is the primary target, so the cell-intrinsic determinant of thalamic vulnerability is unknown.

open_questions/1.rationale: Serial FDG-PET places the start of measurable thalamic neurodegeneration 13-21 months before onset, implying that intervention must be pre-symptomatic. But the preventive doxycycline study had to compare against a historical dataset precisely because no validated surrogate endpoint exists, and that gap now blocks efficient trials of the mechanistically stronger PrP-lowering agents.

open_questions/2.rationale: Sporadic fatal insomnia patients are codon-129 methionine homozygotes without D178N, yet reproduce the FFI phenotype - implying the 19 kDa conformer, not the mutation, specifies the disease. The reproducible absence of unglycosylated-isoform underrepresentation is an unexplained molecular discrepancy that bears directly on whether glycosylation pattern is part of strain identity or a consequence of the mutant substrate.

steps/1.description: Post-zygotic activating GNAS variants cause constitutive Gs-alpha/cAMP signaling in a mosaic population of skeletal progenitors. Mosaicism is essential to viability and determines whether disease is monostotic, polyostotic, or syndromic with extraskeletal manifestations.

steps/2.description: GNAS-activated osteogenic progenitors fail to mature normally. Normal marrow and trabecular bone are replaced by fibro-osseous tissue containing fibrous stroma and immature woven bone, weakening the affected skeleton.

steps/3.description: Active dysplastic osteogenic cells can overproduce FGF23. FGF23 decreases renal phosphate reabsorption and active vitamin D, causing hypophosphatemia with rickets or osteomalacia in patients with high disease burden.

evidence.snippet: The resulting skeleton is weakened and prone to fractures and deformity, resulting in pain and functional impairment.
evidence.explanation: The review links fibro-osseous lesions to the major skeletal complications.

steps/4.description: FD lesions weaken affected bone and produce pain, deformity, fractures, cortical thinning, bowing, coxa vara, gait disturbance, and axial or craniofacial skeletal morbidity according to lesion location.

steps/5.description: When post-zygotic activating GNAS variants involve extraskeletal tissues, constitutive Gs-alpha/cAMP signaling produces the McCune-Albright spectrum of hyperpigmented skin lesions, hyperfunctioning endocrinopathies, and a small increased risk of neoplasia in affected tissues.

evidence.snippet: Common factors known to trigger episodes include fever, fasting, decreased oral intake, vomiting, infections, and ingestion of large amounts of fructose.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the catabolic triggers. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

evidence.snippet: For most patients, first metabolic decompensation occurred before two years of age with a similar sequence: the triggering factors were fever, fasting, or decrease of food intake.
evidence.explanation: Independently confirms the trigger profile in the French cohort.

evidence.snippet: Although small amounts of fructose (≤2 g/kg/day) are generally well tolerated, single ingestion of a high dose of fructose (>1g/kg) is harmful, especially in younger children.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the fructose exposure threshold that triggers harm. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

evidence.snippet: Disease is mainly revealed by hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, both symptoms being characteristic for an enzymatic block in the last steps of the gluconeogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the proximal lesion as an enzymatic block in the terminal steps of gluconeogenesis, the trigger node of this pathograph.

evidence.snippet: Enzyme activity in leukocytes was dramatically decreased (<10%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the residual enzyme activity in the French diagnostic cohort, supporting the DECREASED modifier on fructose 1,6-bisphosphate 1-phosphatase activity.

steps/3.description: Biallelic loss-of-function FBP1 variants deplete cytosolic fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase activity in the liver. The enzyme hydrolyzes fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to fructose-6-phosphate, the irreversible step that commits carbon to glucose synthesis rather than back to glycolysis, so its loss is an enzymatic block in the last steps of gluconeogenesis. Residual activity in patient leukocytes is typically under 10% of normal.

evidence.snippet: Acute crises are most common in early childhood; nearly half of affected children have hypoglycemia in the neonatal period (especially the first four days) resulting from deficient glycogen stores.
evidence.explanation: Attributes neonatal hypoglycemia specifically to exhaustion of glycogen stores in the setting of a gluconeogenic block, supporting the glycogen-dependent buffering described in this node. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

steps/4.description: With the fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase step blocked, the hepatocyte cannot convert lactate, glycerol, and gluconeogenic amino acids into glucose. Glycogenolysis still works, so glucose homeostasis is maintained in the fed and early-fasted state; the defect becomes clinically apparent only once glycogen stores run down and the liver must switch to de novo glucose production. Neonates are especially vulnerable because glycogen stores are small.

evidence.snippet: In four patients, genetic study was prompted by detection of glycerol or glycerol-3-phosphate in urine organic acids analysis. One patient also had pseudo-hypertriglyceridemia.
evidence.explanation: Documents accumulation of gluconeogenic substrates proximal to the block, including the glycerol-driven pseudo-hypertriglyceridemia artifact.

evidence.snippet: Common factors known to trigger episodes include fever, fasting, decreased oral intake, vomiting, infections, and ingestion of large amounts of fructose.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the catabolic and fructose-load stressors that amplify the block into an acute crisis. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

steps/5.description: Substrates that would normally be consumed by gluconeogenesis build up behind the block. Lactate accumulates and drives a high-anion-gap lactic acidosis; glycerol and glycerol-3-phosphate spill into urine (and can produce spurious pseudo-hypertriglyceridemia on glycerol-blanked triglyceride assays); urate rises. A catabolic stress — fever, fasting, reduced intake, vomiting, infection, or a large fructose load — sharply increases demand for hepatic glucose output and converts the compensated state into a crisis.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, all 18 patients had liver abnormalities either during follow-up
evidence.explanation: Establishes that liver abnormalities were universal in the 18-patient multicenter series and occurred on routine follow-up, not only during crises. The per-finding counts quoted in the node description come from the bracketed figures in the same sentence.

steps/6.description: Liver involvement is near-universal and is not confined to crises. In a French series every one of 18 patients had liver abnormalities — hepatomegaly (8/18), transaminase elevation (6/15), or a bright (steatotic) liver on ultrasound (7/11) — during routine follow-up as well as during acute episodes (hepatomegaly 10/17, transaminase elevation 13/16, bright liver 4/14), and acute liver failure occurred in 6/14 during crises. This reframes FBP1 deficiency as a chronic hepatic disorder warranting long-term liver surveillance, not only an episodic hypoglycemic one.

evidence.snippet: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) deficiency is characterized by episodic acute crises of lactic acidosis and ketotic hypoglycemia, manifesting as respiratory distress or hyperventilation, apneic spells, seizures, and/or lethargy/coma.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ketotic hypoglycemia as the defining episodic metabolic abnormality. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

evidence.snippet: In between acute episodes, children are asymptomatic.
evidence.explanation: Supports the episodic rather than continuous character of the hypoglycemia. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

steps/7.description: Blood glucose falls when fasting outlasts hepatic glycogen. Because lipolysis and ketogenesis remain intact, the hypoglycemia is ketotic — a key discriminator from fatty-acid oxidation defects, which give hypoketotic hypoglycemia. Between episodes children are asymptomatic and normoglycemic.

evidence.snippet: All the patients presented with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia, metabolic acidosis, hyperlactacidemia and hepatomegaly.
evidence.explanation: Defines the composite decompensation phenotype in a molecularly confirmed patient series.

evidence.snippet: All of them had the first metabolic decompensation prior to 2 years old. The common triggering factors were vomiting and infection.
evidence.explanation: Supports the early-childhood timing and the catabolic triggers of the decompensated state.

steps/8.description: The central effector is a stereotyped crisis of ketotic hypoglycemia plus high-anion-gap lactic acidosis, usually with hepatomegaly and transaminase elevation. Unlike the urea-cycle and organic-acidemia conformers of this module, hyperammonemia is not a feature; the acid load is lactate and ketoacid. First decompensation is almost always before two years of age.

evidence.snippet: In untreated individuals, clinical manifestations worsen progressively as continued catabolism leads to multiorgan failure (especially liver, brain, and later heart).
evidence.explanation: Supports progression from decompensation to multiorgan crisis when untreated. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

evidence.snippet: One patient had short stature and another had neurological deficit following status epilepticus due to profound hypoglycemia.
evidence.explanation: Documents permanent neurological injury attributable to profound hypoglycemia in a molecularly confirmed patient.

steps/9.description: Neuroglycopenia combined with lactic acidosis produces hyperventilation, apneic spells, seizures, and lethargy or coma. Most treated children have normal growth and psychomotor development, but profound or prolonged hypoglycemia can leave permanent neurological deficit, and untreated continued catabolism progresses to multiorgan failure involving liver, brain, and later heart, with high mortality.

evidence.snippet: Disease is mainly revealed by hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis, both symptoms being characteristic for an enzymatic block in the last steps of the gluconeogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the enzymatic block to failure of gluconeogenesis.

edges/1.description: Loss of the fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase step directly interrupts flux through hepatic gluconeogenesis.

evidence.snippet: In four patients, genetic study was prompted by detection of glycerol or glycerol-3-phosphate in urine organic acids analysis.
evidence.explanation: Detection of urinary glycerol and glycerol-3-phosphate is direct human evidence that gluconeogenic substrates accumulate behind the block.

edges/2.description: Carbon entering gluconeogenesis stalls proximal to the block, so lactate, glycerol, and glycerol-3-phosphate accumulate while glucose output falls.

evidence.snippet: Acute crises are most common in early childhood; nearly half of affected children have hypoglycemia in the neonatal period (especially the first four days) resulting from deficient glycogen stores.
evidence.explanation: Names glycogen-store depletion as the intermediate that converts the gluconeogenic block into hypoglycemia. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

edges/3.description: Once hepatic glycogen is exhausted, the blocked gluconeogenic pathway cannot sustain blood glucose.

evidence.snippet: For most patients, first metabolic decompensation occurred before two years of age with a similar sequence: the triggering factors were fever, fasting, or decrease of food intake.
evidence.explanation: Links catabolic triggers acting on the metabolic block to the onset of decompensation.

edges/4.description: Accumulating lactate plus failure of glucose output produces the acute decompensated state.

evidence.snippet: There is no clear pathophysiological basis for this fatty liver disease but we postulate that endoplasmic reticulum stress and de novo lipogenesis activation could be key factors, as observed in FBP1 knockout mice.
evidence.explanation: The authors state explicitly that no clear pathophysiological basis is known and offer a mouse-derived postulate, so the intermediate steps of this edge are unknown. Graded INDIRECT because the quote reaches this edge only through an extrapolation from Fbp1 knockout mice, which is also why the edge is typed as having unknown intermediates.

edges/5.description: Chronic carbon accumulation behind the block is associated with fatty liver, but the connecting steps are not established. Endoplasmic reticulum stress and de novo lipogenesis activation have been postulated on the basis of Fbp1 knockout mice; this edge is deliberately typed as having unknown intermediates.

evidence.snippet: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) deficiency is characterized by episodic acute crises of lactic acidosis and ketotic hypoglycemia, manifesting as respiratory distress or hyperventilation, apneic spells, seizures, and/or lethargy/coma.
evidence.explanation: Pairs ketotic hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis as the crisis phenotype. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

edges/6.description: Hypoglycemia is one of the two defining biochemical components of the decompensated crisis.

evidence.snippet: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase 1 (FBP1) deficiency is characterized by episodic acute crises of lactic acidosis and ketotic hypoglycemia, manifesting as respiratory distress or hyperventilation, apneic spells, seizures, and/or lethargy/coma.
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the neurologic and respiratory manifestations that the decompensated state produces. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

edges/7.description: Neuroglycopenia and acidosis produce the neurologic and systemic manifestations of the crisis.

evidence.snippet: Common factors known to trigger episodes include fever, fasting, decreased oral intake, vomiting, infections, and ingestion of large amounts of fructose.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the link from fasting and catabolic stress to acute metabolic decompensation. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

edges/8.description: Fasting, fever, reduced intake, vomiting, and infection directly precipitate acute metabolic decompensation when glycogen is exhausted and gluconeogenic demand rises.

evidence.snippet: Although small amounts of fructose (≤2 g/kg/day) are generally well tolerated, single ingestion of a high dose of fructose (>1g/kg) is harmful, especially in younger children.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the link from a large fructose load to acute metabolic decompensation. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

edges/9.description: A large fructose load directly precipitates acute metabolic decompensation in FBPase deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Biallelic mutations in FBP1 gene (MIM*611570) were identified in all seven patients confirming the diagnosis of FBPase deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports FBP1 as the causal gene with biallelic inheritance in a molecularly confirmed series.

evidence.snippet: We described the first intragenic deletion in FBP1 (g.97,364,754_97,382,011del) in homozygous state.
evidence.explanation: Supports copy-number variation as part of the FBP1 mutational spectrum, which matters because exon-level deletions are missed by sequencing alone.

evidence.snippet: In the Chinese population, c.490G>A and c.355G>A had significantly higher AFs than in the non-Finland European population
evidence.explanation: Supports population-specific FBP1 variant hotspots.

genes/0.notes: Fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency is caused by biallelic pathogenic variants in FBP1. The reported spectrum includes missense, frameshift, splice-site, and copy-number variants, including whole-exon and intragenic deletions; population-specific hotspots exist (c.490G>A and c.355G>A are enriched in Chinese individuals).

evidence.snippet: Acute inpatient treatment includes intravenous glucose with transition to feeds as tolerated; sodium bicarbonate may be required for treatment of acidemia.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the acute inpatient regimen. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/0.description: Acute crises are treated with intravenous glucose, transitioning to feeds as tolerated, with sodium bicarbonate added if acidemia requires correction.

evidence.snippet: Acute inpatient treatment includes intravenous glucose with transition to feeds as tolerated; sodium bicarbonate may be required for treatment of acidemia.
evidence.explanation: Specifies intravenous glucose as the acute treatment that substitutes for absent endogenous glucose production. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Exogenous glucose supplies the glucose that the blocked gluconeogenic pathway cannot produce.

evidence.snippet: Long-term management includes prevention of hypoglycemia with avoidance of fasting, frequent meals, (including use of uncooked cornstarch overnight), and restriction of foods or medicines that contain fructose, sucrose, glycerol, and/or sorbitol
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the long-term dietary management plan. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/1.description: Long-term prevention of hypoglycemia rests on avoiding fasting, frequent meals, and uncooked cornstarch overnight to provide slow-release glucose across the overnight fast.

evidence.snippet: Long-term management includes prevention of hypoglycemia with avoidance of fasting, frequent meals, (including use of uncooked cornstarch overnight), and restriction of foods or medicines that contain fructose, sucrose, glycerol, and/or sorbitol
evidence.explanation: Directly supports fasting avoidance and cornstarch as the preventive strategy against hypoglycemia. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Continuous exogenous carbohydrate supply keeps the fast from ever outlasting glycogen stores, so the gluconeogenic block is never unmasked.

evidence.snippet: Management of acute crisis includes increasing frequency of carbohydrate feedings; intake of glucose polymers; restriction of fructose, sucrose, glycerol, and sorbitol
evidence.explanation: Directly supports substrate restriction as a core management measure. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/2.description: Foods and medicines containing fructose, sucrose, glycerol, or sorbitol are restricted because each feeds carbon into the pathway proximal to the enzymatic block. Antipyretics must be checked for these excipients.

evidence.snippet: treatment with antipyretics for fever that do not contain fructose, sucrose, glycerol, and/or sorbitol
evidence.explanation: Shows the restriction extends to medication excipients, supporting substrate restriction as the mechanism-targeted intervention. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Limiting intake of substrates that must traverse the blocked step reduces further accumulation behind it.

evidence.snippet: Offer molecular genetic testing for the familial FBP1 pathogenic variants to apparently asymptomatic older and younger at-risk sibs of an affected individual in order to identify as early as possible those who would benefit from prompt initiation of measures to prevent acute crises and prompt treatment of infections/febrile illnesses.
evidence.explanation: Supports cascade testing of at-risk relatives as an actionable preventive measure. Evidence source is OTHER because GeneReviews is a synthesizing review.

treatments/3.description: Autosomal recessive recurrence counseling, carrier testing for at-risk relatives, and prenatal or preimplantation testing once the familial variants are known. Presymptomatic molecular testing of at-risk sibs allows preventive measures before a first crisis.

evidence.snippet: There is no clear pathophysiological basis for this fatty liver disease but we postulate that endoplasmic reticulum stress and de novo lipogenesis activation could be key factors, as observed in FBP1 knockout mice.
evidence.explanation: States both the absence of an established mechanism and the specific mouse-derived hypothesis. Graded INDIRECT because the mechanism is offered as a postulate extrapolated from Fbp1 knockout mice and has not been demonstrated in human liver tissue.

hypotheses/0.description: The steatosis of FBP1 deficiency has no established pathophysiological explanation. The leading proposal, extrapolated from Fbp1 knockout mice, is that the gluconeogenic block drives endoplasmic reticulum stress and activation of de novo lipogenesis in hepatocytes. This has not been demonstrated in human liver tissue.

open_questions/0.rationale: Human evidence establishes that steatosis is present and clinically important (all 18 patients in the French series had liver abnormalities), but the proposed mechanism rests entirely on an Fbp1 knockout mouse and is stated by the authors as a postulate. Mice tolerate the gluconeogenic block differently from humans and the human hepatic lipid phenotype has not been mechanistically characterized, so the translational validity of the ER-stress/DNL chain is the open question rather than the existence of the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: The gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor β3 gene (GABRB3) encodes the β3-subunit of the gamma-aminobutyric acid type A (GABAA ) receptor, which mediates inhibitory signalling within the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the gene product and its role as a subunit of the receptor mediating inhibitory signalling, the molecular starting point of this disease chain.

evidence.snippet: GABRB3 is highly expressed early in the developing brain, and its encoded β3 subunit is critical for GABAA receptor assembly and trafficking as well as stem cell differentiation in embryonic brain.
evidence.explanation: Supports the developmental expression and assembly/trafficking role of the beta-3 subunit that makes a heterozygous variant consequential. Evidence source is OTHER because this sentence is background framing citing prior work rather than a result of this study's own experiments.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous, usually de novo, GABRB3 variant (predominantly missense, less often nonsense or truncating) alters the beta-3 subunit of the GABA-A receptor. The beta-3 subunit is highly expressed in the developing brain and is a component of the principal native synaptic (alpha1-beta3-gamma2) and extrasynaptic (alpha5-beta3-gamma2) receptor assemblies, so a single heterozygous variant perturbs a large fraction of brain GABA-A receptors.

evidence.snippet: The gain-of-function cohort (n = 27 patients) presented with a younger age of seizure onset, higher risk of severe intellectual disability, focal seizures at onset, hypotonia, and lower likelihood of seizure freedom in response to treatment.
evidence.explanation: Defines the gain-of-function class and its distinct, more severe clinical profile in a 74-patient cohort.

evidence.snippet: Results showed an atypical gain-of-function molecular phenotype in the GABRB3 p.Glu77Lys and p.Thr287Ile variants characterized by increased potency of γ-aminobutyric acid A without change to the estimated maximum open channel probability, deactivation kinetics or absolute currents.
evidence.explanation: Provides the electrophysiological definition of the gain-of-function phenotype as increased GABA potency rather than increased maximal current.

steps/2.description: Gain-of-function variants raise the potency of GABA at the receptor (a leftward shift in the GABA concentration-response relationship) without necessarily changing maximal open probability or absolute current. Because tonic, extrasynaptic inhibition is driven by low ambient GABA concentrations, a potency increase disproportionately amplifies tonic chloride flux. Counterintuitively for a receptor whose job is inhibition, this class carries the more severe clinical phenotype: younger seizure onset, higher risk of severe intellectual disability, focal seizures at onset, hypotonia, and lower likelihood of seizure freedom.

evidence.snippet: Of the 20 gain-of-function variants assessed, 13 were found to alter receptor desensitization properties. Seven variants reduced desensitization at equilibrium, which acts to worsen gain-of-function traits. Six variants accelerated current decay kinetics, which limits gain-of-function traits.
evidence.explanation: Establishes desensitization as a distinct modifier of the gain-of-function molecular phenotype, in two opposite directions.

evidence.snippet: This included younger age of first seizure onset (median 0.5 months), movement disorders (dystonia and dyskinesia), epilepsy of infancy with migrating focal seizures (EIMFS) and risk of early mortality.
evidence.explanation: Links reduced desensitization at equilibrium to the most severe clinical subgroup, including movement disorder and early-mortality risk.

steps/3.description: Desensitization — the decline of current during sustained agonist exposure — is a second, independent axis of gain-of-function severity. Variants that reduce desensitization at equilibrium sustain the excess conductance and worsen gain-of-function traits; these cluster in the pore-forming transmembrane region and are associated with the most severe outcomes (median first-seizure onset 0.5 months, movement disorder, migrating focal seizures, and risk of early mortality). Variants that instead accelerate current decay limit the gain-of-function effect, cluster in the activation coupling loops, and are associated with later onset and milder phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Febrile seizures at onset are exclusive to the loss-of-function cohort (n = 47 patients).
evidence.explanation: Defines the loss-of-function class as a separable cohort with its own clinical onset signature.

evidence.snippet: These variants are presumed to cause loss-of-function receptors leading to reduced neuronal GABAergic activity.
evidence.explanation: States the prior assumption that GABA-A receptor epilepsy variants act by loss of function — the framing this entry's two-class model revises. Evidence source is OTHER because this sentence states the field's background assumption rather than reporting the study's own data.

steps/4.description: The other functional class reduces GABA-A receptor function, the mechanism originally presumed to account for all GABA-A receptor epilepsies. These patients have a distinct clinical signature: febrile seizures at onset occur exclusively in this group, and treatment response is comparatively better.

evidence.snippet: Interestingly, both mutant β3 subunits impaired postsynaptic clustering of wild-type GABAA receptor γ2 subunits and prevented γ2 subunits from incorporating into GABAA receptors at synapses, although by different cellular mechanisms.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the trans-acting clustering defect by which mutant beta-3 subunits deplete synaptic receptors beyond simple haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that impaired receptor localization to synapses is a common pathophysiological mechanism for GABRB3 mutations, although the extent of impairment may be different among mutant subunits.
evidence.explanation: Generalizes impaired synaptic localization as a shared cellular mechanism across GABRB3 variants, with variant-dependent severity.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, wild-type γ2 subunits were reduced and less clustered at inhibitory synapses in Gabrb3+/- knockout mice.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the synaptic clustering deficit in vivo in a heterozygous Gabrb3 mouse, showing it is not an artifact of heterologous expression.

steps/5.description: Mutant beta-3 subunits reduce surface and synaptic receptor levels and, more strikingly, act in trans on the wild-type receptor pool: they impair postsynaptic clustering of wild-type gamma-2 subunits and prevent gamma-2 from being incorporated into synaptic GABA-A receptors. Because gamma-2 is what anchors GABA-A receptors at the synapse, this converts a heterozygous subunit defect into a broader loss of synaptic inhibitory receptors. The same reduction in synaptic gamma-2 clustering is seen in Gabrb3 heterozygous knockout mice.

evidence.snippet: However, cortical neurons in thalamocortical slices from knock-in mice had reduced miniature inhibitory post-synaptic current amplitude and prolonged spontaneous thalamocortical oscillations.
evidence.explanation: Provides direct circuit-level evidence that a disease-causing GABRB3 variant shifts inhibitory synaptic drive and prolongs thalamocortical oscillations.

evidence.snippet: Thus, the Gabrb3+/D120N knock-in mouse recapitulated human Lennox-Gastaut syndrome seizure types and behavioural abnormalities and was caused by impaired inhibitory GABAergic signalling in the thalamocortical loop.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the modelled human seizure phenotype specifically to impaired inhibitory GABAergic signalling in the thalamocortical loop.

evidence.snippet: GABA(A)-R density is approximately halved in brain of beta3-deficient mice, and GABA(A)-R function is severely impaired.
evidence.explanation: Shows that removing the beta-3 subunit halves brain GABA-A receptor density and severely impairs receptor function, the loss-of-function extreme of this node.

steps/6.description: Both functional classes converge here. GABA-A receptor signalling in developing cortical, hippocampal, and thalamocortical circuits is displaced from its normal set point — reduced in loss-of-function variants, excessive and mistimed (particularly in the tonic, extrasynaptic compartment) in gain-of-function variants. Either displacement destabilizes the balance between excitation and inhibition. In the Gabrb3 D120N knock-in mouse this manifests as reduced miniature inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitude in cortical neurons and prolonged spontaneous thalamocortical oscillations.

evidence.snippet: Electroencephalography demonstrated ictal generalized and interictal multifocal epileptiform abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Documents the hypersynchronous discharges in a molecularly confirmed GABRB3 patient.

evidence.snippet: Disrupting the gabrb3 gene in mice produces electroencephalographic abnormalities, seizures, and behavior that parallel those seen in AS.
evidence.explanation: Shows that beta-3 subunit disruption alone is sufficient to produce electroencephalographic abnormality and seizures in vivo.

steps/7.description: The destabilized network fires excessively and synchronously. In patients this is visible as ictal generalized and interictal multifocal epileptiform abnormalities on EEG; in the D120N knock-in mouse it appears as prolonged spontaneous thalamocortical oscillations underlying atypical absence seizures.

evidence.snippet: The seizure onset age ranged from 1 to 21 months (median age 3.75 months).
evidence.explanation: Establishes infantile seizure onset as the clinical expression of this node.

evidence.snippet: Our patient presented with neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties, then developed pharmacoresistant epileptic encephalopathy, characterized by multiple seizure types from 3 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates the transition from an early non-seizure presentation to pharmacoresistant encephalopathy with multiple seizure types.

steps/8.description: Hypersynchronous discharges become clinical seizures, typically starting in the first year of life and typically of several types in the same child. Because the same receptor defect that generates seizures also disturbs GABAergic signalling during a period when it is shaping circuit development, the developmental impairment is not simply a consequence of seizure burden — which is what the "developmental and epileptic encephalopathy" designation is intended to capture.

evidence.snippet: Clinical features included cluster seizures (80.8%), fever sensitivity (53.8%), and developmental delay (96.2%).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the near-universal developmental delay accompanying the epilepsy.

evidence.snippet: Yet, patients with GABAA receptor variants have diverse clinical phenotypes and many are refractory to treatment despite the availability of drugs that enhance GABAergic activity.
evidence.explanation: Supports treatment refractoriness as a defining feature of the clinical endpoint, despite GABA-enhancing drugs being available.

steps/9.description: The clinical endpoint is chronic epilepsy that frequently resists antiseizure medication, together with global developmental delay and intellectual disability that ranges from mild to profound. Seizure control is achievable in a substantial minority — 57.7% in one cohort — and severity tracks with the variant's functional class and structural location rather than being uniform across the disease.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that 44 pathogenic GABRB3 missense variants segregate into gain-of-function and loss-of-function groups and respective patients display distinct clinical phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that a GABRB3 variant partitions into one of two functional outcomes, of which gain of function is this branch.

edges/1.description: One class of missense variants increases the potency of GABA at the mutant receptor.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that 44 pathogenic GABRB3 missense variants segregate into gain-of-function and loss-of-function groups and respective patients display distinct clinical phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the second of the two functional outcomes a GABRB3 variant can produce.

edges/2.description: The other class reduces receptor function, by lowering GABA-evoked current or by impairing subunit assembly and delivery.

evidence.snippet: Of the 20 gain-of-function variants assessed, 13 were found to alter receptor desensitization properties.
evidence.explanation: Shows that most gain-of-function variants additionally alter desensitization, supporting this edge from the gain-of-function node to the desensitization modifier.

edges/3.description: Within the gain-of-function class, desensitization kinetics further tune how much excess chloride flux persists at equilibrium.

evidence.snippet: Modelling of the activation properties of the receptors indicated that either variant caused increased chloride flux in response to low concentrations of γ-aminobutyric acid that mediate tonic currents.
evidence.explanation: Provides the mechanistic step from increased GABA potency to excess tonic chloride flux, the change that displaces network excitation-inhibition balance. The link is marked INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES because the measurement is of receptor-level flux, not of network balance itself.

edges/4.description: Excess tonic GABAergic conductance in immature cortical and thalamocortical circuits disturbs, rather than restores, network balance.

evidence.snippet: Variants that reduced the desensitization at equilibrium were clustered in the transmembrane regions that constitute the channel pore and correlated with greater disease severity, while variants that accelerated current decay were clustered in the coupling loops responsible for receptor activation and correlated with lesser severity.
evidence.explanation: Ties the direction of the desensitization change to the magnitude of downstream disease severity, supporting desensitization as a modifier of the network-level consequence.

evidence.snippet: This suggests that impaired receptor localization to synapses is a common pathophysiological mechanism for GABRB3 mutations, although the extent of impairment may be different among mutant subunits.
evidence.explanation: Identifies impaired synaptic receptor localization as the common cellular route by which GABRB3 variants lose function.

edges/6.description: A recurrent cellular route to loss of function is failure to deliver and retain receptors at inhibitory synapses.

evidence.snippet: Hyperactivity, lack of coordination, and seizures are consistent with reduced presynaptic inhibition in spinal cord and impaired inhibition in higher cortical centers and/or pleiotropic developmental defects.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the in vivo consequences of beta-3 subunit loss to impaired inhibition in cortical centres, the network-balance node.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, wild-type γ2 subunits were reduced and less clustered at inhibitory synapses in Gabrb3+/- knockout mice.
evidence.explanation: Shows in vivo that the clustering defect depletes receptors at inhibitory synapses, which is what reduces inhibitory drive at the network node.

evidence.snippet: However, cortical neurons in thalamocortical slices from knock-in mice had reduced miniature inhibitory post-synaptic current amplitude and prolonged spontaneous thalamocortical oscillations.
evidence.explanation: Couples the reduction in inhibitory synaptic drive directly to prolonged hypersynchronous thalamocortical oscillations in the same preparation.

evidence.snippet: Electroencephalography demonstrated ictal generalized and interictal multifocal epileptiform abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Links the hypersynchronous discharges recorded on EEG to the clinical ictal events they accompany in a molecularly confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: Our patient presented with neonatal hypotonia and feeding difficulties, then developed pharmacoresistant epileptic encephalopathy, characterized by multiple seizure types from 3 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Documents progression from seizure onset to established pharmacoresistant encephalopathy, the transition this edge represents.

evidence.snippet: Using a SureSelectXT custom multiple gene panel covering 48 early infantile epileptic encephalopathy/developmental delay genes, a novel de novo GABRB3 heterozygous missense mutation, c.860C>T (p.Thr287Ile), was identified and confirmed on Sanger sequencing.
evidence.explanation: Documents a de novo heterozygous GABRB3 missense variant causing early infantile epileptic encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that 44 pathogenic GABRB3 missense variants segregate into gain-of-function and loss-of-function groups and respective patients display distinct clinical phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two-class functional architecture of the GABRB3 variant landscape across 74 patients.

evidence.snippet: Pathogenic variants in GABRB3 have been associated with a spectrum of phenotypes from severe developmental disorders and epileptic encephalopathies to milder epilepsy syndromes and mild intellectual disability (ID).
evidence.explanation: Summarizes the allelic spectrum of GABRB3, of which this entry curates the encephalopathic end.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were controlled in 57.7% of patients by valproate, levetiracetam, or perampanel in the majority.
evidence.explanation: Directly reports the agents most often associated with seizure control and the proportion of patients controlled.

evidence.snippet: Valproate, levetiracetam and perampanel seem to have positive effects on seizure control for patients with GABRB3 variants.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own summary of which agents appear effective in GABRB3-related epilepsy.

treatments/0.description: Conventional antiseizure medications remain the mainstay, usually as polytherapy. In a 26-patient cohort, seizures were controlled in 57.7% of patients, most often with valproate, levetiracetam, or perampanel, so drug-resistance is common but far from universal.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were controlled in 57.7% of patients by valproate, levetiracetam, or perampanel in the majority.
evidence.explanation: Shows these agents suppress the seizure output of the hyperexcitable network in a majority of the patients who achieved control, without addressing the receptor lesion itself.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: These agents act downstream of the receptor lesion, suppressing network hyperexcitability rather than correcting the GABA-A receptor defect.

evidence.snippet: However, vigabatrin, a drug that inhibits γ-aminobutyric acid transaminase to increase tonic γ-aminobutyric acid currents, has mixed success in treating seizures in patients with GABRB3 variants: some patients experience seizure cessation, but there is hypersensitivity in some patients associated with hypotonia, sedation and respiratory suppression.
evidence.explanation: Documents both the benefit and the specific adverse reaction — hypotonia, sedation, respiratory suppression — that make vigabatrin variant-class dependent.

evidence.snippet: We therefore propose that the hypersensitivity reaction to vigabatrin is a result of GABRB3 variants that exacerbate GABAergic tonic currents and caution is required when prescribing vigabatrin.
evidence.explanation: Gives the mechanistic reason for the contraindication in gain-of-function variants and the explicit prescribing caution.

treatments/1.description: Vigabatrin inhibits GABA transaminase and thereby raises tonic GABAergic current. Its effect in GABRB3-related DEE depends on which functional class the variant belongs to, and getting this wrong is harmful rather than merely ineffective. In loss-of-function variants it is expected to be safe and effective and a truncating-variant patient responded well. In gain-of-function variants it produces a hypersensitivity reaction with hypotonia, sedation, and respiratory suppression, because it further exaggerates an already excessive tonic current. Functional or structural classification of the variant should therefore precede a vigabatrin trial.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, drug strategies increasing tonic currents in loss-of-function variants are likely to be a safe and effective therapy.
evidence.explanation: States that raising tonic current is the appropriate corrective strategy specifically for loss-of-function variants. Evidence source is OTHER because this is the authors' therapeutic recommendation inferred from their electrophysiology, not a measured clinical or in vitro result.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: By raising ambient GABA, vigabatrin compensates for reduced GABA-gated current in loss-of-function variants. The same action is the reason it is hazardous in gain-of-function variants.

evidence.snippet: Benzodiazepines, including nitrazepam, are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors that predominately affect phasic currents, usually through prolonging inhibitory postsynaptic currents
evidence.explanation: Gives the pharmacological basis for why benzodiazepines behave differently from vigabatrin in gain-of-function patients.

evidence.snippet: She was subsequently stabilized and spasms ceased on a combination of nitrazepam and the ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Documents clinical stabilization on nitrazepam plus ketogenic diet in a vigabatrin-hypersensitive gain-of-function patient.

evidence.snippet: Our finding suggested that clonazepam might be a choice for patient with GABRB3-related EOEE.
evidence.explanation: Single-case evidence that clonazepam can control seizures in GABRB3-related early-onset epileptic encephalopathy.

treatments/2.description: Benzodiazepines are also GABA-potentiating, but they act predominantly on phasic synaptic currents rather than the tonic extrasynaptic currents that vigabatrin raises — which is the mechanistic reason they were tolerated by a gain-of-function patient who could not tolerate vigabatrin. A patient with the gain-of-function p.Glu77Lys variant stabilized on nitrazepam plus the ketogenic diet, and a separate case report describes complete seizure cessation on clonazepam.

evidence.snippet: Benzodiazepines, including nitrazepam, are positive allosteric modulators of GABAA receptors that predominately affect phasic currents, usually through prolonging inhibitory postsynaptic currents
evidence.explanation: Specifies the compartment (phasic, not tonic) in which benzodiazepines modulate inhibitory signalling, which is why they act on this node without the vigabatrin hazard.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Positive allosteric modulation of synaptic GABA-A receptors prolongs inhibitory postsynaptic currents, acting on the phasic rather than the tonic compartment.

evidence.snippet: She was subsequently stabilized and spasms ceased on a combination of nitrazepam and the ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Supports adjunctive use of the ketogenic diet. Marked PARTIAL because the diet was given with nitrazepam in a single patient, so its independent contribution cannot be separated.

treatments/3.description: The ketogenic diet is used as an adjunct in refractory GABRB3-related epilepsy; it contributed to seizure cessation in combination with nitrazepam in a vigabatrin-hypersensitive gain-of-function patient.

evidence.snippet: CBD and vigabatrin significantly reduced spasm frequency compared to the vehicle.
evidence.explanation: Reports cannabidiol efficacy against epileptic spasms in the Gabrb3 D120N knock-in mouse. Evidence source is MODEL_ORGANISM; this has not been shown in patients.

evidence.snippet: In addition, treatment with antiepileptic drugs and cannabinoids ameliorated atypical absence seizures in knock-in mice.
evidence.explanation: Independent mouse-model evidence that cannabinoids reduce atypical absence seizures in the same knock-in line.

treatments/4.description: Cannabidiol reduced both atypical absence seizures and epileptic spasms in the Gabrb3 D120N knock-in mouse, which models a human Lennox-Gastaut-phenotype GABRB3 variant. This is a mouse-model result in a single modelled variant and has not been tested clinically in GABRB3-related DEE, so it is recorded as a preclinical rationale rather than as an established therapy.

evidence.snippet: We therefore propose that the hypersensitivity reaction to vigabatrin is a result of GABRB3 variants that exacerbate GABAergic tonic currents and caution is required when prescribing vigabatrin.
evidence.explanation: States the tonic-current-excess model directly, as the proposed explanation for the gain-of-function vigabatrin hypersensitivity.

hypotheses/0.description: Under this model, the reason gain-of-function GABRB3 variants cause the more severe encephalopathy is that increased GABA potency preferentially amplifies tonic currents carried by extrasynaptic receptors responding to low ambient GABA. Excess tonic inhibition during the period when GABAergic signalling patterns developing circuits is proposed to be as damaging as too little. The strongest support is pharmacological and indirect: vigabatrin, which raises tonic GABA current, produces hypotonia, sedation, and respiratory suppression specifically in gain-of-function patients, whereas benzodiazepines, which act mainly on phasic synaptic currents, do not. It is recorded as EMERGING rather than canonical because no study has yet measured the proposed tonic-current excess in patient neurons or shown that normalizing it reverses the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Overall, patients with GABRB3 variants that increase GABAergic activity have more severe developmental and epileptic encephalopathies. This paradoxical finding challenges our current understanding of the GABAergic system in epilepsy and how patients should be treated.
evidence.explanation: States the paradox and its unresolved status in the authors' own words.

open_questions/0.rationale: The excitation-inhibition framework predicts that reduced GABAergic inhibition causes seizures, and GABA-A receptor epilepsy variants were presumed to act that way. GABRB3 breaks the prediction: the class of variants that increases GABAergic activity has the worse outcome. Candidate explanations include preferential amplification of tonic extrasynaptic current, depolarizing GABA responses in immature neurons with high intracellular chloride, and disruption of the developmental patterning role of GABAergic signalling — but these have not been discriminated experimentally, and the answer determines whether GABA-enhancing drugs help or harm a given patient.

evidence.snippet: The loss of the single gene, gabrb3, in these mice is sufficient to cause phenotypic traits that have marked similarities to the clinical features of AS, indicating that impaired expression of the GABRB3 gene in humans probably contributes to the overall phenotype of Angelman syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Shows the knockout is framed and validated as an Angelman syndrome model, not as a model of the human GABRB3 DEE gain-of-function spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Gabrb3+/D120N mice display robust atypical absence seizures and neonatal spasms that respond to antiseizure agents, supporting the predictive validity of this model as a preclinical platform for LGS drug discovery.
evidence.explanation: States the predictive-validity claim that this mismatch discussion asks to be tested across functional classes rather than assumed.

open_questions/1.rationale: Every in vivo Gabrb3 model in current use sits on one side of the human disease. The constitutive knockout removes the subunit entirely, which is a loss-of-function extreme and additionally produces an Angelman-like phenotype rather than DEE43. The two knock-in lines (D120N, N328D) each model a single Lennox-Gastaut-associated human variant. No published model reproduces the reduced-desensitization gain-of-function subgroup that carries the earliest onset, movement disorder, and early-mortality risk in patients. This matters concretely: cannabidiol efficacy has been shown in the D120N line and is being read as a rationale for human use, but the functional class of D120N cannot be assumed to represent the gain-of-function patients in whom GABA-directed drugs behave oppositely.

evidence.snippet: The 6-Minute Walk Test captured gait disturbances and triggered paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia.
evidence.explanation: A standardised exertion protocol provokes the episodes.

evidence.snippet: The factors that frequently aggravated these events were hunger, exercise, fever, and fatigue, in that order.
evidence.explanation: Exercise ranked second among aggravating factors in the nationwide cohort.

evidence.snippet: The factors that frequently aggravated these events were hunger, exercise, fever, and fatigue, in that order.
evidence.explanation: Hunger was the leading aggravating factor.

evidence.snippet: Sensitivity to fasting or exertion in combination with those 3 main symptoms were the main differences between mutated and negative patients (p < 0.001).
evidence.explanation: Fasting sensitivity is a discriminating clinical feature of SLC2A1-positive patients.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of Glut1DS is established in a proband with suggestive clinical findings, hypoglycorrhachia documented by lumbar puncture, and a (usually) heterozygous pathogenic variant in SLC2A1 identified by molecular genetic testing.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews establishes heterozygous SLC2A1 pathogenic variants as the molecular cause of Glut1DS.

evidence.snippet: Several heterozygous mutations resulting in GLUT1 haploinsufficiency have been identified.
evidence.explanation: Review paper documents the haploinsufficiency mechanism underlying heterozygous SLC2A1 mutations.

evidence.snippet: We now report two distinct classes of mutations as the molecular basis for the functional defect of glucose transport: hemizygosity of GLUT1 and nonsense mutations resulting in truncation of the GLUT-1 protein.
evidence.explanation: The founding molecular study identifies whole-gene hemizygosity and truncating nonsense alleles as the first two classes of causal SLC2A1 lesion.

evidence.snippet: GLUT1 immunoreactivity was normal, but 3-O-methyl-D-glucose uptake into erythrocytes was significantly reduced, suggesting a quantitatively normal, but functionally impaired, GLUT1 protein at the cell membrane.
evidence.explanation: A missense allele (Gly91Asp) shows that loss of transport function, not only loss of protein, produces the haploinsufficient state.

evidence.snippet: Functional studies in Xenopus oocytes and human erythrocytes revealed that this mutation decreased glucose transport and caused a cation leak that alters intracellular concentrations of sodium, potassium, and calcium.
evidence.explanation: Heterologous expression confirms that PED-associated SLC2A1 alleles are loss-of-function for glucose transport, with an additional cation-leak gain in the pore-region deletion.

evidence.snippet: Red blood cell glucose uptake residual activity, a surrogate of haploinsufficiency, correlated with the clinical severity.
evidence.explanation: The degree of residual transporter activity, rather than the variant class, scales the clinical phenotype.

steps/3.description: Heterozygous (rarely biallelic) pathogenic variants in SLC2A1 reduce the amount or function of the GLUT1 facilitative glucose transporter protein, typically through haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Glucose, the essential metabolic fuel for the brain, is transported into the brain exclusively by the protein glucose transporter type 1 (Glut1) across the endothelial cells forming the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Glut1DS results from the inability of Glut1 to transfer sufficient glucose across the BBB to meet the glucose demands of the brain.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews defines the core defect as insufficient GLUT1-mediated glucose transfer across the blood-brain barrier.

evidence.snippet: Glut1 deficiency syndrome (Glut1DS) is a brain energy failure syndrome caused by impaired glucose transport across brain tissue barriers.
evidence.explanation: International consensus statement (expert consensus, hence OTHER) restates the barrier-transport lesion as the disease-defining step.

steps/4.description: GLUT1 is the transporter responsible for facilitated glucose diffusion across the endothelial cells that form the blood-brain barrier, as well as glucose uptake into erythrocytes. Reduced GLUT1 activity impairs the rate at which glucose can be delivered from blood to brain, independent of blood glucose concentration.

evidence.snippet: The mean V(max) for the 3-O-methyl-D-glucose uptake into erythrocytes was 996 fmol/10(6) red blood cells per second, significantly less (54 +/- 11%; t test, p < 0.05) than the mean control value of 1,847. The mean Km value for the patient group (1.4 +/- 0.5mM) was similar to the control group (1.7 +/- 0.5mM; t test, p > 0.05).
evidence.explanation: Kinetic assay in 16 patients shows roughly half-normal transport capacity with unchanged affinity, the erythrocyte signature of haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: We also noted a significant correlation between the mean erythrocyte 3-OMG uptake and clinical severity (R(2) = 0.94).
evidence.explanation: In 109 suspected cases, residual erythrocyte uptake correlates tightly with clinical severity.

evidence.snippet: the hemolysis with echinocytosis may result from alterations in intracellular electrolytes caused by a cation leak through mutant GLUT1.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the cation-leak branch by which a pore-region GLUT1 allele damages the erythrocyte itself.

steps/5.description: Erythrocytes express the same GLUT1 transporter as the brain endothelium, so the haploinsufficient state is measurable outside the brain as reduced 3-O-methyl-D-glucose uptake (typically about half of control Vmax with an unchanged Km) and, with flow cytometry, as reduced surface GLUT1. Residual uptake tracks clinical severity. Certain pore-region alleles additionally render the mutant transporter leaky to cations, disturbing red-cell sodium, potassium and calcium and producing echinocytosis and hemolysis. This node is chiefly a diagnostic surrogate of the primary lesion; only the cation leak branch is itself pathogenic.

evidence.snippet: The needs of the brain for glucose increase rapidly after birth, peaking in early childhood, remaining high until about age 10 years, then gradually decreasing throughout adolescence and plateauing in early adulthood.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews explains why the cerebral energy deficit is most severe in infancy/early childhood when brain glucose demand peaks, framing the developmental basis of the classic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, brain energy metabolism normalised with triheptanoin, that is, increased Pi/PCr ratio during brain activation compared to the recovery phase (p = 0.021), and deteriorated when triheptanoin was withdrawn.
evidence.explanation: 31P-NMR spectroscopy in patients shows an abnormal activation-dependent brain energy profile that normalises with substrate supplementation, a direct in vivo measure of the cerebral energy deficit.

evidence.snippet: glucose transportation was reduced, whereas hexokinase activity and glucose metabolism were enhanced
evidence.explanation: FDG-PET kinetics in a missense mouse model separate the transport-limited supply step from a compensatory rise in downstream hexokinase flux.

evidence.snippet: Research reaches beyond the concept of brain energy depletion by impaired GLUT1-mediated glucose transfer across the blood-brain barrier. Novel concepts investigate alternative substrates, transport mechanisms, and metabolic interactions of different brain cell types.
evidence.explanation: Recent review frames energy depletion as the canonical model while flagging that astrocyte-neuron metabolic interactions are an active refinement of it.

steps/6.description: Chronic under-supply of glucose to neurons and glia produces a state of cerebral energy insufficiency during the period of childhood brain development when glucose demand is highest, driving neuronal hyperexcitability, impaired neurodevelopment, and deceleration of brain (and hence head) growth.

evidence.snippet: the predominant clinical findings of Glut1DS are paroxysmal eye-head movements, pharmacoresistant seizures of varying types, deceleration of head growth, and developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents pharmacoresistant seizures as the predominant early clinical finding reflecting cortical hyperexcitability.

evidence.snippet: During 24-h EEGs, background activity showed generalized 2.5- to 4-Hz spike-wave discharges (41%), generalized slowing or attenuation (34%), no abnormalities (34%), focal epileptiform discharges (13%), or focal slowing or attenuation (9%).
evidence.explanation: 24-hour EEG in 20 children quantifies the hypersynchronous generalized spike-wave and focal epileptiform signatures of the network state.

evidence.snippet: Electroencephalography (EEG) may show 2.5-4Hz spike-waves improving on food intake.
evidence.explanation: The food-responsive EEG ties the hypersynchronous discharge directly to the fuel state of the cortex.

evidence.snippet: GLUT-1+/- mice have epileptiform discharges on electroencephalography (EEG), impaired motor activity, incoordination, hypoglycorrhachia, microencephaly, decreased brain glucose uptake as measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scan and decreased brain Glut-1 expression by western blot (66%).
evidence.explanation: Haploinsufficient mice reproduce epileptiform discharges, showing that a 34% loss of brain GLUT1 is sufficient for network hyperexcitability.

steps/7.description: Cortical and subcortical neuronal networks deprived of adequate glucose fuel become hyperexcitable, producing hypersynchronous discharges that manifest as pharmacoresistant seizures of varying semiology. This node conforms to the shared epilepsy excitation-inhibition-imbalance final common pathway, substituting a metabolic (energy-deficit) upstream driver rather than a primary ion-channel lesion.

evidence.snippet: Studies to define the temporal requirements for Glut1 reveal that pre-symptomatic, AAV9-mediated repletion of the protein averts brain microvasculature defects and prevents disease, whereas augmenting the protein late, during adulthood, is devoid of benefit.
evidence.explanation: Temporal rescue experiments show the microvascular defect is GLUT1-dependent and has a developmental window.

evidence.snippet: Impaired development of the brain microvasculature is one such complication of delayed Glut1DS treatment in the postnatal period.
evidence.explanation: The consensus statement carries the mouse finding into the clinical framing of untreated early disease; it is expert opinion, not human vascular measurement.

steps/8.description: In Glut1-deficient mice, low endothelial GLUT1 arrests postnatal cerebral angiogenesis and leaves a profoundly reduced brain microvasculature while barrier integrity is preserved. Pre-symptomatic AAV9-mediated GLUT1 repletion averts the vascular defect and the disease; late (adult) repletion does not. The 2020 consensus statement adopts impaired microvascular development as a complication of delayed treatment, but direct human vascular data are lacking, so this node is provisional and is the structural basis of an emerging, non-fuel mechanism.

evidence.snippet: the predominant clinical findings of Glut1DS are usually complex paroxysmal movement disorders, spasticity, ataxia, dystonia, speech difficulty, and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the later-onset movement-disorder-predominant clinical picture directly arising from the same energy-deficit mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonic, ataxic, and dystonic features are most prominent. Speech is often severely affected. Some patients develop spasticity and secondary microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 published cases summarises the motor, speech and head-growth consequences of the developmental energy deficit.

evidence.snippet: Epilepsy dominated infancy and improved during childhood. Dystonia emerged during childhood or adolescence.
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal follow-up (mean 14 years) shows the movement disorder emerging as the dominant later manifestation.

evidence.snippet: The GLUT-1+/- murine phenotype mimics the classical human presentation of Glut-1 DS.
evidence.explanation: Haploinsufficient mice with microencephaly and incoordination recapitulate the developmental and motor consequences.

steps/9.description: Chronic cerebral energy deficit produces a complex, often paroxysmal movement disorder (ataxia, dystonia, spasticity), speech difficulty, and intellectual disability that can present alone or alongside epilepsy, reflecting the breadth of the GLUT1DS phenotypic spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Functional imaging studies implicated alterations in glucose metabolism in the corticostriate pathways in the pathophysiology of PED and in the frontal lobe cortex in the pathophysiology of epileptic seizures.
evidence.explanation: Imaging in SLC2A1 PED families localises the metabolic disturbance behind dyskinesia to corticostriatal circuits.

evidence.snippet: Sensitivity to fasting or exertion in combination with those 3 main symptoms were the main differences between mutated and negative patients (p < 0.001).
evidence.explanation: In a national laboratory cohort, trigger sensitivity to fasting and exertion discriminates SLC2A1-positive from negative patients.

evidence.snippet: A clue to the diagnosis in patients with paroxysmal symptoms may be the triggering of episodes during fasting or exercise.
evidence.explanation: Review confirms fasting and exercise as the characteristic provocations of the paroxysmal phenotype.

steps/10.description: Under sustained exertion or fasting, the marginal glucose supply of the energy-deficient brain is transiently overwhelmed in corticostriatal circuits, producing episodes of choreoathetosis or dystonia affecting mainly the legs (paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia). The same triggers aggravate seizures and paroxysmal ataxia. Functional imaging in PED families implicates altered glucose metabolism in the corticostriate pathways; the exertion-induced energy-deficit model is proposed rather than directly measured in the basal ganglia.

evidence.snippet: The initial symptom was convulsive seizures, which occurred in 15 cases, and was followed by abnormal eye movements in 7 cases and apneic or cyanotic attacks in 4 cases.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide Japanese survey documents convulsive seizures as the most frequent presenting symptom.

evidence.snippet: Patients present with an early-onset epilepsy resistant to anticonvulsants, developmental delay, and a complex movement disorder.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 cases confirms early-onset, anticonvulsant-resistant epilepsy as the presenting endpoint.

evidence.snippet: Seizure types were generalized tonic or clonic (14), absence (10), partial (nine), myoclonic (six), or astatic (four).
evidence.explanation: Chart review of 20 children enumerates the seizure semiologies that make up the endpoint.

steps/11.description: The clinical endpoint of cortical hyperexcitability is recurrent, typically pharmacoresistant, epileptic seizures of varying types beginning in infancy or early childhood.

evidence.snippet: Thirty-two patients (97%) exhibited some type of epileptic seizure.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort of 33 confirmed GLUT1DS patients documents seizures in 97% of individuals, directly supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: Three different phenotypes were recognized: (i) the classical phenotype (84%), subdivided into early-onset (<2 years) (65%) and late-onset (18%); (ii) a non-classical phenotype, with mental retardation and movement disorder, without epilepsy (15%)
evidence.explanation: In 57 genetically confirmed patients, 84% had the epilepsy-containing classical phenotype and 15% had no epilepsy, keeping seizures in the VERY_FREQUENT band while documenting the epilepsy-free minority.

evidence.snippet: Patients present with an early-onset epilepsy resistant to anticonvulsants, developmental delay, and a complex movement disorder.
evidence.explanation: Supports the pharmacoresistance qualifier.

steps/12.description: Seizures of varying types (often including absence, myoclonic, or generalized tonic-clonic seizures), typically beginning in infancy and frequently resistant to conventional anti-seizure medications, but responsive to ketogenic diet therapy.

evidence.snippet: Mild to severe mental retardation was detected in all 33 cases.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents developmental/cognitive impairment in all 33 confirmed cases.

steps/13.description: Delayed acquisition of motor and cognitive milestones, typically apparent from infancy, with mild-to-severe intellectual disability persisting into later childhood and adulthood.

evidence.snippet: the predominant clinical findings of Glut1DS are paroxysmal eye-head movements, pharmacoresistant seizures of varying types, deceleration of head growth, and developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists deceleration of head growth as a predominant early clinical finding.

evidence.snippet: characterized by infantile seizures, developmental delay, acquired microcephaly, spasticity, ataxia, and hypoglycorrhachia
evidence.explanation: Names the microcephaly as acquired, i.e. postnatal.

evidence.snippet: Some patients develop spasticity and secondary microcephaly.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 cases classifies it as secondary microcephaly and as occurring in some rather than all patients, so no frequency band is asserted.

steps/14.description: Deceleration of head growth after a normal birth head circumference, reflecting impaired postnatal brain growth from the underlying cerebral energy deficit.

evidence.snippet: Neurological findings revealed that most patients had muscle hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and spastic paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents cerebellar ataxia as a common neurological finding in most patients.

steps/15.description: Impaired coordination of voluntary movement, part of the complex movement disorder that emerges as GLUT1DS progresses.

evidence.snippet: Neurological findings revealed that most patients had muscle hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and spastic paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents dystonia as a common neurological finding.

evidence.snippet: Hypotonic, ataxic, and dystonic features are most prominent.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 published cases ranks dystonic features among the most prominent motor findings.

steps/16.description: Sustained or intermittent muscle contractions causing abnormal, often repetitive movements or postures; part of the complex movement disorder of GLUT1DS and the dominant feature of the paroxysmal-dyskinesia-predominant subtype.

evidence.snippet: Neurological findings revealed that most patients had muscle hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and spastic paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents spastic paralysis as a common neurological finding.

steps/17.description: Increased muscle tone contributing to the complex movement disorder of GLUT1DS.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, paroxysmal episodes of ataxia, dystonia/dyskinesia, and motor paralysis were described in approximately 1/3 of all patients. The factors that frequently aggravated these events were hunger, exercise, fever, and fatigue, in that order.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort quantifies paroxysmal dyskinetic episodes in about a third of patients and identifies exertion/hunger/fever/fatigue as triggers.

evidence.snippet: PED was characterized by choreoathetosis, dystonia or both, affecting mainly the legs.
evidence.explanation: Defines the semiology of PED in SLC2A1 families.

evidence.snippet: The 6-Minute Walk Test captured gait disturbances and triggered paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia.
evidence.explanation: A standardised exertion test reproducibly provokes the episodes in long-term follow-up.

evidence.snippet: In particular, paroxysmal exertional dyskinesia is now a well-documented clinical feature that occurs in individuals with Glut1 DS.
evidence.explanation: Review establishes PED as a recognised feature across the spectrum, not only in GLUT1DS2.

steps/18.description: Episodic dystonic or dyskinetic attacks of the extremities triggered by prolonged physical exertion, hunger, fever, or fatigue; the dominant presenting feature of the milder GLUT1DS2/DYT18 phenotype but also reported in classic disease.

evidence.snippet: the predominant clinical findings of Glut1DS are usually complex paroxysmal movement disorders, spasticity, ataxia, dystonia, speech difficulty, and intellectual disability.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists speech difficulty among predominant clinical findings in the later-onset presentation.

steps/19.description: Dysarthria and other speech production difficulties associated with the movement disorder and developmental impairment of GLUT1DS.

evidence.snippet: Neurological findings revealed that most patients had muscle hypotonia, cerebellar ataxia, dystonia, and spastic paralysis.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents muscle hypotonia as a common neurological finding.

steps/20.description: Reduced muscle tone, frequently observed alongside ataxia and dystonia.

evidence.snippet: Subsequently children develop complex movement disorders and intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents intellectual disability across a mild-to-severe range.

evidence.snippet: Mild to severe mental retardation was detected in all 33 cases.
evidence.explanation: All 33 confirmed cases had cognitive impairment, supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: Most patients (87.5%) exhibited classic phenotype with intellectual deficiency (41.7%), epilepsy (75%) or movement disorder (29%) as initial symptoms at a medium age of 7.5 months
evidence.explanation: French cohort shows intellectual deficiency as the presenting symptom in 41.7%.

steps/21.description: Cognitive impairment ranging from mild learning difficulty to severe intellectual disability, present in essentially all classic cases and in the non-classical movement-disorder phenotype; it was the initial symptom in over 40% of a French national cohort.

evidence.snippet: Seizure types were generalized tonic or clonic (14), absence (10), partial (nine), myoclonic (six), or astatic (four).
evidence.explanation: Absence seizures in 10 of 20 children with Glut1DS.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in SLC2A1 were detected in 5 (10%) of 50 patients with absence epilepsy
evidence.explanation: Shows the converse association, that absence epilepsy is a recognised Glut1DS presentation.

evidence.snippet: Absence epilepsy and other idiopathic generalized epilepsy syndromes may occur with seizure onset in childhood or adulthood.
evidence.explanation: Review places absence epilepsy within the milder end of the spectrum.

steps/22.description: Absence seizures, including early-onset absence epilepsy beginning before age four, are a characteristic seizure type; SLC2A1 variants account for about one in ten cases of absence epilepsy screened in a Danish series.

evidence.snippet: Seizure types were generalized tonic or clonic (14), absence (10), partial (nine), myoclonic (six), or astatic (four).
evidence.explanation: Myoclonic seizures in 6 of 20 children.

evidence.snippet: Patients with myoclonic seizures (52%) evolved with more severe intellectual deficiency and movement disorders compared with those with Early Onset Absence Epilepsy (38%).
evidence.explanation: Myoclonic seizures identify a more severe subgroup.

steps/23.description: Myoclonic seizures occur in a substantial minority and mark the more severe end of the spectrum, with worse intellectual and motor outcome than early-onset absence epilepsy in the French national cohort.

evidence.snippet: Seizure types were generalized tonic or clonic (14), absence (10), partial (nine), myoclonic (six), or astatic (four).
evidence.explanation: Generalized tonic or clonic seizures in 14 of 20 children.

steps/24.description: Generalized tonic or clonic seizures were the most frequent seizure type in a 20-child series.

evidence.snippet: Seizure types were generalized tonic or clonic (14), absence (10), partial (nine), myoclonic (six), or astatic (four).
evidence.explanation: Partial seizures in 9 of 20 children.

steps/25.description: Partial (focal-onset) seizures occur alongside the generalized seizure types, particularly in infancy.

evidence.snippet: In all ages, a normal interictal EEG was the most common EEG finding. When abnormalities occurred, focal slowing or epileptiform discharges were more prevalent in the infant. In older children (2 years or older), a generalized 2.5- to 4-Hz spike-wave pattern emerged.
evidence.explanation: Defines the age-dependent EEG signature and its low sensitivity.

evidence.snippet: Electroencephalography (EEG) may show 2.5-4Hz spike-waves improving on food intake.
evidence.explanation: Documents the food-responsive property of the discharge.

steps/26.description: Interictal EEG is most often normal, but when abnormal the characteristic finding from about two years of age is generalized 2.5-4 Hz spike-wave discharges, which improve after food intake; focal discharges and slowing predominate in infants.

evidence.snippet: When first diagnosed in infancy to early childhood, the predominant clinical findings of Glut1DS are paroxysmal eye-head movements, pharmacoresistant seizures of varying types, deceleration of head growth, and developmental delay.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists paroxysmal eye-head movements first among infantile findings.

evidence.snippet: The initial symptom was convulsive seizures, which occurred in 15 cases, and was followed by abnormal eye movements in 7 cases and apneic or cyanotic attacks in 4 cases.
