evidence.explanation: Abnormal eye movements were the presenting symptom in 7 of 33 nationwide cases.

steps/27.description: Paroxysmal, often multidirectional eye movements accompanied by head movements in the same direction are among the earliest signs in infancy and are frequently misread as seizures.

evidence.snippet: Percent-predicted 6-Minute Walk Test distance correlated significantly with Columbia Neurological Scores.
evidence.explanation: Walking performance is a quantitative correlate of neurological burden in long-term follow-up.

steps/28.description: Gait disturbance reflecting the combined ataxia, dystonia and spasticity; percent-predicted 6-Minute Walk distance tracks overall neurological severity.

evidence.snippet: Cerebrospinal fluid glucose was below 2.5 mmol/l (range 0.9-2.4 mmol/l) in all patients and cerebrospinal fluid : blood glucose ratio was below 0.50 in all but one patient (range 0.19-0.52).
evidence.explanation: All 57 genetically confirmed patients had hypoglycorrhachia, supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: The CSF glucose levels ranged from 16.2 to 50.5 mg/dL and were at or below the 10th percentile for all 147 patients.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of 147 genetically proven patients confirms universally low CSF glucose against age-specific percentiles.

evidence.snippet: The essential biochemical finding is a low glucose concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid
evidence.explanation: Gives the pooled mean CSF glucose across 84 published cases.

steps/29.description: Low CSF glucose (typically below 2.5 mmol/L, mean about 1.7 mmol/L) with a CSF:blood glucose ratio usually below 0.5 in the presence of normal blood glucose. Present in essentially all genetically confirmed patients when age-specific reference values are applied, so it is the diagnostic laboratory phenotype; rare reports of apparently normal CSF glucose exist.

evidence.snippet: The CSF lactate levels ranged from 5.4 to 13.5 mg/dL and were at or below the 10th percentile for 59 of 73 patients (81%).
evidence.explanation: 81% of patients with reported values had low CSF lactate, supporting VERY_FREQUENT.

evidence.snippet: The mean cerebrospinal fluid lactate concentration was 1.0 +/- 0.3mM, which was less than the normal mean value of 1.63mM.
evidence.explanation: Mean CSF lactate in 16 new patients was below the normal mean.

evidence.snippet: in the setting of normoglycaemia. CSF lactate is normal.
evidence.explanation: The 2007 review reports CSF lactate as normal rather than reduced; the value is low-to-normal, never elevated, which is the diagnostically useful point.

steps/30.description: CSF lactate is low-to-normal, at or below the 10th percentile in about 80% of patients with reported values, in contrast to the raised CSF lactate of mitochondrial encephalopathies; this helps separate a transport defect from an oxidative one.

evidence.snippet: Their PED was accompanied by epilepsy, mild developmental delay, reduced CSF glucose levels, hemolytic anemia with echinocytosis, and altered erythrocyte ion concentrations.
evidence.explanation: Three-generation family with the Q282_S285del pore-region allele documents the hemolytic phenotype.

steps/31.description: Hemolytic anemia with echinocytosis and altered erythrocyte ion concentrations occurs in the subset of families whose SLC2A1 allele creates a cation leak through the mutant transporter; it is absent with alleles that only reduce glucose transport.

evidence.snippet: It is caused by a defect in glucose transport into brain, mediated by the facilitative glucose transporter GLUT1.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the SLC2A1/GLUT1 defect to impaired glucose transport into the brain.

evidence.snippet: GLUT-1, whose sequence was originally deduced from cDNAs cloned from human hepatoma and rat brain, is present at high levels in primate erythrocytes and brain endothelial cells.
evidence.explanation: Places the mutated carrier at the brain endothelium, the site where the transport lesion acts.

edges/1.description: Loss-of-function SLC2A1 variants reduce the density or activity of GLUT1 transporters expressed on brain microvascular endothelial cells.

evidence.snippet: These findings validate the erythrocyte glucose uptake assay as a confirmatory functional test for Glut1 DS and as a surrogate marker for GLUT1 haploinsufficiency.
evidence.explanation: Establishes reduced erythrocyte uptake as a direct read-out of the same haploinsufficient transporter.

edges/2.description: The same haploinsufficient transporter is expressed on erythrocytes, so red-cell hexose uptake falls in parallel with brain transport and serves as the accessible functional surrogate of the lesion.

evidence.snippet: Facilitated glucose transporter protein type 1 (GLUT1) deficiency syndrome (MIM 138140) defines a prototype of a novel group of disorders resulting from impaired glucose transport across blood-tissue barriers.
evidence.explanation: Review frames Glut1DS as the prototypic disorder of impaired glucose transport across blood-tissue barriers, i.e., a cerebral energy-deficit disease.

evidence.snippet: Impaired glucose transport across brain tissue barriers is reflected by hypoglycorrhachia and results in an epileptic encephalopathy with developmental delay and motor disorders.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from barrier transport failure to the low-CSF-glucose, energy-deprived brain.

edges/3.description: Insufficient transendothelial glucose flux starves brain tissue of its principal metabolic substrate, independent of normal peripheral blood glucose levels.

evidence.snippet: The essential biochemical finding is a low glucose concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid
evidence.explanation: Low CSF glucose with normal blood glucose is the direct biochemical signature of the barrier transport defect.

edges/4.description: Reduced endothelial glucose flux lowers glucose in the CSF and brain interstitium while blood glucose stays normal, so the CSF:blood glucose ratio falls.

evidence.snippet: We used model mice to demonstrate that low Glut1 protein arrests cerebral angiogenesis, resulting in a profound diminution of the brain microvasculature without compromising the blood-brain barrier.
evidence.explanation: Mouse evidence that low GLUT1 itself, independent of barrier integrity, arrests cerebral angiogenesis.

edges/5.description: Beyond fuel delivery, endothelial GLUT1 is required for postnatal cerebral angiogenesis; low GLUT1 arrests microvessel expansion in model mice.

evidence.snippet: we propose that the dyskinesias result from an exertion-induced energy deficit that may cause episodic dysfunction of the basal ganglia
evidence.explanation: Proposes, from combined genetic, functional and brain-imaging data, that exertion converts the chronic deficit into episodic basal ganglia failure.

edges/6.description: When energy demand rises (sustained exertion) or substrate supply falls (fasting), the marginal glucose supply to metabolically expensive basal ganglia circuits is transiently exceeded.

edges/7.description: Lower glycolytic substrate delivery is the presumed reason CSF lactate is low-to-normal rather than raised; the intermediate steps are inferred, and the finding distinguishes Glut1DS from mitochondrial disease.

evidence.snippet: Key clinical features signaling the onset of Glut1DS are eye-head movement abnormalities, seizures, neurodevelopmental impairment, deceleration of head growth, and movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: Consensus statement lists eye-head movement abnormalities among the earliest onset features of the energy-deficient brain.

edges/8.description: Paroxysmal eye-head movements are among the earliest signs of the infantile energy deficit; the circuit through which they arise is not established.

evidence.snippet: Thirty-two patients (97%) exhibited some type of epileptic seizure.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents near-universal seizure occurrence, the clinical readout of energy-deficit-driven cortical hyperexcitability.

edges/9.description: Energy-deficient neurons and cortical circuits become hyperexcitable and hypersynchronous, generating the pharmacoresistant seizures characteristic of Glut1DS.

evidence.snippet: Subsequently children develop complex movement disorders and intellectual disability ranging from mild to severe.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents the progression from early seizures/developmental delay to complex movement disorder and intellectual disability.

edges/10.description: Sustained cerebral energy insufficiency during critical developmental windows impairs neurodevelopment and produces a complex movement disorder combining ataxia, dystonia, and spasticity, together with deceleration of head growth (acquired/progressive microcephaly).

evidence.snippet: Thirty-two patients (97%) exhibited some type of epileptic seizure.
evidence.explanation: Nationwide cohort documents near-universal seizure occurrence as the clinical manifestation of cortical hyperexcitability.

edges/11.description: Hyperexcitable, hypersynchronous cortical networks manifest clinically as recurrent seizures.

evidence.snippet: In older children (2 years or older), a generalized 2.5- to 4-Hz spike-wave pattern emerged.
evidence.explanation: Documents the age-dependent emergence of the generalized spike-wave pattern.

edges/12.description: The interictal electrographic signature of the hypersynchronous network, most prominent from about two years of age.

evidence.snippet: Glut-1 deficiency syndrome (Glut-1 DS, OMIM #606777) is characterized by infantile seizures, developmental delay, acquired microcephaly and hypoglycorrhachia.
evidence.explanation: Acquired microcephaly is a defining consequence in both the human syndrome and the haploinsufficient mouse (microencephaly).

edges/13.description: Reduced postnatal brain growth is expressed as deceleration of head growth.

edges/21.description: Gait disturbance is the functional composite of ataxia, dystonia and spasticity.

evidence.snippet: We screened 4 additional families, in which PED is combined with epilepsy, developmental delay, or migraine, but not with hemolysis or echinocytosis, and identified 2 additional GLUT1 mutations (A275T, G314S) that decreased glucose transport but did not affect cation permeability.
evidence.explanation: Allele-level dissociation shows hemolysis follows the cation leak, not the transport loss per se.

edges/27.description: Restricted to alleles that create a cation leak (e.g. Q282_S285del); alleles that only reduce transport (A275T, G314S) do not cause hemolysis.

evidence.snippet: Glut1 repletion in early-symptomatic mutants that have experienced sustained periods of low brain glucose nevertheless restores the cerebral microvasculature and ameliorates disease.
evidence.explanation: Restoring the microvasculature ameliorates disease in symptomatic mutants, linking the vascular node to the neurodevelopmental outcome.

edges/28.description: A diminished microvascular bed is proposed to compound the fuel deficit and contribute to cognitive dysfunction; the human contribution is unquantified.

evidence.snippet: PED was characterized by choreoathetosis, dystonia or both, affecting mainly the legs.
evidence.explanation: Describes the clinical form of the exertion-triggered episodes produced by this mechanism.

evidence.snippet: we propose that the dyskinesias result from an exertion-induced energy deficit that may cause episodic dysfunction of the basal ganglia
evidence.explanation: The proposed mechanism by which exertion acts on this node.

edges/30.description: Sustained muscular activity raises whole-body and cerebral glucose demand beyond what the haploinsufficient transporter can deliver to corticostriatal circuits.

evidence.snippet: A clue to the diagnosis in patients with paroxysmal symptoms may be the triggering of episodes during fasting or exercise.
evidence.explanation: Fasting as a trigger of the paroxysmal events produced by this node.

edges/31.description: Reduced blood glucose availability lowers an already marginal cerebral supply.

evidence.snippet: Electroencephalography (EEG) may show 2.5-4Hz spike-waves improving on food intake.
evidence.explanation: Feeding reverses the electrographic abnormality.

edges/32.description: Pre-prandial worsening and post-prandial improvement of spike-wave discharges tie network hyperexcitability to the fuel state.

evidence.snippet: Glut1DS is most commonly caused by a heterozygous SLC2A1 pathogenic variant and inherited in an autosomal dominant manner. About 90% of individuals with Glut1DS have the disorder as the result of a de novo SLC2A1 pathogenic variant; about 10% of individuals have the disorder as the result of a pathogenic variant inherited from a parent.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews genetic counseling section quantifies the de novo versus inherited variant origin split.

evidence.snippet: Pathological mutations in the SLC2A1 gene were identified in 28 out of 32 cases (87.5%).
evidence.explanation: Nationwide Japanese cohort documents the molecular diagnostic yield of SLC2A1 testing among clinically suspected patients.

evidence.snippet: In these 57 patients we identified 49 different mutations, including six multiple exon deletions, six known mutations and 37 novel mutations (13 missense, five nonsense, 13 frame shift, four splice site and two translation initiation mutations).
evidence.explanation: Largest single-laboratory series enumerates the allelic spectrum, including multi-exon deletions detectable only by MLPA.

evidence.snippet: We now report two distinct classes of mutations as the molecular basis for the functional defect of glucose transport: hemizygosity of GLUT1 and nonsense mutations resulting in truncation of the GLUT-1 protein.
evidence.explanation: Founding gene-discovery report.

evidence.snippet: We identified 16 rearrangements, including seven missense, one nonsense, one insertion, and seven deletion mutations. Fourteen were novel mutations. There were no obvious correlations between phenotype, genotype, or biochemical measures.
evidence.explanation: Adds the deletion-heavy spectrum of a further 16 patients and the absence of genotype-phenotype correlation in that series.

genes/0.notes: Allelic spectrum: whole-gene hemizygosity, nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, translation-initiation, multi-exon deletion and missense alleles, all converging on haploinsufficiency of transport. Biallelic (compound heterozygous or homozygous) genotypes with asymptomatic heterozygous parents account for the rare recessive families. Whether variant class predicts severity is contested (see the genotype-phenotype discussion).

evidence.snippet: All patients were seizure-free within a month of receiving the diet therapy. All patients were followed up for six months, three were followed up for 12 months after the treatment, and there was no recurrence of epilepsy during this period.
evidence.explanation: Retrospective single-center cohort of SLC2A1-mutation patients demonstrates rapid and durable seizure control with ketogenic diet therapy.

evidence.snippet: Typically, the earlier the treatment the better the long-term clinical outcome.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews documents that earlier ketogenic diet initiation yields better long-term neurologic outcome.

evidence.snippet: a ketogenic diet was effective in most of the patients with epilepsy (86%) and also reduced movement disorders in 48% of the patients with a classical phenotype and 71% of the patients with a non-classical phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies response of both seizures and movement disorder in 57 confirmed patients.

evidence.snippet: Of those with seizures, 95% of the children had >50% seizure reduction and 80% had >90% seizure reduction.
evidence.explanation: Largest (92-family, parent-reported) series of dietary therapy in Glut1DS.

evidence.snippet: The ketogenic diet is the treatment of choice as it provides an alternative fuel to the brain. It should be introduced early and maintained into puberty. Seizures are effectively controlled with the onset of ketosis, but might recur and require comedication.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 cases states duration guidance and the possibility of seizure recurrence needing co-medication.

evidence.snippet: Earlier introduction of the ketogenic diet correlated with better long-term outcomes on some measures.
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal cohort (mean 14 years) supports the early-treatment claim with outcome data rather than expert statement.

evidence.snippet: KDT represent standard choices with Glut1DS-specific recommendations regarding duration, composition, and management.
evidence.explanation: International consensus designates KDT as standard of care.

treatments/0.description: Age-specific ketogenic diet therapies (KDTs) supply ketone bodies as an alternative fuel for brain energy metabolism, bypassing the GLUT1 transport defect. Earlier initiation, ideally in infancy, is associated with better seizure control and long-term neurologic outcome. Effective for both seizure control and the movement disorder.

evidence.snippet: Targeted therapy: Age-specific KDTs primarily provide a supplemental fuel, namely, ketone bodies, for brain energy metabolism.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the ketogenic diet mechanism of action as supplying an alternative cerebral fuel that bypasses the GLUT1 transport defect.

evidence.snippet: Diets used were extremely varied: 59 were treated with the classic ketogenic diet (KD), 29 with the Modified Atkins Diet (MAD), 4 with the Medium-chain Triglyceride (MCT) Diet and 2 with the low glycemic index treatment.
evidence.explanation: Documents real-world use of the dietary variants.

evidence.snippet: There was an equal percentage of children seizure-free receiving the KD/MCT Diets compared to the MAD/Low Glycemic Index Treatment (74% vs. 63%, p=0.30).
evidence.explanation: No significant difference in seizure freedom between classic and less restrictive diets in this parent-reported survey.

treatments/1.description: Less restrictive ketogenic dietary therapies (modified Atkins diet, medium-chain-triglyceride diet, low-glycaemic-index treatment) are used, particularly in older children and adults, and in a large family survey gave seizure-freedom rates comparable to the classic 4:1 diet. They act by the same ketone-supply mechanism as the classic diet.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Supplies ketone bodies as an alternative cerebral fuel, as the classic ketogenic diet does.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with triheptanoin resulted in a 90% clinical improvement in non-epileptic paroxysmal manifestations and a normalised brain bioenergetics profile in patients with GLUT1-DS.
evidence.explanation: Open-label pilot study supports triheptanoin efficacy against the non-epileptic paroxysmal (movement-disorder) manifestations of GLUT1DS.

evidence.snippet: Triheptanoin did not significantly reduce seizure frequency in patients with Glut1DS not on the ketogenic diet.
evidence.explanation: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial qualifies the treatment claim by showing no significant seizure-frequency benefit for the epilepsy phenotype.

treatments/2.description: Triheptanoin is an anaplerotic odd-chain (C7) medium-chain triglyceride that provides Krebs-cycle substrates and an alternative brain fuel independent of GLUT1. An open-label study reported marked reduction of non-epileptic paroxysmal manifestations and normalized brain bioenergetics, but a subsequent randomized placebo-controlled trial did not show a significant reduction in seizure frequency in patients not on a ketogenic diet, leaving its efficacy for the epilepsy phenotype unproven.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with triheptanoin resulted in a 90% clinical improvement in non-epileptic paroxysmal manifestations and a normalised brain bioenergetics profile in patients with GLUT1-DS.
evidence.explanation: Open-label study demonstrates triheptanoin supplies anaplerotic Krebs-cycle substrates that bypass the GLUT1 defect and normalize brain energy metabolism.

evidence.snippet: Agents/circumstances to avoid: In individuals on KDTs: (1) avoidance of treatment of seizures with valproic acid, because it increases the risk of a Reye-like illness and may also inhibit glucose transport; (2) other anti-seizure medications (ASMs) including phenobarbital, acetazolamide, topiramate, and zonisamide may be relatively contraindicated as adjunctive treatment.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews Agents/Circumstances to Avoid section directly documents these drug-safety warnings for GLUT1DS patients on ketogenic diet therapy.

treatments/3.description: In individuals on ketogenic diet therapy, valproic acid should be avoided because it increases the risk of a Reye-like illness and may also inhibit glucose transport; phenobarbital, acetazolamide, topiramate, and zonisamide may be relatively contraindicated as adjunctive treatment. This is a "circumstance to avoid" (GeneReviews Agents/Circumstances to Avoid section) rather than a recommended treatment; retained here as a treatment-adjacent drug-safety note.

evidence.snippet: Supportive care: In addition to educational programs to address the individual's needs, multidisciplinary care by specialists in neurology familiar with KDTs, physical medicine and rehabilitation, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech and therapy, and clinical genetics and genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews management section documents the multidisciplinary supportive care regimen recommended alongside ketogenic diet therapy.

treatments/4.description: Physical medicine and rehabilitation, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, educational programs, and clinical genetics/genetic counseling, alongside routine neurology follow-up to monitor response to ketogenic diet therapy and identify new manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Each child of an individual with autosomal dominant Glut1DS has a 50% chance of inheriting the SLC2A1 pathogenic variant and being clinically affected.
evidence.explanation: Recurrence risk for offspring of an affected individual.

evidence.snippet: Once the SLC2A1 pathogenic variant(s) have been identified in an affected family member, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing for Glut1DS are possible.
evidence.explanation: Reproductive options.

treatments/5.description: Each child of an individual with autosomal dominant Glut1DS has a 50% chance of inheriting the SLC2A1 variant; because about 90% of cases are de novo and transmitting parents may be mildly affected or unaffected (possible mosaicism), parental testing is informative. Prenatal and preimplantation testing are possible once the familial variant is known.

evidence.snippet: It is appropriate to evaluate at-risk newborns, infants, and other relatives of a proband to identify as early as possible those who would benefit from initiation of treatment and preventive measures.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews recommendation to evaluate relatives at risk.

evidence.snippet: Early initiation of KDTs, ideally in infancy, results in better seizure control and improves long-term neurologic outcome.
evidence.explanation: The rationale for presymptomatic identification.

treatments/6.description: Because early ketogenic diet therapy improves seizure control and long-term neurological outcome, at-risk newborns, infants and other relatives of a proband should be tested for the familial SLC2A1 variant so that treatment can begin before or at the first manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Surveillance: Routinely scheduled evaluations with a neurologist (to determine response to KDTs and identify any new manifestations) as well as follow up per treating physical therapists, occupational therapists, and speech-language therapists.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews surveillance recommendation.

treatments/7.description: Routinely scheduled neurology review to judge response to ketogenic diet therapy and to detect new manifestations, especially the movement disorder that emerges in later childhood and adolescence, with follow-up by the treating physical, occupational and speech-language therapists.

evidence.snippet: Timely Glut1 repletion may thus constitute an effective treatment for Glut1 DS.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion from the temporal rescue series; preclinical.

treatments/8.description: Experimental, preclinical only. In Glut1-deficient mice, pre-symptomatic AAV9-mediated repletion of GLUT1 averts the brain microvascular defect and prevents disease, and repletion in early-symptomatic animals still restores the microvasculature and ameliorates disease, whereas adult repletion gives no benefit. The 2020 consensus notes that interventions to restore GLUT1 protein content and function are in development. No human trial of GLUT1 gene replacement is cited here.

evidence.snippet: Ongoing research has identified future interventions to restore Glut1 protein content and function.
evidence.explanation: Consensus statement records protein-restoring interventions as the direction of therapeutic research.

treatments/8/targets/0.description: Vector-delivered SLC2A1 restores GLUT1 protein content in the deficient brain.

evidence.snippet: Glut1 repletion in early-symptomatic mutants that have experienced sustained periods of low brain glucose nevertheless restores the cerebral microvasculature and ameliorates disease.
evidence.explanation: Direct rescue of the vascular node by gene replacement in symptomatic mice.

treatments/8/targets/1.description: Early GLUT1 repletion restores the cerebral microvasculature in model mice.

evidence.snippet: Glut1 deficiency syndrome (Glut1DS) is a brain energy failure syndrome caused by impaired glucose transport across brain tissue barriers.
evidence.explanation: Consensus definition of the canonical mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These symptoms suggested the existence of a defect in glucose transport across the blood brain barrier.
evidence.explanation: The founding formulation of the hypothesis, confirmed by the mutations reported in the same paper.

hypotheses/0.description: Haploinsufficient GLUT1 at the brain endothelium limits glucose delivery, producing hypoglycorrhachia and a chronic brain energy deficit that is greatest when developmental glucose demand peaks; the deficit drives cortical hyperexcitability, impaired neurodevelopment and, under exertion or fasting, episodic basal ganglia failure. Ketogenic diet therapy works by supplying ketone bodies that bypass the transporter.

evidence.snippet: We used model mice to demonstrate that low Glut1 protein arrests cerebral angiogenesis, resulting in a profound diminution of the brain microvasculature without compromising the blood-brain barrier.
evidence.explanation: Primary mouse evidence for the hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: Research reaches beyond the concept of brain energy depletion by impaired GLUT1-mediated glucose transfer across the blood-brain barrier.
evidence.explanation: 2025 review frames non-fuel mechanisms as an active, still-emerging area.

hypotheses/1.description: Beyond its fuel-transport role, endothelial GLUT1 is required for postnatal cerebral angiogenesis; in model mice low GLUT1 arrests microvessel growth and early, but not late, repletion averts disease. The consensus statement has adopted impaired microvascular development as a complication of delayed treatment, but the human contribution is unmeasured, and this model may partly explain why fuel substitution rescues seizures more completely than cognition.

evidence.snippet: the hemolysis with echinocytosis may result from alterations in intracellular electrolytes caused by a cation leak through mutant GLUT1
evidence.explanation: The authors' mechanistic proposal from oocyte and erythrocyte studies.

hypotheses/2.description: Specific pore-region SLC2A1 alleles render the mutant transporter permeable to sodium, potassium and calcium; the resulting erythrocyte electrolyte disturbance produces echinocytosis and hemolytic anemia. Alleles that only reduce transport do not cause hemolysis, so this is an allele-specific gain of an abnormal function layered on haploinsufficiency, established in one family plus heterologous expression.

evidence.snippet: Glucose, the essential metabolic fuel for the brain, is transported into the brain exclusively by the protein glucose transporter type 1 (Glut1) across the endothelial cells forming the blood-brain barrier (BBB).
evidence.explanation: Establishes the exclusive GLUT1 route for cerebral glucose, framing why the deficit is global; the open question is which cell type first converts that global shortfall into focal-onset hyperexcitability.

evidence.snippet: GLUT-1+/- mice have epileptiform discharges on electroencephalography (EEG), impaired motor activity, incoordination, hypoglycorrhachia, microencephaly, decreased brain glucose uptake as measured by positron emission tomography (PET) scan and decreased brain Glut-1 expression by western blot (66%).
evidence.explanation: Provides a tractable in vivo system in which the epileptiform phenotype is reproduced, i.e., a model where the missing cellular intermediate could be dissected with cell-type-specific readouts.

open_questions/0.rationale: The causal edge from "Cerebral Glucose Energy Deficit" to "Neuronal Hyperexcitability and Hypersynchrony" is curated as INDIRECT_KNOWN_INTERMEDIATES, but the identity of that intermediate is not actually established. Glucose reaches the brain almost exclusively through GLUT1, yet why a global fuel shortfall produces the particular Glut1DS electroclinical signature (including 2.5-4 Hz generalized spike-wave and absence-like seizures) rather than diffuse depression is unresolved. Candidate mechanisms — astrocytic lactate-supply failure, preferential ATP starvation of parvalbumin interneurons whose high firing rates make them metabolically expensive, and adenosine-mediated network effects — carry different therapeutic implications, so resolving the intermediate would materially sharpen the mechanism model.

evidence.snippet: Targeted therapy: Age-specific KDTs primarily provide a supplemental fuel, namely, ketone bodies, for brain energy metabolism.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that ketogenic therapy acts by fuel substitution, framing the question of why fuel substitution rescues seizures more completely than neurodevelopmental outcomes.

evidence.snippet: Typically, the earlier the treatment the better the long-term clinical outcome.
evidence.explanation: Documents the developmental-window dependence of outcome, one of the competing explanations for the residual neurodevelopmental deficit.

evidence.snippet: Restoring the protein to 2-week old mutants, in which certain disease characteristics are readily apparent, is less effective in shaping normal brain microvasculature.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism evidence that later restoration incompletely reverses structural brain defects, supporting a developmental-window contribution to residual, seizure-independent morbidity.

evidence.snippet: The effect on neurodevelopment appears less impressive.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 cases records the seizure-versus-neurodevelopment dissociation that this gap is about.

evidence.snippet: KDT are ineffective in some patients for reasons yet unknown.
evidence.explanation: 2025 review states that the determinants of KDT non-response are unknown, confirming the gap remains open.

open_questions/1.rationale: Ketogenic diet therapy is the mainstay treatment and supplies ketone bodies as an alternative cerebral fuel that bypasses the GLUT1 transport defect. In practice it controls seizures far more completely than it reverses the paroxysmal movement disorder, ataxia/dystonia, or cognitive outcome, and outcomes are consistently better with earlier treatment. Whether the residual, seizure-independent morbidity reflects irreversible injury incurred before diagnosis (a developmental-window effect), inadequate ketone delivery to specific circuits, or a role of glucose beyond bulk fuel (e.g., biosynthetic/pentose-phosphate demands) is unresolved — and it determines whether earlier or supplemental (e.g., anaplerotic) therapy could close the gap.

evidence.snippet: The GLUT-1+/- murine phenotype mimics the classical human presentation of Glut-1 DS.
evidence.explanation: Documents fidelity to the classical core phenotype; the open question is whether the paroxysmal and spectrum-defining human features are also captured.

open_questions/2.rationale: The GLUT-1+/- mouse reproduces epileptiform EEG, motor impairment, hypoglycorrhachia and microencephaly and is described as mimicking the classical human presentation, making it the workhorse model for Glut1DS. But the human disorder is defined as much by paroxysmal, activity- and fasting-triggered phenomena and by a wide phenotypic spectrum (paroxysmal exercise-induced dyskinesia, early-onset absence epilepsy, isolated movement disorder) that depend on human-specific behavioral repertoire and developmental glucose-demand timing. Whether these paroxysmal and spectrum-defining features are recapitulated — and thus whether the model can validate therapies aimed at them — is the open translational question, distinct from a claim that evidence is simply absent.

evidence.snippet: Type of mutation was related to the severity of mental retardation and the presence of complex movement disorders.
evidence.explanation: Supports the claim that variant class predicts severity, in 57 genetically confirmed patients.

evidence.snippet: There were no obvious correlations between phenotype, genotype, or biochemical measures.
evidence.explanation: Refutes the claim in an independent series of 16 patients.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal dominant transmission and several mutational hot spots have been identified, but phenotype-genotype correlations are not yet apparent.
evidence.explanation: Review of 84 published cases found no apparent correlation.

evidence.snippet: thus making it difficult to identify definite genotype-phenotype correlations
evidence.explanation: French national cohort argues phenotypes overlap along a continuum rather than segregating by genotype.

evidence.snippet: We also noted a significant correlation between the mean erythrocyte 3-OMG uptake and clinical severity (R(2) = 0.94).
evidence.explanation: Supports the alternative position that residual transporter function, rather than variant class, predicts severity.

open_questions/3.rationale: The largest laboratory series reported that mutation type was related to the severity of intellectual disability and to the presence of complex movement disorders, whereas the Columbia series of 16 new patients and the 2007 review of 84 published cases found no correlation between genotype, phenotype and biochemical measures, and the French national cohort found overlapping phenotypes that resist genotype-phenotype assignment. What does correlate across series is residual erythrocyte glucose uptake, which even determines whether a family presents as dominant or recessive. The resolution matters for counselling and for how the has_subtypes entries are read: they are phenotype clusters on a continuum, not variant-defined entities.

evidence.snippet: In vitro, CSF-1 stimulation resulted in rapid autophosphorylation of selected tyrosine residues in the kinase domain of wild-type but not mutant CSF1R, suggesting that HDLS may result from partial loss of CSF1R function.
evidence.explanation: The discovery paper shows that HDLS-causing CSF1R mutations abolish CSF-1-stimulated autophosphorylation, establishing partial loss of CSF1R function as the molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: As CSF1R is a crucial mediator of microglial proliferation and differentiation in the brain, our findings suggest an important role for microglial dysfunction in HDLS pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Links impaired CSF1R signaling to microglial dysfunction as the central pathogenic mechanism.

steps/1.description: CSF1R encodes the colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase expressed predominantly on microglia. Disease-causing variants cluster in the tyrosine kinase domain and impair CSF-1-stimulated receptor autophosphorylation, producing partial loss of CSF1R function (haploinsufficiency). Because CSF1R is a crucial mediator of microglial proliferation, survival, and differentiation, impaired signaling causes microglial dysfunction that initiates the disease.

evidence.snippet: Primary axonopathy followed by demyelination was suggested by pathology.
evidence.explanation: Describes the neuropathologic sequence of axonal degeneration preceding demyelination in CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Given that CSF1R mainly expresses in microglia, CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy is representative of primary microgliopathies
evidence.explanation: Establishes the disease as a primary microgliopathy driven by microglial CSF1R dysfunction.

evidence.snippet: monoallelic deletion of Csf2 rescues most behavioral deficits and histopathological changes in Csf1r+/- mice by preventing microgliosis and eliminating most microglial transcriptomic alterations, including those indicative of oxidative stress and demyelination
evidence.explanation: Mouse model evidence that unbalanced CSF-1R/CSF-2 signaling drives microgliosis and demyelination, with rescue by lowering CSF-2.

evidence.snippet: We also show elevation of Csf2 transcripts and of several CSF-2 downstream targets in the brains of ALSP patients, demonstrating that the mechanisms identified in the mouse model are functional in humans.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in human ALSP brains the elevated CSF-2 signaling implicated in the mouse model, supporting human relevance of the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: we generated a xenotolerant mouse model lacking the fms-intronic regulatory element (FIRE) enhancer within Csf1r, which develops nearly all the hallmark pathologies associated with ALSP
evidence.explanation: A Csf1r-FIRE-enhancer-deficient (microglia-depleted) mouse recapitulates nearly all hallmark ALSP pathologies, confirming that loss of microglial CSF1R function is sufficient to drive the white-matter neurodegeneration.

steps/2.description: As a primary microgliopathy, microglial dysfunction from impaired CSF1R signaling drives white-matter neurodegeneration. Pathology shows primary axonopathy followed by demyelination, with characteristic axonal spheroids and pigmented glia in affected cerebral white matter. In the Csf1r+/- mouse model, microgliosis and microglial transcriptomic alterations indicative of oxidative stress and demyelination are central, with elevated cerebral CSF-2 (GM-CSF) signaling implicated; monoallelic CSF2 deletion rescues most deficits, and elevated CSF2 is confirmed in human ALSP brains.

evidence.snippet: Given that CSF1R mainly expresses in microglia, CSF1R-related leukoencephalopathy is representative of primary microgliopathies
evidence.explanation: Establishes that microglial CSF1R dysfunction is the upstream driver of the downstream white-matter neurodegeneration, supporting this causal edge.

edges/1.description: Microglial dysfunction from impaired CSF1R signaling drives downstream white-matter neurodegeneration with axonal spheroids and pigmented glia.

evidence.snippet: We combined genome-wide linkage analysis with exome sequencing and identified 14 different mutations affecting the tyrosine kinase domain of the colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (encoded by CSF1R) in 14 families with HDLS.
evidence.explanation: Identifies CSF1R tyrosine-kinase-domain mutations as the cause of HDLS in 14 families.

evidence.snippet: Late-onset CSF1R-related disorder is typically caused by a heterozygous pathogenic variant and inherited in an autosomal dominant manner
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews confirms autosomal dominant inheritance for the typical late-onset form.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous pathogenic variants in CSF1R, clustering in the tyrosine kinase domain, are the most common cause of ALSP/HDLS. More than 70 different mutations have been identified worldwide.

evidence.snippet: Hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) has been increasingly offered to patients with CSF1R-ALSP.
evidence.explanation: Documents HSCT as an emerging therapy increasingly used in CSF1R-ALSP.

evidence.snippet: gait problems indicated a milder phenotype with better response to HSCT and good therapy outcomes. In contrast, patients with a higher burden of cognitive symptoms were most likely not to benefit from HSCT.
evidence.explanation: Outcomes are variable and depend on phenotype/timing, so HSCT benefit is partial and patient-dependent.

evidence.snippet: Allogeneic HSCT may be beneficial in ALSP by providing a supply of bone marrow-derived brain-engrafting myeloid cells with donor wild-type CSF1R to repopulate the microglial niche.
evidence.explanation: Provides the mechanistic rationale for HSCT in ALSP: donor-derived myeloid cells with wild-type CSF1R engraft the brain and repopulate the dysfunctional microglial niche. The two-patient series showed MRI stabilization and partial clinical stabilization at >2 years.

treatments/0.description: HSCT is an emerging disease-modifying therapy increasingly offered to patients with CSF1R-ALSP, aiming to replace dysfunctional CSF1R-mutant microglia/brain macrophages with donor-derived cells. Outcomes are variable: gait problems as the predominant manifestation and younger age at transplant predict better outcomes, whereas a high burden of cognitive symptoms predicts worse outcomes.

evidence.snippet: Multidisciplinary care by specialists in neurology, psychotherapy, neuropsychological rehabilitation, physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language therapy, social services for family support, and genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews specifies multidisciplinary supportive care as the management approach.

evidence.snippet: sedatives, antipsychotics, and other medications that may decrease alertness and increase the risk of falling should be used cautiously
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews "Agents/circumstances to avoid": caution with sedatives and antipsychotics in patients with gait problems and cognitive decline.

treatments/1.description: Mainstay management is multidisciplinary supportive care, including neurology, neuropsychological rehabilitation, physical, occupational, and speech-language therapy, psychotherapy, social support, and genetic counseling. Sedatives, antipsychotics, and other medications that decrease alertness or increase fall risk should be used cautiously in individuals with gait problems and cognitive decline.

evidence.snippet: predictive testing for at-risk relatives and prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing for CSF1R-related disorder are possible
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews supports genetic counseling and predictive/prenatal testing once the familial variant is identified.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is recommended given autosomal dominant (and, for biallelic early-onset disease, autosomal recessive) inheritance; predictive and prenatal/preimplantation genetic testing are possible once the familial CSF1R variant is known.

evidence.snippet: transplantation of human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived microglial (iMG) progenitors restores a homeostatic microglial signature and prevents the development of axonal spheroids, white matter abnormalities, reactive astrocytosis, and brain calcifications
evidence.explanation: Preclinical proof of concept that iMG transplantation prevents ALSP-like neuropathology in the FIRE mouse model.

evidence.snippet: transplantation of CRISPR-corrected ALSP-patient-derived iMG reverses pre-existing spheroids, astrogliosis, and calcification pathologies
evidence.explanation: Transplantation of CRISPR-corrected patient-derived iMG into the ALSP mouse model reverses established pathology, supporting gene-corrected autologous microglia replacement as a therapeutic avenue.

treatments/3.description: An emerging, preclinical microglia-replacement strategy. Transplantation of human iPSC-derived microglial (iMG) progenitors into a microglia-deficient (Csf1r FIRE-enhancer-deleted) ALSP mouse model restores a homeostatic microglial signature and prevents axonal spheroids, white-matter abnormalities, reactive astrocytosis, and brain calcifications. CRISPR-corrected ALSP-patient-derived iMG can reverse pre-existing pathology, supporting iMG transplantation as a candidate disease-modifying therapy. Not yet in human use.

evidence.snippet: Women with HHT considering pregnancy are screened and treated for pulmonary and cerebral AVMs; sizable pulmonary AVMs discovered during pregnancy are treated during the second trimester.
evidence.explanation: The management response to this exposure, which is the practical evidence that pregnancy is treated as a risk period in HHT.

evidence.snippet: A second locus, designated ORW2, was mapped to chromosome 12.
evidence.explanation: Localises the HHT2 locus to chromosome 12, where ACVRL1 lies.

steps/2.description: The initiating lesion is a heterozygous germline loss-of-function variant in ACVRL1 on chromosome 12q13, present in every cell of the body. Reported classes include nonsense, frameshift, missense within the kinase domain, and whole-gene deletion.

evidence.snippet: Somatic mosaic lesion-specific ACVRL1 variants were identified in four hepatic AVM samples and in one telangiectasia.
evidence.explanation: Direct human evidence for lesion-restricted somatic ACVRL1 variants in HHT2 tissue, in both the hepatic and mucocutaneous compartments.

evidence.snippet: Increasing evidence points to the importance of a second genetic hit to generate biallelic mutations, and the sporadic nature of such somatic mutations would explain the localised formation of vascular lesions.
evidence.explanation: Gives the reasoning that ties the second hit specifically to the focal distribution of lesions.

steps/3.description: Individual lesions acquire a somatic mutation in the remaining wild-type ACVRL1 allele, producing local biallelic loss. This is what reconciles a germline variant present in every endothelial cell with a disease that is focal: telangiectases and AVMs arise where a second hit has occurred, not everywhere. Lesion-specific somatic ACVRL1 variants have been recovered from hepatic AVMs and from a skin telangiectasia in a patient whose germline lesion was a whole-gene ACVRL1 deletion, with different somatic variants in different lesions of the same person.

evidence.snippet: We suggest that BMP10 is the most relevant physiological ligand of the ENG-ALK1 signaling pathway pertinent to HHT pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Identifies which ligand actually drives this receptor arm, supporting the node's statement that BMP10 loss is what reproduces the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Bmp10-iKO and Bmp9/10-dKO mice showed AVMs in developing retina, postnatal brain, and adult wounded skin, while Bmp9-KO did not display any noticeable vascular defects.
evidence.explanation: The ligand-knockout comparison behind the BMP10-over-BMP9 claim; graded MODEL_ORGANISM because it is mouse data.

evidence.snippet: Immunohistochemical analysis in four subjects and one control showed pulmonary vascular endothelial expression of activin-receptor-like kinase 1 in normal and diseased pulmonary arteries.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in human tissue that ALK1 is expressed where this node places it, the vascular endothelium.

steps/4.description: ALK1 is the type I receptor for the circulating ligands BMP9 and BMP10. Ligand is captured by the co-receptor endoglin and handed to ALK1, a type II receptor joins and phosphorylates ALK1, and activated ALK1 phosphorylates SMAD1/5. With less functional ALK1, flux through this specific BMP9/10-ENG-ALK1 arm falls. Mouse work indicates BMP10 rather than BMP9 is the ligand whose loss reproduces the AVM phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Similar phenotypes develop following combined EC specific loss of SMAD1 and 5, or EC loss of SMAD4.
evidence.explanation: The genetic epistasis that places SMAD1/5-SMAD4 in the same functional unit as ALK1 for this phenotype.

steps/5.description: Phospho-SMAD1/5 partners SMAD4 and moves to the nucleus to run the transcriptional programme that keeps endothelium quiescent. That the whole BMP9/10-ENG-ALK1-SMAD1/5-SMAD4 axis is one functional unit is shown by the convergence of the mouse phenotypes: endothelial loss of ENG, of ALK1, of SMAD4, or of SMAD1 and SMAD5 together each produces the same arteriovenous malformation phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Thus in the absence of BMP9/10 signalling there is increased PI3K activity leading to increased EC proliferation and survival.
evidence.explanation: Supports the PI3K/AKT-mediated proliferation arm described in this node.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of the ENG/ALK1 signalling pathway also affects EC responses to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and crosstalk between ECs and vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence.explanation: Supports the VEGF-responsiveness arm, which is the target of anti-VEGF treatment.

evidence.snippet: Bmp10 deficiency resulted in increased proliferation and size of endothelial cells in AVM vessels.
evidence.explanation: Independent mouse evidence that interrupting this ligand-receptor arm increases endothelial proliferation inside the lesions themselves.

evidence.snippet: ALK1-dependent SMAD signaling synergizes with activated Notch in stalk cells to induce expression of the Notch targets HEY1 and HEY2, thereby repressing VEGF signaling, tip cell formation, and endothelial sprouting.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the ALK1-Notch-HEY1/HEY2 mechanism by which this node's brake on sprouting is applied, and therefore what its loss releases.

evidence.snippet: Blocking Alk1 signaling during postnatal development in mice leads to retinal hypervascularization and the appearance of arteriovenous malformations (AVMs).
evidence.explanation: The loss-of-function result: removing ALK1 signalling produces exactly the excess angiogenic drive this node describes, and the AVM that follows.

evidence.snippet: loss of SMAD4 disinhibits flow-mediated KLF4-TIE2-PI3K/Akt signaling, leading to cell cycle progression-mediated loss of arterial identity due to KLF4-mediated repression of cyclin dependent Kinase (CDK) inhibitors CDKN2A and CDKN2B.
evidence.explanation: Gives the shear-stress-set-point mechanism named in this description. Graded INDIRECT for HHT2 because it was shown by deleting SMAD4 rather than ALK1; SMAD4 is the downstream node of the same axis, so the result bears on this node through that shared pathway rather than by testing ACVRL1 itself.

steps/6.description: Two endothelial-cell-autonomous defects follow. First, endothelial cells normally polarise against the direction of blood flow and migrate upstream; without ALK1 signalling that shear-directed migration is lost and the cells stall. Second, the stalled cells keep proliferating - in part because BMP9/10 signalling normally restrains PI3K/AKT, so its loss increases endothelial proliferation and survival. The pathway also normally damps endothelial responses to VEGF, which is why anti-VEGF therapy is effective downstream. In adult vessels this only becomes visible when an angiogenic trigger is present. Two mechanisms have been resolved for how the brake is applied. ALK1-driven SMAD signalling cooperates with Notch in stalk cells to induce HEY1 and HEY2, which repress VEGF signalling, tip-cell formation and sprouting - so blocking Alk1 gives retinal hypervascularisation and AVMs, and activating it with BMP9 rescues hypersprouting caused by Notch inhibition. Separately, the pathway sets the fluid-shear-stress set point at which endothelium is stable; losing the downstream node SMAD4 lowers that set point and disinhibits flow-driven KLF4-TIE2-PI3K/Akt signalling, so cells proliferate and lose arterial identity under flow that would otherwise be quiescent.

evidence.snippet: Loss of the ENG (HHT1) or ALK1 (HHT2) gene in ECs leads to aberrant arteriovenous connections or malformations (AVMs) in developing blood vessels.
evidence.explanation: Names ALK1 loss specifically (HHT2) as the cause of aberrant arteriovenous connections, which is this node.

evidence.snippet: Where present, AVMs allow arterial blood to bypass the normal capillary bed and reach the vein at abnormally high pressure.
evidence.explanation: Supports the haemodynamic description - capillary bypass and high venous pressure - that makes these lesions bleed.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is characterized by the presence of multiple arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) that lack intervening capillaries and result in direct connections between arteries and veins.
evidence.explanation: The human-disease definition of the lesion this node describes.

steps/7.description: A direct connection forms between an artery and a vein with no intervening capillary bed. Blood preferentially takes this low-resistance channel, so the feeding artery and draining vein enlarge under haemodynamic load while the bypassed capillary plexus regresses. The vein receives blood at abnormally high pressure, which is why these lesions bleed. The same lesion at different calibre gives either a mucocutaneous telangiectasis or a visceral AVM.

evidence.snippet: Telangiectases (small AVMs) are characteristically found on the lips, tongue, buccal and gastrointestinal (GI) mucosa, fingers, and nose.
evidence.explanation: Gives the anatomical distribution this node records.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that HHT2 has a later onset than HHT1 and the former may disproportionately involve smaller vessels in tissues with more significant vascular remodeling.
evidence.explanation: Supports the later appearance of lesions in HHT2 and the authors' proposal that HHT2 preferentially affects the smaller-calibre vessels this node describes.

steps/8.description: Small superficial arteriovenous connections in the nasal, oral, gastrointestinal and skin surfaces present as telangiectases. Because they deliver arterial pressure into thin-walled superficial vessels, mucosal telangiectases rupture readily; this, not the large AVMs, is the source of the recurrent bleeding that dominates day-to-day disease. In HHT2 these lesions appear later than in HHT1, and truncating ACVRL1 variants carry a higher telangiectasis burden than non-truncating ones.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic hepatic involvement was only seen in HHT2 patients.
evidence.explanation: The strongest single statement of the hepatic tropism this node asserts; in a cohort of 93 HHT1 and 250 HHT2 patients, symptomatic liver disease was confined to the ACVRL1 genotype.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic vascular malformations were more common in patients with HHT2.
evidence.explanation: Independent cohort replication of the hepatic predominance in HHT2.

steps/9.description: Diffuse hepatic vascular malformations create hepatic artery-to-hepatic vein, hepatic artery-to-portal vein, and portal vein-to-hepatic vein shunts. This is the compartment that most distinguishes HHT2 from HHT1: symptomatic hepatic involvement is characteristic of ACVRL1 disease, and in the French-Italian cohort it was seen only in HHT2 patients. Depending on which shunt predominates the consequence is high cardiac output, portal hypertension, or liver failure.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic PAVMs were more frequent in HHT1 (34.4 vs. 5.2%, P<0.001), as were cerebral abscesses (7.5 vs. 0.8%, P=0.002).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the lower but non-zero pulmonary AVM burden of HHT2 stated in this node, together with the downstream abscess rate.

evidence.snippet: ENG patients were significantly younger at diagnosis (36.9 vs 45.7 years) and had pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) (71.4% vs 24.4%) and cerebral AVMs (17.6% vs 2%) more often than patients with ACVRL1 variants.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the lower pulmonary AVM frequency in ACVRL1 patients, here on screened rather than symptomatic lesions.

steps/10.description: Pulmonary AVMs connect a pulmonary artery to a pulmonary vein, so venous blood bypasses the alveolar capillary bed and enters the systemic circulation unfiltered and incompletely oxygenated. Pulmonary AVMs occur in HHT2 but are markedly less frequent than in HHT1 - about 5% versus 34% for symptomatic lesions in the French-Italian cohort. That lower frequency does not remove the need for screening, because the consequences of an unscreened lesion are catastrophic rather than gradual.

evidence.snippet: Cerebral arteriovenous malformations were more common in patients with HHT1, but spinal arteriovenous malformations were seen only in patients with HHT2.
evidence.explanation: Carries both halves of this node's neurovascular claim - the lower cerebral and the distinctive spinal burden of HHT2.

evidence.snippet: In addition, cerebral AVMs carry an intrinsic risk of haemorrhagic stroke
evidence.explanation: Supports the intrinsic haemorrhagic risk attributed to the cerebral lesions themselves.

evidence.snippet: Using endothelial-specific inducible Alk1 knockout mice (Alk1iECKO) and regionally resolved single-cell RNA sequencing, we show that loss of ALK1 signaling induces bAVMs predominantly in the perineural vascular plexus (PNVP).
evidence.explanation: Shows that ALK1 loss alone is sufficient to produce brain AVMs, and that they are regionally patterned - the mechanistic counterpart of the cerebral lesion this node represents.

evidence.snippet: Cross-species analyses and validation in human samples demonstrate that KIT expression is conserved in endothelial cells from both sporadic and HHT2 brain AVMs.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in human HHT2 brain AVM tissue the endothelial state that the mouse work identifies, which is the rare point at which this node's cell biology is anchored in human material.

steps/11.description: Arteriovenous malformations arising within the brain or spinal cord itself, distinct from the embolic cerebral complications of a pulmonary shunt. The cerebral lesions are substantially less frequent in HHT2 than in HHT1 - roughly 2% versus 18% in the Spanish registry - but carry an intrinsic risk of haemorrhagic stroke where present. The spinal lesions run the other way: in one cohort they were seen only in HHT2. The two are grouped in one node because the single cohort that separates them reports them together, and because the reciprocal direction of the two genotype effects is the point.

evidence.snippet: Pulmonary hypertension in association with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia can involve mutations in ALK1.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ACVRL1 as a cause of pulmonary hypertension in HHT.

evidence.snippet: We identified amino acid changes in activin-receptor-like kinase 1 that were inherited in subjects who had a disorder with clinical and histologic features indistinguishable from those of primary pulmonary hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Supports the histological identity with idiopathic PAH that makes this a distinct arteriopathy rather than a shunt effect.

steps/12.description: A separate and opposite pulmonary lesion from the pulmonary AVM: obliterative remodelling of small pulmonary arteries producing pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension histologically indistinguishable from the idiopathic disease. ACVRL1 is the HHT gene for which this second disease phenotype is best established, and it means that pulmonary hypertension in an HHT2 patient has two candidate mechanisms - this arteriopathy, and the post-capillary pressure rise from a high-output hepatic shunt - which are managed differently. Marked PROVISIONAL because the intermediate steps linking reduced ALK1 signalling to an occlusive rather than a dilating lesion are not established.

evidence.snippet: ACVRL1 patients developed symptomatic liver disease and anemia more often than ENG patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports the HHT2-specific claim that the anaemia burden is higher in the ACVRL1 genotype.

steps/13.description: Repeated small-volume losses from nasal and gastrointestinal telangiectases exceed dietary iron replacement, depleting iron stores and producing iron-deficiency anaemia. In adults this is the single most common consequence of the disease, and it is more frequent in HHT2 than in HHT1 because of the greater gastrointestinal bleeding burden.

evidence.snippet: Patients with ACVRL1 variants had a higher cardiac index (2.62 vs 3.46), higher levels of hepatic functional blood tests, and anemia (28.5% vs 56.7%) more often than ENG patients.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the elevated cardiac index in ACVRL1 patients alongside the hepatic laboratory abnormality, supporting this node as an HHT2-associated state.

evidence.snippet: left-to-right through systemic AVMs (causing high cardiac output)
evidence.explanation: Names the shunt direction and its haemodynamic consequence.

steps/14.description: Sustained left-to-right shunting through hepatic vascular malformations raises cardiac index. This is a measurable, genotype-associated haemodynamic state - cardiac index is higher in ACVRL1 than in ENG patients - and it is the physiological target of anti-VEGF therapy, which lowers cardiac index rather than removing the malformations.

evidence.snippet: which is right-to-left through pulmonary AVMs (causing ischaemic stroke or cerebral abscess)
evidence.explanation: Names the shunt direction and both cerebral consequences this node routes to.

steps/15.description: With a right-to-left pulmonary shunt in place, particulate matter and bacteraemia that the pulmonary capillary bed would normally clear reach the systemic and cerebral arterial circulation directly, causing paradoxical embolic stroke and metastatic brain abscess. This is the rationale for antibiotic prophylaxis before dental and non-sterile procedures, for air-bubble precautions in intravenous lines, and for the advice against scuba diving in unscreened patients.

evidence.snippet: The most common clinical manifestation is recurrent nosebleeds (epistaxis) beginning on average at age 12 years.
evidence.explanation: Establishes epistaxis as the cardinal manifestation of HHT and gives the syndrome-level age of onset against which the HHT2 delay is measured.

evidence.snippet: Epistaxis occurred later in HHT2, with incomplete penetrance (P<0.0001).
evidence.explanation: The HHT2-specific onset and penetrance claim in this description.

evidence.snippet: We found that epistaxis had an earlier onset in patients with HHT1 than those with HHT2, but the severity by middle ages was similar.
evidence.explanation: Replicates the later onset in HHT2 and adds the important qualifier that the eventual severity converges - so this is a difference in timing, not in ultimate burden.

steps/16.description: Recurrent spontaneous nosebleeds from ruptured nasal mucosal telangiectases; the cardinal and usually earliest manifestation of HHT, and the first Curacao criterion. In HHT2 it begins later than in HHT1 and is incompletely penetrant, so its absence in a young ACVRL1 carrier does not exclude the diagnosis. No frequency is recorded here because the HHT2-specific sources report incomplete penetrance without a percentage.

evidence.snippet: The appearance of telangiectases is generally later than epistaxis but may be during childhood.
evidence.explanation: Gives the relative timing of this feature stated in the description.

evidence.snippet: Truncating mutations were associated with a higher frequency of epistaxis and telangiectasis, in HHT2.
evidence.explanation: Supports the intra-HHT2 variant-class gradient in telangiectasis burden.

steps/17.description: Clusters of dilated post-capillary venules connected directly to dilated arterioles, on the lips, tongue, buccal mucosa, fingers and nose. The second Curacao criterion. In HHT2 they appear later than in HHT1, and truncating ACVRL1 variants carry a higher telangiectasis burden than other variant classes.

evidence.snippet: Gastrointestinal bleeding occurred more frequently in HHT2 (16.4 vs. 6.5%, P=0.017).
evidence.explanation: Source of both the HHT2-specific frequency band recorded here and the genotype comparison in the description.

evidence.snippet: Some individuals with HHT have GI bleeding, which is rarely seen before age 50 years.
evidence.explanation: Supports the age of presentation given in the description.

steps/18.description: Bleeding from gastrointestinal mucosal telangiectases, typically presenting after age 50. Notably more frequent in HHT2 than in HHT1 (16.4% versus 6.5% in the French-Italian cohort), and a major contributor to the higher anaemia burden of the ACVRL1 genotype.

evidence.snippet: Patients with ACVRL1 variants had a higher cardiac index (2.62 vs 3.46), higher levels of hepatic functional blood tests, and anemia (28.5% vs 56.7%) more often than ENG patients.
evidence.explanation: Source of the 56.7% ACVRL1 figure behind the FREQUENT band and of the genotype comparison.

evidence.snippet: In adults, the most frequent HHT manifestations relate to iron deficiency and anaemia owing to recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds) or bleeding from gastrointestinal telangiectases.
evidence.explanation: Supports this being the most frequent adult manifestation, and its bleeding origin.

steps/19.description: Iron-deficiency anaemia from chronic mucosal blood loss, the most frequent adult manifestation of the disease and significantly more common in ACVRL1 than in ENG patients (56.7% versus 28.5% in the Spanish registry).

evidence.snippet: The most common symptoms were epistaxis 521/565 (92%) and fatigue 446/565 (79%).
evidence.explanation: Source of the 79% figure and of the ranking of fatigue immediately behind epistaxis. The cohort is HHT overall, which is why no HHT2 frequency band is claimed.

steps/20.description: Fatigue, reported by 79% of respondents in an international HHT quality-of-life survey and second only to epistaxis as a symptom. It tracks epistaxis severity and is a principal driver of the disability of the disease, over and above the bleeding itself. No frequency band is recorded because the cohort was HHT overall, not genotyped to ACVRL1; it is curated here because chronic anaemia, which HHT2 has more of than HHT1, is one of its causes.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic hepatic involvement was only seen in HHT2 patients.
evidence.explanation: The genotype restriction stated in this description.

evidence.snippet: Hepatic vascular malformations were more common in patients with HHT2.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication in a separate cohort.

steps/21.description: Diffuse hepatic arteriovenous, arterioportal and portovenous shunting. The defining organ involvement of HHT2: in the French-Italian cohort symptomatic hepatic disease occurred only in HHT2 patients, and ACVRL1 patients had higher hepatic laboratory abnormality than ENG patients. Frequency is left unrecorded because the HHT2-specific sources report the genotype contrast rather than a percentage of ACVRL1 carriers affected.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic hepatic AVMs are managed medically; liver transplantation is recommended for individuals who do not respond to medical therapy and who develop refractory high-output heart failure.
evidence.explanation: Confirms refractory high-output heart failure as a recognised hepatic-AVM complication, and its management endpoint.

evidence.snippet: By contrast, ALK1/HHT2 patients are more likely to have liver AVMs and consequent high output heart failure
evidence.explanation: States the HHT2 attribution of this complication and its hepatic derivation in one sentence.

steps/22.description: Decompensated high-output heart failure driven by the volume load of hepatic left-to-right shunting. Historically the indication for liver transplantation, and now the principal indication for systemic anti-VEGF therapy in HHT. Because the shunt is hepatic, this is disproportionately an HHT2 complication.

evidence.snippet: Arteriovenous shunts in the liver may lead to high-output cardiac failure, liver failure, or portal hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Names portal hypertension as a consequence of hepatic arteriovenous shunting, which is the derivation this phenotype records. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the authors' background statement of the human clinical picture rather than a result of the mouse experiments they report.

steps/23.description: Portal hypertension arising from arterioportal shunting within the hepatic vascular malformations, one of the alternative hepatic presentations alongside high cardiac output.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic PAVMs were more frequent in HHT1 (34.4 vs. 5.2%, P<0.001), as were cerebral abscesses (7.5 vs. 0.8%, P=0.002).
evidence.explanation: Source of the symptomatic HHT2 figure behind the OCCASIONAL band.

evidence.snippet: ENG patients were significantly younger at diagnosis (36.9 vs 45.7 years) and had pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) (71.4% vs 24.4%) and cerebral AVMs (17.6% vs 2%) more often than patients with ACVRL1 variants.
evidence.explanation: Source of the screened 24.4% figure, which lands in the same frequency band as the symptomatic estimate.

steps/24.description: Direct pulmonary artery-to-pulmonary vein connection producing a right-to-left shunt. Present in HHT2 but much less often than in HHT1 - 5.2% symptomatic in the French-Italian cohort and 24.4% on screening in the Spanish registry, against 34.4% and 71.4% respectively for HHT1. Screening is still indicated in ACVRL1 carriers because the complications are abrupt.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic PAVMs were more frequent in HHT1 (34.4 vs. 5.2%, P<0.001), as were cerebral abscesses (7.5 vs. 0.8%, P=0.002).
evidence.explanation: Gives the HHT2 abscess rate and shows it tracking the pulmonary AVM difference between the genotypes.

steps/25.description: Metastatic cerebral abscess from bacteraemia crossing an unfiltered right-to-left pulmonary shunt. Rare in HHT2 (0.8% versus 7.5% in HHT1), consistent with the lower pulmonary AVM burden; frequency is omitted because the reported rate is below 1%.

evidence.snippet: which is right-to-left through pulmonary AVMs (causing ischaemic stroke or cerebral abscess)
evidence.explanation: Names the shunt mechanism and the ischaemic outcome recorded here.

steps/26.description: Ischaemic stroke from paradoxical embolism through a right-to-left pulmonary arteriovenous shunt - the reason pulmonary AVMs with a feeding vessel of 2-3 mm or more are occluded prophylactically.

evidence.snippet: ENG patients were significantly younger at diagnosis (36.9 vs 45.7 years) and had pulmonary arteriovenous malformations (AVMs) (71.4% vs 24.4%) and cerebral AVMs (17.6% vs 2%) more often than patients with ACVRL1 variants.
evidence.explanation: Source of the 2% ACVRL1 figure behind the VERY_RARE band.

evidence.snippet: Cerebral arteriovenous malformations were more common in patients with HHT1, but spinal arteriovenous malformations were seen only in patients with HHT2.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication of the lower cerebral AVM burden in HHT2.

steps/27.description: Arteriovenous malformation within the brain, carrying an intrinsic risk of haemorrhagic stroke. Uncommon in HHT2 - 2% of ACVRL1 patients in the Spanish registry against 17.6% of ENG patients.

evidence.snippet: Cerebral arteriovenous malformations were more common in patients with HHT1, but spinal arteriovenous malformations were seen only in patients with HHT2.
evidence.explanation: The sole source for the HHT2 selectivity claim, which is why the description flags it as single-cohort.

steps/28.description: Spinal arteriovenous malformation. Reported as an HHT2-selective lesion: in a US cohort of 111 patients from 34 families, spinal AVMs were seen only in HHT2. This is a single-cohort observation and should be read as a signal rather than a settled genotype restriction.

evidence.snippet: We identified amino acid changes in activin-receptor-like kinase 1 that were inherited in subjects who had a disorder with clinical and histologic features indistinguishable from those of primary pulmonary hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the ACVRL1 attribution and the histological identity with idiopathic PAH stated in the description.

evidence.snippet: We identified suggestive linkage of pulmonary hypertension with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia on chromosome 12q13, a region that includes ALK1.
evidence.explanation: The genetic mapping that ties this phenotype to the ACVRL1 locus rather than to BMPR2.

evidence.snippet: Approximately 20% of patients with ACVRL1-associated HHT develop pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH).
evidence.explanation: The circulating penetrance figure for PAH in ACVRL1 disease. Graded OTHER and flagged INDIRECT because the sentence is a case report's introductory statement citing a further source, not a result of the report itself - the number is recorded with that provenance, and no frequency band is set from it.

evidence.snippet: The reduced penetrance of PAH among ACVRL1 mutation carriers suggests that additional modifiers account for PAH development.
evidence.explanation: Records that PAH is an incompletely penetrant consequence of the ACVRL1 genotype rather than an obligate one, which is why it is curated as a phenotype of HHT2 without a frequency claim.

steps/29.description: Pre-capillary pulmonary arterial hypertension from obliterative remodelling of small pulmonary arteries, clinically and histologically indistinguishable from idiopathic PAH. Among the HHT genes this is best established for ACVRL1, and it is mechanistically distinct from - though it can coexist with - the post-capillary pressure elevation of a high-output hepatic shunt. A figure of about 20% of ACVRL1-associated HHT patients developing PAH is in circulation; the citable statement of it available here is a background sentence in a case report, itself citing a further source, so the number is reported with that provenance rather than used to set a frequency band.

evidence.snippet: Our data suggest a critical role for ALK1 in the control of blood vessel development or repair.
evidence.explanation: The original ACVRL1 report draws exactly this inference - that the mutations act by compromising ALK1's role in vessel development - which is the edge from variant to reduced receptor signalling.

edges/2.description: A single functional ACVRL1 allele delivers less ALK1 receptor to the endothelial surface than the vasculature requires during remodelling.

evidence.snippet: These data further support the second-hit pathophysiological mechanism to explain the multifocality of vascular lesions in HHT.
evidence.explanation: States the causal role of the second hit in lesion genesis, which is the claim this edge makes.

edges/3.description: Loss of the second allele drops ALK1 signalling below the haploinsufficient level within the clone, which is where the lesion forms.

evidence.snippet: The type II receptor phosphorylates ALK1, which in turn phosphorylates SMAD1/5 transcription factors that can then bind to SMAD4 and move to the nucleus to regulate gene expression.
evidence.explanation: Sets out the receptor-to-transcription-factor step that this edge asserts.

edges/4.description: Activated ALK1 is the kinase for SMAD1/5, so less ALK1 activity means less phospho-SMAD1/5 available to partner SMAD4 and enter the nucleus.

evidence.snippet: These mutations are associated with diverse effects, including the vascular dilatation characteristic of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and the occlusion of small pulmonary arteries that is typical of primary pulmonary hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Explicitly attributes both the dilating and the occluding lesion to the same ALK1 mutations, which is the branch this edge records.

edges/5.description: A divergent, and clinically counterintuitive, consequence of ALK1 loss: instead of dilating, small pulmonary arteries occlude. ACVRL1 variants cause a pulmonary vascular disease clinically and histologically indistinguishable from idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension. The intermediate steps that make the pulmonary arterial bed respond this way are not established, which is why the link type is indirect with unknown intermediates rather than direct.

evidence.snippet: Taken together these data point to the essential role of the BMP9/10-ENG-ALK1-SMAD1/5-SMAD4 pathway in protecting the vasculature from AVMs.
evidence.explanation: States the protective function whose loss this edge asserts, drawn from the convergent endothelial-knockout mouse models the review summarises.

edges/6.description: The transcriptional programme this axis maintains is what restrains endothelial proliferation and enforces flow-directed migration; losing it releases both.

evidence.snippet: Altered directional migration of ECs in response to shear stress and increased EC proliferation are now recognised as critical factors driving AVM formation.
evidence.explanation: Names these two cellular defects as the drivers of AVM formation, which is precisely this edge.

edges/7.description: Stalled, over-proliferating endothelium is what builds the direct artery-to-vein channel.

evidence.snippet: Small superficial AVMs in the skin, mouth, nose and gastrointestinal tract are known as telangiectases, and those found in the mucosal tissues are particularly prone to rupture and bleeding, with severe cases leading to anaemia.
evidence.explanation: Makes the causal step from mucosal telangiectasis to rupture and bleeding that both this edge and the gastrointestinal one assert.

edges/13.description: Rupture of nasal mucosal telangiectases is the direct source of the nosebleeds.

evidence.snippet: In adults, the most frequent HHT manifestations relate to iron deficiency and anaemia owing to recurrent epistaxis (nosebleeds) or bleeding from gastrointestinal telangiectases.
evidence.explanation: States the causal chain from mucosal bleeding to iron deficiency and anaemia that this edge records.

evidence.snippet: whilst multiple vascular malformations in the liver can increase venous return to the heart that may result in high output heart failure
evidence.explanation: States the haemodynamic step from hepatic shunting to increased venous return and high-output failure that this edge and the next one carry.

edges/18.description: Hepatic artery-to-hepatic vein shunting returns blood to the right heart without traversing a capillary bed, raising venous return and cardiac output.

evidence.snippet: The only treatment available to restore normal cardiac output in patients with hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) and cardiac failure is liver transplant.
evidence.explanation: Ties the cardiac failure of HHT to the liver as its source - transplant of the liver is what restores cardiac output - which is the direction of causation this edge asserts.

edges/20.description: When the volume load exceeds what the heart can sustain, decompensated high-output failure follows; this is the indication for which liver transplantation was historically the only remedy.

evidence.snippet: even small AVMs increase risk of stroke and brain abscess due to reduced filtering of micro-thrombi and bacteria by pulmonary capillaries
