evidence.explanation: States the loss-of-filtration mechanism, and that even small lesions suffice, which is the claim this edge carries.

edges/22.description: The bypassed alveolar capillary bed is also the filter that removes micro-thrombi and bacteria from returning venous blood.

edges/28.description: Chronic anaemia is one route to the fatigue that dominates patient-reported burden in this disease.

evidence.snippet: Such complications occur most often in the second and third trimesters when maternal changes such as peripheral vasodilation and increased cardiac output are at their maximum.
evidence.explanation: Names the haemodynamic changes - peripheral vasodilation and increased cardiac output - by which pregnancy loads this node, and ties the timing of complications to when they peak.

edges/29.description: The physiological rise in cardiac output and fall in systemic vascular resistance add to the volume load already imposed by hepatic shunting.

evidence.snippet: We report three mutations in the coding sequence of the ALK1 gene in those families which show linkage of the ORW phenotype to chromosome 12.
evidence.explanation: The founding demonstration that ACVRL1 is the HHT2 gene, establishing the gene-disease relationship this block asserts.

evidence.snippet: It includes the activin receptor like kinase 1 gene (ACVRLK1 or ALK1), a member of the serine-threonine kinase receptor family expressed in endothelium.
evidence.explanation: Supports the receptor class and endothelial expression stated in the notes.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in ACVRL1 cluster largely in exons 7 and 8, but ENG mutations were widely distributed within that gene.
evidence.explanation: Supports the statement that reported ACVRL1 variants cluster within the gene.

evidence.snippet: Up to 90% of disease-causal variants are observed in ENG and ACVRL1, with SMAD4 and GDF2 less frequently responsible for HHT.
evidence.explanation: Supports the frequency statement and places ACVRL1 among the two major HHT genes.

genes/0.notes: ACVRL1 (12q13) encodes activin receptor-like kinase 1 (ALK1), a transmembrane serine/threonine kinase type I receptor expressed in vascular endothelium. Germline variants are heterozygous and loss-of-function; both truncating and missense classes occur, and reported variants cluster in the kinase-domain exons. Do not import ENG (9q34, HHT1), SMAD4 (18q21, juvenile polyposis/HHT overlap) or GDF2 (10q11) into this block - those genes define other HHT entities.

evidence.snippet: Oral tranexamic acid or intravenous bevacizumab for epistaxis and GI bleeding; pomalidomide or pazopanib for refractory epistaxis and GI bleeding.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews lists oral tranexamic acid among the targeted therapies for the two bleeding indications recorded here.

treatments/0.description: Oral antifibrinolytic used first-line for epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding. It acts on the consequence of the lesions - haemostasis at the bleeding site - and not on the vascular malformation itself.

evidence.snippet: In this preliminary study of patients with HHT associated with severe hepatic vascular malformations and high cardiac output, administration of bevacizumab was associated with a decrease in cardiac output and reduced duration and number of episodes of epistaxis.
evidence.explanation: The trial's own conclusion, covering both indications recorded here.

evidence.snippet: The most severe adverse events were 2 cases of grade 3 systemic hypertension, which were successfully treated.
evidence.explanation: Records the safety signal reported alongside the efficacy result.

treatments/1.description: Intravenous anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody. The most HHT2-relevant systemic therapy: in a phase II trial of patients with severe hepatic vascular malformations and high cardiac output, bevacizumab lowered cardiac index in 20 of 24 patients and also reduced epistaxis duration. Before this, liver transplantation was the only way to restore cardiac output in these patients. It works upstream of the bleeding, on the excess VEGF-driven angiogenic drive released by loss of ALK1 signalling, rather than on haemostasis.

evidence.snippet: Of the 24 patients who had echocardiograms available for reread, there was a response in 20 of 24 patients with normalization of cardiac index (complete response [CR]) in 3 of 24, partial response (PR) in 17 of 24, and no response in 4 cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the effect on the exact haemodynamic node this treatment targets.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: The measured endpoint of the phase II trial was cardiac index, which this node represents.

evidence.snippet: Disruption of the ENG/ALK1 signalling pathway also affects EC responses to vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) and crosstalk between ECs and vascular smooth muscle cells.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the VEGF-responsiveness change that makes this node an anti-VEGF target; indirect in that it explains why the drug works rather than reporting the clinical effect.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Mechanistic rationale: the BMP9/10-ALK1 pathway normally damps endothelial responses to VEGF, so sequestering VEGF substitutes for part of what the lost pathway did.

evidence.snippet: At 24 weeks, the mean difference between the pomalidomide group and the placebo group in the change from baseline in the Epistaxis Severity Score was -0.94 points (95% confidence interval [CI], -1.57 to -0.31; P = 0.004).
evidence.explanation: The randomised efficacy estimate recorded in this description.

evidence.snippet: Adverse events that were more common in the pomalidomide group than in the placebo group included neutropenia, constipation, and rash.
evidence.explanation: The toxicity profile recorded alongside the efficacy claim.

evidence.snippet: Characteristics associated with a less robust response were older age (0.29 [95% CI, 0.05-0.53] per 10 years older, P = .02) and underlying ACVRL1 germ line mutation (0.62 [95% CI, -0.04 to 1.27] vs ENG, SMAD4, or mutation not known, P = .06]
evidence.explanation: The ACVRL1 response signal recorded in this description, with the effect size and the P value that make it a trend rather than a finding. This is the only place in the therapeutic literature where HHT2 genotype is reported to matter.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, pomalidomide was effective for HHT-associated epistaxis over extended durations, albeit with nontrivial potential toxicities, and may be considered for certain patients with HHT.
evidence.explanation: The durability conclusion recorded in this description, from a cohort of 62 patients followed for up to 4.4 years.

evidence.snippet: Pomalidomide was less effective for gastrointestinal bleeding than for epistaxis, particularly in patients with high red blood cell transfusion requirements.
evidence.explanation: The compartment-specific limitation, which matters here because gastrointestinal bleeding is the compartment HHT2 has more of.

treatments/2.description: Oral immunomodulatory agent for refractory epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding. In a randomised placebo-controlled trial it reduced the Epistaxis Severity Score by 0.94 points more than placebo - above the 0.71-point threshold considered clinically significant - with neutropenia, constipation and rash as the excess adverse events. The trial was stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy. It was not stratified by genotype, but a post-hoc response analysis found ACVRL1 germline mutation among the characteristics associated with a *less* robust response (+0.62 ESS points versus ENG, SMAD4 or unknown genotype). That is a trend at P=0.06, not a result - but it is the first genotype signal for treatment stratification in HHT, and it points the wrong way for this entity, so it is recorded here rather than left in the trial literature. An open-label extension followed 62 patients for up to 4.4 years and found the epistaxis benefit durable, while noting that pomalidomide was less effective for gastrointestinal bleeding - the bleeding compartment that is disproportionately HHT2's.

evidence.snippet: Intravenous bevacizumab, oral pazopanib, and oral thalidomide are the three targeted primary angiogenesis inhibitors, with multiple studies describing both reassuring safety and impressive effectiveness in the treatment of moderate-to-severe HHT-associated bleeding.
evidence.explanation: Places pazopanib among the established antiangiogenic options for HHT bleeding, which is the claim this treatment records.

evidence.snippet: Oral tranexamic acid or intravenous bevacizumab for epistaxis and GI bleeding; pomalidomide or pazopanib for refractory epistaxis and GI bleeding.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews places pazopanib in the refractory-bleeding line recorded here.

treatments/3.description: Oral multikinase VEGFR inhibitor, listed by GeneReviews alongside pomalidomide for refractory epistaxis and gastrointestinal bleeding, and one of the three primary angiogenesis inhibitors in current HHT practice. Evidence is observational rather than randomised.

evidence.snippet: Intravenous bevacizumab, oral pazopanib, and oral thalidomide are the three targeted primary angiogenesis inhibitors, with multiple studies describing both reassuring safety and impressive effectiveness in the treatment of moderate-to-severe HHT-associated bleeding.
evidence.explanation: Places thalidomide among the established antiangiogenic options for HHT bleeding.

evidence.snippet: bevacizumab and pazopanib inhibit angiogenesis, while thalidomide bolsters blood vessel maturation
evidence.explanation: Source of the mechanistic distinction drawn in this description between thalidomide and the VEGF-directed agents.

treatments/4.description: Oral antiangiogenic used for HHT-associated bleeding, described as acting by bolstering blood-vessel maturation rather than by blocking VEGF outright. The third of the three established angiogenesis inhibitors in HHT practice.

evidence.snippet: GI bleeding and anemia is treated with iron replacement therapy and (if needed) blood transfusions.
evidence.explanation: The management recorded here.

treatments/5.description: Iron replacement, with red-cell transfusion where symptomatic anaemia persists, for the chronic blood loss that dominates adult HHT2. Iron replacement is preferred over transfusion, including in pregnancy.

evidence.snippet: Pulmonary AVMs with a feeding vessel 2-3 mm or greater in diameter typically require occlusion for stroke prevention.
evidence.explanation: The size threshold and the prophylactic indication recorded here.

treatments/6.description: Occlusion of pulmonary AVMs with a feeding vessel of 2-3 mm or greater, done for stroke prevention rather than for symptoms. This is prophylaxis against the paradoxical-embolism pathway, and it remains indicated in HHT2 despite the lower lesion frequency.

treatments/6/targets/0.description: Occluding the shunt restores passage of returning venous blood through the alveolar capillary filter.

evidence.snippet: Symptomatic hepatic AVMs are managed medically; liver transplantation is recommended for individuals who do not respond to medical therapy and who develop refractory high-output heart failure.
evidence.explanation: The indication and its position after medical therapy, as recorded here.

treatments/7.description: Reserved for refractory high-output heart failure from hepatic vascular malformations that has not responded to medical therapy. Because the hepatic burden is the HHT2-predominant one, this is disproportionately a consideration in ACVRL1 patients.

treatments/7/targets/0.description: Transplantation removes the shunting organ, which is the source of the volume load.

evidence.snippet: When pulmonary shunting is present, use antibiotic prophylaxis for dental and non-sterile invasive procedures, taking care to prevent air bubbles from being introduced in intravenous lines; this may include an air filter when available and compatible with the medication being administered.
evidence.explanation: The prophylaxis recommendation recorded here.

evidence.snippet: anticoagulant and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory agents that interfere with clotting (including aspirin) should be avoided in individuals with significant nose or GI bleeding unless required for treatment of other medical condition; scuba diving unless TCE within the last five years was negative for evidence of a right-to-left shunt; liver biopsy.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews Agents/Circumstances to Avoid list, captured here because it is drug-safety guidance rather than general advice.

treatments/8.description: Where pulmonary shunting is present, antibiotic prophylaxis before dental and non-sterile invasive procedures and prevention of air bubbles in intravenous lines. GeneReviews additionally lists agents and circumstances to avoid in HHT: vigorous nose blowing, heavy lifting, straining at stool, finger manipulation in the nose, anticoagulants and NSAIDs including aspirin in those with significant bleeding unless otherwise required, scuba diving unless contrast echocardiography within five years was negative for right-to-left shunt, and liver biopsy.

evidence.snippet: Molecular genetic testing should be offered to at-risk family members if the germline pathogenic variant has been identified in the family.
evidence.explanation: The cascade-testing recommendation recorded here.

treatments/9.description: Autosomal dominant transmission with a 50% recurrence risk per child, and age-dependent penetrance that makes clinical assessment of young relatives unreliable, together make predictive ACVRL1 testing the primary route to identifying affected family members once the familial variant is known.

evidence.snippet: In this latter context, high local BMP9 concentrations (BMP9 is made in the liver) could make hepatic ECs less dependent on ENG and more dependent on ALK1 activity.
evidence.explanation: States the hypothesis in the reviewers' own words, and its hedged phrasing ("could make") is why this is recorded as EMERGING rather than canonical. Graded OTHER because the sentence is the review authors' proposed explanation rather than a result from any single study design.

evidence.snippet: It is possible that ENG and ALK1 interact with different partner proteins in different vascular beds to elicit differential downstream signalling.
evidence.explanation: Records the competing bed-specific-partner account named in the description.

hypotheses/0.description: Why HHT2 is the hepatic form of HHT is not settled. Endoglin facilitates but is not strictly required for BMP9/BMP10 signalling through ALK1, so if the two proteins acted purely in series HHT1 and HHT2 should look alike, and they do not. One proposed explanation is regional ligand availability: BMP9 is produced in the liver, so hepatic endothelial cells sit in a high-ligand environment in which the ligand-capturing contribution of endoglin matters less and the signalling contribution of ALK1 matters more. Losing one ACVRL1 allele would then bite harder in the liver than losing one ENG allele does. An alternative, not mutually exclusive, account is that ENG and ALK1 recruit different partner proteins in different vascular beds. Both are hypotheses about the ligand/receptor economy of specific vascular beds; neither has been demonstrated in human hepatic tissue.

evidence.snippet: However, this is not the case and there are clear genotype/phenotype correlations in HHT that are not understood.
evidence.explanation: The review states plainly that the genotype-phenotype split this entry curates is unexplained, which is the gap recorded here.

open_questions/0.rationale: Endoglin and ALK1 act in the same BMP9/10 receptor complex, with endoglin facilitating rather than being strictly required for ALK1 signalling. On a simple series model HHT1 and HHT2 should therefore differ in severity, not in organ distribution - and yet the organ distribution is exactly what separates them, reproducibly, across independent French-Italian, US and Spanish cohorts. The candidate explanations on offer are hypotheses about vascular-bed-specific ligand economy (BMP9 is made in the liver, so hepatic endothelium may lean on ALK1 rather than on endoglin for ligand capture) and about bed-specific interaction partners. Neither has been tested in human hepatic tissue, and neither predicts the reciprocal pulmonary and cerebral bias of HHT1. Until one is established, the genotype-phenotype correlation that drives HHT2 surveillance is an empirical regularity rather than a mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These mutations are associated with diverse effects, including the vascular dilatation characteristic of hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia and the occlusion of small pulmonary arteries that is typical of primary pulmonary hypertension.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the same ACVRL1 mutations produce both a dilating and an occluding vascular lesion, which is what creates the ambiguity this discussion records.

open_questions/1.rationale: ACVRL1 is the one HHT gene in which pulmonary hypertension has two mechanistically opposite routes. One is a pre-capillary arteriopathy in which small pulmonary arteries occlude, histologically indistinguishable from idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension - the mirror image of the vascular dilatation that defines HHT everywhere else in the body. The other is the elevated pulmonary pressure that follows the volume load of hepatic left-to-right shunting, which is the HHT2-predominant complication. The two coexist in the same genotype and are separated by right heart catheterisation rather than by genetics, and they diverge in management: the hepatic route responds to reducing the shunt burden, the arteriopathy does not. This entry models them as separate nodes deliberately so that the distinction is not collapsed into a single "pulmonary hypertension in HHT2" claim.

evidence.snippet: The recommendations highlight new evidence in existing topics from the first International HHT Guidelines and provide guidance in 3 new areas: anemia, pediatrics, and pregnancy and delivery.
evidence.explanation: The guideline structure is organised by clinical domain rather than by causal gene, which is the observation this gap rests on.

evidence.snippet: Characteristics associated with a less robust response were older age (0.29 [95% CI, 0.05-0.53] per 10 years older, P = .02) and underlying ACVRL1 germ line mutation (0.62 [95% CI, -0.04 to 1.27] vs ENG, SMAD4, or mutation not known, P = .06]
evidence.explanation: The one genotype signal this gap points at, with the P value that keeps it a trend.

evidence.snippet: In conclusion, several baseline patient and disease characteristics were associated with pomalidomide response, findings that may help guide patient selection for the use of pomalidomide in HHT.
evidence.explanation: The authors frame their own result as hypothesis-generating for patient selection, which is why this entry records it as a gap rather than as a recommendation.

open_questions/2.rationale: The therapeutic evidence base for HHT is enrolled on phenotype, not genotype. The pomalidomide trial randomised on epistaxis severity and anaemia; the guideline recommendations are written for HHT as a whole. The one partial exception runs the other way and favours this entity: the bevacizumab trial selected patients with severe hepatic vascular malformations and high cardiac output, which is the HHT2-predominant presentation, without stating genotype. So the treatments recorded in this entry are ones with established efficacy in HHT that are applied to HHT2 patients. Reading any of them as an ACVRL1-specific recommendation would overstate what the trials tested. One signal does exist and it runs against this entity: a post-hoc analysis of PATH-HHT found ACVRL1 germline mutation among the characteristics associated with a less robust pomalidomide response, at P=0.06. A trend in a post-hoc analysis of a trial that did not randomise on genotype is not a basis for withholding an effective drug from HHT2 patients, and the entry does not treat it as one. It is recorded because it is the only genotype signal in HHT therapeutics and because the study that would settle it - a prospective genotype-stratified trial - has not been done.

evidence.snippet: The mutations induce a permanent shift in the substrate preference from L-serine to L-alanine, which results in the pathological formation of atypical and neurotoxic 1-deoxy-sphingolipids (1-deoxySL).
evidence.explanation: States the substrate shift and the novel product, which is what makes this a neomorphic rather than a loss-of-function change.

evidence.snippet: Despite earlier reports, canonical activity with l-serine was not reduced in any of the investigated SPT mutants.
evidence.explanation: A uniform isotope-labelling re-assay of eleven SPTLC1 and six SPTLC2 mutants finds canonical activity intact, which is the specific evidence against grading these variants as loss of function.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrate that these mutations result in a partial to complete loss of SPT activity in vitro and in vivo.
evidence.explanation: The founding SPTLC2 report's contrary finding of reduced SPT activity, curated as REFUTE against the neomorphic reading rather than omitted. The later uniform re-assay above is why the entry follows the substrate-shift model; both are kept so the disagreement stays visible.

steps/1.description: Serine palmitoyltransferase condenses palmitoyl-CoA with L-serine in the first and rate-limiting step of de novo sphingolipid synthesis. HSAN1 missense variants in the SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 subunits impose a permanent shift in substrate preference from L-serine towards L-alanine. The variant enzyme therefore acquires an activity the wild-type enzyme does not have, which is why the genetic context is recorded as NEOMORPHIC rather than as a loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, they cause the accumulation of the atypical and neurotoxic sphingoid metabolite 1-deoxy-sphinganine.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the SPTLC2 variants generate the atypical metabolite, independently of the disputed activity finding in the same paper.

evidence.snippet: Affected family members showed elevated 1-deoxysphingolipid plasma levels.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the accumulation in affected people rather than only in a cell-based assay, which is what makes the node a human disease mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Levels of these abnormal compounds are elevated in blood of HSN-1 patients
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation that the metabolites are elevated in patients. The statement summarises prior work rather than this paper's own measurement, which is its own in vitro neurotoxicity result.

steps/2.description: 1-deoxysphingolipids lack the C1 hydroxyl group of a canonical sphingoid base. That hydroxyl is required both for conversion into complex sphingolipids and for entry into the normal degradation route, so these metabolites accumulate rather than turning over. They are measurable in patient plasma by LC-MS, which makes this node the disease's accessible biomarker as well as its mechanism.

evidence.snippet: we show that exogenous application of these deoxysphingoid bases causes dose- and time-dependent neurotoxicity in primary mammalian neurons, as determined by analysis of cell survival and neurite length
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that the accumulated metabolites kill neurons, with a dose-response, which is the evidence that the accumulation node causes this one.

evidence.snippet: The changes in intracellular Ca2+ handling are accompanied by an early loss of mitochondrial membrane potential in deoxysphingoid base-treated motor and sensory neurons.
evidence.explanation: Names the proximate subcellular mechanism this node asserts.

steps/3.description: Deoxysphingoid bases are toxic to primary sensory and motor neurons, with disturbed endoplasmic-reticulum and mitochondrial calcium handling and loss of mitochondrial membrane potential as proximate cellular effects. Degeneration is length-dependent, so the longest sensory axons in the lower limbs fail first, which is why the clinical picture begins in the feet.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type 1 (HSAN1) causes sensory loss that predominantly affects the lower limbs, often preceded by hyperpathia and spontaneous shooting or lancinating pain.
evidence.explanation: Describes the distribution and the pain that often precedes it. The sentence is the paper's framing of the disease rather than its own measurement.

steps/4.description: Length-dependent distal sensory loss predominantly affecting the lower limbs, spreading proximally, and often preceded by spontaneous lancinating pain. This is the presenting feature of HSAN1.

evidence.snippet: Hereditary sensory and autonomic neuropathy type I (HSAN-I) is an axonal peripheral neuropathy associated with progressive distal sensory loss and severe ulcerations.
evidence.explanation: Names severe ulceration as a defining feature of the disease the SPTLC2 families present with. The sentence introduces the disease rather than reporting this paper's own finding.

evidence.snippet: most patients develop complications, such as recurrent ulcers and osteomyelitis, making amputations commonplace
evidence.explanation: Establishes that ulceration and its sequelae affect most patients, which is the basis for treating this as a dominant clinical problem rather than an occasional one.

steps/5.description: Severe ulceration of insensate distal extremities. This is the complication that dominates long-term morbidity; osteomyelitis and amputation follow from it.

edges/1.description: Condensation of palmitoyl-CoA with L-alanine instead of L-serine yields deoxysphinganine, and with glycine yields deoxymethylsphinganine.

edges/2.description: Accumulated deoxysphingoid bases are directly neurotoxic to sensory neurons.

edges/3.description: Loss of the longest sensory axons produces the length-dependent distal sensory deficit.

edges/4.description: Insensate feet sustain unnoticed injury, which ulcerates and heals poorly.

evidence.snippet: No mutations were found in SPTLC3, but we identified three heterozygous missense mutations in the SPTLC2 subunit of SPT in four families presenting with a typical HSAN-I phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Establishes SPTLC2 as causative and, in the same sentence, excludes SPTLC3, which is why HSAN1C is an SPTLC2 entity specifically.

evidence.snippet: This study identifies the SPTLC2 N177D variant as a novel disease-causing mutation with increased 1-deoxySL formation and its association with a typical HSAN1 phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Adds a further causative allele and ties it to the same biochemical mechanism.

genes/0.notes: Heterozygous missense variants. The founding report screened 78 HSAN patients and found three SPTLC2 variants in four families; SPTLC3, the third SPT subunit, carried none, and none has been found there since. Later reports add N177D and others, and patients with SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 variants are described as clinically indistinguishable.

evidence.snippet: In mice bearing a transgene expressing the C133W SPTLC1 mutant linked to HSAN1, a 10% L-serine–enriched diet reduced dSL levels. L-serine supplementation also improved measures of motor and sensory performance as well as measures of male fertility.
evidence.explanation: The functional-outcome evidence comes from the mouse arm, not from patients, and the transgene is an SPTLC1 mutant rather than SPTLC2. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM for that reason.

evidence.snippet: In contrast, a 10% L-alanine–enriched diet increased dSL levels and led to severe peripheral neuropathy.
evidence.explanation: The reciprocal alanine arm moves both the metabolite and the phenotype in the opposite direction, which is the strongest available test that substrate competition is the operative mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that oral supplementation of L-serine decreases 1-deoxySL in HSAN1C without major global effects on metabolism.
evidence.explanation: The only study of this treatment in HSAN1C itself rather than in HSAN1A or the SPTLC1 mouse. Establishes the biochemical effect and the safety profile in an SPTLC2 carrier.

evidence.snippet: Based on this single case and one-year follow-up, we cannot conclude whether the achieved 1-deoxySL reduction was sufficient to stop or slow the progression of the disease.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own limit on what the study establishes. Curated as SUPPORT for the treatment while recording that the functional question is open - this is the sentence that makes the metabolite a surrogate rather than an outcome.

evidence.snippet: Our patient underwent a 52-wk treatment in which the L-serine dose was titrated up to 400 mg/kg/day.
evidence.explanation: Records the dose and duration, which the entry previously did not carry anywhere.

treatments/0.description: Substrate competition rather than enzyme replacement: supplying excess L-serine shifts the mutant enzyme back towards its canonical substrate and lowers 1-deoxysphingolipid production. Shown in a transgenic mouse model and in a 14-patient pilot study, and reported in HSAN1C itself in a 52-week single-patient study that titrated to 400 mg/kg/day and halved serum 1-deoxysphingolipid without demonstrating a functional benefit.

evidence.snippet: In a pilot study with 14 HSAN1 patients, L-serine supplementation similarly reduced dSL levels.
evidence.explanation: Shows the intervention lowers the mechanistic metabolite in patients, which is the specific claim this link makes. It does not show a clinical benefit; see the attached discussion.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Excess dietary L-serine competes with L-alanine at the mutant enzyme's active site, reducing formation of the neurotoxic metabolite.

open_questions/0.rationale: The founding SPTLC2 report measured partial to complete loss of SPT activity; a later study re-assaying eleven SPTLC1 and six SPTLC2 mutants by a uniform isotope-labelling method found canonical activity was not reduced in any of them, and that three variants showed increased canonical activity. The two are not reconciled in the literature, and the difference is not cosmetic: it decides whether this is a neomorphic or a loss-of-function disease, and therefore whether substrate competition alone is the right therapeutic principle. This entry follows the later uniform re-assay, on the grounds that it compares mutants under one method, and keeps the earlier result as a REFUTE item rather than discarding it.

open_questions/1.rationale: The only evidence that L-serine improves sensory and motor function, as opposed to lowering the metabolite, comes from a mouse carrying an SPTLC1 mutation. The human pilot study reports the biochemical effect only, and that effect is a surrogate endpoint. Since HSAN1C is by definition an SPTLC2 disease, both the species and the subunit differ from the model that carries the functional claim. The shared downstream metabolite is the reason to expect transfer, and the observation that SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 patients are clinically indistinguishable strengthens it. The gap is narrower than absence: a 52-week single-patient study in an SPTLC2 p.(Arg183Trp) carrier did record functional outcomes alongside the metabolite, and they were inconclusive - the neuropathy score did not improve and the authors decline to say whether progression was slowed. So the question is not whether SPTLC2 human data exist but whether an n-of-1 year-long observation can answer it, and the answer is no.

open_questions/2.rationale: Principal component analysis of sphingoid bases clustered SPT mutations into three groups corresponding to no, mild and severe phenotype, and the clusters mapped onto position in a homology model, with active-site mutations mild and surface mutations severe. That is a strong claim for a disease this rare, and it was made across SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 mutants together. Whether it holds within the SPTLC2 subset alone, and prospectively rather than on the mutants used to derive it, has not been tested.

evidence.snippet: A 2010 review of the literature identified several risk factors that had been consistently identified as occurring more frequently among cases of HPE, including maternal diabetes, twinning, and a predominance of females
evidence.explanation: A CDC systematic review of the epidemiologic literature identifies maternal diabetes as one of the risk factors consistently associated with holoprosencephaly.

evidence.snippet: Pregnancy associated risk associated with holoprosencephaly included maternal pregestational diabetes (9.2% of cases and 0 controls, p = .02)
evidence.explanation: A case-control study quantifies the association: pregestational diabetes in 9.2% of holoprosencephaly cases versus none of the controls.

evidence.snippet: Following ethanol exposure, mean dysmorphology scores were increased by 3.2- and 6.6-fold in Shh(+/-) and Gli2(+/-) groups, respectively, relative to their wildtype littermates.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the gene-environment amplification of ethanol teratogenicity by Gli2 haploinsufficiency in mice.

evidence.snippet: mice with single-allele Gli2 mutations exhibit increased penetrance and severity of HPE in response to low-dose teratogen exposure
evidence.explanation: Establishes low-dose teratogen exposure as the environmental arm of the gene-environment interaction.

evidence.snippet: All predict a truncated protein with loss of the C-terminal activator domain.
evidence.explanation: Identifies loss of the C-terminal activator domain as the shared molecular consequence of the pathogenic truncating alleles.

evidence.snippet: We also demonstrate that these mutations lack GLI2 activity.
evidence.explanation: Frog-embryo and C3H10T1/2 osteogenic-induction assays show the patient alleles have no GLI2 activity, confirming loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in the human GLI2 gene are associated with a distinctive phenotype (within the HPE spectrum) whose primary features include defective anterior pituitary formation and pan-hypopituitarism, with or without overt forebrain cleavage abnormalities, and HPE-like midfacial hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: Gene-discovery paper characterising the causal GLI2 alleles as loss of function.

steps/4.description: A heterozygous truncating variant, pathogenic zinc-finger missense variant, or whole-gene 2q14.2 deletion removes or inactivates one GLI2 allele. Truncating alleles delete the C-terminal transcriptional activation domain, so the residual protein cannot drive Hedgehog target-gene transcription.

evidence.snippet: Gli2 is one of three vertebrate transcription factors implicated as obligatory mediators of Shh signal transduction.
evidence.explanation: Places GLI2 as an obligatory transducer of the Hedgehog signal, the step that is dose-reduced here.

evidence.snippet: None of the mutant alleles manifested dominant negative activity in these studies.
evidence.explanation: Co-injection experiments with wild-type GLI2 found no dominant-negative activity, supporting simple haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Functional assays confirmed the pathogenicity of the identified variant and revealed a dominant-negative effect of mutant GLI2 on Hedgehog signalling.
evidence.explanation: A C-terminal frameshift allele (p.P1167LfsX52) behaved as a dominant negative in cell-based assays, so haploinsufficiency may not be the mechanism for every pathogenic allele. Marked PARTIAL because it qualifies rather than supports the haploinsufficiency model.

steps/5.description: GLI2 is the principal activator among the three vertebrate GLI transcription factors that transduce the Hedgehog signal. With one allele inactivated, the dose of full-length GLI2 activator available for nuclear translocation and target-gene activation falls. The mutant alleles show no dominant-negative activity in the original functional assays, so the mechanism is haploinsufficiency rather than poisoning of the wild-type product - although a later C-terminal frameshift allele did display a dominant-negative effect, leaving room for allele-specific mechanisms.

evidence.snippet: This genetic predisposition is associated with a Gli2 dosage-dependent attenuation of Hedgehog ligand responsiveness at the cellular level.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates that Gli2 gene dosage sets the magnitude of cellular Hedgehog responsiveness, the central effector step of this disease.

evidence.snippet: GLI2 is a downstream transcription factor in Sonic Hedgehog signalling, acting early in ventral forebrain and pituitary development.
evidence.explanation: Locates GLI2 in the Hedgehog cascade and names the two tissues whose development is most dependent on it.

steps/6.description: Reduced GLI2 activator dose lowers transcriptional output of the Hedgehog pathway in responding cells. Mouse work shows this is not an all-or-nothing switch: Gli2 heterozygosity produces a dosage-dependent attenuation of Hedgehog ligand responsiveness at the cellular level, which is compatible with normal development at baseline but leaves the pathway with less reserve.

evidence.snippet: The secreted protein Shh acts as a crucial factor that patterns the ventral forebrain and is required for the division of the primordial eye field and brain into two discrete halves.
evidence.explanation: States the developmental process that GLI2-dependent Hedgehog output serves in the ventral forebrain.

evidence.snippet: We have found that the floor plate throughout the midbrain, hindbrain and spinal cord does not form in Gli2 homozygotes.
evidence.explanation: Mouse null data show Gli2 is required for ventral midline (floor plate) induction, the CNS-patterning step disrupted in this node.

evidence.snippet: On the C57BL/6J background, homozygous GLI2 loss of function results in the characteristic brain and facial features seen in severe human HPE, including midfacial hypoplasia, hypotelorism and medial forebrain deficiency with loss of ventral neurospecification.
evidence.explanation: Shows that complete Gli2 loss reproduces the human midline forebrain and face phenotype, linking this node to its clinical consequence.

steps/7.description: Hedgehog signalling from the prechordal plate ventralizes the rostral neuroepithelium and drives the midline separation of the eye field and prosencephalon. Reduced GLI2-dependent output impairs this midline induction. In the mouse, complete Gli2 loss abolishes the floor plate and, on a permissive genetic background, reproduces the medial forebrain deficiency and midfacial hypoplasia of severe human holoprosencephaly; in humans the heterozygous state usually leaves cleavage intact and manifests only as midfacial hypoplasia and hypotelorism.

evidence.snippet: Our data support a growing body of evidence that Shh signaling is necessary for an early step in pituitary formation
evidence.explanation: Places the GLI2-dependent requirement at an early step of pituitary organogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Gli2 mutant mice have hypoplastic anterior and absent posterior pituitary glands.
evidence.explanation: Mouse data directly demonstrate that Gli2 loss disrupts development of both pituitary lobes.

evidence.snippet: The observation argues that overall inhibition of Shh-Gli signaling leads the adenohypophysis anlage to transdifferentiate into lens.
evidence.explanation: Zebrafish gli2 (you-too) mutants show that Shh-Gli signalling maintains adenohypophyseal identity; its loss redirects the pituitary primordium to a lens fate.

evidence.snippet: It is the pituitary and facial structures that are the most sensitive to a reduction in GLI2 activity.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the pituitary as the tissue most sensitive to reduced GLI2 dose in humans, explaining why hypopituitarism dominates the phenotype.

steps/8.description: Hedgehog signalling is required at an early step of pituitary formation, when Rathke pouch is induced from the oral ectoderm beneath the ventral diencephalon. Reduced GLI2 activator output impairs anterior pituitary specification and growth and disturbs the descent/positioning of the posterior lobe, producing anterior pituitary hypoplasia with an ectopic posterior pituitary and interrupted stalk. Gli2 mutant mice have hypoplastic anterior and absent posterior pituitary glands, and in zebrafish loss of Gli-mediated signalling causes the adenohypophyseal anlage to transdifferentiate into lens.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent phenotypic feature is post-axial polydactyly (65%) which is also the mildest phenotypic expression of the condition, reported in many parents of individuals with systemic findings.
evidence.explanation: Establishes postaxial polydactyly as the most frequent and mildest expression of a pathogenic GLI2 variant.

evidence.snippet: His father and a six-year-old brother with the identical mutation also had unilateral postaxial polydactyly and mid-facial hypoplasia although there was no pituitary hormone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Shows postaxial polydactyly occurring as the isolated manifestation in relatives carrying the identical GLI2 splice variant.

steps/9.description: Hedgehog signalling from the zone of polarizing activity, read out through the GLI transcription factors, specifies digit number and identity along the anteroposterior axis of the limb bud. Reduced GLI2 activator dose perturbs this readout and produces an extra postaxial digit. This is the most prevalent manifestation of a pathogenic GLI2 variant and the mildest expression of the condition - frequently the only finding in a transmitting parent.

evidence.snippet: Subsequently, anophthalmia plus orbital anomalies, heminasal aplasia, branchial arch anomalies and polydactyly have also been incorporated into the general phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Documents branchial arch and orbital anomalies as part of the GLI2 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Novel sequence variants were found in the GLI2 gene in patients with marked involvement of the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), a new clinical finding observed with mutations of this gene.
evidence.explanation: Adds temporomandibular joint involvement, a first-arch derivative, to the craniofacial arm of the phenotype.

steps/10.description: Beyond the midline, reduced Hedgehog output perturbs patterning of the first branchial arch and its derivatives and of the developing palate and orbit, producing midface hypoplasia, orofacial clefting, temporomandibular joint anomalies, and - at the severe end - orbital anomalies with anophthalmia or microphthalmia and heminasal aplasia.

evidence.snippet: Although normally indistinguishable from wild-type littermates, we demonstrate that mice with single-allele Gli2 mutations exhibit increased penetrance and severity of HPE in response to low-dose teratogen exposure.
evidence.explanation: The defining gene-environment experiment: Gli2 heterozygosity is silent alone but converts a subthreshold teratogen exposure into holoprosencephaly.

evidence.snippet: While Shh(+/-) and Gli2(+/-) mice have been described as phenotypically normal, these results illustrate a functional haploinsufficiency of both genes in combination with ethanol exposure.
evidence.explanation: Independent replication with prenatal ethanol as the second hit, supporting the reduced-buffering model.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with prior reports, we observed incomplete penetrance of the deletion in the family, illustrating the multifactorial etiology of holoprosencephaly spectrum features.
evidence.explanation: Human family data showing the same incomplete penetrance the mouse model explains.

steps/11.description: A single functional GLI2 allele is usually sufficient for normal development, which is why so many carriers are unaffected. What haploinsufficiency removes is reserve: the pathway becomes dose-limited and therefore vulnerable to a second genetic or environmental hit during the first-trimester patterning window. Mice heterozygous for a Gli2 null allele are indistinguishable from wild-type littermates at baseline but show markedly increased penetrance and severity of holoprosencephaly after low-dose teratogen or ethanol exposure. This provides the mechanistic account of the incomplete penetrance that defines the human disorder, but the specific human second hits remain unidentified.

evidence.snippet: The index case of family 1 had polydactyly, hypoglycemia, and seizures, and GH, TSH, prolactin, ACTH, LH, and FSH deficiencies.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates the multi-axis anterior pituitary hormone deficiency produced by a truncating GLI2 variant.

evidence.snippet: Most patients with a GLI2 variant (21/23, 91%) had hypopituitarism, including 21.7% (5/23) presenting isolated growth hormone deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the hormonal phenotype in the largest cohort of pathogenic GLI2 variants, including the isolated-GH-deficiency subset.

steps/12.description: Structural anterior pituitary failure translates into deficiency of one or more anterior pituitary hormones - most often growth hormone, frequently combined with TSH, ACTH, prolactin and gonadotropin deficiency, and occasionally with antidiuretic hormone deficiency (diabetes insipidus) when the posterior lobe axis is involved. Clinically this presents as neonatal hypoglycaemia and cholestasis, micropenis and cryptorchidism in male infants, and growth failure in childhood.

evidence.snippet: A common facial phenotype was seen in individuals (with midface hypoplasia, cleft lip/palate and hypotelorism) with truncating mutations.
evidence.explanation: Defines the recurrent midline facial gestalt of GLI2 truncating variants.

evidence.snippet: HPE (6%) or other brain structure abnormalities (15%)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how much of the GLI2 morbidity spectrum is structural brain malformation.

steps/13.description: The structural end-point of impaired midline patterning: most commonly subtle midface hypoplasia, hypotelorism, orofacial clefting and a solitary median maxillary central incisor, and less commonly overt lobar or semilobar holoprosencephaly. The severity of the brain malformation is the dominant determinant of neurodevelopmental outcome.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent phenotypic feature is post-axial polydactyly (65%)
evidence.explanation: Postaxial polydactyly is the most prevalent manifestation across 60 individuals with pathogenic GLI2 variants.

steps/14.description: An extra digit on the ulnar or fibular side of the hand or foot, unilateral or bilateral. It is the single most frequent finding in GLI2 variant carriers and is often the only clue that an apparently unaffected parent is a carrier.

evidence.snippet: Pregnancy associated risk associated with holoprosencephaly included maternal pregestational diabetes (9.2% of cases and 0 controls, p = .02)
evidence.explanation: Reports maternal pregestational diabetes in 9.2% of holoprosencephaly cases versus none of the controls, a human association with the malformation.

edges/13.description: This entry models a dose-limited pathway with no reserve, which is the substrate on which environmental insults act. Maternal diabetes is the best-replicated such insult and raises the chance that a carrier crosses into the affected range.

evidence.snippet: Following ethanol exposure, mean dysmorphology scores were increased by 3.2- and 6.6-fold in Shh(+/-) and Gli2(+/-) groups, respectively, relative to their wildtype littermates.
evidence.explanation: Ethanol raised dysmorphology scores several-fold in Shh and Gli2 heterozygotes relative to wild type, demonstrating the gene-environment interaction. Support is PARTIAL because the demonstration is in mice and has not been shown in human carriers.

edges/14.description: Ethanol worsens the phenotype specifically on a Hedgehog-sensitised background, which is what this node describes: the same dose produces far more dysmorphology when one Shh or Gli2 allele is already lost.

evidence.snippet: mice with single-allele Gli2 mutations exhibit increased penetrance and severity of HPE in response to low-dose teratogen exposure
evidence.explanation: Single-allele Gli2 mutant mice showed increased penetrance and severity of holoprosencephaly after low-dose teratogen exposure. Support is PARTIAL because this is a mouse demonstration rather than human data.

edges/15.description: Low-dose teratogen exposure that a normal embryo tolerates becomes damaging once buffering is lost, increasing both penetrance and severity. This is the mechanism by which an unaffected carrier parent can have a severely affected child.

evidence.snippet: Here, we show that loss-of-function mutations in the human GLI2 gene are associated with a distinctive phenotype (within the HPE spectrum) whose primary features include defective anterior pituitary formation and pan-hypopituitarism, with or without overt forebrain cleavage abnormalities, and HPE-like midfacial hypoplasia.
evidence.explanation: The founding report establishing GLI2 loss of function as the cause of this distinctive HPE-spectrum phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We show that most of the 31 missense variants previously reported as pathogenic are likely benign or, at most, low-risk variants.
evidence.explanation: Reclassification of the missense variant burden; important for interpreting the historically high reported frequency of GLI2 "variants" in HPE cohorts.

evidence.snippet: Our findings confirm the association of haploinsufficiency of GLI2 and mild HPE spectrum features.
evidence.explanation: A 1.3 Mb 2q14.2 deletion encompassing GLI2 reproduces the phenotype, establishing gene dosage (haploinsufficiency) rather than an allele-specific effect as the disease mechanism.

genes/0.notes: GLI2 is also somatically activated in Hedgehog-driven cancers (e.g. medulloblastoma, basal cell carcinoma); that gain-of-signal role is mechanistically opposite to the loss-of-function developmental disorder curated here.

evidence.snippet: Once diagnosed, individualized hormone replacement treatment is required for each patient.
evidence.explanation: Individualised hormone replacement is the management principle for GLI2-related (Culler-Jones) disease.

treatments/0.description: Recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin) for the growth hormone deficiency that is the most consistent hormonal deficit, restoring growth velocity and final height.

evidence.snippet: These phenotypes support partial penetrance, variable polydactyly, midline facial defects, and pituitary hormone deficiencies, including diabetes insipidus, conferred by heterozygous frameshift or nonsense GLI2 mutations.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the range of hormone axes - including ADH - that require replacement in GLI2-related disease.

treatments/1.description: Replacement of the remaining deficient axes as identified - hydrocortisone for ACTH deficiency (with stress dosing and adrenal crisis education, the most safety-critical element), levothyroxine for central hypothyroidism, desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus, and sex steroids at the age of puberty for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent phenotypic feature is post-axial polydactyly (65%)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the frequency of the anomaly this treatment addresses. Marked PARTIAL because the source documents the indication, not the intervention.

treatments/2.description: Excision or reconstruction of the supernumerary postaxial digit, usually in infancy or early childhood, for function and appearance. This is standard orthopaedic practice rather than a GLI2-specific intervention.

evidence.snippet: orofacial clefting (17%)
evidence.explanation: Establishes the frequency of the anomaly this treatment addresses. Marked PARTIAL because repair follows generic craniofacial protocols not evaluated in this source.

treatments/3.description: Staged surgical repair of cleft lip and palate along standard craniofacial protocols, with speech and feeding support.

evidence.snippet: Our approach clarifies clinical risks and the important messages to discuss in counseling for a pathogenic GLI2 variant.
evidence.explanation: Frames genotype-informed counselling as the explicit clinical deliverable of GLI2 genotype-phenotype analysis.

evidence.snippet: The mutation was frequently inherited from an asymptomatic parent.
evidence.explanation: The counselling fact that most complicates recurrence-risk discussion.

treatments/4.description: Counselling must address the two facts that make GLI2 unusual: a phenotypically normal parent may carry the variant (so a negative family history does not lower recurrence risk), and a carrier child's phenotype cannot be predicted from the genotype. Cascade testing and the reclassification of most GLI2 missense variants as benign are both central to the discussion.

evidence.snippet: None of the mutant alleles manifested dominant negative activity in these studies.
evidence.explanation: No dominant-negative activity was demonstrable for any patient allele, favouring haploinsufficiency.

evidence.snippet: Our findings confirm the association of haploinsufficiency of GLI2 and mild HPE spectrum features.
evidence.explanation: Whole-gene deletion phenocopies intragenic truncating variants, the classic argument for haploinsufficiency.

hypotheses/0.description: The dominant model: pathogenic alleles are functionally null, the wild-type allele is unaffected, and disease results from a halved dose of GLI2 activator. Supported by the absence of dominant-negative activity in the original functional assays and by the fact that whole-gene deletions reproduce the phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Functional assays confirmed the pathogenicity of the identified variant and revealed a dominant-negative effect of mutant GLI2 on Hedgehog signalling.
evidence.explanation: Cell-based assays show a dominant-negative effect for this specific truncating allele.

hypotheses/1.description: An alternative, probably allele-restricted mechanism in which a truncated GLI2 protein retaining the N-terminal repressor domain actively interferes with Hedgehog signalling rather than simply being inert. Reported for the C-terminal frameshift p.P1167LfsX52 in a Culler-Jones family, but not demonstrated for the alleles tested in the founding functional study.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that mutations in Gli2, which encodes a Hedgehog pathway transcription factor, can cause or predispose to HPE depending upon gene dosage.
evidence.explanation: Frames Gli2 lesions as either causal or predisposing depending on dosage and additional exposure.

evidence.snippet: A possible digenic origin (GLI2/HESX1) is proposed in one family.
evidence.explanation: A single reported family suggests a human second-locus contribution; marked PARTIAL because it is a proposal in one family, not established digenic inheritance.

hypotheses/2.description: Penetrance and severity are set not by the GLI2 allele alone but by whether a second genetic or environmental insult perturbs the already dose-limited Hedgehog pathway during the first-trimester patterning window. Strong support in the mouse; in humans the specific modifiers remain unidentified, and a possible digenic GLI2/HESX1 family has been reported.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with truncating mutations in GLI2 typically present with pituitary anomalies, polydactyly and subtle facial features rather than HPE.
evidence.explanation: The finding that motivates the nomenclature question.

open_questions/0.rationale: The HPE9 designation predates the large genotype-phenotype series and reflects the ascertainment of the original cohorts, which were screened for holoprosencephaly. Subsequent series consistently show that pituitary anomalies and postaxial polydactyly, not forebrain non-cleavage, are the modal presentation, which is why the milder presentation was split out as Culler-Jones syndrome. dismech keeps a single entry under the MONDO label holoprosencephaly 9 with the two presentations modelled as subtypes, but the naming remains a live question and a curator considering a separate Culler-Jones entry should read this note first.

evidence.snippet: A possible digenic origin (GLI2/HESX1) is proposed in one family.
evidence.explanation: The only human second-locus lead currently reported; marked PARTIAL because it is a single proposed family.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mouse work establishes that a second hit converts silent Gli2 heterozygosity into overt disease, but the human modifiers are unknown. No modifier locus has been validated, only a single family with a proposed digenic GLI2/HESX1 contribution, and no human study has tested the teratogen interaction directly. Identifying the modifiers would convert an unpredictable counselling situation into a stratifiable one.

evidence.snippet: Although normally indistinguishable from wild-type littermates, we demonstrate that mice with single-allele Gli2 mutations exhibit increased penetrance and severity of HPE in response to low-dose teratogen exposure.
evidence.explanation: States the mouse heterozygote baseline that differs from the human carrier state.

evidence.snippet: The most prevalent phenotypic feature is post-axial polydactyly (65%)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that most human heterozygotes are not phenotypically silent, unlike the mouse.

open_questions/2.rationale: The human disorder is dominant with roughly 65% of pathogenic-variant carriers showing postaxial polydactyly, whereas Gli2 heterozygous mice are described as indistinguishable from wild-type littermates without a second insult, and the murine phenotype that does resemble severe human holoprosencephaly requires homozygous loss on a permissive background. The species therefore differ in where the developmental threshold sits relative to a single functional allele. This matters because the second-hit model of human non-penetrance rests largely on heterozygous-mouse data; if the human heterozygote is already below threshold in the limb, the environmental component may be less necessary for the human phenotype than the mouse experiments imply.

evidence.snippet: Yet, MSLT is neither sensitive nor specific and the polysomnographic diagnostic criteria require continuous readjustment and biologic markers are still lacking.
evidence.explanation: States the absence of a biological marker directly, which is the evidence for curating this node as an unidentified process rather than assigning it a mechanism.

evidence.snippet: A familial background is often present but rigorous studies are still lacking.
evidence.explanation: Records the familial signal and, in the same sentence, that it has not been characterised - so this entry curates no inheritance mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Healthy controls and subjects with other sleep disorders all had normal levels.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the key negative constraint on this node - normal CSF hypocretin-1 in hypersomnias other than narcolepsy-cataplexy - which is why this entry does not conform to orexin_arousal_instability.

steps/0.description: The trigger node, and it is deliberately named for what is not known. No structural lesion, neurotransmitter deficiency, autoimmune target, or causative gene has been established in idiopathic hypersomnia. What is established is negative and constraining: CSF hypocretin-1 is normal, which excludes the orexin-deficiency mechanism; there is no HLA association of the strength seen in narcolepsy type 1; and no consistent neuropathology has been reported. Onset is typically in adolescence or young adulthood, a familial background is frequently reported but has never been rigorously characterised, and no biological marker exists. Curating this node as unknown rather than assigning it a plausible mechanism is the honest position and is what the disorder's name records.

evidence.snippet: Idiopathic hypersomnia is a central hypersomnolence disorder of unknown origin characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness despite normal or long sleep time, and frequent severe sleep inertia.
evidence.explanation: States both halves of this node - pathological sleepiness coexisting with normal or increased sleep - which is the combination that defines the disorder.

evidence.snippet: cases with IH had more severe sleepiness and sleep propensity, despite similar or longer sleep times
evidence.explanation: Population-cohort confirmation with objective polysomnography and multiple sleep latency testing that the sleepiness is not explained by reduced sleep, which is what the node asserts.

steps/1.description: The central and defining physiological abnormality: sleep propensity is pathologically elevated, but sleep architecture, efficiency, and continuity are normal or better than normal. This combination is what separates idiopathic hypersomnia from every other cause of daytime sleepiness. In narcolepsy type 1 the sleep-wake switch is unstable in both directions, so nocturnal sleep is fragmented; in sleep-disordered breathing it is destroyed by respiratory events; in circadian disorders it is displaced in time. Here sleep is abundant, consolidated, and still insufficient. Sleep is extended rather than curtailed, and the extension does not relieve the sleepiness - which is the observation that makes a simple sleep-debt model untenable.

evidence.snippet: It is often accompanied by sleep of long duration and debilitating sleep inertia.
evidence.explanation: Names sleep inertia as a defining accompaniment of the disorder rather than an incidental feature, supporting its curation as a separate node.

evidence.snippet: Idiopathic hypersomnia continues to evolve from the concept of "sleep drunkenness" introduced by Bedrich Roth in Prague in 1956
evidence.explanation: Documents that the arousal abnormality, not the sleepiness, was the founding observation of the disease concept.

steps/2.description: A partly separable abnormality, and one that a pure sleep-drive model does not predict. Waking is prolonged, confused, and incomplete: patients are difficult to rouse, may require multiple alarms or another person, and remain impaired for tens of minutes to hours after rising - the "sleep drunkenness" Roth described in the original 1956 account. It is curated as its own node because it dissociates from sleepiness in treatment response as well as in phenomenology, and because it, rather than the sleepiness, is often the most disabling symptom and the one that most reliably distinguishes idiopathic hypersomnia from narcolepsy at the bedside.

evidence.snippet: as well as a 24 h PSG or a 2-wk actigraphy in association with a sleep log to ensure a total 24-h sleep time longer than or equal to 66O minutes
evidence.explanation: Gives the operational threshold (a 24-hour sleep time of at least 660 minutes) by which extended sleep is established, which is how this node is measured. Note the source text contains a typographic error, printing the letter O for the final zero of "660"; the snippet reproduces the cached text verbatim as required and the correct value is 660 minutes.

steps/3.description: Sleep in idiopathic hypersomnia fails at its restorative function while succeeding at its structural one. Nocturnal sleep may extend well beyond ten hours, and daytime naps - which in narcolepsy are short and briefly restorative - are here long and leave the patient no better. This is the feature clinicians use to separate the two disorders in the consulting room, and it constrains any candidate mechanism: whatever is wrong is not a failure to obtain sleep but a failure of obtained sleep to discharge sleep pressure.

evidence.snippet: The condition is disabling, sometimes even more so than narcolepsy type 1 or 2.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the magnitude of disability relative to the better-recognised comparator disorder.

evidence.snippet: Longitudinal data (spanning 12.1 ± 4.3 years) demonstrated a chronic course of sleepiness for most of the cases with IH, though pathologic somnolence remitted in roughly 40% of cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies both the chronicity and the substantial remission rate, which together define the natural history recorded at this node.

steps/4.description: The clinical endpoint. Idiopathic hypersomnia is most often a chronic condition of adolescent or young-adult onset with substantial occupational, educational, and social disability - sometimes rated by patients as greater than that of narcolepsy, in part because the disorder is less recognised and its severity less readily believed. It is not, however, uniformly permanent: in the only population-based longitudinal series, pathological somnolence remitted in roughly 40% of cases over about twelve years, which is a prognostically important finding and one that any mechanistic account must accommodate.

edges/0.description: Whatever the somnogenic process is, its measurable effect is an increase in sleep propensity that does not degrade sleep quality or continuity.

edges/1.description: The same unidentified process is presumed to underlie the difficulty in transitioning out of sleep, which does not follow from sleep drive alone.

edges/2.description: Elevated sleep drive that is not discharged by sleep produces prolonged sleep episodes and long naps from which the patient does not wake refreshed.

edges/3.description: Prolonged post-waking impairment interferes with employment, education, and driving independently of the daytime sleepiness.

edges/4.description: Long unrefreshing sleep consumes the day and does not relieve the sleepiness, compounding disability.

evidence.snippet: Patients treated with modafinil experienced a significantly prolonged mean sleep latency on the MWT at the end of the study compared with placebo
evidence.explanation: Randomised placebo-controlled evidence of objective benefit on daytime wakefulness in the subtype studied.

evidence.snippet: Modafinil, which was approved for idiopathic hypersomnia until 2011 in Europe, is the most commonly used treatment and improved sleepiness in two recent randomized placebo-controlled trials.
evidence.explanation: Establishes modafinil's place in practice and that two randomised trials support it, while recording its off-label regulatory status.

treatments/0.description: A wake-promoting agent and the most commonly used treatment, prescribed off-label in most jurisdictions since its European idiopathic hypersomnia indication was withdrawn in 2011. It improves objective and subjective sleepiness but is not directed at sleep inertia, which is the symptom patients most often rate as most disabling - a therapeutic gap this entry records deliberately.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Wake promotion opposes the elevated sleep propensity symptomatically; it does not act on the unidentified upstream process and is not disease-modifying.

evidence.snippet: In a placebo-controlled, double-blind, randomized withdrawal study, LXB reduced daytime sleepiness and sleep inertia, and improved daily functioning.
evidence.explanation: Randomised-withdrawal evidence that the agent acts on both curated symptom nodes, which is what distinguishes it from the wake-promoting agents.

evidence.snippet: Efficacy and safety of low-sodium oxybate were maintained or improved during the 6-month OLE, supporting long-term treatment with low-sodium oxybate in adults with idiopathic hypersomnia.
evidence.explanation: Cited as PARTIAL because the durability claim comes from an open-label extension without a control arm, so it supports persistence of benefit more weakly than the randomised-withdrawal result above.

treatments/1.description: The only agent approved specifically for idiopathic hypersomnia (United States, 2021). Notable mechanistically as well as clinically, because it reduces sleep inertia as well as daytime sleepiness - the only treatment shown to act on both nodes - and because a GABA-B agonist improving a disorder hypothesised to involve excessive GABA-A potentiation is a genuine puzzle that the entry's mechanistic hypothesis does not resolve.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Reduces sleep inertia in randomised withdrawal, distinguishing it from the wake-promoting agents, which do not address this node.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Reduces daytime sleepiness alongside the effect on sleep inertia.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that a naturally occurring substance in CSF augments inhibitory GABA signaling, thus revealing a new pathophysiology associated with excessive daytime sleepiness.
evidence.explanation: The primary claim of the hypothesis, stated by its originators, and the basis for curating it as a candidate mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, flumazenil normalized vigilance in seven hypersomnolent patients.
evidence.explanation: Cited as PARTIAL because it is the clinical arm of the hypothesis and is an open-label observation in seven patients - suggestive, and explicitly not sufficient to establish the mechanism.

evidence.snippet: The bioactive CSF component had a mass of 500 to 3000 daltons and was neutralized by trypsin.
evidence.explanation: Records how far characterisation of the putative somnogen got - a mass range and protease sensitivity - and therefore that no molecular identity was established, which is the principal reason the hypothesis remains EMERGING.

hypotheses/0.description: The leading positive hypothesis, and the reason idiopathic hypersomnia is sometimes described as the mirror image of narcolepsy. Cerebrospinal fluid from hypersomnolent patients was reported to potentiate GABA-A receptor function in vitro in the presence of GABA, with the bioactivity attributable to a trypsin-sensitive component of 500-3000 daltons whose identity was never established. On this model the disorder is one of excessive endogenous somnogenic inhibition rather than deficient arousal drive - which would explain why it coexists with normal orexin, why sleep is abundant rather than fragmented, and why arousal from sleep is specifically impaired. The supporting flumazenil result is mechanistically striking, since flumazenil is conventionally regarded as lacking intrinsic activity, and it reversed the enhancement in vitro and normalised vigilance in an open-label series of seven patients. It is curated as EMERGING and not as the mechanism: the finding rests substantially on one laboratory's assay, the bioactive substance was never identified, and the clinical arm was small and unblinded.

open_questions/0.rationale: The two diagnoses are separated by a single polysomnographic count - two or more sleep-onset REM periods on the multiple sleep latency test - applied to a test its own reviewers describe as neither sensitive nor specific, and the count is unstable on repeat testing. Neither disorder has a biological marker, both have normal CSF hypocretin-1, and they respond to the same drugs. This is not a nosological quibble: it determines whether mechanistic studies of either are being conducted in a homogeneous population, and a negative replication in a mixed cohort would be uninterpretable. It is the principal reason this entry's trigger node is curated as unknown rather than inheriting a mechanism from narcolepsy research.

open_questions/1.rationale: The gabaergic_potentiation hypothesis is the only mechanistic account of idiopathic hypersomnia with direct experimental support, and it is curated here as EMERGING rather than canonical for two specific reasons that are resolvable rather than permanent. The bioactive substance was characterised only as a trypsin-sensitive species of 500-3000 daltons and has never been identified, so there is no assay a second laboratory can run on the analyte itself; and the supporting clinical observation was open-label in seven patients. Until both are addressed, a conforming or citing entry should not treat GABA-A potentiation as established.

evidence.snippet: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia, also related to smoking, is characterized by exertional dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive lung function, and ground-glass opacities on high-resolution CT.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that the exposure drives a second member of the family, not only respiratory bronchiolitis-interstitial lung disease.

evidence.snippet: Organizing pneumonia (OP) is a nonspecific lung parenchymal response to any form of injury, with its idiopathic variant coined as cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (COP).
evidence.explanation: Directly states the logic this node encodes for one member of the family — the lesion is a stereotyped, cause-agnostic parenchymal response to injury, and the idiopathic entity is what remains once a cause cannot be found. Recorded as PARTIAL because the source argues it for organizing pneumonia rather than for the whole IIP family.

evidence.snippet: Diagnostic evaluation relies on excluding secondary causes of organizing pneumonia and includes a thorough history including medications, exposures, and signs or symptoms of underlying rheumatologic disease.
evidence.explanation: Documents the diagnosis-by-exclusion step this node asserts, naming the specific alternative causes that must be ruled out before an interstitial pneumonia is called idiopathic.

steps/1.description: The shared initiating step of the family. Injury reaches the alveolar epithelium and the surrounding interstitium, and the search for a cause — connective tissue disease, inhaled antigen, drug, infection, occupational exposure — returns nothing. What makes an interstitial pneumonia idiopathic is therefore not a distinct kind of injury but the exhaustion of the differential, which is why every entity in this family is defined partly by exclusion.

evidence.snippet: In 2002 the American Thoracic Society/European Respiratory Society (ATS/ERS) classification of idiopathic interstitial pneumonias (IIPs) defined seven specific entities, and provided standardized terminology and diagnostic criteria. In addition, the historical "gold standard" of histologic diagnosis was replaced by a multidisciplinary approach.
evidence.explanation: Both halves of this node come from one sentence pair — that the family resolves into a fixed, small set of defined entities, and that the entity is assigned by multidisciplinary discussion rather than by histology alone.

evidence.snippet: It is identified histologically by the nonspecific interstitial pneumonia pattern.
evidence.explanation: A worked instance of the pattern-assigns-entity rule this node states, for the idiopathic NSIP member of the family.

steps/2.description: The pivot of the whole family, and the reason it is a classification rather than a single disease. The injured lung has only a small repertoire of histopathologic responses — usual interstitial pneumonia, nonspecific interstitial pneumonia, organizing pneumonia, diffuse alveolar damage, respiratory bronchiolitis, desquamative interstitial pneumonia, lymphoid interstitial pneumonia — and which one it adopts, not the (absent) cause, assigns the clinicopathologic entity together with its natural history and its treatment. Since 2002 that assignment has been made by multidisciplinary discussion integrating clinical, radiologic, and pathologic data rather than by histology alone.

evidence.snippet: Respiratory bronchiolitis-associated ILD mainly affects smokers, showing ground-glass opacities on chest computed tomography (CT) scans and pigmented macrophages in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid.
evidence.explanation: Names the cell, the pigment, and the smoking association that together define this arm of the classification.

evidence.snippet: Desquamative interstitial pneumonia, also related to smoking, is characterized by exertional dyspnea, dry cough, restrictive lung function, and ground-glass opacities on high-resolution CT.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the second smoking-related entity shares the same driver, supporting their treatment as one lesion at two extents.

steps/3.description: The lesion shared by the two smoking-related IIPs. Pigmented ("smoker's") macrophages accumulate in respiratory bronchioles and the surrounding alveoli. Confined to the bronchiolar region the lesion is respiratory bronchiolitis-interstitial lung disease; when the same accumulation becomes diffuse and fills alveolar spaces it is desquamative interstitial pneumonia. This is the one arm of the classification with an identified and removable driver, which is why its first-line therapy is an exposure intervention rather than a drug.

evidence.snippet: Lymphoid interstitial pneumonia involves lymphocytic proliferation and is associated with autoimmune diseases or infections, treated with corticosteroids.
evidence.explanation: Gives the cellular lesion, the secondary associations that must be excluded before calling it idiopathic, and the therapy that follows from it.

steps/4.description: The lesion of lymphoid interstitial pneumonia. Polyclonal lymphocytes and plasma cells diffusely infiltrate and widen the alveolar septa. Truly idiopathic LIP is rare; most cases sit downstream of an autoimmune disease (classically Sjogren syndrome) or an infection, so the same caveat that governs the whole family — idiopathic means the search failed — is at its most demanding here.

evidence.snippet: The hallmark pathological features are presence of polypoid granulation tissue, or Masson bodies, in the alveolar spaces, with lung architecture preserved in most patients with good clinical outcomes poststeroid treatment.
evidence.explanation: Supplies the lesion, its location, the preservation of architecture, and the good steroid-treated outcome that follows from it.

steps/5.description: The lesion of cryptogenic organizing pneumonia. Polypoid plugs of fibroblastic granulation tissue (Masson bodies) fill alveolar spaces, alveolar ducts, and distal bronchioles while the underlying alveolar architecture is preserved. Because the scaffold survives, the lesion is reversible — this is the mechanistic basis for the steroid responsiveness that separates COP from the chronic fibrosing entities.

evidence.snippet: Acute interstitial pneumonia (AIP) is a term used for an idiopathic form of acute lung injury characterized clinically by acute respiratory failure with bilateral lung infiltrates and histologically by diffuse alveolar damage (DAD), a combination of findings previously known as the Hamman-Rich syndrome.
evidence.explanation: States the lesion, its clinical expression, and that the entity is the idiopathic member of the acute lung injury family.

steps/6.description: The lesion of acute interstitial pneumonia. Alveolar-capillary barrier disruption with hyaline membrane formation produces fulminant respiratory failure clinically indistinguishable from ARDS; survivors pass into an organizing phase that can leave fibrosis. AIP is the idiopathic form, so its diagnosis requires DAD on histology plus exclusion of every recognised ARDS trigger.

evidence.snippet: Key cells in the pathogenesis involve alveolar type 2 (AT2) cells, club cells and myofibroblasts; however, to what extent these cells are affected by telomere shortening and DNA damage is not yet known.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the epithelial and myofibroblast cell types this node asserts as the effectors of fibrogenesis across different types of progressive fibrosing interstitial lung disease, not only in IPF.
