evidence.snippet: We found increased severity is strongly associated with variants occurring in protein regions involved with ATP and MT binding: the P loop, switch I, and switch II.
evidence.explanation: Reports a genotype-severity association.

evidence.snippet: Seventeen mutations occurred in the motor domain of the Kinesin-1A protein, but location of mutation did not correlate with neurological and imaging presentations.
evidence.explanation: Finds no location-phenotype correlation.

open_questions/0.rationale: Genotype-severity correlation matters for counseling and for selecting patients for allele-specific therapy. A 100-patient cohort links P-loop, switch I and switch II variants and rigor motility to severe disease, while a 28-patient Italian series found no correlation between mutation location and neurological or imaging presentation. Both are cross-sectional, and severity rises with age in a progressive disease.

evidence.snippet: Heterozygous variants leading to KIF1A haploinsufficiency are associated only with adult onset hereditary spastic paraplegia without seizures or cognitive impairment, a phenotype significantly milder than that associated with missense variants9 suggesting that gapmer ASO mediated therapy might provide a bridging therapeutic approach for dominant negative missense variants in KIF1A until other treatment options are available.
evidence.explanation: States the therapeutic rationale and its dependence on haploinsufficiency being mild.

evidence.snippet: However, unlike these allelic disorders, dominant spastic paraplegia was also caused by loss-of-function variants outside this domain in six families.
evidence.explanation: Loss-of-function heterozygosity is itself pathogenic.

open_questions/1.rationale: Allele-specific knockdown converts a dominant-negative genotype into a haploinsufficient one. Loss-of-function carriers have a much milder, pure spastic paraplegia, but they do develop disease, sometimes from infancy, so the ceiling of benefit and the long-term outcome of knockdown are unknown.

evidence.snippet: On the other hand, we have suggested that KIF1A(V8M), KIF1A(A255V), and KIF1A(R350G) mutations (all of them are familial) result in a gain of function (25).
evidence.explanation: Prior model data suggest hyperactivation for A255V.

evidence.snippet: we established in vitro motility assays with purified full-length human KIF1A and found that KIF1A mutations associated with the hereditary SPG lead to hyperactivation of KIF1A motility.
evidence.explanation: SPG-associated variants hyperactivate purified KIF1A.

evidence.snippet: Introduction of the corresponding mutations into the Caenorhabditis elegans KIF1A homolog unc-104 revealed abnormal accumulation of SVPs at the tips of axons and increased anterograde axonal transport of SVPs.
evidence.explanation: Increased, not decreased, SVP transport in worm knock-ins.

open_questions/2.rationale: The recessive SPG30B allele p.Ala255Val lies in the motor domain, yet worm studies have suggested that it and other familial alleles cause gain of function. The functional class of recessive alleles determines whether SPG30B shares the transport-loss mechanism of the dominant subtypes.

evidence.snippet: KIF1A mutants died mostly within a day after birth showing motor and sensory disturbances.
evidence.explanation: Null mice are neonatal lethal, unlike the heterozygous human disease.

open_questions/3.rationale: Kif1a-null mice die within a day of birth, a genotype no patient has, while KAND knock-in worms reproduce the dominant-negative transport defect but lack the corticospinal, optic and cerebellar systems that degenerate in patients. Neither model can test which neurons degenerate first or whether reducing the mutant allele halts degeneration.

evidence.snippet: K85 and K35 are the first hair keratins expressed in cortical cells at the early stage of the differentiation. Two types of mutations in the gene encoding K85 are associated with ectodermal dysplasia of hair and nail type
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that K85 and K35 are the earliest hair keratins expressed in cortical cells, and that K85 mutations cause ectodermal dysplasia.

evidence.snippet: The K85-K35 pair formed short filaments in the cytoplasm, which gradually elongated and became thicker and entangled around the nucleus, indicating that K85-K35 promotes lateral association of short intermediate filaments (IFs) into bundles but cannot form IF networks in the cytoplasm
evidence.explanation: Characterization of K85-K35 intermediate filament assembly shows unique bundling behavior distinct from cytokeratin networks, essential for proto-macrofibril formation in hair cortex.

evidence.snippet: The disease locus was mapped to a 16.6 centimorgan region on chromosome 12q12-q14.1 (Zmax = 8.2), which harbours six type II hair keratin genes
evidence.explanation: Linkage mapping localized the disease to the type II hair keratin gene cluster on chromosome 12q, confirming hair keratin disruption as the molecular basis.

steps/0.description: KRT85 is a type II keratin that heterodimerizes with type I keratins (particularly KRT35) to form intermediate filaments in the hair cortex. K85 and K35 are the first hair keratins expressed in cortical cells at the early stage of differentiation and are critical for proto-macrofibril formation. Loss of KRT85 disrupts the structural integrity of keratin intermediate filaments in the hair shaft cortex, leading to mechanically fragile, poorly formed hair shafts.

evidence.snippet: Molecular defects in cutaneous keratin genes encoding for keratin intermediate filaments (KIFs) causes keratinocytes and tissue-specific fragility, accounting for a large number of genetic disorders in human skin and its appendages
evidence.explanation: Review establishing that keratin intermediate filament defects cause tissue-specific fragility in skin appendages including nails.

steps/1.description: KRT85 is also expressed in the nail matrix, where it contributes to nail plate formation. Loss of KRT85 leads to structurally abnormal nail plates manifesting as nail dystrophy, with brittle, ridged, or malformed nails.

evidence.snippet: four different types of ectodermal dysplasia involving only hair and nails have been described
evidence.explanation: Establishes that KRT85-related ectodermal dysplasia involves hair (hypotrichosis) as a defining feature of this pure hair-nail subtype.

steps/2.description: Sparse scalp hair (hypotrichosis) present from birth, reflecting disrupted hair shaft formation due to defective keratin intermediate filament assembly in the hair cortex. Sparse eyebrows, eyelashes, and body hair have also been observed in some families (Shimomura 2010, Amico 2019).

evidence.snippet: four different types of ectodermal dysplasia involving only hair and nails have been described
evidence.explanation: Establishes nail involvement as a defining feature of KRT85-related pure hair-nail ectodermal dysplasia.

steps/3.description: Abnormal nail plate formation with ridging, brittleness, or malformation affecting fingernails and toenails from birth, resulting from defective keratinization in the nail matrix.

evidence.snippet: a two-nucleotide (C1448 T1449) deletion (delCT) in the protein tail domain of K85 interfered with the K85-K35 filament formation and gave only aggregates
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that KRT85 mutations can completely disrupt filament formation, producing only aggregates rather than normal intermediate filaments, which would manifest as abnormal hair shaft morphology.

steps/4.description: Structural abnormalities of the hair shaft visible on light or electron microscopy, reflecting disrupted keratin intermediate filament organization within the cortex.

steps/5.description: Progressive or complete loss of scalp hair. Complete alopecia has been reported with certain KRT85 mutations, particularly the R78H missense mutation in the head domain. Some individuals show partial improvement after puberty.

evidence.snippet: This report provides the first direct evidence relating to the molecular pathogenesis of pure hair-nail ectodermal dysplasias
evidence.explanation: Establishes KRT85 as a causative gene for pure hair-nail ectodermal dysplasia through linkage analysis and mutation identification.

evidence.snippet: ectodermal dysplasia (ED; K85)
evidence.explanation: Review confirming K85 (KRT85) as the gene responsible for ectodermal dysplasia of hair and nail type within the broader keratin genodermatosis classification.

treatments/0.description: No specific treatment exists for the underlying keratin defect. Management is supportive and includes gentle hair care to minimize breakage, nail care, and cosmetic interventions such as wigs.

evidence.snippet: The identification of specific pathogenic mutations in keratin disorders formed the basis of our understanding that led to re-classification, improved diagnosis with prognostic implications, prenatal testing and genetic counseling in severe keratin genodermatoses
evidence.explanation: Review confirming that identification of keratin gene mutations enables genetic counseling and prenatal testing for keratin genodermatoses.

treatments/1.description: Genetic counseling for autosomal recessive inheritance pattern, carrier testing for family members, and prenatal diagnosis when the familial mutations are known.

evidence.snippet:
Initial studies suggested a 
central role of anosmin-1, in GnRH neuron ontogeny - specifically in GnRH 
neuronal migration from the cribriform plate area into the brain - as well as in 
olfactory bulb development.
evidence.explanation: Supports anosmin-1's role in GnRH neuron migration and olfactory bulb development.

evidence.snippet:
we suggest that the KAL1 gene product, the
extracellular matrix protein anosmin-1, is involved in FGF signaling
evidence.explanation: Links anosmin-1 to the FGFR1 signaling pathway that guides GnRH neuron migration.

evidence.snippet: While loss-of-function mutations in FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1) cause human GnRH deficiency, to date no specific ligand for FGFR1 has been identified in GnRH neuron ontogeny.
evidence.explanation: Places FGF8 at this node as the FGFR1 ligand acting in GnRH neuron ontogeny, which is why both genes are bound here rather than only the receptor.

evidence.snippet:
These findings reveal that insufficient 
prokineticin-signaling through PROKR2 leads to abnormal development of the 
olfactory system and reproductive axis in man.
evidence.explanation: Places the PROK2/PROKR2 pair at this node as a second, independent signalling axis whose loss disrupts the same olfactory and reproductive development.

evidence.snippet:
CHD7's role is further 
corroborated by specific expression in IHH/KS-relevant tissues and appropriate 
developmental expression.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding CHD7 at this node. INDIRECT deliberately: it establishes that CHD7 is expressed in the tissues and at the developmental stages this node describes, not that CHD7 loss was observed to arrest GnRH neuron migration.

evidence.snippet: In addition, we discovered that WDR11 interacts with EMX1, a homeodomain transcription factor involved in the development of olfactory neurons, and that missense alterations reduce or abolish this interaction.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding WDR11 at this node. INDIRECT deliberately: the demonstrated step is loss of an interaction with an olfactory-neuron developmental transcription factor, not an observed arrest of GnRH neuron migration.

evidence.snippet: These findings are consistent with a model in which KAL1 can act as a modulatory coligand with FGF to activate the FGF receptor in an HS-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding HS6ST1 at this node, and for the direction: heparan sulfate modification is required for anosmin-1 to help activate FGFR1, so reduced 6-O-sulfotransferase activity reduces signalling through the axis already bound here.

evidence.snippet: Mice lacking semaphorin 3A expression have been showed to have a Kallmann-like phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding SEMA3A at this node: loss of the semaphorin in mouse reproduces the human developmental phenotype this node describes.

evidence.snippet: Because a subset of axons in these tracks is the migratory pathway for GnRH neurons, in FEZF1 deficiency, GnRH neurons also fail to enter the brain.
evidence.explanation: The basis for binding FEZF1 at this node, and the most direct statement of this node's own claim that any gene on the entry supplies: loss of FEZF1 stops the GnRH neurons entering the brain.

steps/10.description: During embryogenesis GnRH neurons originate in the olfactory placode and migrate along olfactory/vomeronasal axons to the hypothalamus. Kallmann syndrome genes disrupt the molecular guidance, adhesion, and growth-factor signaling required for this co-migration and for olfactory bulb formation. Anosmin-1 (ANOS1) is an extracellular matrix protein that binds heparan sulfate proteoglycans and modulates FGFR1 signaling; FGF8 is the cognate FGFR1 ligand; and prokineticin-2/PROKR2 signaling is also required, so loss of any of these arrests GnRH neuron migration and impairs olfactory bulb morphogenesis.

evidence.snippet:
Isolated gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) 
deficiency (IGD) is characterized by inappropriately low serum concentrations of 
the gonadotropins LH (luteinizing hormone) and FSH (follicle-stimulating 
hormone) in the presence of low circulating concentrations of sex steroids.
evidence.explanation: Defines the core endocrine defect downstream of GnRH deficiency.

steps/11.description: Deficient hypothalamic GnRH leads to inappropriately low pituitary secretion of gonadotropins (LH and FSH) and consequently low sex steroid levels, producing absent or incomplete puberty, hypogonadism, and infertility.

evidence.snippet:
Kallmann syndrome combines anosmia, related to defective olfactory bulb 
morphogenesis, and hypogonadism due to gonadotropin-releasing hormone 
deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Attributes anosmia to defective olfactory bulb morphogenesis.

steps/12.description: Disrupted migration of olfactory axons and failure of olfactory bulb morphogenesis cause absent or hypoplastic olfactory bulbs, the anatomic basis of the anosmia that defines Kallmann syndrome.

edges/10.description: Failure of GnRH neurons to reach the hypothalamus results in deficient hypothalamic GnRH secretion.

edges/11.description: The same migratory/developmental defect that prevents olfactory axons from reaching the forebrain also disrupts olfactory bulb formation.

evidence.snippet:
The gene for X-linked Kallmann's syndrome (KAL-1, encoding anosmin-1) was cloned 
in 1991.
evidence.explanation: Establishes KAL1/ANOS1 (anosmin-1) as the X-linked Kallmann syndrome gene.

evidence.snippet: ANOS1 | HGNC:6211 | hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 1 with or without anosmia | MONDO:0010635 | XL | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the ANOS1-HH1 gene-disease relationship as definitive with X-linked inheritance, matching this subtype's MONDO binding.

genes/0.notes: Loss-of-function variants in ANOS1 (KAL1) cause X-linked Kallmann syndrome via loss of anosmin-1, an extracellular matrix protein required for GnRH neuron migration and olfactory bulb development.

evidence.snippet:
We establish here that loss-of-function mutations in FGFR1 underlie KAL2 whereas a
gain-of-function mutation in FGFR1 has been shown to cause a form of
craniosynostosis.
evidence.explanation: Direct evidence that FGFR1 loss-of-function causes Kallmann syndrome type 2.

genes/1.notes: Loss-of-function variants in FGFR1 cause autosomal dominant Kallmann syndrome (KAL2).

evidence.snippet:
These findings reveal that insufficient 
prokineticin-signaling through PROKR2 leads to abnormal development of the 
olfactory system and reproductive axis in man.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the PROKR2/PROK2 prokineticin pathway in Kallmann syndrome pathogenesis.

evidence.snippet: PROKR2 | HGNC:15836 | hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 3 with or without anosmia | MONDO:0009482 | AD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the PROKR2-HH3 gene-disease relationship as definitive, which is the MONDO class this subtype row spans.

genes/2.notes: Variants in the prokineticin receptor PROKR2 (KAL3) cause Kallmann syndrome; insufficient prokineticin signaling through PROKR2 impairs olfactory system and reproductive axis development. PROKR2 and its ligand PROK2 previously shared one `genetic:` record here, which meant the ligand was named in prose but bound to no HGNC identifier and so was invisible to any machine reading of this entry. They are split into two records because `gene_term` is single-valued; both still point at the one `PROKR2_PROK2` subtype row, which now carries both genes.

evidence.snippet:
we took a 
candidate gene strategy and identified ten and four different point mutations in 
the genes encoding the G protein-coupled prokineticin receptor-2 (PROKR2) and 
one of its ligands, prokineticin-2 (PROK2), respectively.
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort's own result identifying point mutations in PROK2 itself, not only in its receptor.

evidence.snippet:
The mutations in PROK2 
were detected in the heterozygous state, whereas PROKR2 mutations were found in 
the heterozygous, homozygous, or compound heterozygous state.
evidence.explanation: The zygosity split between the ligand and the receptor in the founding cohort, recorded because it is the point on which ClinGen's semidominant grading for PROK2 cannot be read off this paper.

evidence.snippet: PROK2 | HGNC:18455 | hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 4 with or without anosmia | MONDO:0012528 | SD | Definitive
evidence.explanation: ClinGen classifies the PROK2-HH4 gene-disease relationship as definitive with semidominant inheritance.

genes/3.notes: PROK2 (KAL4) encodes prokineticin-2, the ligand for PROKR2. It is the ligand half of the same signalling axis as the PROKR2 record above and shares the `PROKR2_PROK2` subtype row. ClinGen's assertion is recorded against hypogonadotropic hypogonadism 4 (MONDO:0012528) and carries a semidominant mode of inheritance. Note that this does not come from the founding cohort's PROK2 zygosity data, which points the other way: in that series every PROK2 mutation was heterozygous, and it was PROKR2 that was found heterozygous, homozygous and compound heterozygous. The same cohort reported a patient carrying both a PROKR2 and a KAL1 mutation, which is one of the observations behind this entry's digenic/oligogenic modelling.

evidence.snippet: While loss-of-function mutations in FGF receptor 1 (FGFR1) cause human GnRH deficiency, to date no specific ligand for FGFR1 has been identified in GnRH neuron ontogeny.
evidence.explanation: Establishes FGF8 as the FGFR1 ligand whose deficiency causes GnRH deficiency.

genes/4.notes: Decreased FGF8 signaling causes GnRH deficiency in humans and mice; FGF8 is the principal FGFR1 ligand in GnRH neuron ontogeny.

evidence.snippet:
Seven heterozygous mutations, two splice and 
five missense, which were absent in > or = 180 controls, were identified in 
three sporadic KS and four sporadic normosmic IHH patients.
evidence.explanation: CHD7 mutations were identified in sporadic Kallmann syndrome patients.

genes/5.notes:
Heterozygous CHD7 variants cause Kallmann syndrome / IHH; isolated disease can represent a milder allelic variant of CHARGE syndrome.
ClinGen has no gene-disease validity assertion for CHD7 against Kallmann syndrome or any hypogonadotropic hypogonadism class - checked against the ClinGen gene-validity download retrieved 2026-09-19, in which the only CHD7 row is CHARGE syndrome (MONDO:0008965, Definitive). The KS relationship is therefore cited to the primary mutation-screening study rather than to ClinGen.

evidence.snippet: these data emphasize that like the other mutations associated with Kallmann syndrome the described Spry4 mutation creates a hyperactive version of a selective inhibitory molecule and can thereby contribute to a weakened FGF signaling.
evidence.explanation: States the gain-of-inhibition reading directly for the S241Y allele, and is the reason this subtype is modelled as converging on decreased FGFR1 signalling rather than as a loss of FGF restraint.

evidence.snippet: Spry4 gains the capability of inhibiting FGF, but not epithelial growth factor (EGF)-induced signaling as a consequence of the tyrosine substitution.
evidence.explanation: The inhibition gained by the variant is FGF-selective rather than a general dampening of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling, which is what makes it disease-relevant here.

evidence.snippet: The inhibition of these processes was accompanied by lower relative phospho-extracellular-signal-regulated kinases (pERK) levels in response to serum induction, indicating that activation of MAPK was less efficient.
evidence.explanation: Shows the Kallmann-associated Sprouty4 K177R protein reduces ERK activation, the gain-of-inhibition step that reconciles an antagonist variant with a decreased-FGFR1-signalling disease.

evidence.snippet: This mutation was found in two independent studies, and in both cases associated with the Kallmann syndrome
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the variant tested in that functional work is one reported in Kallmann syndrome patients, not an arbitrary substitution.

evidence.snippet: Knockout mice of Spry1, Spry2 and Spry4 show characteristic phenotypes often similar to the one observed with FGF overdose
evidence.explanation: The independent argument that simple SPRY4 loss of function is the wrong reading for this disease. Deleting the antagonist in mouse produces an FGF-EXCESS phenotype, the opposite direction from the decreased FGFR1 signalling Kallmann syndrome requires, so the human variants have to be doing something other than abolishing Sprouty4.

evidence.snippet: One rare SPRY4 variant (p.T68S) was found in a female patient with Kallmann syndrome who also carried a PLXNA1 mutation.
evidence.explanation: A worked instance of the contributory pattern - the SPRY4 carrier in this cohort also carried a variant at a second IHH locus.

genes/6.notes:
SPRY4 encodes Sprouty4, an intracellular antagonist of receptor tyrosine kinase signalling that restrains FGFR1-driven MAPK/ERK activation. The naive reading - that losing an antagonist raises FGF signalling - points the wrong way for this disease, because Kallmann syndrome is a DECREASED-FGFR1-signalling disorder. The published functional work points the other way. Two Kallmann-reported Sprouty4 substitutions - S241Y and K177R - have each been characterised as HYPERACTIVE inhibitors, suppressing migration, proliferation and serum- or FGF-induced ERK activation where wild-type Sprouty4 does not, and S241Y does so selectively for FGF rather than EGF signalling. Gain of inhibitory function in the antagonist therefore converges on the same decreased FGFR1 signalling node as FGFR1 and FGF8 loss of function, which is why this subtype needs no separate pathograph.
`relationship_type: SUSCEPTIBILITY` rather than `CAUSATIVE` is deliberate. There is no ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion for SPRY4; GenCC submitters classify it Limited to Moderate, and Genomics England PanelApp lists it amber on both hypogonadotropic hypogonadism panels. The reported architecture is contributory - usually a second or third locus alongside - which is what the SUSCEPTIBILITY value describes.

evidence.snippet: We confirmed this by showing that all FLRTs can interact with FGFR1 and FLRTs can be induced by the activation of FGF signalling by FGF-2.
evidence.explanation: The physical link to the FGFR1 axis this disease runs on, which is what made FLRT3 a candidate at all. INDIRECT because the interaction was shown in mouse development rather than in a GnRH neuron or in a patient.

evidence.snippet: While thalamic axons lacking FLRT3 are insensitive to Netrin-1, thalamic axons containing FLRT3 can modulate their Netrin-1 responsiveness in a context-dependent manner.
evidence.explanation: The second candidate mechanism, axon guidance, which is the process this disease is about. INDIRECT because it is a thalamic axon in a mouse rather than an olfactory or GnRH axon in a patient.

evidence.snippet: we show that mouse embryos with a double deletion of FLRT2 and FLRT3 genes encoding cell adhesion molecules exhibit an abnormal distribution of interneurons within the streams during development
evidence.explanation: That FLRT3 loss disturbs tangential neuronal migration, which is the class of process that fails in Kallmann syndrome. INDIRECT, and doubly so - a double knockout in mouse cortex, not a single FLRT3 patient allele in the olfactory system.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in genes encoding components of the FGF pathway are associated with complex modes of CHH inheritance and act primarily as contributors to an oligogenic genetic architecture underlying CHH.
evidence.explanation: The founding cohort's own conclusion about the class of gene FLRT3 belongs to, which is what the SUSCEPTIBILITY typing records.

evidence.snippet: Previously reported heterozygous variants were also found in the PROK2 (c.163del, p.Ile55*), CHD7 (c.c.2750C>T, p.Thr917Met and c.7891C>T, p.Arg2631*), FLRT3 (c.1106C>T, p.Ala369Val), and CCDC103 (c.461A>C, p.His154Pro) genes.
evidence.explanation: A worked instance of the contributory pattern - the FLRT3 allele in this series is one of several heterozygous findings in a five-patient cohort, reported alongside PROK2 and CHD7 variants rather than as a solitary cause.

genes/7.notes:
FLRT3 encodes fibronectin leucine-rich transmembrane protein 3, a cell-surface molecule with two documented activities that both point at this disease. It interacts with FGFR1 and is itself induced by FGF signalling, which is why it was selected into the FGF8-synexpression candidate screen that found it in CHH. And it is an axon-guidance and neuronal-migration receptor: it is a Robo1 coreceptor whose absence makes thalamic axons insensitive to Netrin-1 and produces axon guidance defects in vivo, and it acts with FLRT2 through Unc5 receptors to control the tangential migratory streams of cortical interneurons. Defective co-migration of GnRH neurons and olfactory axons is exactly the node this entry's pathograph already carries, so no separate mechanism is needed for this subtype.
The direction of effect is not established, and this entry does not assert one. FLRT3 is a positive modulator of FGF signalling on the first reading, so losing it would lower FGFR1 pathway output and converge on the same decreased-signalling node as ANOS1, FGFR1 and FGF8. But no functional study of a CHH-associated FLRT3 variant has been published - the founding paper performed in vitro work on FGF17 and IL17RD variants and not on the FLRT3 ones - so whether the reported alleles reduce, raise or leave unchanged either the FGFR1 interaction or the guidance function is unknown. The guidance data cited here come from mouse and from Flrt3-null systems, not from patient alleles.
`relationship_type: SUSCEPTIBILITY` rather than `CAUSATIVE` is deliberate and is the same call made for SPRY4 on weaker grounds. There is no ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion for FLRT3 - checked against the ClinGen gene-validity download of 2026-09-08 - the founding cohort found variants in 3 of 386 individuals and concluded that the FGF-pathway genes act as contributors to an oligogenic architecture, and the later cohorts that report FLRT3 classify the variants as rare or of uncertain significance. Typing it causative would assert a sufficiency nobody has claimed.

evidence.snippet: We found six patients with a total of five different heterozygous WDR11 missense mutations, including three alterations (A435T, R448Q, and H690Q) in WD domains important for β propeller formation and protein-protein interaction.
evidence.explanation: Establishes heterozygous WDR11 missense variants as a cause of IHH and Kallmann syndrome.

genes/8.notes: Heterozygous WDR11 missense variants were found in six patients after a balanced t(10;12) translocation in a Kallmann syndrome patient pointed at the locus. The functional route to this entry's mechanism is WDR11's interaction with EMX1, a homeodomain transcription factor involved in olfactory neuron development, which the patient alterations reduce or abolish. There is no ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion for WDR11 in the current Gene-Disease Validity table (file created 2026-09-25, downloaded from the unversioned URL pinned in data/clingen/MANIFEST.yaml); ClinGen has classified none of those nine genes, so that silence is about the panel's coverage of congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism rather than about any one gene.

evidence.snippet: We report here mutations in HS 6-O-sulfotransferase 1 (HS6ST1) in families with idiopathic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (IHH).
evidence.explanation: The founding human observation that establishes HS6ST1 as an IHH gene, in families rather than in a functional assay.

evidence.snippet: IHH-associated HS6ST1 mutations display reduced activity in vitro and in vivo, suggesting that HS6ST1 and the complex modifications of extracellular sugars are critical for normal development in humans.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the loss-of-activity direction of the disease alleles, which is what makes this gene consistent with a decreased-FGFR1-signalling disease. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM because the "in vivo" half of this sentence is the Caenorhabditis elegans work the same abstract describes, not a human observation; the enzyme assays are the in vitro half, and the sentence covers both.

genes/9.notes: HS6ST1 6-O-sulfates heparan sulfate, the modification that lets anosmin-1 act as a modulatory coligand with FGF in activating FGFR1. The IHH-associated alleles reduce enzyme activity in vitro and in vivo, so the direction of effect - less FGFR1 activation - is sourced rather than inferred, which is why this gene is bound at the migration node where SPRY4, FLRT3 and DUSP6 are not. MONDO records HS6ST1 against MONDO:0013946 with a `contributes_to` predicate rather than `causes`; this record is typed CAUSATIVE on the strength of an independent 158-patient exome cohort that counted HS6ST1 among the genes whose pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants it judged sufficient to cause disease.

evidence.snippet: This deletion cosegregated in the propositus' family with the KS phenotype, that was transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion and was not associated with other neurological or non-neurological clinical disorders.
evidence.explanation: Establishes dominant cosegregation of a SEMA3A deletion with Kallmann syndrome.

genes/10.notes:
A heterozygous 213 kb deletion removing 11 of the 17 SEMA3A exons cosegregated with Kallmann syndrome in an autosomal dominant family, and mice lacking semaphorin 3A have a Kallmann-like phenotype. That mouse phenotype is what puts the mechanism on the olfactory-axon and GnRH-neuron migration step this entry models, and is why the gene is bound at that node.
Two things qualify the CAUSATIVE typing without overturning it. MONDO records SEMA3A against MONDO:0013961 with a `contributes_to` predicate rather than `causes`, and a 158-patient exome cohort found SEMA3A in one of its two digenic combinations (with SEMA3E). The same cohort also counts SEMA3A among the genes whose variants it judged sufficient to cause disease, and the founding evidence is a segregating whole-gene-region deletion rather than a missense association, which is why the typing follows the dominant reading with the digenic report kept as evidence on the subtype row.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in DUSP6 alone seem sufficient to cause IHH in an autosomal dominant manner, whereas IL17RD or SPRY4 mutations may cause IHH phenotypes in synergy with variants in other IHH-associated genes.
evidence.explanation: The cohort conclusion that separates DUSP6 from the other FGF-pathway modulators. Recorded as the sufficiency claim that exists for DUSP6 and not for IL17RD or SPRY4; it does not determine this record's typing, which stays SUSCEPTIBILITY because the founding screen concludes FGF-pathway genes act primarily as contributors to an oligogenic architecture.

genes/11.notes:
DUSP6 encodes an ERK2 phosphatase that negatively modulates FGF8-FGFR1 signalling. Of the three FGF-pathway modulator loci curated as subtypes here - SPRY4, FLRT3 and DUSP6 - it is the only one for which a cohort has argued that variants are sufficient alone, but it is typed SUSCEPTIBILITY on the same footing as SPRY4, FLRT3 and IL17RD, because the founding screen's own conclusion is that these genes act primarily as oligogenic contributors, because two of that screen's five DUSP6 carriers also carried an SPRY4 allele (recounted in the discussion of PMID:37108593, not in the screen's own abstract), and because the one structurally characterised congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism DUSP6 allele is a variant of uncertain significance whose reporting authors say functional studies are needed. The sufficiency claim is kept as evidence on the subtype row rather than discarded.
DUSP6 is not bound at the migration pathophysiology node. Losing a negative modulator of FGF signalling would raise rather than lower FGFR1 output, the opposite of the decreased signalling that node asserts, and the one published direction-of-effect analysis of a disease allele agrees with the naive reading: molecular dynamics on DUSP6 p.Leu145Arg predicts loss of the interaction needed for ERK2 binding. SPRY4's record resolves its own version of this paradox with published characterisation of two Kallmann-reported Sprouty4 substitutions as hyperactive inhibitors; nothing equivalent exists for DUSP6, so the direction is left unasserted.

evidence.snippet: Most of the FGF17 and IL17RD mutations altered protein function in vitro.
evidence.explanation: The functional support for the FGF17 alleles, which is what raises this above a list-only association.

genes/12.notes: FGF17 is an FGF8-subfamily ligand, so it is a plausible participant in the FGFR1 axis this entry models, and most of the reported FGF17 alleles altered protein function in vitro. It is typed SUSCEPTIBILITY rather than CAUSATIVE on the same grounds as SPRY4 and FLRT3: three individuals in a screen of 386, the founding cohort's own conclusion that the FGF-pathway genes act primarily as oligogenic contributors, later recurrence only under the heading of rare variants, and no ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion in the current Gene-Disease Validity table (file created 2026-09-25). DUSP6, from the same screen, carries the same typing here, and the difference between them is only that one cohort has argued DUSP6 variants are sufficient alone while none has argued that for FGF17.

evidence.snippet: We identified homozygous loss-of-function mutations in FEZF1 in two independent consanguineous families each with two affected siblings.
evidence.explanation: Establishes biallelic FEZF1 loss of function as a cause of Kallmann syndrome.

genes/13.notes: Homozygous loss-of-function FEZF1 variants in two independent consanguineous families, each with two affected siblings. The mechanism is stated directly in the founding report and is this entry's own node: the FEZF1 product lets olfactory receptor neuron axons cross the CNS basal lamina, and because a subset of those axons carries the migrating GnRH neurons, FEZF1 deficiency stops them entering the brain. Inheritance is autosomal recessive, unlike most of this entry.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that NELF is associated with normosmic IHH and KS, either singly or in combination with a mutation in another gene.
evidence.explanation: The screen's own conclusion, which is what the SUSCEPTIBILITY typing records.

genes/14.notes:
NSMF is the gene originally described as NELF, nasal embryonic LHRH factor, isolated from migratory GnRH neurons. Typed SUSCEPTIBILITY: the dedicated screen found three alleles in 168 IHH/KS patients, and both of its two Kallmann (anosmic) patients carried the NELF variant together with a variant at a second locus - KAL1 in one, TACR3 in the other - while the single solitary finding was in a normosmic IHH patient. The screen's conclusion is that NELF is associated with IHH and KS either singly or in combination with a mutation in another gene. There is no ClinGen gene-disease validity assertion for NSMF in the current Gene-Disease Validity table (file created 2026-09-25).
The NELF/TACR3 pair is worth noting alongside this entry's TACR3 ruling: a TACR3 nonsense allele does appear in an anosmic patient, as the second locus in an oligogenic combination. That is consistent with TACR3 contributing to a Kallmann phenotype in combination, and not with TACR3 being a Kallmann gene in its own right.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the situation in these cells of mesenchymal origin, in lung cancer-derived cell lines both variants of Spry4 were able to interfere with proliferation of tested cells
evidence.explanation: The authors' own cell-type contrast is the mismatch - the variant-specific effect is not reproduced across the lines tested, and no GnRH-neuron model was used.

open_questions/0.rationale: The mechanism that makes SPRY4 coherent as a Kallmann gene - a variant antagonist that inhibits FGFR1/ERK output more strongly than wild-type - rests on ectopic expression in lung fibroblasts, osteosarcoma cells and lung cancer lines. The same paper reports that the direction of effect is cell-type dependent: in the lung cancer lines both wild-type and variant Sprouty4 inhibited proliferation, and the variant's advantage appeared only where FGFR1 was highly expressed. The disease-relevant cell, the migrating GnRH neuron, has not been tested, so whether the effect size or even the sign carries over is unknown. This is a model-fidelity question rather than an absence of evidence, which is why it is recorded as HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH and not KNOWLEDGE_GAP.

evidence.snippet: which confirmed a prominent smoking-related signature (signature 4
evidence.explanation: Confirms the tobacco mutational signature as the dominant mutational process in LCNEC.

evidence.snippet: On average, LCNECs exhibited an exonic mutation rate of 8.6 non-synonymous mutations per million base pairs and a C:G > A:T transversion rate of 38.7%
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the tobacco-type mutational burden in a genomically profiled LCNEC cohort.

evidence.snippet: LCNEC and SCLC are clinically aggressive tumors presenting in elderly heavy-smokers
evidence.explanation: Establishes heavy smoking as the near-universal clinical context of LCNEC.

steps/6.description: Pulmonary LCNEC arises almost exclusively in older heavy smokers. Whole-exome and whole-genome sequencing shows a high exonic mutation rate dominated by C:G>A:T transversions and by COSMIC mutational signature 4, the canonical tobacco-carcinogen signature. This mutagenic burden is what generates the tumour-suppressor loss-of-function events that define both molecular subgroups.

evidence.snippet: Commonly altered genes in LCNEC included TP53 (78%), RB1 (38%), STK11 (33%), KEAP1 (31%), and KRAS (22%)
evidence.explanation: Gives the mutation frequency of TP53 and of the genes defining the downstream branches.

evidence.snippet: TP53 was the most frequently mutated gene (92%)
evidence.explanation: Independent whole-exome confirmation that TP53 loss is near universal.

steps/7.description: Biallelic TP53 loss of function is the near-universal first hit in LCNEC, reported in 78% of tumours by targeted sequencing and 92% by whole-exome sequencing. Loss of p53 abrogates DNA-damage checkpoint control and apoptosis, licensing both the genomic instability and the second-hit bifurcation that follow.

evidence.snippet: Analyses of chromosomal gene copy numbers revealed statistically significant amplifications of 1p34 (containing the MYCL1 gene, 12%), 8p12 (containing FGFR1, 7%), 8q24.21 (containing MYC, 5%)
evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent copy-number changes that constitute chromosomal instability in LCNEC.

evidence.snippet: Large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (12.7 mutations/Mb) and SCLC (11.9 mutations/Mb) showed higher tumor mutational burdens than TC (2.4 mutations/Mb) and AC (7.1 mutations/Mb)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the mutator phenotype, showing that LCNEC carries a tumour mutational burden comparable to SCLC and several-fold above the low- and intermediate-grade carcinoids.

steps/8.description: Following p53 loss, LCNEC accumulates a high mutation burden together with recurrent focal amplifications (MYCL1 at 1p34, FGFR1 at 8p12, MYC at 8q24.21, NKX2-1 at 14q13) and deletions (CDKN2A at 9p21), i.e. the mutator phenotype and chromosomal instability that the genome-instability module describes.

evidence.snippet: SCLC-like (n = 18), characterized by TP53+RB1 co-mutation/loss and other SCLC-type alterations, including MYCL amplification
evidence.explanation: Defines the SCLC-like subset by TP53+RB1 co-alteration.

evidence.snippet: RB1 mutation and protein loss were detected in 47% (n = 37) and 72% (n = 78) of the cases, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Gives the frequency of RB1 mutation and of Rb protein loss in a registry-based LCNEC cohort.

evidence.snippet: somatic alterations of RB1 and STK11/KEAP1 were detected in 82% of the cases (n = 49) and occurred in a mutually exclusive fashion
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the RB1 and STK11/KEAP1 branches are mutually exclusive.

evidence.snippet: The presence of RB1 and TP53 genomic alterations (GAs) were used to define a SCLC-like subtype (n = 557).
evidence.explanation: Confirms the TP53+RB1 SCLC-like subtype in a 1,426-sample clinical comprehensive genomic profiling series, far larger than the original discovery cohorts.

steps/9.description: Biallelic RB1 inactivation, co-occurring with TP53 loss, defines the SCLC-like (Rekhtman) or type II (George) subgroup. RB1 mutation is reported in 38-47% of cases and loss of nuclear Rb protein in up to 72%. This branch is mutually exclusive with the STK11/KEAP1 branch. Note the counterintuitive transcriptional consequence: despite the SCLC-like genotype, type II tumours show reduced neuroendocrine marker expression.

evidence.snippet: NSCLC-like (n = 25), characterized by the lack of coaltered TP53+RB1 and nearly universal occurrence of NSCLC-type mutations (STK11, KRAS, and KEAP1)
evidence.explanation: Defines the NSCLC-like subset by STK11/KRAS/KEAP1 alteration without TP53+RB1 co-alteration.

evidence.snippet: Combined with loss-of-heterozygosity (LOH), bi-allelic alterations of STK11 and KEAP1 were found in 37% of the cases
evidence.explanation: Quantifies biallelic STK11/KEAP1 alteration as the defining lesion of the type I subgroup.

evidence.snippet: These NSCLC-like subtype-defining GAs included SMARCA4, KRAS, FGF3/4/19, STK11, CDKN2A/B, MTAP, and CCND1.
evidence.explanation: Extends the NSCLC-like lesion set beyond STK11/KEAP1/KRAS in a large clinical genomic profiling cohort.

steps/10.description: Biallelic inactivation of STK11 (LKB1) and/or KEAP1, in the absence of RB1 co-alteration, defines the NSCLC-like (Rekhtman) or type I (George) subgroup. STK11 loss deregulates LKB1-AMPK-mTOR energy sensing and KEAP1 loss constitutively activates NRF2 antioxidant signalling. This branch frequently also carries activating KRAS mutations.

evidence.snippet: more frequent mutations in NOTCH family genes (28%), implicated as key regulators of neuroendocrine differentiation
evidence.explanation: Quantifies NOTCH-family mutation in LCNEC and names its role in neuroendocrine differentiation.

steps/11.description: Inactivating NOTCH-family mutations occur in about a quarter of NSCLC-like LCNEC, and NOTCH pathway activity is high in the type II subgroup that shows low neuroendocrine marker expression. NOTCH signalling is an established regulator of the neuroendocrine-versus-non-neuroendocrine fate switch in lung epithelium, which makes it the most plausible link between the genomic subgroups and their divergent lineage states.

evidence.snippet: higher proliferative activity in SCLC-like tumors (P < 0.0001)
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that the TP53+RB1 branch translates into a measurably higher proliferative rate.

steps/12.description: Combined TP53 and RB1 inactivation removes both the p53 damage checkpoint and the Rb-enforced G1/S restriction point, the canonical evading-growth-suppressors lesion. In LCNEC this is the SCLC-like branch and is accompanied by measurably higher proliferative activity than in the STK11/KEAP1 branch.

evidence.snippet: instead LCNECs form distinct transcriptional subgroups with closest similarity to SCLC
evidence.explanation: Establishes that LCNEC's transcriptional identity is neuroendocrine and SCLC-proximate.

evidence.snippet: positive staining for greater than or equal to two of three neuroendocrine IHC markers increased the sensitivity for LCNEC from 47% to 93% on paired biopsy specimens
evidence.explanation: Shows that the neuroendocrine programme is demonstrable immunohistochemically and is diagnostically decisive.

steps/13.description: LCNEC expresses a neuroendocrine differentiation programme demonstrable as chromogranin A, synaptophysin and CD56 immunoreactivity, and transcriptionally as ASCL1 and DLL3 expression in the neuroendocrine-high subgroup. This programme, not the genomic lesion set, is what places LCNEC transcriptionally closest to small cell lung carcinoma and justifies its WHO classification as a neuroendocrine carcinoma rather than an NSCLC variant. DLL3 expression in this branch is the rationale for DLL3-directed therapy.

evidence.snippet: a subtype of lung cancer with neuroendocrine morphology, neuroendocrine differentiation on immunohistochemistry, a high mitotic rate
evidence.explanation: States the defining combination of neuroendocrine features with a high mitotic rate.

steps/14.description: A mitotic rate above 10 mitoses per 2 square millimetres together with extensive, often geographic necrosis is a defining diagnostic criterion of LCNEC and separates it from the low-grade (typical carcinoid) and intermediate-grade (atypical carcinoid) neuroendocrine tumours.

evidence.snippet: The tumors with invasion of the segmental and/or lobar bronchus were classified as central LCNEC and those without as peripheral LCNEC.
evidence.explanation: Defines the central versus peripheral growth patterns by bronchial invasion.

evidence.snippet: The majority of LCNEC proved to be of the peripheral type (64.3%, 81/126). Central tumors were associated with smoking habit (p = 0.047), higher TNM-stage (p = 0.014) and larger tumor size (p < 0.001).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the peripheral predominance and the clinical correlates of central growth.

steps/15.description: The primary tumour grows as either a peripheral mass, which is the majority pattern, or a central tumour invading the segmental or lobar bronchus. The distinction is prognostically and biologically real: central tumours are more strongly associated with smoking, present at higher stage and larger size, and carry markedly worse survival, while peripheral tumours more often retain Rb protein and harbour EGFR mutations.

evidence.snippet: LCNEC was more common among male subjects, and disease usually presented at stage IV (55%)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that most patients present with disseminated disease.

evidence.snippet: Brain metastasis occurred more frequently in LCNEC (19.2%) than SCLC (16.7%, P < .001) or NSCLC (13%, P < .001)
evidence.explanation: Documents the disproportionate brain tropism of LCNEC.

steps/16.description: LCNEC disseminates early and widely. In population data the majority of patients present at stage IV, and brain metastasis is more frequent than in either small cell or non-small cell lung cancer, making the central nervous system a characteristic site of colonisation.

evidence.snippet: Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (LCNEC) accounts for approximately 3% of lung malignancies.

steps/17.description: The pulmonary primary tumour, most often presenting as a peripheral mass but with a substantial minority arising centrally.

evidence.snippet: Brain metastasis occurred more frequently in LCNEC (19.2%) than SCLC (16.7%, P < .001) or NSCLC (13%, P < .001)
evidence.explanation: Reports brain metastasis in 19.2% of LCNEC, which maps to the OCCASIONAL band (5-29%).

steps/18.description: Metastatic involvement of the brain, disproportionately frequent in LCNEC compared with both small cell and non-small cell lung cancer.

evidence.explanation: Reports the association of the RB1-altered subgroup with a NOTCH-high, neuroendocrine-low state. Curated as PARTIAL because the study establishes co-occurrence, not a causal mechanism.

evidence.explanation: Reports KRAS mutation in 22% of LCNEC, within the NSCLC-like branch.

evidence.snippet: In advanced disease, the historical regimen of platinum based therapy in combination with etoposide or irinotecan remains among the commonly used first line therapies
evidence.explanation: Documents the standard-of-care status of platinum-etoposide in advanced LCNEC.

treatments/0.description: Small cell lung cancer-type chemotherapy, historically the default first-line regimen for advanced LCNEC by extrapolation from SCLC. Note that its superiority is not established, and in RB1 wild-type tumours it performs worse than NSCLC-type chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: the historical regimen of platinum based therapy in combination with etoposide or irinotecan remains among the commonly used first line therapies
evidence.explanation: Establishes platinum-etoposide as a standard first-line cytotoxic regimen in advanced LCNEC.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Cytotoxic chemotherapy targets the rapidly proliferating compartment that defines the high-grade phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Patients with RB1 wild-type LCNEC treated with NSCLC-GEM/TAX had a significantly longer OS [9.6; 95% confidence interval (CI), 7.7-11.6 months] than those treated with SCLC-PE [5.8 (5.5-6.1); P = 0.026]
evidence.explanation: Gives the survival difference by RB1 status between NSCLC-type and SCLC-type chemotherapy.

evidence.snippet: In patients with LCNEC, NSCLC-t chemotherapy results in longer overall survival compared to NSCLC-pt and SCLC-t chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: Independent registry evidence that NSCLC-type chemotherapy gives the longest overall survival.

treatments/1.description: Platinum combined with gemcitabine or a taxane. In a national registry cohort this produced longer overall survival than either pemetrexed-based or etoposide-based treatment, and in RB1 wild-type tumours it significantly outperformed platinum-etoposide. This is the clearest example in LCNEC of molecular subtype guiding chemotherapy choice.

evidence.snippet: Patients with LCNEC tumors that carry a wild-type RB1 gene or express the RB1 protein do better with NSCLC-GEM/TAX treatment than with SCLC-PE chemotherapy.
evidence.explanation: Establishes RB1 status as predictive of differential benefit between the two chemotherapy strategies.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Cytotoxic chemotherapy targets the proliferating tumour compartment. RB1 status does not change the drug target but predicts which cytotoxic strategy performs better.

evidence.snippet: Ipilimumab plus nivolumab demonstrated a 26% ORR in patients with high-grade neuroendocrine neoplasms, with durable responses seen in patients with refractory disease.
evidence.explanation: Reports prospective activity of dual checkpoint blockade in high-grade neuroendocrine neoplasms. Curated as PARTIAL because the 19-patient cohort was not LCNEC-specific.

treatments/2.description: Ipilimumab plus nivolumab, studied prospectively in the high-grade neuroendocrine neoplasm cohort of the DART SWOG S1609 basket trial. Activity is real but modest, and the cohort was histologically and anatomically mixed rather than LCNEC-specific.

evidence.snippet: Stage I-III LCNEC behaves similarly to NSCLC, whereas stage IV is more akin to SCLC.
evidence.explanation: Supports an NSCLC-like, resection-oriented approach at stages I-III. PARTIAL because this population study reports behaviour rather than directly comparing surgical against non-surgical management.

treatments/3.description: Complete resection is the treatment of choice for early-stage, resectable LCNEC, consistent with the observation that stage I-III LCNEC behaves like non-small cell lung cancer.

evidence.snippet: however for extra thoracic LCNEC regimens like FOLFOX, FOLFOIRI and CAPTEM can also be used
evidence.explanation: Documents the site-adapted chemotherapy options for extrapulmonary LCNEC.

treatments/4.description: For extrathoracic primaries, gastrointestinal-type regimens are used in addition to the platinum backbone, reflecting the site rather than the pulmonary paradigm.

evidence.snippet: Under this schema, 530 samples were classified as NSCLC-like and 314 remained unclassified.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the proportion of LCNEC that does not fit either genomic subtype, which is the empirical basis for treating the binary as incomplete.

open_questions/0.rationale: The subgroup framework rests on retrospective cohorts, and the one treatment-relevant finding (RB1 wild-type tumours doing better with NSCLC-type than with SCLC-type chemotherapy) comes from a registry analysis, not a randomised trial. The two branches are reported as mutually exclusive in 82% of cases, which leaves a substantial residue that fits neither, and the discordance between the genomic label and the transcriptional phenotype suggests a continuum of neuroendocrine differentiation rather than two classes. The largest clinical genomic series to date makes the residue explicit: of 1,426 profiled LCNEC samples, 557 were SCLC-like, 530 NSCLC-like, 25 carcinoid-like and 314 could not be classified at all. No prospective biomarker-stratified trial has yet tested assigning chemotherapy by RB1 status.

open_questions/1.rationale: Neuroendocrine morphology is absent in roughly half of biopsies from tumours that prove to be LCNEC on resection, and registry-coded frequency (0.9% of lung cancers) is well below the pathology-reviewed estimate (about 3%). Population statistics on incidence, stage distribution and survival are therefore drawn from a systematically incomplete and probably resection-biased case set, and the apparent rise in incidence may partly reflect improving recognition rather than changing biology.

evidence.snippet: Sequence analysis of the SC5D gene in the patient's DNA, showing the presence of two missense mutations (R29Q and G211D), confirmed that the patient is affected by a novel defect of cholesterol biosynthesis.
evidence.explanation: The original molecular confirmation of the disease gene.

steps/1.description: Homozygous or compound heterozygous SC5D variants. Reported alleles are predominantly missense, and residual activity tracks with severity across the small reported cohort.

evidence.snippet: The biosynthesis of cholesterol in the patient's fibroblasts was defective, showing a block in the conversion of lathosterol into 7-dehydrocholesterol.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the enzymatic block directly in patient fibroblasts.

steps/2.description: The conversion of lathosterol to 7-dehydrocholesterol, the penultimate step of cholesterol synthesis, is blocked.

evidence.snippet: The plasma lathosterol concentration was markedly raised at 219.8 μmol/L (control range 0.53-16.0), confirming the diagnosis.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the accumulation against a stated control range.

steps/3.description: Plasma and tissue lathosterol rise, in the reported mild case to more than tenfold above the upper limit of the control range. Accumulation is the diagnostic signature and appears to drive the storage arm of the disease specifically.

evidence.snippet: Sc5d (-/-) pups were stillborn, had elevated lathosterol and decreased cholesterol levels, had craniofacial defects including cleft palate and micrognathia, and limb patterning defects.
evidence.explanation: Establishes both the biochemical changes and the malformation phenotype.

steps/4.description: Cellular cholesterol falls. In the mouse knockout this, rather than the accumulated precursor, is what accounts for the malformation phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Many of the malformations found in Sc5d (-/-) mice are consistent with impaired hedgehog signaling, and appear to be a result of decreased cholesterol rather than increased lathosterol.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the malformations to the pathway and, importantly, adjudicates between the two candidate biochemical causes.

steps/5.description: The route by which a biosynthetic block becomes a malformation syndrome rather than a purely degenerative disease. This is the mechanism shared with Smith-Lemli-Opitz and the other post-squalene defects.

evidence.snippet: An unique aspect of the lathosterolosis phenotype is the combination of a malformation syndrome with an intracellular storage defect.
evidence.explanation: States the combination that distinguishes this disease from its neighbours.

steps/6.description: Lamellar inclusions on electron microscopy, with a mucolipidosis-like appearance on light microscopy in the most severely affected. This storage component is what makes lathosterolosis unusual among the cholesterol biosynthesis defects.

evidence.snippet: Liver involvement is variable and can range from normal liver function tests to portal fibrosis and cirrhosis.
evidence.explanation: Describes the range of hepatic involvement across reported cases.

steps/7.description: Ranges from normal liver function tests through transaminitis to portal fibrosis and cirrhosis. It is the arm that responds to lowering the accumulated sterol.

evidence.snippet: The LS phenotype appears to be characterized by the distinctive association of a recognizable pattern of congenital anomalies, involving axial and appendicular skeleton, liver, central nervous and urogenital systems, and lysosomal storage.
evidence.explanation: Defines the malformation pattern and couples it to the storage finding.

steps/8.description: A recognisable pattern involving the axial and appendicular skeleton, liver, central nervous and urogenital systems.

edges/1.description: The variants reduce activity of the encoded desaturase.

edges/2.description: Substrate upstream of the block accumulates.

edges/3.description: Flux to the end product falls.

edges/4.description: The storage picture tracks with the most severe biochemical defects, suggesting it follows accumulation rather than cholesterol shortage.

edges/5.description: Lowering lathosterol pharmacologically improved transaminases and fibrosis grade in one patient, which is the observation that implicates accumulation in the hepatic arm.

edges/6.description: Sonic hedgehog requires covalent cholesterol modification, so a cholesterol shortfall impairs the morphogen pathway.

edges/7.description: Disrupted morphogen signalling produces the craniofacial and limb anomalies.

evidence.snippet: A missense variant, NM_006918.4 (SC5D):c.212A>T;p.(Asn71Ile) and a nonsense variant, NM_006918.4(SC5D):c.214C>T; p.(Gln72*) were identified in exon 3 of the SC5D gene.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the one reported allele that is a true null. The entry's genotype-phenotype reading rests on residual activity, so an allele with none is the informative extreme.

evidence.snippet: The mutation leads to a relatively conservative amino acid substitution, consistent with some residual enzyme activity.
evidence.explanation: Links a specific allele's chemistry to the milder phenotype, which is the genotype-phenotype logic available in a disease with this few patients.

genes/0.notes: Biallelic variants, predominantly missense. Reported alleles include R29Q, G211D, Y46S, P160R, D210E and L219S. D210E is a conservative substitution reported in two patients who both had relatively mild disease, consistent with residual activity. The one reported allele that cannot encode a functional enzyme is the nonsense variant Q72*, carried in trans with the missense N71I by a patient whose FibroScan read 15.6 kPa against a paediatric normal of 2.5 to 8.5. It anchors the severe end of the same residual-activity argument that D210E anchors at the mild end. No patient homozygous for a null has been reported, which is consistent with the Sc5d-null mouse being stillborn.

evidence.snippet: Medications and chemicals that are hepatotoxic
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews agents-and-circumstances-to-avoid instruction.

treatments/0.description: GeneReviews lists hepatotoxic medications and chemicals as agents to avoid. This carries more weight in this disease than the generic version of the advice: the hepatic arm is the dominant morbidity driver, it is the arm liver transplantation addresses, and the entry's only pharmacotherapy is a statin - so protecting the liver is a management instruction about the same organ the treatment plan turns on.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Avoids additional hepatocellular injury on top of the sterol-driven disease; it does not act on the biosynthetic block.

evidence.snippet: Simvastatin treatment resulted in lowering of plasma lathosterol levels, improvement in transaminitis, and liver fibrosis grade, suggesting that children with this condition should be actively treated in order to prevent progression of liver disease.
evidence.explanation: The single most substantive treatment observation available: a biochemical response coupled to a histological one.

evidence.snippet: Our patient's family did not notice any benefit from treatment with simvastatin.
evidence.explanation: A contrary observation in a different patient, curated as REFUTE so the entry does not present the treatment as uniformly effective.

treatments/1.description: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase upstream of the block, reducing flux into the pathway and so lowering the accumulated lathosterol. It does not restore the missing enzyme, and reported benefit is inconsistent.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Reducing proximal cholesterol synthesis lowers the substrate that accumulates behind the block.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Improvement in transaminases and fibrosis grade followed the fall in plasma lathosterol in the treated patient.

evidence.snippet: annual ophthalmology evaluation; liver enzymes at each visit; liver imaging including ultrasound and FibroScan® every six months or per hepatologist; plasma sterol profile before initiating simvastatin and every one to two months while on therapy
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews Surveillance section verbatim, giving each interval rather than a general instruction to follow up.

treatments/2.description: GeneReviews sets a monitoring plan that is unusually specific for a disease with this few patients, and its shape follows the mechanism: the ophthalmologic and hepatic arms are both progressive and both actionable, so each gets an interval. Developmental milestones at every visit; annual ophthalmology; liver enzymes at every visit with ultrasound and FibroScan every six months; and a plasma sterol profile before starting simvastatin and every one to two months on it. That last interval is the one that carries mechanistic weight - it monitors the substrate behind the block, because the clinical endpoint the statin is meant to change has never been established.

evidence.snippet: Potential targeted therapies include simvastatin (the safety and/or efficacy of simvastatin has not been proven in lathosterolosis) and liver transplantation.
evidence.explanation: The GeneReviews Management section naming both targeted options, and stating plainly that simvastatin is unproven.

treatments/3.description: Named alongside simvastatin as a potential targeted therapy. It addresses the hepatic arm definitively by replacing the affected organ, while doing nothing for the malformation or storage arms - which is consistent with the entry's reading that those arms have different biochemical causes.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Replaces the organ in which the hepatic arm manifests.

hypotheses/0.description: The malformations follow from insufficient cholesterol for hedgehog morphogen modification. The Sc5d-null mouse supports this over the alternative directly, reporting that the defects appear to result from decreased cholesterol rather than increased lathosterol.

hypotheses/1.description: The lysosomal storage picture is not a general feature of cholesterol biosynthesis defects, and within lathosterolosis it tracks with the most severe biochemical defects rather than with cholesterol shortage. The hepatic response to lowering plasma lathosterol points the same way. Modeled as a separate group because the two arms of this disease appear to have different biochemical causes, which is unusual and worth keeping visible.

open_questions/0.rationale: A biosynthetic block produces both a shortage and a surplus, and lathosterolosis is unusual in giving evidence that they act on different arms. The Sc5d-null mouse attributes the malformations to decreased cholesterol rather than increased lathosterol. The storage picture points the other way: it is not a general feature of cholesterol synthesis defects, it tracks with the most severe biochemical defects, and the hepatic disease improved when plasma lathosterol was lowered without the enzyme being restored. The entry models these as separate hypothesis groups rather than collapsing them, because a treatment that lowers flux would be expected to help the accumulation arm and do nothing for the cholesterol arm - which is testable and matters clinically.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The mismatch is not a weakness of the mouse, it is a statement about which arm of the disease each system can see. Homozygous nulls are stillborn with craniofacial and limb patterning defects, which is exactly the window in which the malformation arm is decided, and the model earns its place by attributing those defects to decreased cholesterol rather than to accumulated lathosterol. But the same lethality means it cannot report on the hepatic course, the cataracts, or the response to simvastatin, and those are what patients present with and what treatment targets.
The allele is also more severe than the human lesion. Every reported patient carries at least one missense allele with some residual activity; no patient homozygous for a null has been described. So the mouse models a genotype that may not be compatible with human live birth either, which is a further reason its silence on the postnatal course is uninformative rather than reassuring.
The practical consequence for this entry: the mouse supports the cholesterol-driven malformation hypothesis and must not be read as evidence about the accumulation arm, which is where the entry's two hypothesis groups differ.

open_questions/2.rationale:
Two reports disagree. In one, simvastatin lowered plasma lathosterol and was accompanied by improvement in transaminases and in fibrosis grade on repeat imaging. In another, the family noticed no benefit. Both are single patients, the endpoints are not the same, and the second reports absence of perceived benefit rather than a measured non-response - so the two are not strictly contradictory. With fewer than a dozen patients worldwide a trial is not realistic, which makes consistent sterol and liver endpoints across reported cases the only practical route to an answer.
GeneReviews does not adjudicate between the two reports but states the field's position plainly: simvastatin is a potential targeted therapy whose safety and efficacy have not been proven in this disease. It nonetheless recommends a plasma sterol profile before starting and every one to two months on therapy - which is the practical shape of the uncertainty, monitoring a biochemical surrogate because the clinical endpoint is not established.

evidence.snippet: we identified six different homozygous loss-of-function mutations in the extracellular matrix protein 1 gene (ECM1)
evidence.explanation: Establishes that biallelic loss-of-function mutations in ECM1 are the molecular cause of lipoid proteinosis.

steps/1.description: Lipoid proteinosis is caused by biallelic (homozygous or compound heterozygous) loss-of-function mutations in ECM1, which encodes the secreted glycoprotein extracellular matrix protein 1. The gene was mapped to 1q21 and identified as causal by genome-wide linkage and candidate-gene sequencing in consanguineous families, with recurrent founder alleles in some populations (e.g., the Q276X nonsense allele in Namaqualand, South Africa).

evidence.snippet: It has a role in the structural organization of the dermis (binding to perlecan, matrix metalloproteinase-9 and fibulin)
evidence.explanation: Identifies the ECM1 protein-protein interactions (perlecan, MMP-9, fibulin) whose loss is proposed to disrupt dermal matrix organization.

evidence.snippet: the ECM1 protein can normally bind to various extracellular matrix proteins and glycosaminoglycans as well as certain enzymes, including matrix metalloproteinase 9. Loss of key protein-protein interactions may underscore some of the disease pathophysiology
evidence.explanation: States that loss of ECM1's matrix and enzyme interactions is thought to underlie the disease pathophysiology.

steps/2.description: ECM1 normally participates in the structural organization of the dermis through protein-protein interactions with perlecan, fibulin, and matrix metalloproteinase-9, and it binds glycosaminoglycans. Loss of these interactions disrupts extracellular-matrix and basement-membrane physiology, the proposed proximate basis of the tissue pathology.

evidence.snippet: there is widespread deposition of hyaline (glycoprotein) material and disruption/reduplication of basement membrane
evidence.explanation: Documents the widespread hyaline deposition and basement-membrane reduplication that define the tissue pathology.

evidence.snippet: This results in the deposition of periodic acid-Schiff (PAS)-positive, hyaline-like material on the skin, mucosae and internal organs.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the PAS-positive hyaline material deposits in skin, mucosae, and internal organs.

steps/3.description: Widespread deposition of amorphous, PAS-positive hyaline (glycoprotein) material in the dermis and around blood vessels and appendages, accompanied by disruption and reduplication of basement membranes. This histopathologic hallmark occurs across skin, mucosae, and internal organs and is the tissue substrate for the organ-specific manifestations.

evidence.snippet: Classical features include beaded eyelid papules and laryngeal infiltration leading to hoarseness.
evidence.explanation: Identifies laryngeal infiltration as the cause of the characteristic hoarseness.

steps/4.description: Infiltration of the vocal folds and larynx by hyaline material thickens the tissue and impairs phonation, producing a weak or hoarse cry from early infancy — typically the earliest and most consistent sign of the disease and a potential cause of airway compromise.

evidence.snippet: The most consistent clinical signs for a diagnosis of LiP in this group were a hoarse voice and thickened sublingual frenulum leading to restricted tongue movement.
evidence.explanation: Documents the thickened sublingual frenulum and restricted tongue movement as consistent cutaneous/mucosal signs.

steps/5.description: Hyaline deposition in the skin and mucosae produces waxy and verrucous papules and plaques (favoring extensor surfaces and the face), beaded papules along the eyelid margins (moniliform blepharosis), acneiform/pock-like scarring, and a thickened sublingual frenulum that restricts tongue movement.

evidence.snippet: There may be bean- or comma-shaped intracranial calcifications, often selectively affecting the amygdala.

evidence.snippet: Neuroimaging studies have revealed a pattern of brain calcification often but not exclusively leading to selective bilateral amygdala damage.
evidence.explanation: Links the intracranial calcification pattern to selective bilateral amygdala damage in Urbach-Wiethe disease.

steps/6.description: Many patients develop bean- or comma-shaped intracranial calcifications that selectively involve the amygdalae and medial temporal lobes, typically bilateral and symmetric and more prominent with longer disease duration. evidence.snippet: On no occasion did SM exhibit fear, and she never endorsed feeling more than minimal levels of fear.
evidence.explanation: Patient SM, a bilateral-amygdala-lesion case, shows an absence of fear induction and experience, demonstrating the amygdala's pivotal role. (SM's bilateral amygdala damage results from lipoid proteinosis; the disease link is established in the amygdala-calcification node.)

evidence.snippet: Patients with lipoid proteinosis therefore have been used as models for demonstrating physiologic and pathologic abnormalities of the amygdala with respect to fear processing, affect and cognition, anxiety and memory.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that lipoid-proteinosis patients are models for amygdala abnormalities in fear processing, affect, and cognition.

steps/7.description: Bilateral amygdala damage in lipoid proteinosis produces a distinctive neurobehavioral phenotype in which affected individuals fail to induce or experience fear in response to normally frightening stimuli, while other basic emotions are preserved. Lipoid-proteinosis patients with bilateral amygdala calcification have served as key human models of amygdala function in fear processing.

evidence.snippet: verrucous and keratotic cutaneous lesions on extensor surfaces (especially the elbows)

evidence.snippet: Lipoid proteinosis (LiP) is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by a hoarse voice, warty skin infiltration and scarring.

evidence.snippet: On no occasion did SM exhibit fear, and she never endorsed feeling more than minimal levels of fear.

evidence.snippet: Homozygosity for a nonsense mutation in exon 7 of the ECM1 gene, Q276X, was identified in all patients

genes/0.notes: Biallelic loss-of-function variants in ECM1 (extracellular matrix protein 1) cause lipoid proteinosis. evidence.snippet: We present a case report of a 48-year-old man with LP who exhibited significant improvement after oral acitretin therapy.

evidence.explanation: GeneReviews independently corroborates oral retinoid use, noting benefit for mucosal lesions and hoarseness.

treatments/0.description: Low-dose oral acitretin (a systemic retinoid, ~0.5 mg/kg/day) is the best-evidenced pharmacologic option, used off-label; benefit is more consistent for mucosal/laryngeal symptoms (voice) than for established cutaneous lesions, with variable individual response. Historically reported skin-directed agents (oral dimethyl sulfoxide, D-penicillamine) have only limited/anecdotal evidence.

evidence.snippet: Microlaryngoscopic excision of laryngeal deposits can improve airway access and voice quality.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes microlaryngoscopic excision of laryngeal deposits.

Resolving whether calcification is the proximate cause or a marker of a broader ECM1-dependent CNS process would sharpen the mechanism model and determine whether the neuropsychiatric burden is potentially modifiable.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of 27 patients revealed that LV patients had an increased Body Mass Index (BMI; 11/27), hypertension (19/27) and increased levels of lipoprotein (a) (5/12) and homocysteine (10/12) in the blood.

evidence.snippet: Histopathologically, it shows intraluminal fibrin deposition and thrombosis, segmental hyalinization, and endothelial proliferation.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports thrombosis and fibrin deposition in dermal vessels as central tissue pathology.

evidence.snippet: Clinically, it is characterized by the presence of painful purpuric ulcers on the lower extremities.
