evidence.explanation: This establishes MCM9 as the causal gene and links it mechanistically to homologous-recombination repair.

evidence.snippet: Our study identified two novel homozygous loss-of-function (LoF) mutations in MCM9 in two unrelated NOA patients presenting with Sertoli cell-only syndrome (SCOS).
evidence.explanation: This extends the causal role of biallelic MCM9 loss-of-function variants to the male infertility branch.

genes/0.notes: MCM9 encodes minichromosome maintenance 9 homologous recombination repair factor and functions in homologous recombination and mismatch repair.

evidence.snippet: Autosomal-recessive variants in MCM9 cause a genomic-instability syndrome associated with hypergonadotropic hypogonadism and short stature.
evidence.explanation: This directly anchors the ovarian-failure branch of MCM9 deficiency to the hypergonadotropic hypogonadism that drives hormone-replacement treatment.

evidence.snippet: This review outlines key diagnostic criteria, initial investigations, referral pathways and management options including hormone therapy, chronic disease risk reduction, fertility counselling and psychosocial support.
evidence.explanation: This provides condition-level management evidence that hormone therapy is part of standard care for primary ovarian insufficiency, the core female branch of MCM9-related disease.

treatments/0.description: Estrogen-based hormone replacement is used to treat hypoestrogenism in the ovarian-failure branch, support pubertal development, and reduce osteoporosis risk.

evidence.snippet: Early screening protocols may be beneficial for carriers.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports gastrointestinal cancer-screening and surveillance for MCM9-variant carriers.

evidence.snippet: These findings underscore the importance of including MCM8/MCM9 in diagnostic gene panels for certain clinical contexts and suggest that biallelic carriers may benefit from cancer surveillance.
evidence.explanation: This refines the surveillance recommendation for the broadened MCM9 cancer-predisposition spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Active screening for potential colorectal and other cancer risks in the homozygotic MCM9 subjects has been instigated.
evidence.explanation: This adds MCM9-specific clinical support for proactive gastrointestinal and cancer surveillance in biallelic carriers.

treatments/1.description: Because biallelic MCM9 deficiency confers polyposis plus gastric and early-onset colorectal cancer risk, affected individuals may benefit from structured gastrointestinal surveillance including colonoscopic and endoscopic screening.

evidence.snippet: These findings enhance our understanding of the genetic basis of human NOA, particularly SCOS, and provide valuable insights for genetic counseling and fertility guidance tailored to these patients.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports genetic counseling as part of management for MCM9-associated gonadal failure.

treatments/2.description: Genetic counseling is appropriate for affected families because the condition is recessive, causes infertility, and carries implications for cancer surveillance and reproductive planning.

evidence.snippet: Given the poor outcomes of microdissection testicular sperm extraction (micro-TESE) observed in both probands, we propose that biallelic LoF mutations in MCM9 may serve as non-invasive molecular biomarkers for predicting micro-TESE failure.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports counseling male patients on the expected poor outcome of testicular sperm extraction and the need for alternative fertility planning.

treatments/3.description: Male patients with MCM9-related azoospermia should receive reproductive counseling that specifically addresses the poor prognosis for sperm retrieval. Biallelic MCM9 loss-of-function is associated with Sertoli cell-only syndrome, and microdissection testicular sperm extraction (micro-TESE) has yielded unsuccessful outcomes in reported cases. Counseling should therefore address alternative family-building options such as donor sperm or adoption.

evidence.snippet: both biallelic MCM8 and MCM9 variants are linked to hypogonadism and the early development of germ cell tumors.
evidence.explanation: This establishes the germ cell tumor risk in MCM9 deficiency as a surveillance target distinct from the gastrointestinal malignancy already modeled in the GI cancer surveillance treatment.

evidence.snippet: biallelic carriers may benefit from cancer surveillance.
evidence.explanation: This supports broad multi-organ cancer surveillance including for germ cell tumors.

treatments/4.description: In addition to gastrointestinal cancer surveillance, biallelic MCM8 and MCM9 variant carriers show an association with early-onset germ cell tumors, particularly occurring before age 15. Surveillance protocols for affected individuals may include imaging to detect gonadal or extra-gonadal germ cell tumors, in addition to the colonoscopic and endoscopic gastrointestinal screening already warranted.

evidence.snippet: The resulting allele Ndufa1S55A introduced systemic serine-55-alanine (S55A) mutation within the MWFE protein, which is essential for Complex I assembly and stability.
evidence.explanation: States the role of the MWFE protein product in complex I assembly and stability.

evidence.snippet: Exome sequencing and a complementation study of the latter patient identified a novel c.55C>T hemizygous missense mutation in the nuclear-encoded gene NDUFA1.
evidence.explanation: Adds a further hemizygous pathogenic allele, identified with functional complementation support.

steps/1.description: NDUFA1 encodes MWFE, a small accessory (non-catalytic) subunit of complex I that is nonetheless essential for the holoenzyme to assemble and remain stable. Reported pathogenic alleles are missense — p.Gly8Arg and p.Arg37Ser hemizygously in the index males, c.55C>T identified later by exome sequencing, and p.Gly32Arg in an affected heterozygous female.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of the cDNA showed that 72% of the expressed mRNA was mutated in the muscle biopsy sample.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the allelic expression skew in the affected tissue.

evidence.snippet: Investigation of the X-inactivation pattern demonstrated that 74% of the paternally inherited allele was active in the muscle.
evidence.explanation: Directly demonstrates skewed X-inactivation as the reason a heterozygote is affected.

evidence.snippet: This is the first report of an X-chromosomally inherited respiratory chain defect in a heterozygous female.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that heterozygous females can manifest this respiratory chain defect.

steps/2.description: Because NDUFA1 is X-linked, a heterozygous female is a mosaic of cells expressing either the wild-type or the mutant allele, and her phenotype depends on which allele is active in the affected tissue. In the reported affected girl, 72% of NDUFA1 mRNA in muscle carried the mutation and 74% of the active allele in that muscle was the paternally inherited one — skewing toward the mutant allele in the very tissue that was biochemically deficient. This is why heterozygous females cannot be assumed to be unaffected carriers, and it modifies the whole chain rather than sitting at one point in it.

evidence.snippet: Two-dimensional blue native gel electrophoresis showed decreased levels of intact complex I with no accumulation of lower molecular weight subcomplexes, indicating that assembly, stability, or both are compromised.
evidence.explanation: The direct demonstration of the assembly/stability lesion, including the absent-subcomplex finding that constrains its interpretation.

evidence.snippet: Assembly/stability studies in fibroblasts were performed using two-dimensional blue native gel electrophoresis.
evidence.explanation: Records the assay and the patient cell type in which it was performed.

steps/3.description: Two-dimensional blue native gel electrophoresis of patient fibroblasts shows reduced amounts of fully assembled complex I with no accumulation of lower-molecular-weight subcomplexes. That negative finding is the mechanistically informative one: an assembly pathway blocked at a defined intermediate would leave that intermediate behind, so its absence points to failure of assembly, destabilization of the assembled holoenzyme, or both, rather than a discrete arrest point.

evidence.snippet: The S55A mutation caused systemic partial Complex I deficiency of ∼50% in both sexes.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the residual complex I activity in an equivalent-allele model, supporting a partial rather than complete deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical investigations of a muscle biopsy revealed a deficiency in the amount and activity of complex I.
evidence.explanation: Confirms that both the quantity and the enzymatic activity of complex I fall in patient muscle.

steps/4.description: Less intact complex I means less NADH oxidation and less electron delivery to ubiquinone, reducing proton pumping and oxidative phosphorylation capacity. NADH that cannot be reoxidized through the respiratory chain is instead consumed by cytosolic lactate dehydrogenase, which is why the biochemical signature is lactic acidosis and a raised lactate-to-pyruvate ratio. The deficiency is partial rather than complete — the mouse model of an equivalent allele shows roughly 50% residual activity — consistent with survival to presentation rather than embryonic lethality.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the X-linked NDUFA1 gene result in complex I defect and encephalomyopathy.
evidence.explanation: States the causal link from gene to clinical syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Assembly/stability analysis might give an explanation for the different clinical phenotypes and become useful for future diagnostic purposes.
evidence.explanation: Records the authors' proposal that assembly/stability differences underlie the phenotypic variability between alleles.

steps/5.description: The clinical endpoint. Neurons and muscle are the tissues least able to tolerate reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity, so the disease presents as encephalomyopathy: Leigh syndrome in one index patient, myoclonic epilepsy with developmental delay in the other, and muscular hypotonia with lactic acidosis in the affected heterozygous girl. Phenotypic variability between patients carrying different NDUFA1 alleles was noted from the outset.

evidence.snippet: Two of these are X-chromosome linked nuclear (nDNA) genes (NDUFA1 and NDUFB11), and 7 are mitochondrial (mtDNA, MT-ND1-6, -4L) genes, which may be responsible for sex-dependent variation in the presentation of mitochondrial diseases.
evidence.explanation: Places NDUFA1 as one of only two X-linked nuclear complex I genes and links that to sex-dependent presentation.

evidence.snippet: Mutation screening of all structural subunits of complex I identified a heterozygous mutation c.94G>C, p.Gly32Arg in the X-chromosomal NDUFA1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the allele found in the affected heterozygous female.

genes/0.notes: NDUFA1 (Xq24) encodes MWFE, an accessory subunit of complex I. It is one of only two X-chromosomal nuclear genes among the 58 that control complex I biogenesis — NDUFB11 is the other — which is what makes this entity's inheritance pattern unusual within the complex I series and offers a mechanism for sex-dependent variation in presentation. Reported alleles are missense: p.Gly8Arg, p.Arg37Ser, c.55C>T (hemizygous males) and p.Gly32Arg (affected heterozygous female).

open_questions/0.rationale: The two index hemizygous patients had clearly different neurological syndromes from different NDUFA1 missense alleles, and the reporting authors proposed that assembly and stability analysis might explain the difference and become diagnostically useful. That proposal has not been tested across an allelic series. It matters because complex I deficiency is genetically heterogeneous and clinically unpredictable, and a biochemical assay that predicted phenotype from allele would be prognostically valuable. The difficulty is that only a handful of NDUFA1 patients have been reported, so an allele-to-phenotype correlation cannot presently be powered from clinical data alone.

open_questions/1.rationale: Heterozygous females were initially assumed unaffected, and one affected girl with demonstrably skewed X-inactivation overturned that assumption. Because the skew is tissue-specific and was measured in the biopsied muscle, the relationship between a blood-derived X-inactivation result and disease risk in brain or muscle is unclear. The practical consequence is a counselling question with no evidence base: a carrier mother cannot currently be given a quantitative risk of manifesting, and a symptomatic female relative may be dismissed as a carrier. Systematic biochemical assessment of obligate carriers has not been reported.

open_questions/2.rationale: Evidence exists in the model, but its translational validity to the human phenotype is the open question. The mouse reproduces the biochemistry well — systemic partial complex I deficiency of about 50%, in an X-linked architecture matching the human gene — yet its neurological phenotype is late-onset cerebellar Purkinje degeneration, whereas the human disease is an infantile or early childhood encephalopathy with basal ganglia and brainstem involvement or with myoclonic seizures. The engineered S55A allele is also not a human patient allele. The model may therefore be a good platform for the metabolic consequences of MWFE dysfunction while being a poor one for the neuropathology that defines the disease.

evidence.snippet: This FAD-dependent oxidoreductase, which has never previously been associated with human disease, is now shown to be a complex I-specific molecular chaperone.
evidence.explanation: Establishes FOXRED1's identity as a complex-I-specific chaperone, which is what this node claims is lost.

evidence.snippet: mutations in FOXRED1 leading to partial loss of function cause defects in complex I biogenesis
evidence.explanation: Supports grading the variant consequence as partial rather than complete loss of function.

steps/1.description: Biallelic FOXRED1 variants reduce or abolish the function of an FAD-dependent oxidoreductase that acts specifically as a complex I assembly chaperone. The protein has no counterpart role in the other respiratory chain complexes, which is why the biochemical defect is isolated to complex I.

evidence.snippet: In the absence of FOXRED1, mtDNA-encoded complex I subunits are still translated and transiently assembled into a late stage ∼815 kDa intermediate; but instead of transitioning further to the mature complex I, the intermediate breaks down to an ∼475 kDa complex.
evidence.explanation: The whole of this node in one sentence: translation and early incorporation are intact, the late intermediate forms, and it is the final maturation step that fails, after which what was built comes apart.

evidence.snippet: FOXRED1 mutations resulted in 50% reduction in complex I activity, dissasembly of complex I, mitochondrial depolarization, oxidative stress, and NAD+/NADH imbalance.
evidence.explanation: Confirms disassembly in patient-derived cells. Quoted including the source's misspelling of "disassembly", since a snippet reproduces its source rather than correcting it.

steps/2.description: Without FOXRED1 the mitochondrially encoded subunits are still translated and are still incorporated into a late-stage assembly intermediate of roughly 815 kDa. That intermediate then fails to mature into the holoenzyme and instead breaks down into a smaller complex of roughly 475 kDa. The same smaller species is detectable in patient cells, so the cellular model and the patient material agree on where the pathway stops.

evidence.snippet: Silencing of FOXRED1 in human fibroblasts resulted in reduced complex I steady-state levels and activity, while lentiviral-mediated FOXRED1 transgene expression rescued complex I deficiency in the patient fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Loss of function and rescue in the same system, which is the strongest available demonstration that the complex I deficiency is caused by the FOXRED1 defect rather than merely correlated with it.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of complex I was demonstrated by the absence of complex I on Blue Native Gel Electrophoresis and by a significantly reduced complex I enzyme activity in the patient's fibroblasts.
evidence.explanation: Direct biochemical confirmation in patient fibroblasts, at the severe end of the residual-activity range.

evidence.snippet: FOXRED1 mutations resulted in 50% reduction in complex I activity
evidence.explanation: Quantifies residual activity in patient peripheral blood mononuclear cells at the milder end of the range.

steps/3.description: Steady-state levels and catalytic activity of complex I fall while the other respiratory chain complexes are spared. Residual activity is partial rather than absent in patient cells carrying the recurrent hypomorphic alleles, and complete absence of assembled complex I on native gels has been reported in at least one more severely affected infant.

evidence.snippet: mitochondrial depolarization, oxidative stress, and NAD+/NADH imbalance
evidence.explanation: Names the three measured cellular consequences that constitute this node.

steps/4.description: With complex I unable to oxidise NADH at normal rates, electron entry into the respiratory chain is restricted. The measured consequences in patient cells are mitochondrial depolarization, raised reactive oxygen species and a disturbed NAD+/NADH ratio. The redox arm matters clinically as well as mechanistically, because it is the step niacin supplementation is aimed at.

evidence.snippet: The neuroimaging results ranged from normal to severe cerebral atrophy and polycystic encephalomalacia in early infancy.
evidence.explanation: States the structural brain consequence and its range across reported patients.

evidence.snippet: Both patients exhibited early-onset refractory seizures, basal ganglia lesions, hyperlacticemia, and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: Records basal ganglia involvement, the lesion distribution shared with Leigh syndrome spectrum disorders.

steps/5.description: Neurons, with high and inflexible ATP demand, are the tissue in which the oxidative-phosphorylation deficit becomes structural damage. The reported imaging correlates span basal ganglia lesions, diffuse cerebral atrophy and polycystic encephalomalacia, and in one infant prenatal-onset periventricular cysts. The range across patients is wide and is recorded as such.

evidence.snippet: Both patients exhibited early-onset refractory seizures, basal ganglia lesions, hyperlacticemia, and developmental regression.
evidence.explanation: Documents hyperlactatemia as part of the core presentation.

steps/6.description: Systemic and central nervous system lactate rise. Presentation ranges from hyperlactatemia noted on routine testing to congenital lactic acidosis severe enough to dominate the neonatal course.

evidence.snippet: Here, we demonstrate that FOXRED1 is involved in mid-late stages of complex I assembly.
evidence.explanation: Places the chaperone's action at the assembly step whose failure is the next node.

edges/1.description: Loss of the chaperone removes the activity needed to complete the final maturation step.

evidence.snippet: Cells lacking FOXRED1 had ∼10% complex I levels, reduced complex I activity, and were unable to grow on galactose media.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the consequence of the assembly arrest: gene-edited FOXRED1-null cells retain about a tenth of normal complex I and cannot respire on galactose, which is the functional endpoint of this edge.

edges/4.description: A blocked NADH-oxidising step forces cytosolic reduction of pyruvate to lactate.

evidence.snippet: including cDNA complementation to show that mutations in NUBPL and FOXRED1 can cause complex I deficiency
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation, by cDNA complementation in patient cells, that FOXRED1 mutations cause complex I deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Eleven pathogenic variants in FOXRED1 have been reported, comprising six missense variants, two non-sense variants, two frameshift variants, and one splice variant
evidence.explanation: Establishes the size and composition of the allelic spectrum.

genes/0.notes: Encodes an FAD-dependent oxidoreductase domain-containing protein that functions as a complex-I-specific assembly chaperone rather than as a structural subunit. The recurrent c.1054C>T (p.R352W) allele was identified in the original report and recurs in unrelated later families; c.612_615dupAGTG (p.A206SfsX15) is the second recurrent allele.

evidence.snippet: while clinical supplementation reduced blood lactate levels, suggesting it may be a potential therapeutic option
evidence.explanation: Quoted with the authors' hedge intact. The evidence is one series with an in vitro correlate, which does not establish clinical benefit.

treatments/0.description: Aimed at the NAD+/NADH imbalance rather than at the assembly defect. Niacin restored the NAD+/NADH ratio in patient cells in vitro, and clinical supplementation lowered blood lactate. This is a single small report proposing a candidate therapy, not an established treatment, and the source frames it that way.

evidence.snippet: Niacin restored the NAD+/NADH ratio in vitro
evidence.explanation: The cell-based half of the claim, and the half that bears on this mechanism node directly: niacin corrects the measured redox imbalance in patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: while clinical supplementation reduced blood lactate levels, suggesting it may be a potential therapeutic option
evidence.explanation: The clinical half, graded separately because it is a different kind of evidence from the in vitro redox measurement. Quoted with the authors' hedge intact: a lactate fall in supplemented patients is not a demonstration of clinical benefit.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replenishes NAD precursor supply to correct the redox imbalance downstream of the complex I block.

evidence.snippet: her blood lactate levels decreased from 18.3 mmol/L to 3.3 mmol/L
evidence.explanation: The reported biochemical response to dichloroacetate in a single infant.

evidence.snippet: Concerning the application of dichloroacetic acid (DCA) it is well known that it is neurotoxic in MID patients
evidence.explanation: Records the published safety objection to using dichloroacetate in this disorder. Graded REFUTE against the claim that this is an appropriate intervention, not against the observed lactate response. Marked REVIEW_SYNTHESIS because the letter restates toxicity findings from elsewhere rather than reporting its own.

treatments/1.description: Used in one reported infant, where blood lactate fell from 18.3 to 3.3 mmol/L after four doses and stayed in range for five weeks after discontinuation. A subsequent letter objected that dichloroacetate is neurotoxic in mitochondrial disease patients and questioned the rationale, so this is recorded as a reported intervention with a documented safety objection rather than as a recommendation.

evidence.snippet: Treatment with biotin 20 mg (q12 hrs), levocarnitine 100 mg (q12 hrs), thiamine 200 mg (q12 hrs), riboflavin 100 mg (q6 hrs), coenzyme Q10 90 mg (q6 hrs), and alpha lipoic acid 25 mg (q12 hrs) did not improve blood lactic acid levels.
evidence.explanation: A negative result: the vitamin and cofactor cocktail, riboflavin included, failed to lower lactate in the one FOXRED1 patient in whom it is reported. Graded REFUTE against the claim that this is an effective intervention. It is a single patient and a combination regimen, so it does not exclude a riboflavin effect in another patient or on another endpoint.

treatments/2.description: Biotin, levocarnitine, thiamine, riboflavin, coenzyme Q10 and alpha-lipoic acid were given together to the infant with congenital lactic acidosis and did not lower blood lactate. Riboflavin is the component with the most FOXRED1-specific rationale, since FOXRED1 is itself an FAD-dependent flavoprotein and riboflavin is the FAD precursor, but that rationale was not borne out in the one patient in whom it was tried. Recorded here because a negative result in the only reported attempt is more informative than the untested mechanistic argument, and because the cocktail design means the failure cannot be attributed to riboflavin alone.

open_questions/0.rationale: The only reported case attributed the pulmonary hypertension to the complex I defect. A published letter objected that echocardiography on the second day of life showed a patent ductus arteriosus and a patent foramen ovale, which could raise pulmonary artery pressure and later reverse the shunt direction, and noted that the follow-up echocardiogram reported the ductus but not the foramen ovale. With one patient and a confounded cardiac anatomy, neither attribution is established. The distinction matters because a mitochondrial cause would make pulmonary hypertension a surveillance target in this disorder and a shunt cause would not.

evidence.snippet: The nuclear-encoded NDUFS8 (TYKY) subunit of complex I is highly conserved among eukaryotes and prokaryotes and contains two 4Fe4S ferredoxin consensus patterns, which have long been thought to provide the binding site for the iron-sulfur cluster N-2.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the conservation and the proposed iron-sulfur cluster-binding role of the affected subunit.

evidence.snippet: The first mutation was a C236T (P79L), and the second mutation was a G305A (R102H).
evidence.explanation: Records the two alleles of the index compound heterozygote.

evidence.snippet: NDUFS8 is a nuclear-encoded structural core protein of complex I, and mutations are expected to cause infantile onset and severe disease.
evidence.explanation: States the core-subunit status and the severity that status was expected to imply - the expectation the same paper then contradicts.

steps/1.description:
NDUFS8 encodes TYKY, a structural core subunit of complex I rather than an accessory one. Two features make it a plausible point of failure. It is highly conserved across eukaryotes and prokaryotes, which is the signature of a subunit whose sequence is constrained by an essential function rather than tolerated as scaffolding. And it carries two 4Fe4S ferredoxin consensus patterns that have long been thought to provide the binding site for iron-sulfur cluster N-2 - the terminal cluster of the electron relay, the one that delivers electrons to ubiquinone.
Reported pathogenic alleles are missense: C236T (p.Pro79Leu) and G305A (p.Arg102His) as compound heterozygotes in the index patient, two further novel missense changes in the late-onset patient, and homozygous variants in the consanguineous "PEO plus" family.

evidence.snippet: Western blot analysis revealed a deficiency in the NDUFS8 polypeptide, but also reductions in other nuclear subunits of complex I, suggesting that this subunit is essential for either the assembly or stability of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The assembly/stability lesion and the explicit statement that the two cannot be told apart from this evidence.

evidence.snippet: Patient cells displayed increased ROS levels and a variable decrease in complex I activity and amount.
evidence.explanation: Confirms in a panel including NDUFS8-mutant fibroblasts that the amount of complex I falls, and records that the decrease is variable between patients.

evidence.snippet: our patient had reduced levels of all complex I subunits examined consistent with a proposed function for the NDUFS8 subunit in complex I assembly, specifically in connecting the membrane and peripheral domains of complex I.
evidence.explanation: Gives the structural proposal for what TYKY does - joining the membrane and peripheral arms - which is why losing it destabilises the whole assembly rather than removing one step.

evidence.snippet: It has been suggested that the 39-kDa subunit, like the NDUFS8 23-kDa subunit, is located at the boundary of the peripheral and the membrane domains.
evidence.explanation: Places the 39-kDa subunit at the same domain boundary, which is the basis for the proposed direct interaction with TYKY.

steps/2.description:
Western blotting of patient material shows not only a deficiency of the NDUFS8 polypeptide itself - which a mutation in its own gene would produce trivially - but reductions in other nuclear-encoded subunits of complex I as well. That second observation is the informative one: the rest of the complex cannot be maintained without TYKY, so the subunit is required for assembly, for stability of the assembled enzyme, or for both. The available data do not distinguish those alternatives, and the reporting authors do not claim to.
There is a structural proposal for what the subunit is doing. NDUFS8/TYKY is thought to connect the membrane and peripheral domains of complex I - the boundary between the arm embedded in the inner membrane and the arm that carries the electron relay. A subunit at that junction is exactly the kind whose loss would destabilise the whole assembly rather than remove one catalytic step. Consistent with that, the late-onset patient also showed a drastic reduction in the 39-kDa subunit, which is proposed to sit at the same domain boundary and may interact with TYKY directly.

evidence.snippet: For control cells, the ratio between activity and amount was 1 whereas for the patients this ratio was below 1, indicating a defect in intrinsic catalytic activity of complex I in the latter cells.
evidence.explanation: The measurement that separates a quantity defect from a quality defect, and shows both are present.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, they provide evidence that both the amount and intrinsic activity of complex I are decreased in inherited complex I deficiency.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own summary of the two-component deficit this node curates.

steps/3.description:
The step at which this entity's biochemistry says something the assembly story alone does not. In control fibroblasts the ratio between complex I enzymatic activity and complex I amount is exactly one - enzyme present is enzyme working. In fibroblasts from children with nuclear complex I gene defects including NDUFS8 that ratio falls below one. The enzyme that does get assembled is therefore intrinsically impaired, not merely scarce.
That is what a core subunit carrying the terminal iron-sulfur cluster would be expected to do, and it distinguishes this entity mechanistically from the accessory-subunit deficiencies elsewhere in the nuclear complex I series, where the lesion is essentially one of quantity. Practically, it also predicts a ceiling on any therapy that works by increasing the amount of complex I - see the antioxidant node.

evidence.snippet: Functionally, in LS cells glucose-by-galactose replacement increased mitochondrial fragmentation and mass, depolarized the mitochondrial membrane potential
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates the bioenergetic failure in patient fibroblasts, including NDUFS8-mutant lines, once glycolytic compensation is removed.

evidence.snippet: LS cell death was dose-dependently inhibited by pyruvate, malate, oxaloacetate, α-ketoglutarate, aspartate, and exogenous NAD+ (eNAD), but not by lactate, succinate, α-ketobutyrate, and uridine.
evidence.explanation: The rescue profile - NAD+-regenerating substrates work, others do not - identifies redox rather than carbon supply as the limiting problem.

steps/4.description: Reduced NADH oxidation and electron delivery to ubiquinone lower proton pumping and oxidative phosphorylation capacity. Two consequences follow that are visible in patient cells: the mitochondrial membrane potential falls, and NADH that cannot be reoxidized through the respiratory chain accumulates - which is why exogenous NAD+ and pyruvate, both of which restore cytosolic NAD+ regeneration, rescue these cells.

evidence.snippet: Cell models of mitochondrial complex I (CI) deficiency display activation of glycolysis to compensate for the loss in mitochondrial ATP production. This adaptation can mask other relevant deficiency-induced aberrations in cell physiology.
evidence.explanation: States both the compensation and the fact that it conceals the underlying defect.

evidence.snippet: Following optimization of the cell culture protocol, LS fibroblasts died in the galactose medium, whereas control cells did not.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that removing the glycolytic escape route unmasks a lethal deficit in patient cells specifically.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the complex I protein, the complex IV COI subunit was elevated in the patient's skeletal muscle.
evidence.explanation: The measured observation - one complex down, another up - in patient muscle.

evidence.snippet: Perhaps this induction of mitochondrial gene expression is an attempt to compensate for the complex I defect.
evidence.explanation: The authors' proposed interpretation, quoted with their own hedge intact - "perhaps" - which is why both items are PARTIAL.

steps/5.description:
A compensatory response that is also a methodological trap, and the reason it is curated as a node rather than left as a footnote. Cells with complex I deficiency upregulate glycolysis to replace lost mitochondrial ATP, and that adaptation masks other consequences of the deficiency. Replacing glucose with galactose in a pyruvate-free medium removes the glycolytic escape route: under those conditions patient fibroblasts die while control cells do not.
Clinically the same logic explains why these patients decompensate under catabolic stress, and why a resting biochemical measurement can understate how close to the edge a tissue is.
Glycolysis is not the only compensatory response in play. In the late-onset patient's skeletal muscle the mitochondrially encoded complex IV COI subunit was ELEVATED while complex I protein was reduced, which the reporting authors read as an attempt to compensate by inducing mitochondrial gene expression. That is hedged as a reading rather than a demonstration, but it is worth recording: an assay that finds one respiratory complex up and another down should not be assumed to have gone wrong.

evidence.snippet: Trolox treatment dramatically reduced ROS levels in both control and patient cells, which was paralleled by a substantial increase in the amount of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The paired observation that grounds the proposed feedback from ROS onto complex I amount.

evidence.snippet: Circumstantial evidence suggests that increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels contribute to the pathogenesis of these disorders.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own characterisation of the evidence as circumstantial, which is why this node is provisional.

evidence.snippet: increased H2DCFDA-oxidizing ROS levels, increased mitochondrial ATP generation, and reduced the total cellular ATP content
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation of raised ROS in Leigh syndrome patient fibroblasts under bioenergetic stress.

steps/6.description:
Fibroblasts from children with nuclear complex I gene defects, including NDUFS8, show raised reactive oxygen species. The interesting finding is not the ROS itself but what happens when it is removed: chronic treatment with the water-soluble vitamin E derivative Trolox dramatically lowers ROS and is accompanied by a substantial increase in the amount of complex I. The reporting authors read that as evidence that complex I expression is itself regulated by ROS, which makes this node a feedback modifier on the assembly node rather than a terminal consequence.
It is curated PROVISIONAL because the causal claim rests on the correlated response to one intervention in cultured fibroblasts, and because the authors describe the contribution of ROS to pathogenesis as supported by circumstantial evidence.

evidence.snippet: A progressive clinical phenotype proceeding to death in the first months of life was expressed in the patient.
evidence.explanation: The severe end of the clinical range.

evidence.snippet: Analysis of the complex I NDUFS8 gene from Leigh syndrome patients with isolated complex I deficiency revealed that one patient with late-onset disease and partial complex I defect was a compound heterozygote for two novel mutations in NDUFS8 gene.
evidence.explanation: Documents a late-onset case with a partial rather than complete biochemical defect.

evidence.snippet: Our patients had a later onset, milder and a clinically distinct phenotype, and this gene would not normally be considered in this context.
evidence.explanation: Records the mildest and least expected end of the range, and the diagnostic consequence.

steps/7.description: The clinical endpoint, and the striking thing about it in this entity is its range rather than its severity. The index patient had neuropathologically proven Leigh syndrome with a progressive course ending in death in the first months of life - the presentation a core-subunit defect predicts. But a second patient had late-onset disease with only a partial complex I defect, and three siblings from a consanguineous family presented as "progressive external ophthalmoplegia plus", a picture in which nobody would have thought to sequence this gene. The authors of that report make the methodological point explicitly: untargeted exome analysis can re-write a phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Western blot analysis revealed a deficiency in the NDUFS8 polypeptide, but also reductions in other nuclear subunits of complex I, suggesting that this subunit is essential for either the assembly or stability of complex I.
evidence.explanation: The direct demonstration that losing this subunit drags down the rest of the complex.

edges/1.description: Loss of a structural core subunit prevents the holoenzyme from assembling or from remaining assembled.

edges/2.description: Less assembled enzyme, and enzyme that is intrinsically less catalytically competent, are two separable consequences of a defective core subunit.

edges/3.description: Less enzyme, working less well, oxidizes less NADH and delivers fewer electrons to ubiquinone.

edges/4.description: Cells respond to falling mitochondrial ATP production by upregulating glycolysis.

edges/5.description: A partially blocked, over-reduced electron transport chain leaks electrons to oxygen.

edges/6.description: Neurons and muscle are the tissues least able to tolerate reduced oxidative phosphorylation capacity.

edges/7.description: Proposed negative feedback: lowering ROS raises the amount of assembled complex I, so raised ROS is inferred to suppress it. Curated as an inference from one interventional experiment, not as an established loop.

evidence.snippet: The NDUFS8 cDNA contains an open reading frame of 633 bp, coding for 210 amino acids.
evidence.explanation: Records the coding sequence of the gene.

evidence.snippet: In the 19 other patients with enzymatic complex I deficiency, no mutations were found in the NDUFS8 cDNA.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies how small a share of isolated complex I deficiency this gene explained in the original screen - one of twenty.

evidence.snippet: This article describes the first molecular genetic link between a nuclear-encoded subunit of complex I and Leigh syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Records the historical status of this gene-disease relationship as the first of its kind.

evidence.snippet: Only the proband of this study with late-onset LS was a compound heterozygote harboring two base substitutions in NDUFS8: a C254T which replaced a proline at position 85 with a leucine (P85L) and a G413A which replaced an arginine at position 138 with a histidine (R138H).
evidence.explanation: Names the two late-onset alleles at nucleotide and protein level.

evidence.snippet: Each parent was heterozygous for one of the two missense mutations. These mutations were absent in 100 DNA controls and were not found in any available EST databases.
evidence.explanation: The segregation and control-allele evidence for the late-onset pair.

evidence.snippet: pathogenic variants of the NDUFS8 can be responsible for LS, including homozygous (c.236C > T/p.Pro79Leu, c.460G > A/p.Gly154Ser, c.187G > C/p.Glu63Gln, c.160C > T/p.Arg54Trp, c.281C > T het/p.Arg94Cys) and compound heterozygous (c.236C > T/p.Pro79Leu and c.305G > A/p.Arg102His, c.254C > T/p.Pro85Leu and c.413G > A/p.Arg138His, c.229C > T/p.Arg77Trp and c.476C > A/p.Ala159Asp, c.52C > T/p.Arg18Cys, c.484G > T/p.Val162Met, c.457T > C/p.Cys153Arg) variations in NDUFS8
evidence.explanation: The complete reported allelic series at nucleotide and protein level, in both zygosity classes - the denominator for any genotype-phenotype work.

evidence.snippet: To date, all identified mutations were missense mutations, and no patients were reported with nonsense mutations in NDUFS8, which suggested that a complete absence of this protein might lead to intrauterine lethality
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the reported allelic series is entirely missense, and gives the proposed reason - a selection effect that shapes what this disease looks like in living patients.

evidence.snippet: 16 patients with Leigh syndrome carrying NDUFS8 mutations and 1 patient with encephalomyopathy carrying NDUFS8 mutations have been displayed
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the size of the reported patient series, which bounds what any genotype-phenotype analysis can be powered to detect.

evidence.snippet: the R138H amino acid substitution is located between these two iron sulfur clusters which have been shown to generate the complex I N2 clusters.
evidence.explanation: Places R138H between the two iron-sulfur clusters that generate N2. The companion clause about P85L lying upstream of the cysteine motifs is not quoted here because it contains a bracketed span ("[4Fe-4S]") that the snippet matcher strips; the same point is carried by the cysteine-motif quote on the genotype-phenotype discussion.

genes/0.notes:
NDUFS8 (11q13.2) encodes TYKY, a structural core subunit of complex I with an open reading frame of 633 bp coding for 210 amino acids. It is the gene MONDO uses to define this entity - MONDO:0032606 is an intersection class, "mitochondrial complex I deficiency, nuclear type" AND has-causal-agent NDUFS8 - so the gene is not merely associated with the concept but constitutive of it.
Reported alleles are missense and biallelic: C236T (p.Pro79Leu) with G305A (p.Arg102His) in the 1998 index compound heterozygote; C254T (p.Pro85Leu) with G413A (p.Arg138His) in the late-onset compound heterozygote, each parent carrying one and neither found in 100 control DNAs; and homozygous variants in the consanguineous PEO-plus family. Worth noting how rare this is: in the original screen of 20 patients with isolated enzymatic complex I deficiency, NDUFS8 explained exactly one.
The full reported allelic series, homozygous and compound heterozygous together, is: p.Pro79Leu, p.Gly154Ser, p.Glu63Gln, p.Arg54Trp and p.Arg94Cys as homozygotes; p.Pro79Leu with p.Arg102His, p.Pro85Leu with p.Arg138His, p.Arg77Trp with p.Ala159Asp, and p.Arg18Cys, p.Val162Met and p.Cys153Arg as compound heterozygotes. That is the set any genotype-phenotype analysis has to work with, and it is larger than the two families this entry's primary reports describe.
A striking feature of the whole reported allelic series: every identified NDUFS8 mutation is missense, and no patient has been reported with a nonsense variant. The proposed explanation is that complete absence of the protein may be lethal in utero, so the living patient population is by construction hypomorphic. That is a selection effect worth holding in mind whenever this entity's phenotypic range is discussed - the severe end of the observable range may not be the severe end of the biological one.
The positions of the late-onset pair relative to the iron-sulfur machinery are what make them mechanistically interesting rather than merely two more variants: P85L lies upstream of the two cysteine motifs thought to coordinate the [4Fe-4S] clusters, and R138H lies between them. Neither disrupts a cysteine motif, which is the reporting authors' explanation for why this patient's disease was milder - see the genotype-phenotype discussion.

evidence.snippet: NDUFS8 is a nuclear-encoded structural core protein of complex I, and mutations are expected to cause infantile onset and severe disease.
evidence.explanation: States the expectation that the observed phenotypic range contradicts.

evidence.snippet: Our patients had a later onset, milder and a clinically distinct phenotype, and this gene would not normally be considered in this context.
evidence.explanation: The observation refuting that expectation, in genetically confirmed patients.

evidence.snippet: For control cells, the ratio between activity and amount was 1 whereas for the patients this ratio was below 1, indicating a defect in intrinsic catalytic activity of complex I in the latter cells.
evidence.explanation: The candidate quantitative explanation the proposed experiment would test.

evidence.snippet: Hence, electron transport through this subunit should be partially preserved.
evidence.explanation: The structural partial answer, quoted as its conclusion: the authors argue that because neither substitution disrupts the cysteine motifs coordinating the iron-sulfur clusters, electron transport through the subunit should be partially preserved. That gives an allele-level criterion predicting milder disease. Recorded as PARTIAL because it is an inference from residue position, not a measurement. (The preceding clause naming the cysteine motifs is not quoted because it contains a bracketed "[4Fe-4S]" that the snippet matcher strips.)

evidence.snippet: The reduced pathogenicity of our patient's complex I disease might be attributable to the nature of the two new missense mutations.
evidence.explanation: States the authors' framing directly - that allele identity, not chance, is what they take to explain the milder course.

evidence.snippet: Our patient differed from the previous NDUFS8 compound heterozygote patient in having a drastic reduction in the 39-kDa subunit.
evidence.explanation: A directly measured protein-level difference between the two genotyped patients with different courses - the most tractable of the three candidate explanations, because it is a western blot rather than an inference.

evidence.snippet: To date, all identified mutations were missense mutations, and no patients were reported with nonsense mutations in NDUFS8, which suggested that a complete absence of this protein might lead to intrauterine lethality
evidence.explanation: Bounds the allelic series that any genotype-phenotype study could use, and supplies a reason for the bound: complete loss of NDUFS8 may not be compatible with life, so every reported patient retains some protein.

open_questions/0.rationale:
The expectation is explicit in the literature and it is wrong: NDUFS8 is a structural core protein and mutations were expected to cause infantile onset and severe disease. The index patient met that expectation. A second patient had late-onset disease with a partial biochemical defect. Three siblings presented as progressive external ophthalmoplegia, a phenotype so far from expectation that the gene would not normally have been considered.
Two candidate explanations are available in this entry's own data, and they are not the same kind of answer.
The first is structural and allele-specific, and it is the closest thing to a partial answer that exists. The late-onset patient's two substitutions, P85L and R138H, both change highly conserved residues - but NEITHER disrupts the cysteine motifs that coordinate the [4Fe-4S] clusters, so the reporting authors argue that electron transport through the subunit should be partially preserved. That is a concrete, testable structural criterion: alleles that spare the cysteine motifs should be milder than alleles that do not. It has not been tested across an allelic series, and it does not obviously explain the PEO-plus family, whose variants are not characterised in this way.
The second is quantitative and gene-agnostic: patients differ in how much of their complex I deficit is loss of enzyme versus loss of intrinsic catalytic competence, and that activity-to-amount ratio varies between individuals. If the ratio tracked clinical severity it would be both an explanation and a prognostic assay.
A third observation sits between them and may be the most tractable. The late-onset patient differed from the infantile index patient in one specific respect at the protein level: a drastic reduction in the 39-kDa subunit, which is proposed to occupy the same membrane-peripheral domain boundary as TYKY and to interact with it. If which partner subunits an allele destabilises varies by allele, that is a measurable intermediate between "where the substitution sits" and "how severe the disease is" - and it is measurable by western blot on the fibroblasts these patients already have.
None of the three has been tested across an NDUFS8 allelic series, and the series is tiny - roughly 17 patients described in the literature to date, all carrying missense alleles - so none can be powered from clinical data alone. The proposed experiment below is designed to test them together, since the structural hypothesis predicts which alleles should show which ratio.

evidence.snippet: NDUFS8 is pivotal for Akt-mTOR cascade activation in endothelial cells. Depleting NDUFS8 inhibited Akt-mTOR activation, reversible with exogenous ATP in HUVECs.
evidence.explanation: The causal link from NDUFS8 through ATP to Akt-mTOR, with the rescue that establishes the direction.

evidence.snippet: revealed that endothelial knockdown of NDUFS8 inhibited retinal angiogenesis
evidence.explanation: The in vivo vascular phenotype, in mouse retina - the strongest form of the claim available, and still not a patient observation.

evidence.snippet: Lastly, we observed an increase in NDUFS8 expression in retinal proliferative membrane tissues obtained from human patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy.
evidence.explanation: The only human tissue observation in the paper, and it is from diabetic retinopathy rather than from mitochondrial disease - which is precisely why this axis is not curated as an MC1DN2 mechanism.

open_questions/1.rationale:
A 2024 study did to NDUFS8 what the patient literature cannot: silenced and knocked it out on its own, in a single cell type, with rescue experiments. It found that NDUFS8 loss inhibits endothelial proliferation, migration and tube formation; that the mechanism runs through failure of Akt-mTOR activation; that exogenous ATP restores Akt-mTOR signalling and constitutively active Akt1 rescues the cellular phenotypes; and that endothelial-specific knockdown inhibits retinal angiogenesis in mice. That is a well-controlled causal chain from this entity's gene to a vascular phenotype.
None of it has been observed in a patient. Vascular maldevelopment is not a reported feature of MC1DN2; the affected tissues are brain, muscle and heart; and the paper's own framing is angiogenesis biology, with its human tissue observation coming from proliferative diabetic retinopathy rather than from mitochondrial disease. The mismatch matters in a specific way rather than generically: if the ATP-Akt-mTOR link is real in patients it would predict vascular contributions to the brain lesions - the symmetric basal ganglia necrosis of Leigh syndrome has long been argued to have a perfusion component - and would make ATP-restoring or mTOR-directed intervention mechanistically motivated rather than empirical. If it is endothelium-specific biology, the axis belongs to angiogenesis research and not to this entry, and should stay out of the pathograph. It is currently kept out.

evidence.snippet: The finding that Trolox treatment increased the amount of complex I might aid the future development of antioxidant treatment strategies for patients.
evidence.explanation: The therapeutic lead the model generates.

evidence.snippet: However, such treatment may only be beneficial to patients with a relatively small reduction in intrinsic catalytic defect of the complex.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own bound on that lead, which is the stratification hypothesis the proposed experiment tests.

open_questions/2.rationale:
This is a model-to-human question with an unusually well-specified answer already sketched in the model. Chronic antioxidant treatment of complex I-deficient fibroblasts lowers ROS and substantially increases the amount of complex I, which reads as a therapeutic lead. But the same experiment measures the catch: in control cells the increase in activity matched the increase in amount exactly, whereas in patient cells the ratio ran between 0.1 and 0.8. More enzyme does not reliably mean more function, because the enzyme that is restored still carries the intrinsic catalytic defect. The authors draw the conclusion themselves - such treatment may only benefit patients with a relatively small intrinsic defect.
Two things make this a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than a plain knowledge gap. The evidence exists and is quantitative; what is unknown is whether it holds in an organism. And the mismatch is directional and predictable: the model says who should not be expected to respond, which is a testable stratification hypothesis rather than a generic call for more research. The fibroblast panel also pooled five genes, so no NDUFS8-specific ratio is available.

evidence.snippet: The diagnosis of Mobitz type II block AVB requires a stable sinus rate, which is an important criterion because a vagal surge (generally benign) can cause simultaneous sinus slowing and AV nodal block, which can resemble Mobitz type II AVB.
evidence.explanation: Supports AV nodal conduction slowing, often vagally mediated, as the physiologic mechanism underlying Wenckebach-like atrioventricular block.

evidence.snippet: Remifentanil is known to cause sinus bradycardia, however, because it has a direct negative chronotropic effect on the cardiac conduction system and there is an indirect negative chronotropic effect via the parasympathetic nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Supports parasympathetic and direct conduction-system suppression as a reversible AV nodal depression mechanism.

steps/0.description: Vagal or parasympathetic surges can slow sinus rate and suppress atrioventricular nodal conduction, producing a generally nodal form of Wenckebach physiology.

evidence.snippet: We report on twelve patients with alternating Wenckebach periods (AWP) occurring during an acute inferior myocardial infarction (AIMI).
evidence.explanation: This clinical series supports acute inferior myocardial infarction as an ischemic context for Wenckebach-type atrioventricular block.

steps/1.description: Acute inferior myocardial infarction can produce ischemic atrioventricular nodal conduction depression with Wenckebach periodicity, converging on the progressive PR-prolongation cascade.

evidence.snippet: The classic pattern of the typical WP's consists of (1) progressive lengthening of the P-R intervals with the largest increment occuring in the second conducted beat
evidence.explanation: Supports progressive PR interval lengthening as the defining Wenckebach conduction pattern.

steps/2.description: In Wenckebach periodicity, successive conducted beats show progressive PR interval lengthening before a nonconducted atrial impulse.

evidence.snippet: the pause produced by the nonconducted P-wave is less than two P-P intervals.
evidence.explanation: Supports the nonconducted P wave as the dropped-beat event in Wenckebach periodicity.

steps/3.description: The Wenckebach cycle culminates in a nonconducted P wave and dropped ventricular beat, lowering the effective ventricular rate.

evidence.snippet: Remifentanil is known to cause sinus bradycardia, however, because it has a direct negative chronotropic effect on the cardiac conduction system and there is an indirect negative chronotropic effect via the parasympathetic nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Supports bradycardia as a conduction-system manifestation that can accompany AV nodal depression.

steps/4.description: Intermittent dropped ventricular beats can produce a slow ventricular rate.

evidence.snippet: In general, patients with second degree AV block may have no symptoms or may experience symptoms like syncope and lightheadedness.
evidence.explanation: Supports syncope as a possible symptom of second-degree atrioventricular block, including Mobitz I presentations.

steps/5.description: Symptomatic episodes may occur when bradycardia causes transient cerebral hypoperfusion.

evidence.snippet: In general, patients with second degree AV block may have no symptoms or may experience symptoms like syncope and lightheadedness.
evidence.explanation: Supports lightheadedness as a symptom of second-degree AV block, including Mobitz I presentations.

steps/6.description: Presyncopal lightheadedness may occur when intermittent dropped beats reduce cardiac output without causing frank syncope.

edges/0.description: AV nodal suppression increases conduction delay across successive beats.

edges/1.description: Ischemic atrioventricular nodal depression produces progressive conduction delay across successive beats.

edges/2.description: Progressive AV nodal conduction delay culminates in a nonconducted atrial impulse.

edges/3.description: Intermittent dropped beats can reduce ventricular rate and contribute to bradycardic symptoms.

edges/4.description: A ventricular rate slow enough to drop cerebral perfusion below the autoregulatory threshold causes transient loss of consciousness.

edges/5.description: Lesser reductions in cerebral perfusion from intermittent dropped beats produce presyncopal lightheadedness without frank syncope.

evidence.snippet: Remifentanil was immediately discontinued, and we administered atropine sulfate. Complete atrioventricular block was restored to sinus rhythm.
evidence.explanation: Supports atropine as acute pharmacotherapy in a reversible AV nodal block sequence that included Wenckebach-type AV block.

treatments/0.description: Atropine may be used in acute vagally mediated or drug-associated AV nodal bradyarrhythmia while removing the reversible trigger; this is not evidence for chronic treatment of asymptomatic nodal Wenckebach.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist, so it removes the parasympathetic input that is depressing atrioventricular nodal conduction in the vagally mediated form of Wenckebach block.

evidence.snippet: Pacemaker therapy was initiated prophylactically in two patients, because of syncope in six, because of hemodynamic deterioration in two, and for syncope and hemodynamic deterioration in two.
evidence.explanation: Supports pacemaker therapy in symptomatic or hemodynamically unstable alternating Wenckebach periods in acute inferior myocardial infarction.

treatments/1.description: Pacemaker therapy can be used for symptomatic or hemodynamically unstable Wenckebach presentations, especially in acute ischemic or non-benign contexts; this is conditional and distinct from asymptomatic nodal Wenckebach, where pacing may be inappropriate.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Pacing supplies a ventricular beat when an atrial impulse fails to conduct, so the dropped beat no longer lowers the effective ventricular rate; the diseased atrioventricular nodal conduction itself is unchanged.

evidence.snippet: Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant hair disorder caused by mutations in the hard keratins KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86.
evidence.explanation: Establishes hair-cortex keratin variants as the causal lesion.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in KRT81 and KRT86 are the most common.
evidence.explanation: Records the relative contribution of the three causal keratin genes.

evidence.snippet: This study is the first to identify pathogenic variants in KRT31 as a cause of autosomal dominant monilethrix.
evidence.explanation: Adds the type I hair keratin KRT31 to the set of genes whose variants produce this lesion, which is why KRT31 is bound among this node's genes.

evidence.snippet: Immunoblotting demonstrated that when co-expressed with its binding partner keratin 85, the truncated keratin 31 was still expressed, albeit less abundantly than the wildtype protein.
evidence.explanation: Cell-culture co-expression shows the truncated chain is produced rather than degraded, which is the condition a dominant-negative lesion requires and the basis for the statement in this node's description.

steps/4.description: A heterozygous variant in one of the hair-cortex keratins KRT81, KRT83 or KRT86 alters a residue required for keratin filament assembly. KRT81 and KRT86 variants are the most commonly reported. These are the same class of filament-assembly lesion that produces epidermolysis bullosa simplex and pachyonychia congenita in other keratin pairs; what differs is the tissue in which the affected pair is expressed. A nonsense variant in the type I hair-cortex keratin KRT31 reaches the same node from the partner side of the obligate heterodimer: it removes the last three residues of the 2B subdomain and the whole C-terminal tail domain, and the shortened chain is still expressed, without nonsense-mediated decay, but localises abnormally.

evidence.snippet: Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant hair disorder caused by mutations in the hard keratins KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the causal proteins are hard keratins, which assemble as obligate heterodimers and so admit the dominant-negative mechanism this node asserts.

steps/5.description: The mutant hard-keratin chain is incorporated into the obligate type-I/type-II heterodimer of the hair cortex, so filament assembly is disrupted throughout the network rather than in the mutant protein alone. This is the dominant-negative step, and it is what makes a single variant allele sufficient.

evidence.snippet: The affected hairs are fragile and break easily
evidence.explanation: Documents the loss of mechanical resilience in the affected structure. The quote is deliberately truncated before the source's phrase "leading to scarring alopecia": monilethrix alopecia is NON-scarring, because the hair fractures above a preserved follicle, and quoting that clause would have the entry cite a claim its own phenotype description refutes.

steps/6.description: The cortical keratin network of the developing hair shaft is assembled abnormally, so the shaft loses the mechanical resilience that its densely packed keratin filaments normally provide. Unlike the epidermal keratinopathies, the affected cells are not lysed in a living tissue plane - the hair shaft is already a dead, keratinized structure - so the mechanical failure presents as fracture of a structure rather than as cytolysis and blistering.

evidence.snippet: it is characterized by a regular, periodic thinning of the hair shaft, leading to a characteristic beaded appearance of the hair
evidence.explanation: Documents the periodic shaft narrowing that defines this node and gives the disorder its name.

steps/7.description: The hair shaft develops regular, periodic constrictions alternating with normal-calibre nodes, giving the beaded or necklace-like appearance on microscopy that is diagnostic. The internodal constrictions are the mechanically weak points, and the shaft fractures there.

evidence.snippet: Follicular hyperkeratosis in the neck and on extensor sides of extremities is a frequently associated finding.
evidence.explanation: Documents the associated follicular hyperkeratosis and its characteristic distribution.

steps/8.description: Keratotic follicular papules, characteristically on the nape of the neck and the extensor surfaces of the limbs. This is a follicular keratinization abnormality rather than a consequence of shaft fracture, and it is present in many but not all affected individuals.

evidence.snippet: monilethrix is a rare structural hair shaft disorder characterized by hair fragility and resulting in patchy dystrophic alopecia
evidence.explanation: Documents the alopecia endpoint and attributes it to shaft fragility rather than to follicular loss.

steps/9.description: Hair that breaks before it can grow long, producing patchy alopecia most marked at sites of friction such as the occiput. The alopecia is non-scarring: the shaft fractures above a preserved follicle, so follicular density is normal and regrowth occurs whenever a shaft survives. Severity ranges from near-complete alopecia to changes mild enough to be missed.

evidence.snippet: The affected hairs are fragile and break easily
evidence.explanation: Documents hair fragility and easy breakage as the defining feature. Quote truncated before the source's "scarring alopecia" clause, which is a clinical error in that letter - monilethrix alopecia is non-scarring.

steps/10.description: Hair with regular periodic shaft narrowing giving a beaded appearance, which is fragile and fractures at the internodal constrictions.

edges/4.description: The variant chain is incorporated into the cortical keratin network and disrupts its assembly.

edges/5.description: A disrupted network cannot build a mechanically sound cortex.

edges/6.description: A mechanically incompetent cortex yields a shaft that thins periodically and fractures at the thinned points.

edges/7.description: The alternation of normal-calibre nodes with internodal constrictions is what presents clinically as beaded, easily broken hair.

edges/8.description: Hair that fractures close to the scalp cannot achieve length, so alopecia results despite normal follicular density.

edges/9.description: The same follicles show keratotic plugging, a claim about follicular keratinization rather than about shaft fracture and therefore modelled separately.

evidence.snippet: In the French and Dutch patients, we found novel KRT86 and KRT83 mutations. Our findings expand the mutational spectrum associated with monilethrix.
evidence.explanation: Reports novel causal KRT86 variants in independent kindreds.

genes/0.notes: KRT86 encodes a type II hair-cortex keratin. Along with KRT81 it accounts for most reported monilethrix, and novel variants continue to be described.

evidence.snippet: Monilethrix is an autosomal dominant hair disorder caused by mutations in the hard keratins KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86.
evidence.explanation: Asserts KRT81 variants as a cause of autosomal dominant monilethrix. The statement covers the three-gene set rather than KRT81 alone, which is why the CAUSATIVE typing rests on it together with the frequency statement below rather than on either alone.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in KRT81 and KRT86 are the most common.
evidence.explanation: Establishes KRT81 as one of the two most frequent causal genes.

genes/1.notes: KRT81 encodes a type II hair-cortex keratin and is, with KRT86, one of the two most commonly implicated genes.

evidence.snippet: In the French and Dutch patients, we found novel KRT86 and KRT83 mutations. Our findings expand the mutational spectrum associated with monilethrix.
evidence.explanation: Reports novel causal KRT83 variants.

genes/2.notes: KRT83 encodes a type II hair-cortex keratin and is the least commonly implicated of the three.

evidence.snippet: Monilethrix typically transmits in an autosomal dominant mode
evidence.explanation: Supports only that dominant transmission is the typical mode, which is the contrast against which the recessive DSG4 form is recorded.

evidence.snippet: Mutations in the desmoglein 4 (DSG4) gene reportedly underlie the autosomal recessive form of the disease.
evidence.explanation: States the DSG4 gene-disease relationship on which the CAUSATIVE typing of this record rests. The sentence is the citing paper's framing of earlier work rather than its own result, hence BACKGROUND.

evidence.snippet: Observation of her hair shaft by means of transmission electron microscopy showed fewer desmosomes and abnormal keratinization.
evidence.explanation: Electron microscopy of a DSG4-homozygous patient's own hair shaft shows the desmosome deficit, which is the reason this gene's route is treated as desmosomal rather than as a keratin assembly lesion.

genes/3.notes: DSG4 (desmoglein 4) causes a recessive form of monilethrix that reaches the same beaded-hair phenotype through desmosomal rather than keratin failure. This entry's pathophysiology models the dominant keratin-associated disease only, so DSG4 is deliberately not bound to a pathophysiology node here; the route belongs mechanistically with `desmosomal_adhesion_failure`. MONDO files the DSG4 disease as hypotrichosis 6, recorded on this entry as a related match, so there is no monilethrix subtype row for it.

evidence.snippet: This study is the first to identify pathogenic variants in KRT31 as a cause of autosomal dominant monilethrix.
evidence.explanation: The report that establishes KRT31 as a monilethrix gene, which is the basis for the CAUSATIVE typing here.

evidence.snippet: Nine affected individuals from four unrelated families were included.
evidence.explanation: Records the size of the series behind the KRT31 claim, which is the reason it is curated as causal rather than as a single-family report.

genes/4.notes: KRT31 encodes a type I hair-cortex keratin, the obligate partner class of the type II keratins KRT81, KRT83 and KRT86; HGNC's previous symbol for it is KRTHA1, keratin hair acidic 1, and the report works with it co-expressed against its type II partner keratin 85. MONDO records no numbered monilethrix class for it: `runoak -i ols:mondo search` returned nothing for "KRT31", "keratin 31", "KRTHA1" or "monilethrix-4" on 2026-09-26, and MONDO:0008009 has exactly three children, the KRT86-, KRT81- and KRT83-defined classes. The gene therefore has no subtype row and is carried as a causal gene on this entry and on the keratin-variant node.

evidence.snippet: Monilethrix remains as a therapeutic challenge for dermatologists.
evidence.explanation: Supports the absence of an established effective therapy, which is the rationale for a supportive approach.

treatments/0.description: No specific therapy corrects the keratin defect. Because breakage is mechanical, gentle hair care and avoidance of physical and chemical trauma are the mainstay. Oral acitretin, topical and oral minoxidil, and oral N-acetylcysteine have all been reported, but only at case-report and small case-series level with inconsistent and often non-sustained benefit, so none is curated here as an effective treatment. They are named rather than silently omitted so a later curator can see what was considered.

treatments/1.description: Counseling for autosomal dominant inheritance with variable penetrance, noting that mildly affected relatives may be unaware they are affected.

evidence.snippet: The ANO1 rare variants were assessed using patch-clamp recordings, and the majority of variants, including ANO1 p.Met658Val, displayed increased sensitivity to intracellular Ca2+.
evidence.explanation: Patch-clamp recordings are the measurement behind the gain-of-function modifier on the channel-activity term.

evidence.snippet: Our studies support that ANO1 gain-of-function pathogenic variants predispose to moyamoya disease and are associated with unique involvement of the posterior circulation.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion links the gain of function to moyamoya disease and to the posterior-circulation pattern named in the node description.

steps/5.description: Rare ANO1 variants increase the sensitivity of the calcium-activated chloride channel anoctamin-1 to intracellular calcium. This gain of function predisposes to moyamoya disease and is reported with involvement of the posterior circulation in addition to the classic features of moyamoya disease.

evidence.snippet: Endothelial knockdown of RNF213 activated the Hippo pathway effector Yes-associated protein (YAP)/tafazzin (TAZ) and promoted the overexpression of the downstream effector VEGFR2.
evidence.explanation: This cell-based component of the study supports Hippo-YAP/TAZ-VEGFR2 activation after RNF213 knockdown.

steps/6.description: Experimental RNF213 loss activates YAP/TAZ and VEGFR2-linked endothelial angiogenic programs, providing a more specific signaling mechanism for pathological angiogenesis in moyamoya disease.

evidence.snippet: This gene encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase with diverse roles in angiogenesis, vascular remodeling, lipid metabolism, and cerebral blood flow regulation, yet its exact mechanisms in cerebrovascular pathology remain incompletely understood.
evidence.explanation: This supports RNF213's proposed involvement in vascular remodeling and angiogenesis while preserving mechanistic uncertainty.

open_questions/0.rationale: RNF213, the major East Asian susceptibility gene for moyamoya disease, is an E3 ubiquitin ligase whose precise pathogenic mechanism is unresolved. Yasuda et al. (2026, PMID:41891799) identify RNF213 as a critical regulator of the IL-6 amplifier (IL6-Amp), an NF-κB/STAT3 inflammatory module active in non-immune cells: RNF213 knockdown selectively suppressed NF-κB target genes and reduced IL-6 expression, and RNF213 depletion attenuated inflammation in an NF-κB-dependent in vivo model. The disease-associated p.R4810K variant strengthens the RNF213-TRAF2 interaction, enhancing TNF-α-NF-κB signaling and IL6-Amp activation, with genotype-dependent NF-κB p65/STAT3 phosphorylation seen in patient superficial temporal arteries. This positions an inflammatory axis alongside the existing angiogenic and Hippo-YAP/TAZ-VEGFR2 mechanisms, but it remains unclear whether NF-κB/IL6-Amp activation is an initiating driver of vascular wall remodeling and stenosis or a parallel/amplifying process, and how it interacts with the angiogenic dysregulation already modeled. The upstream physiological triggers of IL6-Amp induction in cerebral vessels and whether anti-inflammatory or anti-IL-6 strategies can slow steno-occlusive progression in p.R4810K carriers are also unknown.

open_questions/1.rationale: Inflammatory and autoimmune responses are implicated in moyamoya disease (MMD), but the precise molecular mechanisms remain poorly understood. RNF213 is the key MMD susceptibility gene and has been linked to inflammatory signaling, yet its role in NF-κB-driven inflammation was unclear. Yasuda et al. (PMID:41891799) establish that RNF213 acts as a critical regulator of the IL-6 amplifier (IL6-Amp) and directly interacts with TRAF2 to enhance inflammatory NF-κB signaling, with the p.R4810K variant strengthening the RNF213-TRAF2 interaction. What remains unresolved is the upstream side of this axis — which physiological or environmental stimuli (e.g., infection-associated cytokine exposure, TNF-α, IL-6) initiate IL6-Amp induction in cerebral vessel walls — and the downstream side: whether and how sustained NF-κB/IL-6 amplification mechanistically produces the medial and intimal remodeling, smooth-muscle and endothelial changes, and fragile collateral angiogenesis that manifest as progressive steno-occlusive arteriopathy. It is also unclear how RNF213 genetic variation, particularly the dose of p.R4810K, quantitatively tunes the inflammatory cascade and couples genotype to the rate and pattern of stenosis and collateral development. Resolving these upstream triggers and downstream effectors is needed to determine whether anti-inflammatory or anti-IL-6 intervention could modify disease progression.
